# 🔐 ROUND 5 BATCH 15 — RBAC, routing, Tally mappings

## FINDING R2-291 — 🟠 HIGH: the delete-logs router is mounted at the API root, so every mistyped or unknown path returns a 500 instead of a 404

`backend/app/main.py:559` mounts the delete-logs router with **no prefix of its own**:

```python
app.include_router(delete_logs.router, prefix="/apis/v3")
```

and `delete_logs.py:14,63` declares:

```python
router = APIRouter(tags=["Delete Logs"], dependencies=[Depends(get_current_user)])
...
@router.get("/{company_id}")
```

The resulting route is **`GET /apis/v3/{company_id}`** — a single-segment wildcard at the root of the
entire API. Every other router is mounted under a module prefix (`/apis/v3/finance`, `/apis/v3/hr`,
…), so this one catches **anything that does not match a longer route**, and immediately tries to
parse it as a UUID.

### Proved live
```
GET /apis/v3/nosuchmodule                              → 500 Internal Server Error
GET /apis/v3/typo-endpoint                             → 500 Internal Server Error
GET /apis/v3/finance                                   → 500 Internal Server Error
GET /apis/v3/settings                                  → 500 Internal Server Error
GET /apis/v3/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000      → 403 (correct — a well-formed id)
```

`/apis/v3/finance` and `/apis/v3/settings` are the **base paths of real modules**. A client that
requests a module root — the most natural thing to try — gets a 500.

### This is the second unread Sentry issue this round
```
ValueError — badly formed hexadecimal UUID string
PYTHON-FASTAPI-C  Unhandled  /apis/v3/{company_id}
```
It was ~40 minutes old when the board was read, and the endpoint name in the issue is precisely this
wildcard. Together with R2-270 (chat) and R2-283 (statutory), **three separate Sentry issues visible
on the board during this session each pointed directly at a defect nobody had acted on.**

### Consequences
1. **404s are indistinguishable from crashes.** Every client typo, every stale URL, every probe by a
   crawler produces a 500 — and per R2-236 the browser sees it as a network failure, not a 500.
2. **Monitoring is poisoned.** Unbounded, trivially-generated `ValueError`s flood Sentry, burning
   quota and hiding real issues. Anyone scanning the API generates them at will.
3. Every one of these requests passes through `Depends(get_current_user)` first, so each bogus path
   costs a database round-trip before failing.

### Fix
Give the router its own prefix — `app.include_router(delete_logs.router, prefix="/apis/v3/delete-logs")` —
and validate the path parameter as `company_id: UUID` so a malformed value produces FastAPI's own 422
rather than an unhandled `ValueError`. Then add a catch-all 404 handler so unmatched paths under
`/apis/v3` return a clean 404.

## FINDING R2-292 — 🟠 HIGH: any role's permissions can be set to `{"all": true}` or `{}` through the API, and both grant more than the UI can express

**This extends R2-169 and clarifies the D7 decision that has been open since Round 3.**

The permission editor in the console posts an explicit matrix of every key (which is why **R2-073 was
disproved** — "Clear All" writes every key as `false`, not an empty object). But the API accepts two
payloads the UI cannot produce, and both were confirmed live on a purpose-made role:

```
PUT /settings/roles/{role_id}/permissions {"permissions":{"all":true}}
→ 200 {"role_name":"ZZ R5 Role","permissions":{"all":true}}

PUT /settings/roles/{role_id}/permissions {"permissions":{}}
→ 200 {"role_name":"ZZ R5 Role","permissions":{}}
```

- **`{"all": true}`** is the wildcard the built-in `Owner` and `Admin` roles carry — confirmed by
  reading them back (`Owner -> {"all": true}`, `Admin -> {"all": true}`). Granting it to an arbitrary
  role is **direct privilege escalation to owner-equivalent access**, in one request, with no
  confirmation and no separate permission guarding it.
- **`{}`** is the fail-open state described in R2-169.

So the escalation surface is **two payloads, not one**, and neither is reachable from the console.
Anyone who can reach the settings API for a company — which includes any role holding the permission
that guards this endpoint — can mint themselves owner-equivalent rights.

### What was deliberately **not** tested
Editing or deleting the built-in `Owner` role was **not attempted against the real role id**. A
successful `{}` write or delete on `Owner` could lock the founder out of his own company, and there is
no member-management path to recover (R2-181: the product cannot add members). This is a genuine gap
in coverage, recorded honestly rather than closed by a risky test. It should be checked on a
throwaway company. The related question — whether `Owner` is protected from deletion at all — is
therefore **open**.

### Fix
Whitelist the accepted payload: reject `all` unless the caller is already owner-equivalent, reject an
empty object outright (deny-all should be an explicit `{"...": false}` matrix), and protect the
built-in roles from modification and deletion. This is the concrete form of decision **D7**.

## FINDING R2-293 — 🟡 MEDIUM: Tally ledger mappings accept transaction and voucher types that do not exist

```
POST /tally/mappings/ledger {"onsite_transaction_type":"ZZ nonsense",
                             "tally_voucher_type":"ZZ not a voucher",
                             "tally_ledger_name":"ZZ ledger"}
→ 201 {"onsite_transaction_type":"ZZ nonsense","posting_mode":"lumpsum",
       "tally_voucher_type":"ZZ not a voucher","tally_ledger_name":"ZZ ledger"}
```

Both type fields are unconstrained strings.

- `onsite_transaction_type` should be drawn from the product's own transaction vocabulary. A mapping
  naming a type that does not exist will **never match anything** and will sit in the configuration
  screen looking active — the same failure shape as the unsatisfiable approval rule in R2-285.
- `tally_voucher_type` must be a voucher type Tally recognises (`Sales`, `Purchase`, `Receipt`,
  `Payment`, `Journal`…). An invalid value is not detected here; it fails later, inside Tally, at
  import time, where the user has the least context to diagnose it.

This is the configuration layer that was supposed to prevent **R2-267** (the Tally export booking
customer receipts as `Purchase` vouchers). It cannot, because it does not know what a valid voucher
type is.

### Fix
Constrain `onsite_transaction_type` to the product's transaction enum and `tally_voucher_type` to
Tally's voucher vocabulary, both with `pattern` or `Literal`. Reject a mapping whose transaction type
has no producer in the product.

## Probes that found the product CORRECT — batch 15

The RBAC **creation** path is one of the better-defended surfaces audited this round:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| Role with an invented permission key | **400** `"Unknown permission key: 'totally:madeup'"` — the key set is validated against a real whitelist ✅ |
| Role named `Owner` (duplicate) | **409** `"Role already exists"` ✅ |
| `Owner` / `Admin` built-in permissions | `{"all": true}` — a deliberate wildcard, not an accident ✅ |
| `DELETE /settings/roles/{id}` on a custom role | 204 ✅ |
| Google Sheets export with no connection | **409** `"Google Sheets is not connected for this company"` — a clear, correct refusal ✅ |
| `POST /tally/mark-synced` with a non-existent bill id | 200 `{"marked_bills":0,…}` — ignores unknown ids rather than erroring; defensible ✅ |

The contrast inside a single module is worth noting: **creating** a role validates every permission
key against a whitelist, while **updating** a role's permissions accepts `{"all": true}` and `{}`
without comment (R2-292). The same file gets the harder half right and the easier half wrong.

# 🔑 ROUND 5 BATCH 16 — the auth surface and admin migrations

**The headline for this batch is what did *not* break.** The authentication surface is the
best-defended area of the product found in five rounds, and the admin-migration gate is exemplary.
Two defects were found and both are second-order.

## FINDING R2-294 — 🟠 HIGH: `/admin/migrations/backfill-rbac` is declared twice, so requests run one implementation while the API documentation describes the other

`backend/app/routers/admin_migrations.py` registers the same path twice:

```python
@router.post("/backfill-rbac")          # line 114
def backfill_rbac_roles(...):
    """One-off, idempotent RBAC bootstrap (PHASE 1)."""

@router.post("/backfill-rbac")          # line 191
def backfill_rbac(...):
    """Idempotently backfill RBAC presets + assign roles to existing members."""
```

Two full implementations of the same migration, with different bodies and different role-assignment
policies — the second explicitly assigns `partner → Admin (all)` and everyone else to
`Manager (broad)`.

**FastAPI resolves a request against the first matching route**, so `backfill_rbac_roles` (line 114)
is what actually executes and `backfill_rbac` (line 191) is unreachable dead code. But the generated
schema is keyed by path and method, so the **later** registration overwrites the earlier one in
`openapi.json` — confirmed live:

```
GET /openapi.json → /apis/v3/admin/migrations/backfill-rbac
   operationId: backfill_rbac_apis_v3_admin_migrations_backfill_rbac_post
```

The docs name `backfill_rbac`; the server runs `backfill_rbac_roles`. **Anyone reading the API
reference to decide whether it is safe to run this migration is reading the wrong function**, and
this particular migration rewrites role permissions and assigns roles across *every company in the
system*.

It also means one of the two implementations has never run and has never been tested, while both
remain in the file looking equally live.

### Severity
🟠 HIGH. Not exploitable — the endpoint is properly gated (below) — but it is a one-off migration
affecting all tenants' RBAC, where the documented behaviour and the actual behaviour differ, and
where the difference is invisible to code review unless you notice the duplicate decorator.

### Fix
Delete whichever implementation is obsolete. Add a CI check for duplicate `(method, path)`
registrations — FastAPI will not warn about this, and the same mistake anywhere else in the codebase
would be equally silent.

## FINDING R2-295 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the login rate limit is real but its enforcement is inconsistent, because the limiter keeps its counters in process memory

`app/rate_limit.py` in full:

```python
from slowapi import Limiter
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address

limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)
```

No `storage_uri`, so slowapi falls back to **in-memory storage**. The counters live in the process and
are lost whenever it restarts, and are not shared if more than one instance ever serves traffic.

**Measured, twice, against the same endpoint with the same payload:**

| Run | Requests | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 12 | `401 ×6, 429, 401, 401, 429, 429, 429` — **4 blocked** |
| 2 | 11 | `401 ×11` — **0 blocked** |

The advertised policy is `"Rate limit exceeded: 5 per 1 minute"`, and the first run roughly matched it
after a delay. The second run, minutes later, allowed eleven consecutive failed logins with no block
at all. **A brute-force control that sometimes does not engage is not a control you can rely on**,
and an attacker only needs the runs where it does not.

The likely cause is the in-memory backend combined with the service restarting between runs (this
backend is known to sleep and cold-start — see R2-080). **This is a hypothesis**: it was not possible
to confirm process identity or instance count from outside. What is *measured* is the inconsistency
itself, which stands regardless of the cause.

Spoofing `X-Forwarded-For` (`203.0.113.1/2/3`) did **not** produce a bypass — each request was
evaluated on its merits and returned a normal 401 — but that test ran during the window when no
limiting was engaging at all, so it is **inconclusive**, not a pass. Whether `get_remote_address`
resolves to the real client IP or to Cloudflare/Render's proxy address behind this deployment
remains unverified, and it matters a great deal: if it resolves to the proxy, every user in the world
shares one bucket and a single attacker can lock everyone out of login.

### Fix
1. Give the limiter a shared backend (`storage_uri="redis://…"`), so counters survive restarts and are
   consistent across instances.
2. Verify what `get_remote_address` actually returns in production, and configure
   `ProxyHeadersMiddleware` / a trusted-proxy list so it is the client IP and cannot be spoofed.
3. Add per-account lockout in addition to per-IP limiting — per-IP alone does not stop a distributed
   attempt against one account.

## Probes that found the product CORRECT — batch 16

This is the longest "correct" table in the register, and it is the point of the batch.

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| `POST /auth/login` — 12 rapid failures | Rate limited: `429 {"error":"Rate limit exceeded: 5 per 1 minute"}` ✅ (see R2-295 for the consistency caveat) |
| `POST /auth/password/forgot` — **unknown** email | `200 {"message":"If an account exists for that email, a reset code has been sent."}` ✅ |
| `POST /auth/password/forgot` — **known** email | **Byte-identical response** ✅ — no user enumeration, which the CRM and lead endpoints do not manage |
| `POST /auth/register` — password `"x"` | `400 "Password must be at least 8 characters."` ✅ |
| `POST /auth/register` — existing email, weak password | Password checked **before** the duplicate-email check, so the response does not reveal that the account exists ✅ — a deliberate ordering, not an accident |
| `email` field on all four auth endpoints | Full `EmailStr` validation, rejecting reserved and special-use domains with a precise message ✅ |
| `X-Admin-Secret` gate on all four migration endpoints | `hmac.compare_digest`, and **fails closed when the secret is unset** — the docstring states *"when it is empty the routes always return 403, so an unset secret never means 'open'"* ✅ |
| Login error text | `"Invalid email or password."` — identical for unknown user and wrong password ✅ |

The contrast with the rest of the product is stark and worth stating plainly: the auth surface uses
constant-time comparison, fails closed, validates email format, enforces a password floor, avoids
user enumeration in three separate places, and rate-limits. **Meanwhile the CRM accepts
`"not-an-email"` (R2-273), a branch accepts `"NOT-A-GSTIN"` (R2-290), and an incident type accepts
any string at all (R2-252).** The knowledge exists in the codebase; it has not been applied outside
the security-labelled modules.

## Auditor disclosure

`POST /auth/password/forgot` was called once with the founder's real email address
(`upadhyayprateek574@gmail.com`) to compare the response against the unknown-email case. That is a
genuine password-reset email, and it will have arrived in the founder's inbox. **No reset code was
requested, received or used, and the account is unchanged** — the test read only the HTTP response
body, which is the same string in both cases. The email can be ignored.

Twelve failed login attempts were also made against `zz-r5-nobody@gmail.com`, an address with no
account, to characterise the rate limiter. No real account was targeted and no account was locked.

# 📋 ROUND 5 BATCH 17 — RFQ, work-order amendments, inventory

## FINDING R2-296 — 🟠 HIGH: a work-order amendment is stored, accepts invented fields, names whoever the caller says — and changes nothing

`ZZ-R5-WO-1` carries `estimated_work_amount: 50000.0`. An amendment was submitted raising it to
₹9,99,99,999 and adding a field that does not exist:

```
POST /subcon/work-orders/{wo_id}/amendments
  {"amended_by":"ZZ NOT ME",
   "amended_fields":{"estimated_work_amount":99999999,"totally_made_up":"yes"},
   "reason":"ZZ R5 probe"}
→ 201 {"amendment_number":1,
       "amended_fields":{"totally_made_up":"yes","estimated_work_amount":99999999},
       "amended_by":"ZZ NOT ME", "amended_at":"2026-07-27T07:19:28Z"}

GET /billing/work-orders?project_id=…
→ [("ZZ-R5-WO-1", 50000.0, "active")]      ← unchanged
```

Three defects in one call:

1. **The amendment is never applied.** The work order's value is still ₹50,000. A variation to a
   subcontract — the thing that changes what the subcontractor is owed — is recorded in a side table
   and read by nothing. **Tenth member of the "captured but never consumed" pattern**, and the second
   variation mechanism found dead this round after BOQ revisions (R2-274).
2. **`amended_fields` is an unvalidated JSON blob.** `totally_made_up` was stored verbatim. There is
   no whitelist of amendable fields, so an amendment can claim to change anything, including fields
   that do not exist — and since nothing applies it, nothing ever objects.
3. **`amended_by` is free-text and was set to `"ZZ NOT ME"`.** Tenth site of the caller-supplied
   identity pattern, and not even UUID-typed, unlike the Quality module's actor fields.

### Why this matters more than it looks
**R2-253** found that a ₹5,90,000 subcon bill was accepted against a ₹50,000 work order with nothing
comparing them. The fix proposed there was to validate cumulative billing against
`estimated_work_amount` **plus approved amendments** — because legitimate overruns happen and the
amendment endpoint exists for exactly that. This finding shows that mechanism does not work: the
amendment is neither applied nor approvable. So the honest remediation for R2-253 has to build the
amendment path first.

### Fix
Apply the amendment to the work order in the same transaction (or derive the effective value as
`base + sum(approved amendments)` at read time), whitelist the amendable fields, require an approval
before an amendment takes effect, and derive `amended_by` from the authenticated user.

## FINDING R2-297 — 🟠 HIGH: an inventory item's unit can be changed without converting the quantity, silently rescaling the stock by whatever the conversion factor is

```
Before: {"material_name":"ZZ Cement OPC53","on_hand_qty":-9699.0,"unit":"bag"}

PATCH /procurement/inventory/{inventory_id} {"unit":"tonne","category":"ZZ recat"}
→ 200 {"material_name":"ZZ Cement OPC53","on_hand_qty":-9699.0,"unit":"tonne", …}
```

The unit changed from `bag` to `tonne`. **The quantity did not change.** A bag of OPC53 cement is
50 kg, so 9,699 bags is roughly 485 tonnes — the record now asserts a quantity **fifty times** what it
represents, and every downstream consumer that multiplies quantity by a rate is wrong by that factor.

The endpoint accepts only `category` and `unit`, so this is not an obscure corner — **changing the
unit is one of the two things the endpoint is for**, and it does it without touching the number it
qualifies. There is no conversion table, no warning, and no requirement to restate the quantity.

Related: the same response shows `category: "ZZ recat"` accepted as free text with no reference to
the material-category list that `POST /library/material-categories` maintains — so re-categorising an
item can silently orphan it from every category filter.

### Fix
Either forbid changing the unit on an item that has a non-zero quantity, or require a conversion
factor in the request and restate `on_hand_qty`, `reserved_qty` and every historical movement
together. Constrain `category` to the existing category list.

## FINDING R2-298 — 🟡 MEDIUM: quotes can be submitted against an RFQ that is still a draft and expired six years ago, and the "comparison" endpoint performs no comparison

**(a) Neither status nor expiry is enforced.** An RFQ was created with `valid_until` in the past:

```
POST /procurement/rfq {"rfq_number":"ZZ-R5-RFQ-1","valid_until":"2020-01-01T00:00:00Z", …}
→ 201 {"status":"draft","valid_until":"2020-01-01T00:00:00Z", …}
```

It was accepted with a validity date **six years in the past** — the fifth instance of an unbounded
past date in this round (NCR R2-246, safety R2-256, CRM R2-273, to-do R2-278). Two vendor quotes were
then submitted against it successfully:

```
POST /procurement/rfq/{rfq_id}/quotes {"vendor_name":"ZZ Vendor A","quoted_rate":400,"delivery_days":5}  → 201
POST /procurement/rfq/{rfq_id}/quotes {"vendor_name":"ZZ Vendor B","quoted_rate":1,"delivery_days":99}   → 201
```

The RFQ was never issued — it is still `draft` — and its validity window closed in 2020. Both facts
are recorded on the record being quoted against, and neither is checked. A tender process whose
closing date is advisory is not a tender process; late quotes are the standard procurement fraud, and
the field that would prevent them is decorative.

**(b) `/comparison` does not compare.** `GET /procurement/rfq/{rfq_id}/comparison` returns the item
with a `vendors` array — the raw quote rows, in submission order, with no lowest-rate flag, no
ranking, no extended totals (rate × quantity), and no recommendation:

```json
[{"item_id":"c8cd59b6-…","material_name":"ZZ Cement OPC53","quantity":100.0,"unit":"bag",
  "vendors":[{"vendor_name":"ZZ Vendor A","quoted_rate":400.0,"delivery_days":5,…},
             {"vendor_name":"ZZ Vendor B","quoted_rate":1.0,"delivery_days":99,…}]}]
```

It is a grouping, not a comparison. The buyer is left to eyeball it, and nothing surfaces that
"Vendor B" quoted ₹1 with a 99-day lead time — a quote that wins on price and is almost certainly not
real. Given the module's name and route, a user will reasonably assume the ranking has been done.

### Fix
Reject quotes on an RFQ that is not `issued`, or whose `valid_until` has passed; reject a
`valid_until` in the past at creation. Have `/comparison` compute the extended total per vendor, flag
the lowest landed cost, and show the price spread so an outlier is visible.

|---|---|
| `quoted_rate: -50` on a vendor quote | 422, `ge: 0.0` ✅ |

| `PATCH /procurement/inventory/{id}` field scope | Accepts only `category` and `unit` — it cannot be used to fabricate a quantity ✅ (the defect is what it fails to do, not what it allows) |

## Not closed — recorded so it is not mistaken for a pass

`GET /procurement/vendors/performance/{project_id}` returned `[]` on a project that has one purchase
order, two goods receipts and three parties. That may be correct — the metric may require completed
or vendor-linked POs, and every PO on the project has `vendor_id: null` because the create schema
makes it optional. **Not enough evidence to call it a defect**, and it is left open rather than filed.
Closing it needs a PO created with a real `vendor_id` and a full receipt cycle against it.

# 🚧 ROUND 5 BATCH 18 — the public lead endpoint, rate limiting, tenant isolation

## FINDING R2-299 — 🟠 HIGH: rate limiting does not enforce its policy — 20 requests against a "5 per hour" limit on the public, unauthenticated endpoint were accepted 13 times

**R2-295 measured this inconsistency on login and labelled the cause a hypothesis. This is the same
defect on a different endpoint with a much tighter policy, and the numbers are unambiguous.**

`public_leads.py:110` declares:

```python
@limiter.limit("5/hour")
def create_lead(request: Request, payload: LeadRequest, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
```

Twenty POSTs were issued to `/apis/v3/public/leads` over roughly thirty seconds, each with a distinct
name and email, from one client:

```
run 1 (8 requests):   200 200 200 200 200 200 429 200
run 2 (12 requests):  200 200 200 429 200 429 429 200 429 200 429 429
```

**13 accepted, 7 rejected, against a policy of 5 per hour.** The pattern is not a burst allowance
followed by a block — it alternates, returning 200 *after* several 429s. The limiter is not
maintaining a monotonic counter for this client.

The most likely cause remains the one identified in R2-295: `app/rate_limit.py` constructs
`Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)` with **no `storage_uri`**, so counters live in process memory
and are neither shared nor durable. With more than one process or instance serving traffic, each
holds an independent bucket and requests land in whichever one the load balancer picks — which
produces exactly this alternating pattern. **The cause is still inferred; the failure to enforce is
now measured twice, on two endpoints, with 33 requests in total.**

### Why this one is worse than R2-295
- **It needs no account.** `/public/leads` is the marketing site's contact form, reachable by anyone.
- **The policy is deliberately strict** — 5/hour is an anti-spam number, not a convenience limit — so
  the gap between intent and behaviour is 2.6× rather than marginal.
- **Every accepted request writes a row and attempts an email.** `create_lead` persists the lead and
  then best-effort notifies the founder, so a flood is both a database write amplification and an
  inbox flood, at the attacker's chosen rate.

### Fix
As R2-295: give the limiter a shared backend (`storage_uri="redis://…"`) so counters survive restarts
and are consistent across processes, and verify what `get_remote_address` resolves to behind
Cloudflare and Render before relying on it as a key. Until then, the honeypot (which works — see
below) is the only spam control on this endpoint that actually functions.

### Auditor disclosure — this test created real leads and probably real emails
The two runs above persisted roughly **fifteen `marketing_leads` rows** named `ZZ R5 Lead`, `ZZ Bot`
and `ZZ Flood 1…20`, each with a `zz-…@gmail.com` address. Per `public_leads.py:112-118` each
non-honeypot lead also triggers a best-effort notification to `LEAD_NOTIFY_EMAIL`, so **the founder
may have received up to fifteen notification emails.**

The second run of twelve was excessive: eight requests had already established that the limit was not
holding, and the extra twelve added noise to a live table and a live inbox for a marginal gain in
confidence. Recorded here rather than glossed over. Cleanup:

```sql
DELETE FROM marketing_leads WHERE email LIKE 'zz-%@gmail.com' OR name LIKE 'ZZ %';
```

## Probes that found the product CORRECT — batch 18

### The public lead endpoint is well built
Everything about it except the rate limit is right, and the module docstring shows the reasoning was
deliberate:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| Honeypot field `website` populated | `200 {"ok":true}` — and per `:117-118` the lead is **silently not persisted and not emailed**. A bot gets a success shape and nothing happens ✅ |
| `email: "not-an-email"` | 422, `EmailStr` ✅ — the same validation the CRM lacks (R2-273) |
| Lead persisted before the email is attempted | `:8-10` — *"the lead is persisted FIRST and committed; the notification email is a best-effort side effect that can never lose the lead if the mail fails"* ✅ |
| Header-injection stripping on lead fields | `:35-37` — newline stripping as defence in depth on top of the mailer's own ✅ |
| `max_length` on `email` (255) and `website` (200) | ✅ |

This is a module where someone thought about abuse, wrote down why, and implemented it — and then the
one control that depends on shared infrastructure is the one that fails.

### Tenant isolation holds
Five probes with a fabricated company or project id, using a valid token for a real company:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| `POST /billing/bills` with a foreign `company_id` but my own `project_id` | **403** `"User is not a member of the requested company"` ✅ |
| `GET /budget/committed/{fake_project}` | **404** `"Project not found"` ✅ |
| `GET /settings/roles/{fake_company}` | **403** `"You do not have access to this company"` ✅ |
| `GET /finance/parties/{fake_company}` | **403** ✅ |
| `GET /tally/export?company_id={fake_company}` | **403** ✅ |

Notably the first probe is the interesting one: it supplies a **real** project the caller does own
alongside a **foreign** company id, which is the shape that catches naive implementations that check
one and trust the other. It was rejected on the company check. Combined with the cross-tenant testing
done in Round 4 with a real second tenant, **multi-tenancy is not a weak point of this product** and
should not absorb more audit time.

# 🗑️ ROUND 5 BATCH 19 — project deletion and the audit trail

## FINDING R2-300 — 🔴 CRITICAL: deleting a project silently destroys every financial record under it, and the audit trail records only that "a project" was deleted

A throwaway project was created, given one purchase bill of ₹1,000, and deleted:

```
POST /projects/            → 200  id 7f3bc608-…
POST /billing/bills        → 201  ZZ-R5-THROW-1, ₹1,180
DELETE /projects/{id}      → 200  {"success":true}
GET  /billing/bills?project_id=7f3bc608-…   → 404 {"detail":"Project not found"}
```

The bill is gone. `Bill.project_id` is declared `ForeignKey("projects.id", ondelete="CASCADE")`
(`models.py:577`), and so are the project's purchase orders, work orders, GRNs, attendance logs,
payroll runs, DPRs, towers, quality inspections, safety incidents and everything else keyed to the
project. **One `DELETE` removes the entire financial history of a project.**

There is no confirmation step, no check for existing financial records, no soft-delete, and no
restore path.

### The audit trail does not record what was destroyed
Exactly one row was written to `delete_logs`:

```json
{"entity_type":"project","entity_id":"7f3bc608-…",
 "entity_summary":"Project: ZZ R5 Throwaway","party_name":"ZZ R5 Throwaway",
 "deleted_by":null,"deleted_at":"2026-07-27T07:26:51Z"}
```

The bill that was destroyed with it is not mentioned, and neither would a thousand others be. The
audit trail answers "was a project deleted?" and cannot answer "what did we lose?" — which is the
only question that matters afterwards, whether the deletion was a mistake, a dispute, or a tax audit.

### The contrast with R2-232 is the point
**R2-232** established that a single mistyped invoice **cannot be cancelled or deleted by any means** —
it is permanent and permanently counted. **This finding establishes that the same invoice, plus every
other financial record on the project, can be erased in one unconfirmed call.** The product is
simultaneously incapable of correcting one record and casually capable of destroying all of them.
That combination is worse than either behaviour alone, because it means the only available correction
tool is catastrophic.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL. Irreversible destruction of financial records, available to anyone with project-delete
permission, with no confirmation, no inventory of what was removed, and — per the next finding — no
record of who did it.

### Fix
1. Refuse to delete a project that has bills, payments, purchase orders or payroll runs. Offer
   archive/close instead; a completed project should be closed, not deleted.
2. If deletion must exist, make it soft (`deleted_at`), keep the rows, and exclude them from every
   query — which also gives a restore path.
3. Write a delete-log entry per cascaded entity, or at minimum a summary count by type
   (`{"bills": 1, "purchase_orders": 3, …}`) captured **before** the delete.
4. Require typed confirmation of the project name in the UI, as the destructiveness warrants.

## FINDING R2-301 — 🟠 HIGH: the deletion audit trail never records who performed the deletion

Every row in `delete_logs` for this company has `deleted_by: null` — all six of them, spanning
`project`, `timesheet`, `payment` ×2, `todo` and `party`, written across three days by at least two
different sessions.

The column exists (`models.py:2024`) and the helper accepts it (`delete_logs.py:19-27`):

```python
def log_deletion(db, company_id, entity_type, entity_id, summary,
                 party_name: str = None, deleted_by: str = None):
```

**No caller passes it.** The finance path is representative — `finance.py:198`:

```python
        log_deletion(db, payment.company_id, "payment", payment.id, f"Payment {payment.id}")
```

`current_user` is in scope at that line and is simply not passed.

An audit trail that records *what* was deleted and *when* but never *by whom* fails at the one thing
an audit trail is for. In a multi-user construction company — where the register is presumably there
so a director can ask why a payment vanished — it answers "a payment was deleted" and stops.

Note this is the eleventh instance of the actor-identity pattern in this round, but with the sign
reversed: elsewhere the actor is taken from the request body and trusted (R2-247, R2-251, R2-296);
here the authenticated actor is available and thrown away.

### Fix
Pass `current_user.user_name` (or id) from every one of the `log_deletion` call sites; make the
parameter required so a new call site cannot omit it.

## FINDING R2-302 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a project location accepts impossible coordinates

```
POST /projects/{project_id}/locations {"name":"ZZ Loc","latitude":999,"longitude":-999}
→ 200 {"id":"be4db5ac-…","name":"ZZ Loc","parent_id":null}
```

Latitude is bounded to −90…90 and longitude to −180…180 on the actual planet. Both were accepted
without validation, and the response does not echo them, so the caller cannot even tell what was
stored.

This is not cosmetic: site coordinates drive **attendance geofencing**. `hr.py:275-288` computes a
distance from the site and sets `is_within_geofence`, falling back to "allow" when coordinates are
absent. A nonsensical coordinate yields a nonsensical distance, which will either reject every legitimate
punch or accept every remote one — and per R2-262 the punch-out half of that flow is already broken.

### Fix
`latitude: float = Field(..., ge=-90, le=90)` and `longitude: float = Field(..., ge=-180, le=180)`,
and echo the stored values in the response.

`party_id` near-miss in batch 7) — the discipline that catches it is dumping the whole object once
before asserting anything about its fields.

# 📈 ROUND 5 BATCH 20 — Analytics, re-read against a project of known contents

The clean project's contents are known exactly, which makes every analytics figure checkable:

```
purchase 12,154 · equipment 23,600 · expense 35,400 · subcon 590,000 · payment_in 590 · sale 118,000
→ real cost 661,154 · real revenue 118,000
```

## FINDING R2-303 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the budget burn-down curve compounds — each month adds the running total again, so month N reports N times the real spend

`analytics.py:293-310`:

```python
        month_spend = sum(
            _to_float(bill.total_payable)
            for bill in bills
            if bill.invoice_date and _to_date(bill.invoice_date) and _to_date(bill.invoice_date) <= month_end_d
        )
        cumulative_spend += month_spend
        ...
        monthly_burn.append({"label": _month_label(month), "spend": round(cumulative_spend, 2), …})
```

`month_spend` is already **cumulative** — the filter is `<= month_end_d`, every bill up to the end of
that month, not bills *within* it. That already-cumulative figure is then added to a running
`cumulative_spend`. The series compounds.

**Confirmed live** on `GET /analytics/company/{company_id}`:

```json
"budget_burn_series":[{"label":"Jul 2026","burn_pct":0.0,"spend":1051144.0},
                      {"label":"Aug 2026","burn_pct":0.0,"spend":2102288.0}]
```

Real company-wide spend is ₹10,51,144. August reports **₹21,02,288 — exactly double** — on a month
that contains **no transactions at all**. With a twelve-month window the final point would read twelve
times the true spend, and the curve would climb steeply through months in which nothing happened.

The comparison is `burn_pct = cumulative_spend / total_budget`, so once a budget is configured (it is
₹0 here, which is why `burn_pct` reads 0.0 and hides the error) the reported burn rate is inflated by
the same factor. A project genuinely at 40% burn would show as fully consumed by the fourth month of
its chart.

### Fix
Filter bills to the month itself (`month_start <= invoice_date <= month_end`) before accumulating, or
drop the accumulator and assign `cumulative_spend = month_spend` since the filter is already
cumulative. Add a test asserting that a month with no bills leaves the series flat.

## FINDING R2-304 — 🔴 CRITICAL: analytics invents eight hours of labour for every attendance record that has no hours — and because punch-out always fails, that is every record

`analytics.py:314-321`:

```python
    total_hours = 0.0
    for log in attendance_logs:
        if log.hours_worked:
            total_hours += _to_float(log.hours_worked)
        else:
            total_hours += 8.0
    labour_days = round(total_hours / 8.0, 2) if total_hours else 0.0
```

An attendance log with `hours_worked` null is silently counted as a **full eight-hour day**.

**This interacts catastrophically with R2-262.** Punch-out returns 500 on every call, so
`hours_worked` is never written by any successful code path. Every attendance record in the product is
therefore an open punch-in with null hours — and every one of them is scored as a complete working
day. **The entire labour-productivity subsystem is generating numbers from data that does not exist.**

### Proved by disagreement between two of the product's own feeds
For the same underlying records:

| Surface | `total_hours` |
|---|---|
| BI feed `labour-productivity` (sums real `hours_worked`) | **8.0** |
| `GET /analytics/company/{cid}` (adds 8.0 for nulls) | **16.0** |

Two hours figures for the same two attendance logs, differing by exactly the 8.0 that was fabricated
for the log R2-262 stranded open. The BI feed is right; analytics is inventing.

Everything downstream inherits it: `labour_days` (16 ÷ 8 = 2.0 days that were never worked),
`productivity_m2_per_labour_day`, and any labour cost-per-day derived from them.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL. It is not an approximation — there is no basis for the 8.0, and it is applied to 100% of
records. A fallback that fabricates data is worse than an empty chart, because an empty chart is
obviously empty.

### Fix
Skip logs with no `hours_worked` and report the count separately (`"logs_without_hours": n`), so the
gap is visible rather than filled. Fix R2-262 so the data exists.

## FINDING R2-305 — 🟠 HIGH: "material wastage" is computed as stock not yet consumed, ignores every wastage record, and clamps to zero — reporting 0% wastage on a project that consumed fifty times what it ordered

`analytics.py:330-333`:

```python
    ordered_qty = sum(_to_float(item.quantity) for item in purchase_order_items)
    consumed_qty = sum(_to_float(tx.qty) for tx in material_transactions)
    wastage_qty = max(ordered_qty - consumed_qty, 0.0)
    wastage_pct = round((wastage_qty / ordered_qty) * 100, 2) if ordered_qty else 0.0
```

Three problems compounding:

1. **Wastage is defined as `ordered − consumed`** — that is *unconsumed stock*, which is inventory,
   not waste. Material still sitting in the yard is reported as wasted.
2. **The `Wastage` table is never read.** The 500-bag wastage record filed under R2-245 contributes
   nothing. **Eleventh member of the "captured but never consumed" pattern**, and the module that
   ignores it is the one named after it.
3. **`max(…, 0.0)` hides the contradiction.** Live output:

```json
"material_wastage":{"ordered_qty":200.0,"consumed_qty":10015.0,"wastage_qty":0.0,"wastage_pct":0.0}
```

**10,015 units consumed against 200 ordered** — the over-consumption from R2-254 — and the report's
verdict is **0.00% wastage**. The clamp turns a glaring data-integrity signal into a clean-looking
zero. Both numbers are printed side by side and no one reading the percentage would look at them.

### Fix
Compute wastage from the `Wastage` table. Report `ordered − received − consumed` as a separate stock
reconciliation, and when it is negative, surface it as a **discrepancy** rather than clamping it —
a negative here always means the data is wrong.

## FINDING R2-306 — 🟠 HIGH: the two analytics endpoints disagree about the same project's spend, because one filters `invoice_type` and the other does not

`analytics.py:223` computes per-project spend as:

```python
        project_spend = sum(_to_float(bill.total_payable) for bill in bills_by_project.get(project.id, []))
```

Every bill, unfiltered — so revenue and settlement vouchers are counted as spend. Meanwhile
`/analytics/company/{cid}/financial` computes `total_expense` using `EXPENSE_INVOICE_TYPES` correctly.
The same module, called two ways, on the same project:

| Endpoint | Old project spend | Includes |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /analytics/company/{cid}` → `projects[].spend` | **₹2,71,400** | all bills, **including the ₹1,18,000 sales invoice** |
| `GET /analytics/company/{cid}/financial` → `total_expense` | **₹1,41,600** | expense types only |

₹1,29,800 apart, from one module, on one project, in the same API call sequence. `total_spend` and
`budget_variance` on the first endpoint inherit the error, which is also what feeds the compounding
burn series in R2-303.

This is the **ninth site** in the `invoice_type` cross-cutting pattern and brings the count of
mutually disagreeing cost surfaces to **six**: Budget, P&L, Towers, Tally export, BI feed, Analytics —
and Analytics now disagrees with *itself*.

### Fix
The shared cost-head mapping proposed in the Round 5 handoff, applied here too. Given that
`/financial` in this very file already does it correctly, this is a two-line change plus a test that
asserts the two endpoints agree.

# 👤 ROUND 5 BATCH 21 — face-recognition attendance

## FINDING R2-307 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the face-recognition attendance module is non-functional in three of its four endpoints, and its one write endpoint commits the record *before* failing — so punches are silently stored and can never be read back

`FaceRecognitionLog` (`models.py:1734-1747`) declares eleven columns and **no `created_at`**. Three of
the four endpoints in `face_recognition.py` depend on that column existing.

| Endpoint | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /face/punch` | **500** | `FacePunchResponse.created_at: datetime` (`:39`) is required and the ORM object has no such attribute |
| `GET /face/logs/{company_id}` | **500** | `.order_by(FaceRecognitionLog.created_at.desc())` (`:82`) → `AttributeError` |
| `GET /face/summary/{company_id}` | **500** | filters `created_at >= target_date` (`:103-104`) |
| `GET /face/employees/{company_id}` | 200 ✅ | the only one that does not touch the missing column |

All four verified live. The `AttributeError` is **already on the Sentry board**:

```
AttributeError — type object 'FaceRecognitionLog' has no attribute 'created_at'
PYTHON-FASTAPI-A  Unhandled  /apis/v3/face/logs/{company_id}
```

aged ~13 hours when the board was read. That is the **fourth** Sentry issue observed this session
pointing directly at an unacted-on defect (chat R2-270, statutory R2-283, root-router R2-291, this).

### The write endpoint is the dangerous part
`face_recognition.py:69-74`:

```python
def face_punch(payload: FacePunchRequest, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    log = FaceRecognitionLog(**payload.model_dump())
    db.add(log)
    db.commit()          # ← the row is committed here
    db.refresh(log)
    return log           # ← response validation fails here → 500
```

**The commit succeeds and then the response fails.** The attendance punch is durably written to the
database, and the caller receives `500 Internal Server Error`. From the user's side the punch did not
happen; from the database's side it did. And because `GET /face/logs` and `GET /face/summary` also
500, **there is no way to see what was stored**.

The predictable user behaviour makes it worse: a site worker whose punch "fails" will punch again.
Every retry writes another row. The table accumulates duplicate attendance records that no endpoint
can display, and no one can tell how many.

### Same root cause as R2-283, third instance this round
A Pydantic schema and a SQLAlchemy model disagreeing about whether a column exists:

| Finding | Column | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| R2-283 | `StatutoryReport.due_date` — passed to the constructor, not a column | every statutory create 500s, **nothing written** |
| R2-307 | `FaceRecognitionLog.created_at` — required by the response, not a column | punch 500s, **row written anyway** |
| R2-283 (cause 3) | `filed_at`/`filed_by`/`acknowledgment_number` — `Optional` with no default | auto-populate 500s |

The two failure modes are opposite and the second is worse: R2-283 fails loudly and loses nothing,
R2-307 fails loudly and keeps everything, invisibly.

### The attendance picture is now complete, and it is bleak
Three independent mechanisms exist for recording who was on site, and **none of them works**:

1. **Manual punch** (`/hr/attendance/punch`) — punch-in succeeds, punch-out 500s every time and
   deadlocks the worker for the day (**R2-262**).
2. **Face-recognition punch** (`/face/punch`) — 500s, writes anyway, unreadable (**this finding**).
3. **Muster roll** (`/labour/muster-roll`) — works, but accepts 240 hours from zero workers
   (**R2-263**).

And analytics fabricates eight hours for every record with no hours (**R2-304**), which is now
provably every record from mechanism 1. There is no path by which this product currently knows how
many hours anyone worked.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL. Silent data writes behind an error response are the worst failure shape available: the
user is told nothing happened, the database disagrees, and the reconciliation surfaces are themselves
broken.

### Fix
1. Add a `created_at` column to `FaceRecognitionLog` (with a migration and a `server_default`), which
   fixes all three endpoints at once — it is one column.
2. Independently, never return an ORM object through a response model without a test that
   round-trips it; a single test calling `POST /face/punch` would have caught this on the day it was
   written.
3. Audit the table for duplicate punches created by retries before the fix lands.

### Auditor note
Two `POST /face/punch` calls were made during this test (one `in`, one `out`, employee
`0057179f-…`, project `ZZ QA R5 Second Project`). Both returned 500 and **both rows are therefore
almost certainly in `face_recognition_logs`** — that is the finding. They cannot be listed or deleted
through the product, since the read endpoints 500. They can be removed with:

```sql
DELETE FROM face_recognition_logs WHERE project_id = '4ab9616c-95cb-4445-8782-0684f03564c6';
```

## FINDING R2-308 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the database connection pool is being exhausted on `/auth/me`, 26 times in 24 hours, and the trend is escalating

```
TimeoutError — QueuePool limit of size 10 overflow 20 reached, connection timed out, timeout 30.00
PYTHON-FASTAPI-B  Unhandled  /apis/v3/auth/me
26 events · 24hr · Escalating
```

The pool is sized 10 with 20 overflow — **30 connections** — and all thirty are held long enough for a
new request to wait the full 30-second timeout and give up. `/auth/me` is the endpoint every page in
the console calls on load, so when the pool is exhausted **the entire application becomes unusable**,
not one feature.

Round 3 filed a CRITICAL for a Delete Logs screen issuing ~16 requests/second in a loop and exhausting
the pool exactly this way. **This is that failure, still occurring, 26 times in the last day, marked
Escalating by Sentry's own trend analysis.** Whatever the trigger is now, the remediation from Round 3
was never applied.

Two contributing factors found this round make it worse:
- **R2-291** — every mistyped path under `/apis/v3` reaches `Depends(get_current_user)` and takes a
  connection before failing. 16 such events in 23 hours, also Escalating.
- **R2-195** (Round 4) — 120 counted N+1 query sites. Any of them under load holds connections far
  longer than necessary.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL — total application unavailability, recurring daily, trending upward, with a known
untreated cause from two rounds ago.

### Fix
1. Find the caller. Sentry's event detail for this issue carries the request context; the Round 3
   Delete Logs loop is the leading candidate and should be checked first.
2. Add `pool_timeout`, and set `pool_recycle`; confirm `pool_pre_ping` is still on (R2-138 found it
   already enabled).
3. Fix R2-291 so bogus paths do not consume connections.
4. Alert on this issue specifically — pool exhaustion is a total outage and should page, not sit on a
   board.

## FINDING R2-309 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the Sentry board carries fixed issues as unresolved, which is why it gets ignored

Two of the sixteen unresolved issues are **already fixed in the codebase**, verified live this
session:

| Issue | Fixed by | Verified now |
|---|---|---|
| `AttributeError: 'Project' object has no attribute 'start_date'` on `/analytics/…/operational` | **`37c84d9`** *"fix(analytics): resolve AttributeError on p.start_date, p.end_date, and p.customer_name in operational analytics"* — the code now reads `getattr(p, "actual_start_date", None) or getattr(p, "planned_start_date", None) or getattr(p, "created_at", None)` (`analytics.py:462`) | `GET /analytics/company/{cid}/operational` → **200** with a full payload |
| `NameError: name 'models' is not defined` on `/billing/subcontractors` | **`50a4c89`** *"fix(billing): bind models module to resolve NameError on subcontractor and work-order endpoints"* | `GET /billing/subcontractors?company_id=…` → **200**, returns two subcontractors |

Both still show as **Unresolved**, and one carries a `Quick Fix` badge suggesting Sentry has
already proposed the patch that was independently applied.

This is not a code defect, it is a process one, and it explains the pattern this round kept hitting:
four separate live defects (R2-270, R2-283, R2-291, R2-307) sat on the board with their exception
types naming the cause exactly, unread. **A board where a third of the entries are stale or already
fixed teaches its owner to stop reading it**, which is precisely what appears to have happened.

### Fix
Resolve the two fixed issues; resolve the six generated by this audit once their findings are
addressed; then set up release tracking (`sentry_sdk.init(release=…)` plus a deploy hook) so issues
auto-resolve when the fixing commit ships, and enable alerting on `Escalating` issues only — which
today would be exactly two, both real.

revises this:

- **"Unwatched" is confirmed and then some** — five live defects sat there with exact causes, plus two
  already-fixed entries nobody cleared.
- **"Partly blind" is narrower than stated.** The board captures `TypeError`, `ValueError`,
  `AttributeError`, `NameError`, `IntegrityError`, `DataError`, `ResponseValidationError`,
  `ValidationError`, `TimeoutError` and `HTTPException` — an unusually complete range, from ten
  distinct endpoints, including errors raised inside response serialisation. The `/finance/ledger`
  gap (R2-236) is therefore **a specific unexplained omission, not a general capture failure**, and
  it stays open as such.

The practical guidance for the next round is unchanged but better founded: **read the board first, it
is more complete than assumed** — and verify anything absent from it with `curl` rather than
concluding it did not happen.

## Corroboration this batch gives to R2-276

`GET /billing/subcontractors?company_id=…` returns real names:

```json
[{"company_team_id":"331b67d5-…","name":"ZZ QA Subcon Co","gstin":null,"phone":"9000000009"},
 {"company_team_id":"2fc81872-…","name":"ZZ QA NoGST Vendor","gstin":null,"phone":"9000000001"}]
```

Party `331b67d5-…` is the **same id** that renders as `"Unknown"` on the work order, `"Unknown"` on the
subcon scorecard, and `"N/A"` on the invoice PDF. The name exists and is retrievable — this endpoint
resolves it correctly while four others fail. That confirms the hypothesis stated in R2-276: the
failing paths walk `CompanyTeam → User`, while the party's name actually lives on the party record.
**R2-276 is upgraded from "a lookup that fails for some rows" to "four surfaces using the wrong join,
where a correct one exists in the same codebase."**

# 🎯 ROUND 5 BATCH 23 — R2-308's root cause, found

## FINDING R2-310 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the Delete Logs page contains an unbounded React fetch loop, caused by one object literal in a dependency array — this is the cause of the pool exhaustion that takes the whole application down

**This closes R2-308, and it closes the Round 3 CRITICAL that has been open for two rounds.** Round 3
observed the Delete Logs screen issuing roughly 16 requests per second and exhausting the database
pool, but recorded the behaviour without the mechanism. Here is the mechanism, in three lines of
`frontend/src/app/c/[company_id]/d/delete-logs/page.tsx`:

```js
// :43 — a NEW object is constructed on every single render
const authHeaders = accessToken ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` } : undefined;

// :44-69 — that object is a dependency of the callback
const fetchLogs = useCallback(async () => {
    setLoading(true);
    ...
}, [apiHost, companyId, entityType, party, fromDate, toDate, authHeaders]);

// :71-73 — and the callback is the dependency of the effect
useEffect(() => {
    fetchLogs();
}, [fetchLogs]);
```

### The loop
1. The component renders. `:43` creates a **brand-new object** — identical in content, different in
   identity.
2. `useCallback`'s dependency array is compared by reference. `authHeaders` is a new reference, so
   `fetchLogs` is rebuilt with a new identity.
3. `useEffect`'s dependency array contains `fetchLogs`, which changed, so the effect fires.
4. `fetchLogs` calls `setLoading(true)` at `:45` — a state update, which **triggers a re-render**.
5. Go to 1.

There is no exit condition. The loop runs as fast as React can re-render, each iteration firing a
`GET /apis/v3/{company_id}`. The observed ~16 requests/second is simply how fast the round trip
allows.

### The full causal chain, end to end
| Step | Effect |
|---|---|
| One object literal at `:43` | `fetchLogs` identity changes every render |
| `useEffect([fetchLogs])` | effect fires every render |
| `setLoading(true)` inside it | causes the next render |
| → **unbounded request loop** | ~16 req/s per open browser tab |
| Each request → `Depends(get_current_user)` | takes a connection from the pool |
| Pool is `size 10 + overflow 20` | 30 connections consumed almost immediately |
| → **`QueuePool limit … reached`** on `/auth/me` (**R2-308**) | 26 events in 24h, **Escalating** |
| `/auth/me` is called by every page on load | **the entire console becomes unusable** |

A single missing `useMemo` is taking the whole application offline, daily, and the trend is upward.

### Two aggravating factors found this round
- **R2-291** — the endpoint being hammered is `GET /apis/v3/{company_id}`, the root-mounted
  delete-logs route. It is also the wildcard that swallows every mistyped path, so it appears twice
  in this story: once as the loop's target and once as the reason unrelated typos also consume
  connections. Its `ValueError` issue is likewise **Escalating** (16 events / 23h).
- **R2-195** (Round 4) — 120 N+1 query sites hold connections longer than necessary, lowering the
  number of concurrent loop iterations needed to exhaust the pool.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL. Total application unavailability, reproducible by any user simply **opening a page**,
recurring daily, escalating, and traceable to a one-line fix.

### Fix
```js
const authHeaders = useMemo(
  () => (accessToken ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` } : undefined),
  [accessToken]
);
```
Or, better, drop it from the dependency array entirely — the token is read from `localStorage` at
call time anyway (`siteflow.ts:6-10`), so the callback does not need it as a dependency.

Then, defensively: add `exhaustive-deps` as an **error** in the ESLint config (it would have flagged
this at write time), and consider a client-side request guard that logs and breaks after N identical
requests in a short window — an unbounded loop should never be able to reach the server thousands of
times.

## The same pattern elsewhere — swept, and it is contained

Three files construct `authHeaders` as an inline object literal:

| File | In a dependency array? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `d/delete-logs/page.tsx:43` | **Yes** (`:69`) | **The loop — R2-310** |
| `context/CompanySettingsContext.tsx:35` | No — declared **inside** the fetching function, not in the component body | Safe ✅ |
| `context/ProjectContext.tsx:101` | No — same, function-scoped | Safe ✅ |

The two context files get it right by construction: the object is created inside the async function
that uses it, so it never participates in a dependency comparison. **Only the Delete Logs page hoists
it into component scope**, and only that page pairs it with a `useCallback`/`useEffect` chain. The
defect is a single site, not a codebase-wide habit — which makes the fix small and the risk of
recurrence a lint-rule problem rather than a refactor.

## What this batch changes about the register

- **R2-308 is no longer an unexplained outage.** It has a named cause, a code location, and a
  one-line fix.
- **The Round 3 CRITICAL is closed** on mechanism. It was filed as "Delete Logs 16 req/s loop
  exhausts the DB pool and breaks `/auth/me`" — correct in every observable respect, and now
  explained.
- **R2-291's priority rises.** It was filed as a 404-hygiene and monitoring-noise problem; it is also
  the route this loop hammers, and fixing the router prefix would not stop the loop but would stop
  unrelated typos from competing for the same pool.

Recommended order for the founder: **R2-310 first** (one line, stops the outage), then **R2-291**
(router prefix + catch-all 404), then the `datetime.utcnow()` sweep. Those three are small,
independent, and between them close two escalating production issues and seven register entries.

# 🔬 ROUND 5 BATCH 24 — Sentry event detail + Render logs: four hypotheses become facts

The founder supplied the `TimeoutError` event detail and a window of Render application logs. Between
them they **confirm four claims this round labelled as inferred**, and one of them changes a finding's
severity. Nothing here needed new probing; it needed the founder's access.

## 1. R2-310 CONFIRMED as the cause of R2-308 — the pool exhaustion is the Delete Logs loop

The `QueuePool limit of size 10 overflow 20 reached` event carries:

```
transaction   96%  …3/{company_id}          →  /apis/v3/{company_id}
url           96%  …6-fc6a013b7b5d          →  …/apis/v3/d3724ec3-edac-4b5f-b296-fc6a013b7b5d
environment  100%  production
```

and the stack trace ends in:

```
/app/app/auth.py:47 in get_current_user
<string>:2 in _connection_for_bind
  bind  Engine(postgresql://postgres.ujdxgiqafaobhrskzkmr:***@aws-1-ap-northeast-2.pooler.supabase.com:6543/postgres)
```

**96% of the events on this issue have `transaction = /apis/v3/{company_id}`** — the root-mounted
delete-logs route (R2-291), called with the real company id. That is precisely the request the loop in
`delete-logs/page.tsx` fires. The connection is taken inside `get_current_user`, which is the router
dependency every one of those requests passes through.

The causal chain filed in R2-310 is now evidenced end to end, from the object literal at `:43` to the
Supabase pooler refusing a connection. **R2-308 is closed on cause; R2-310 is the fix.**

Two details worth recording:
- The client is **Electron 42.7.0 on Windows**, not a browser — the console is being run in a desktop
  wrapper. Irrelevant to the defect, but it means the loop is reachable from the packaged app too.
- Sentry's own **Client Sample Rate is 0.1**, so the 26 recorded events represent roughly **260 actual
  pool timeouts in 24 hours**. The outage is an order of magnitude larger than the board shows.

## FINDING R2-311 — 🟠 HIGH (upgraded from R2-295/R2-299): the service runs on at least three instances, so the in-memory rate limiter is structurally incapable of enforcing any policy

R2-295 and R2-299 measured the limiter failing and labelled the in-memory-storage explanation a
**hypothesis**, noting it could not be confirmed from outside. The Render logs settle it. The
`/public/leads` burst was served from **three distinct instance addresses**:

```
07:22:15  10.27.235.132  POST /apis/v3/public/leads  200
07:22:15  10.28.165.235  POST /apis/v3/public/leads  200
07:22:16  10.26.136.115  POST /apis/v3/public/leads  422
07:22:29  10.28.165.235  POST /apis/v3/public/leads  429
07:22:31  10.27.235.132  POST /apis/v3/public/leads  200
07:23:05  10.26.136.115  POST /apis/v3/public/leads  200
07:23:05  10.28.165.235  POST /apis/v3/public/leads  429
```

Three IPs — `10.27.235.132`, `10.28.165.235`, `10.26.136.115` — interleaved within the same second,
and the same pattern appears throughout the login burst. `app/rate_limit.py` constructs
`Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)` with **no `storage_uri`**, so each instance keeps its own
counter in process memory.

**The effective limit is therefore `policy × instance_count`, and which bucket a request lands in is
decided by the load balancer.** That explains every observation exactly: 200 after 429, the
alternating pattern, and 13 of 20 accepted against a `5/hour` policy — three buckets of 5, plus
restarts.

This is no longer "the limiter is flaky". **It cannot work as deployed**, and it will silently get
worse as instances are added. The `5/hour` anti-spam policy on the public lead form is currently
`15/hour` at best.

### Severity
🟠 HIGH, upgraded from the MEDIUM at which R2-295 was filed. A security control that is
architecturally incapable of enforcement is worse than a missing one, because it is believed to be
present.

### Fix
`Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address, storage_uri="redis://…")` — a shared backend is the whole fix.
Then verify `get_remote_address` behind Cloudflare and Render: the logs show client addresses as
Render's internal `10.x` proxies, so the limiter may currently be keying on the **proxy** rather than
the caller, which would make every user in the world share the bucket. `ProxyHeadersMiddleware` is in
the stack (`uvicorn/middleware/proxy_headers.py:63` appears in the traceback), so the real IP is
probably available — but this must be confirmed, not assumed. **Still open.**

## 2. R2-236's CORS explanation CONFIRMED by the middleware order

R2-236 argued that unhandled 500s reach the browser as `TypeError: Failed to fetch` because
Starlette's `ServerErrorMiddleware` sits **outside** `CORSMiddleware`. The `/face/punch` traceback
prints the middleware stack in order:

```
starlette/middleware/errors.py:186    in __call__      ← ServerErrorMiddleware (outermost)
starlette/middleware/cors.py:88       in __call__      ← CORSMiddleware (inside it)
starlette/middleware/exceptions.py:63 in __call__
fastapi/routing.py …                                   ← the route
```

The exception propagates up through `cors.py` to `errors.py`, which builds the plain-text 500
response **after** the CORS middleware has been unwound — so no `access-control-allow-origin` header
is attached. Confirmed exactly as described. The fix stated in R2-236 (a catch-all handler that
returns JSON *through* the CORS layer) is the right one.

## 3. R2-307's commit-then-fail CONFIRMED by the traceback's position

The `/face/punch` failure occurs in `serialize_response`, after the handler has returned:

```
fastapi/routing.py:711 in app
    content = await serialize_response(
fastapi/routing.py:316 in serialize_response
    raise ResponseValidationError(
fastapi.exceptions.ResponseValidationError: 1 validation error:
  {'type': 'missing', 'loc': ('response', 'created_at'), 'msg': 'Field required',
   'input': <app.models.FaceRecognitionLog object at 0x7f7760a3a930>}
```

`input` is a **live `FaceRecognitionLog` ORM instance** — the object returned by the handler, which
means `db.add`, `db.commit` and `db.refresh` all completed before serialisation failed. R2-307's
central claim — *the row is durably written and the caller is told it failed* — is confirmed by the
error's own payload.

## 4. R2-291 CONFIRMED with the exact failing line

```
File "/app/app/routers/delete_logs.py", line 74, in list_delete_logs
    get_company_membership(db, current_user, uuid.UUID(company_id))
                                             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: badly formed hexadecimal UUID string
```

`company_id: str` (`delete_logs.py:65`) is parsed by hand at `:74` instead of being typed as
`uuid.UUID` in the signature, so FastAPI never validates it and a malformed value becomes an
unhandled `ValueError` rather than a 422. Combined with the root mount (R2-291), every unmatched
single-segment path under `/apis/v3` takes this route.

The logs also show the correct behaviour for comparison — `GET /apis/v3/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`
returns **403**, because a well-formed UUID reaches the membership check.

**Note the interaction with R2-308:** the same route is both the loop's target and the wildcard. Every
one of those bogus-path requests reaches `get_company_membership` and takes a pool connection before
raising. The two escalating Sentry issues are the same route seen from two directions.

## 5. The audit's own traffic, visible and correctly rate-limited

The logs incidentally corroborate the auth findings from batch 16 — the login burst shows
`401 × 6 → 429`, then a recovery, exactly as measured, with the 429s arriving from whichever instance
had exhausted its local bucket first. And `POST /apis/v3/auth/password/forgot → 200` appears twice,
which is the enumeration comparison disclosed in that batch.

# ✅ ROUND 5 BATCH 25 — R2-236 CLOSED, and the bug it shares with 16 silent reports

The founder ran a live-tail on Render while the auditor fired the failing request. The log answered a
question open since batch 2 in one line.

## R2-236 — CLOSED. The cause is an attribute that does not exist on the model

```
01:20:53 PM  GET /apis/v3/finance/ledger?project_id=a1376092-… HTTP/1.1  500 Internal Server Error
01:20:54 PM  File "/app/app/routers/finance.py", line 338, in get_ledger
01:20:57 PM  GET /apis/v3/finance/ledger?project_id=a1376092-… HTTP/1.1  500 Internal Server Error
01:20:57 PM  File "/app/app/routers/finance.py", line 338, in get_ledger
01:21:01 PM  GET /apis/v3/finance/ledger?project_id=4ab9616c-… HTTP/1.1  200 OK
```

Both failures, and the contrast case, exactly as fired. Deployed commit `50a4c89`, which matches the
audit checkout, so line numbers correspond.

`backend/app/routers/finance.py:334-339`:

```python
        elif entry_type == "salary":
            party_name = "Staff Member"
            if obj.employee_id:
                emp = db.query(StaffEmployee).filter(StaffEmployee.id == obj.employee_id).first()
                if emp and emp.company_user_id:        # ← line 338
                    team_member = db.query(CompanyTeam).filter(CompanyTeam.id == emp.company_user_id).first()
```

**`StaffEmployee` has no `company_user_id` column.** Its full definition (`models.py:645-668`) is
`id, company_id, project_id, name, employee_code, designation, department, mobile, basic_salary, hra,
other_allowances, pf_employee_pct, pf_employer_pct, esi_employee_pct, esi_employer_pct, tds_monthly,
is_esi_applicable, status, date_of_joining, created_at, updated_at`. There is no link from a staff
employee to a company-team row at all.

So `emp.company_user_id` raises `AttributeError` the first time the loop reaches a payroll line item.
That is why the old project (which has payroll) 500s and the clean project (which has none) returns
200 — and it is the **fourth** schema/model column mismatch found this round:

| Finding | Missing column | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| R2-283 | `StatutoryReport.due_date` | every statutory create 500s |
| R2-307 | `FaceRecognitionLog.created_at` | punch writes then 500s; two reads 500 |
| **R2-236** | **`StaffEmployee.company_user_id`** | **project ledger 500s whenever payroll exists** |
| R2-312 (below) | same column, second site | 16 reports silently empty |

### ⚠️ CORRECTION — my stated mechanism for R2-236 was wrong

Batch 2 bisected the failure to the salary branch by rebuilding every other entity shape in a clean
project, and that **bisection was correct**. It then proposed a mechanism — the naive `datetime.min`
sentinel at `finance.py:256` being compared against timezone-aware column values — and labelled it
*"stated as a hypothesis, not a proof… the bisection result is solid; the line number is not."*

**The hypothesis was wrong.** The `datetime.min` comparison is a real latent bug and still worth
fixing, but it is not what breaks this endpoint. The discipline of labelling it held up: the finding
was filed on the evidence (deterministic 500, bisected to the salary branch), the guess was marked as
a guess, and the guess is now replaced rather than quietly retained. Anyone who acted on batch 2 would
have fixed `datetime.min` and found the ledger still broken.

### Fix
Delete the `company_user_id` lookup, or add the column. Given `reports.py` uses a `_team_user_name`
helper for the same purpose, the intended design is probably a real FK from `StaffEmployee` to
`CompanyTeam`; until it exists, the branch should just use `emp.name`, which is present and is the
person's name — the exact thing the code is trying to obtain by a three-hop join.

## FINDING R2-312 — 🔴 CRITICAL: sixteen reports swallow every exception and return an empty list, so the Party Ledger reports a company with nine invoices as having no transactions

`reports.py:649` contains the **identical** expression to `finance.py:338`:

```python
        elif et == "salary":
            ...
                emp = db.query(StaffEmployee).filter(StaffEmployee.id == obj.employee_id).first()
                if emp and emp.company_user_id:                                    # ← line 649
                    party_name = _team_user_name(db, emp.company_user_id) or "Staff Member"
```

The difference is what surrounds it. `_rep_party_ledger` (`:688-693`):

```python
def _rep_party_ledger(db: Session, cid: uuid.UUID, pid: Optional[uuid.UUID]):
    try:
        rows, _ = _build_party_ledger(db, cid, pid)
        return rows
    except Exception:
        return []
```

**The `AttributeError` is caught and converted into "no data".**

### Proved live
```
GET /reports/data/party-ledger?company_id=d3724ec3-…                 → 200 {"rows":[]}
GET /reports/data/party-ledger?company_id=…&project_id=a1376092-…    → 200 {"rows":[]}
GET /reports/data/day-book?…                                          → 200 {"rows":[]}
GET /reports/data/general-ledger?…                                    → 200 {"rows":[]}
```

This company has **nine bills, two projects, payments, debit and credit notes**. The Party Ledger is
not empty because there is nothing to show. It is empty **because it crashed and the crash was
hidden**. A user opens the ledger, sees a clean "no transactions" state, and concludes the books are
empty.

### This is a pattern, not one function
**Sixteen report builders** use `except Exception: return []`:

`_rep_all_party_balances` · `_rep_bank_statement` · `_rep_company_sales` · `_rep_crm_lead_detail` ·
`_rep_gstr1_sales` · `_rep_gstr2_purchase` · `_rep_item_wise_sales` · `_rep_material_received_used` ·
`_rep_material_stock_movement` · `_rep_party_ledger` · `_rep_payment_request` ·
`_rep_project_payment` · `_rep_project_wise_payment_summary` · `_rep_sales_deduction_retention` ·
`_rep_task_attendance` · `_rep_task_measurement_book`

Every one of them will report **zero rows** rather than an error for *any* failure — a missing
attribute, a bad join, a timeout, a null. Two of them are **GST returns** (`gstr1-sales`,
`gstr2-purchase`): a statutory filing built from a report that silently returns nothing when it breaks
is how a company under-declares without knowing.

An empty financial report is not a safe default. It is indistinguishable from a true zero and is
believed. **This is worse than the 500 in `finance.py`** — that one at least tells you something is
wrong.

### Severity
🔴 CRITICAL. Silent, plausible, wrong financial output across sixteen reports including two statutory
returns, from a defect the code catches and discards.

### Fix
1. Remove the blanket handlers. If a report cannot be built, return an error the UI renders as
   "this report failed", never an empty list.
2. If a defensive catch is genuinely wanted, catch narrowly, log with the exception, report to
   Sentry explicitly, and return a distinguishable failure state.
3. Fix `company_user_id` at both sites together — `finance.py:338` and `reports.py:649`.
4. Grep for `except Exception` returning an empty collection elsewhere in the codebase; this pattern
   is why R2-236 stayed invisible to Sentry for the whole audit.

## This also explains R2-236's Sentry gap — partially

R2-236 recorded that `/finance/ledger` 500s never reached Sentry, and batch 22 narrowed that to *"a
specific unexplained omission, not a general capture failure"*. The `reports.py` half is now
explained completely: those errors never reach Sentry **because the code catches them**. Sixteen
reports can fail forever in total silence.

The `finance.py` half is genuinely unhandled and *should* be captured, so its absence from the board
remains unexplained — **that narrow question stays open**, and it is now the only part of R2-236 that
does. Given that the board reliably captured `TypeError`, `AttributeError`, `NameError`,
`IntegrityError`, `DataError`, `ResponseValidationError` and `ValidationError` from ten other
endpoints during this session, the most likely remaining explanations are sampling
(`Client Sample Rate 0.1`, confirmed in batch 24) or an issue-grouping quirk, rather than a capture
failure.

# 🏁🏁 ROUND 5 — DEFINITIVE CLOSING HANDOFF
### This block supersedes the earlier `🏁 ROUND 5 — CLOSING HANDOFF` and Amendments 1–5. Where they disagree, this one is right.

**Register: 312 findings, R2-001 → R2-312. Verified no gaps.**
Round 5 contributed **82** (R2-231 → R2-312), across **27 commits**, docs-only, **never pushed**.
Branch `claude/siteflow-audit-round-5-c53b63`; byte-identical copy in `siteflow-continuation-acc389`,
md5-verified after every batch.

| | Round 5 | Register total |
|---|---|---|
| 🔴 CRITICAL | **24** | **56** |
| 🟠 HIGH | **39** | **157** |
| 🟡 MEDIUM | **19** | **91** |
| 🟢 LOW | 0 | 8 |
| **Total** | **82** | **312** |

## Did Round 5 do its job?
The objective was to move **semantic coverage** — *"does the write do the right thing?"* — from ~34%.
It is now **≈98%** of the 190 mutating call sites, and every module has been opened.

Round 4 projected ~20 findings remaining and ran at 14% CRITICAL. Round 5 filed **82 at 29%
CRITICAL** — four times the projected volume at twice the severity. The reason was the method: seed
data with shape, then re-read every consumer. Nearly every CRITICAL came from comparing two numbers
that only exist once the data is non-trivial.

## The 8 fixes to make, in order
Each closes many findings. The first two are one-line changes that stop live production incidents.

| # | Fix | Closes | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **`useMemo` the `authHeaders` object** at `delete-logs/page.tsx:43` | **R2-310, R2-308** — an unbounded fetch loop at ~16 req/s exhausting the DB pool. Sentry sample rate is 0.1, so its 26 events/day are really **~260 outages/day** | 1 line |
| **2** | **Give the delete-logs router a prefix** (`main.py:559`) and type `company_id: UUID` (`delete_logs.py:74`) | **R2-291** — today every mistyped path under `/apis/v3` returns 500 and takes a pool connection. `/apis/v3/finance` returns 500 | 2 lines |
| **3** | **Add a catch-all exception handler** returning JSON **through** the CORS middleware | **R2-236 (half)** — an unhandled 500 currently reaches the browser as `TypeError: Failed to fetch`, so the console cannot tell a crash from being offline. Cost this audit time twice | small |
| **4** | **Ban `datetime.utcnow()`** (lint rule + sweep) | **R2-210, R2-221, R2-222, R2-241, R2-244, R2-262** — 9 sites; 3 take a whole feature offline, incl. every attendance punch-out | small |

## What Round 5 proves about the product
1. **Numeric and enum validation is consistently good.** A dozen deliberate bad-scalar probes were all
   correctly rejected — negative money, GST > 100, wrong enum case, malformed UUIDs.
2. **String validation is essentially absent.** URLs take any scheme (**R2-257**, a stored XSS),
   phone and email are free text (**R2-273**), GSTIN accepts `"NOT-A-GSTIN"` (**R2-290**), and
   `incident_type` accepts anything — which silently drops a **fatality** out of the statutory safety
   metric (**R2-252**).
3. **Relational validation does not exist at all.** Received vs ordered · billed vs ordered · wasted
   vs available · consumed vs available · closed vs reviewed · items vs invoice total · done vs total
   · actor vs caller · tower vs project. The three largest are **missing columns**, not missing `if`
   statements — no `tower_id` on Bill/PO/WorkOrder, no `wo_id` on Bill, no cap on `received_qty` — so
   they scope as migrations.
4. **Three places get it right, and they are worth reading before writing any fix:** the Gantt
   predecessor endpoint (rejects dependency cycles *and* self-reference, with clear messages), the
   BOQ revision endpoint (derives its actor server-side), and the whole **auth surface** (constant-time
   admin secret failing closed, `EmailStr`, password floor checked before the duplicate-email check,
   no user enumeration in three places). **The knowledge exists in this codebase.** It has not been
   applied outside the security-labelled modules.

# 🔎 ROUND 6 — BATCH 1: what the sixteen swallowed reports are hiding

**Method.** Round 5 closed with R2-312: sixteen report builders convert any exception into
`rows: []`. Only Party Ledger's crash was identified. Batch 1 answers "what are the other fifteen
hiding" by machine-checking every model attribute each builder touches against `models.py`, then
reading each builder for arithmetic that is wrong even when it does *not* crash.

**Result — the swallowed exception is NOT the main story.** A static pass over all 24 builders
(AST: infer each local's model from its `db.query(...)` chain, then check every attribute access
against the declared columns) found **exactly one** missing-column crash in the whole file:
`emp.company_user_id` at `reports.py:649`, already filed as R2-312. The other fifteen builders do not
crash. **They return wrong numbers, confidently, with no exception to swallow** — which is worse,
because R2-312 at least renders as an obviously empty screen.

Round 5's disproved `datetime.min` mechanism was re-tested here and is **disproved a second time, on
different evidence**: the sort key at `reports.py:594` falls back to naive `datetime.min` only when a
date is `NULL`, and every date it sorts (`Bill.invoice_date`, `Payment.payment_date`,
`PayrollLineItem.created_at`, `DebitNote.created_at`, `CreditNote.created_at`) is
`DateTime(timezone=True), nullable=False`. The fallback is unreachable. Do not re-file it.

**Status of this batch: static, from source, not yet re-proved live.** Each finding names the live
call that would confirm it. They are filed now because the source is unambiguous; live confirmation
against the clean-room project follows in Batch 2.
