# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 37: the Tally XML — double entry is correct, and every rupee of GST is booked into the P&L

Fifth document type. `GET /tally/export?company_id=…` returns **17,676 bytes of well-formed
`application/xml`** — a real Tally `Import Data` envelope with ledger-creation messages followed by 18
vouchers. It is the most competently built export in the product, and it has one defect that makes it
unusable.

**What it gets right, recorded first:** the envelope structure is valid, ledgers are created with
correct `PARENT` groups (`Sales Accounts`, `Purchase Accounts`, `Sundry Debtors`, `Sundry Creditors`),
and **every voucher balances** — `Sales A/c −118000.00` against the debtor `+118000.00`,
`Purchase A/c +5900.00` against the creditor `−5900.00`. The double entry is right.

**It also resolves party names correctly** — `ZZ QA NoGST Vendor`, `ZZ QA Subcon Co` — the very
vendor whose bill the invoice PDF printed as `Party: N/A` (R2-400). **Confirmation that the correct
name is reachable and the PDF simply queries the wrong table.**

---

## FINDING R2-410 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the Tally export creates no tax ledgers and posts the GST-inclusive total to Sales/Purchase, so input credit is expensed and output liability is buried in revenue

The complete ledger list emitted by the export:

```
Sales A/c · Purchase A/c · CASH · upadhyayprateek574 · ZZ QA NoGST Vendor · ZZ QA Subcon Co
```

**There is no CGST, SGST, IGST, "Input Tax Credit" or "Duties & Taxes" ledger anywhere in the file** —
`grep -c "CGST\|SGST\|IGST\|Duties" → 0`. And the voucher amounts are the **gross** figures:

| Voucher | Bill subtotal | GST | Total | Posted to Sales/Purchase A/c |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ZZ-QA-EXP-001` | 5,000 | **900** | 5,900 | **5,900.00** |
| `TALLY-001` | 10,000 | **1,800** | 11,800 | **11,800.00** |
| `ZZ-QA-AUDIT-001` | 1,00,000 | **18,000** | 1,18,000 | **1,18,000.00** |

So on the purchase side, **₹900 and ₹1,800 of input GST are booked as expense** rather than to a
Duties & Taxes ledger. In Tally that means:

- **the input tax credit is lost** — it never appears in the tax ledger the GSTR-3B/2B reconciliation
  reads, so the business pays tax it was entitled to offset;
- **the P&L is overstated** by the tax on every purchase;
- on the sales side, **₹18,000 of output tax liability is recorded as revenue**, understating the tax
  payable and overstating turnover — the figure that determines audit thresholds and margins.

The bill records carry `subtotal` and `gst_amount` as separate columns and the export sums them into
one number. **The split the accountant needs is in the database, one field away, and is discarded at
the point of export.**

This is the third instance of the same root gap in this audit: the GST returns fabricate a 50/50
CGST/SGST split (R2-319), the invoice PDF prints no tax breakup (R2-399), and the accounting export
posts no tax at all. **A company using SiteFlow's Tally sync would file wrong returns from correctly
recorded data.**

Related and unfixed by the same omission: no `PARTYGSTIN`, no `TAXCLASS` and no place-of-supply
appear in the XML, so even a hand-corrected import cannot classify the supply.

---

## FINDING R2-411 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the export re-issues `ACTION="Create"` for every ledger on every run, and carries no invoice reference

Two smaller defects in the same file.

**(a)** Each ledger is emitted as `<LEDGER NAME="…" ACTION="Create">` on every export. Tally treats a
`Create` for an existing ledger as an error or a duplicate depending on version and import settings;
the safe idiom is `ACTION="Alter"` with `<ALTERID>`, or a create-if-absent guarded by the
`auto_create_missing_ledgers` flag the connection already stores (`models.py:1247`). That flag is read
when building the envelope but does not change the per-ledger `ACTION`.

**(b)** `<REFERENCE>` is empty on every voucher. The invoice number is carried in `<VOUCHERNUMBER>`,
which Tally uses as its own voucher numbering — so the supplier's document reference, the field an
accountant matches against the physical invoice, is absent. Combined with **R2-369** (the export
advances `last_voucher_seq` without marking anything synced, so a second download re-sends the same
economic events under *different* voucher numbers), a re-import produces duplicate vouchers that
cannot be matched back to a source document by reference either.

---

### Batch 37 tally — R2-410 → R2-411 (2 findings: 1 🔴 CRITICAL · 1 🟡 MEDIUM)

| # | Severity | One line |
|---|---|---|
| R2-410 | 🔴 | No tax ledgers and gross-amount postings — input GST is expensed, output GST is booked as revenue, and the split exists in the database |
| R2-411 | 🟡 | Every ledger is re-emitted as `ACTION="Create"`, and `<REFERENCE>` is empty on every voucher |

**Recorded as correct:** valid envelope structure, correct parent groups, balanced double entry, and
**party names resolved properly** — which independently confirms R2-400's diagnosis of the invoice PDF.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 38: the ZATCA payload — an Indian invoice issued as a Saudi one

Sixth document type. `GET /billing/bills/{id}/zatca` returns a ZATCA (Saudi e-invoicing) QR and a UBL
2.1 XML document. It was fetched for the sale invoice `ZZ-R5-MISMATCH` (₹1,00,000 + ₹18,000 GST) and
the base64 QR was **decoded tag by tag**.

```
QR TLV decoded:
  tag 1 (seller)      = AK Construction
  tag 2 (VAT number)  = 29ABCDE1234F1Z5      ← this is a GSTIN
  tag 3 (timestamp)   = 2026-07-27T00:00:00Z
  tag 4 (total)       = 118000.00
  tag 5 (VAT)         = 18000.00
```

```xml
<cbc:DocumentCurrencyCode>SAR</cbc:DocumentCurrencyCode>
<cac:PartyTaxScheme><cbc:CompanyID>29ABCDE1234F1Z5</cbc:CompanyID>
  <cac:TaxScheme><cbc:ID>VAT</cbc:ID></cac:TaxScheme></cac:PartyTaxScheme>
<cac:TaxTotal><cbc:TaxAmount currencyID="SAR">18000.00</cbc:TaxAmount></cac:TaxTotal>
<cac:LegalMonetaryTotal>
  <cbc:LineExtensionAmount currencyID="SAR">100000.00</cbc:LineExtensionAmount>
  <cbc:PayableAmount     currencyID="SAR">118000.00</cbc:PayableAmount>
</cac:LegalMonetaryTotal>
<cac:InvoiceLine><cbc:ID>1</cbc:ID>
  <cbc:LineExtensionAmount currencyID="SAR">10.00</cbc:LineExtensionAmount>
  <cac:Item><cbc:Name>Item</cbc:Name></cac:Item>
```

---

## FINDING R2-412 — 🟠 HIGH: rupees are labelled `SAR` and an Indian GSTIN is presented as a Saudi VAT registration number

`currency="SAR"` is **hardcoded** at `zatca.py:166`, with the parameter defaulting to `SAR` at `:54`.
Nothing reads a company currency — there is no currency column on `Company` at all. So a ₹1,18,000
Indian invoice is emitted as **`118000.00 SAR`**, roughly 5,000 SAR of real value stated as 118,000.

The tax identifier is worse. `vat_number` is populated from the company's **GSTIN**
(`29ABCDE1234F1Z5`, read live from Settings in Batch 34) and placed in
`PartyTaxScheme/CompanyID` under `<cbc:ID>VAT</cbc:ID>`, and in **QR tag 2**, which ZATCA defines as
the seller's VAT registration number. A Saudi VAT number is 15 digits beginning and ending with `3`;
a GSTIN is a 15-character alphanumeric state-coded PAN. **The document asserts a Saudi tax
registration that does not exist**, in a machine-readable QR designed to be scanned by a tax
authority.

The endpoint is also reachable regardless of configuration: `is_zatca_enable` is `false` on this
company and the payload is returned in full, flagged only by a sibling boolean in the JSON. A caller
who ignores that flag — a print template, an integration — gets a complete, wrong, official-looking
artefact.

**The product has no Indian e-invoicing at all.** Grepping the backend for `IRN`, `e-invoice` or
`NIC IRP` returns one hit: a comment inside `zatca.py` itself. For an ERP sold to Indian construction
companies, the e-invoicing feature that exists is for the wrong country, and the one the customer
needs (IRN/IRP registration above the turnover threshold) is absent.

---

## FINDING R2-413 — 🟠 HIGH: the invoice line is fabricated — one line of `Item` at 10.00 against a 100,000 total

```xml
<cac:InvoiceLine>
  <cbc:ID>1</cbc:ID>
  <cbc:LineExtensionAmount currencyID="SAR">10.00</cbc:LineExtensionAmount>
  <cac:Item><cbc:Name>Item</cbc:Name></cac:Item>
```

The document's own totals say `LineExtensionAmount 100,000.00`. Its only line says **10.00**, for an
item literally named **`Item`**. The lines do not sum to the total — off by a factor of ten thousand —
and any validator that checks `Σ lines = LineExtensionAmount` (which ZATCA's does) rejects the
document.

The cause is **R2-401**: `Bill.items_json` is null for most bills because nothing requires line
detail, so the generator has no lines to emit and **synthesises a placeholder rather than failing**.
The same root gap produced `(No line items)` on the invoice PDF; here it produces a fabricated line
that makes the XML internally inconsistent.

**This is the pattern named in the Rounds 6+7 handoff — "where a column is missing, a feature was
built on top of it anyway and returns confident wrong output rather than an empty state" — reaching
a tax document.**

---

## Assessment: this endpoint should not exist in an Indian deployment

Recorded plainly because it is a product decision rather than a bug. ZATCA support is one of the
"competitor parity" features (`models.py` Phase 17 block), and its implementation is honest about
being offline — `zatca.py:4`, *"e-invoice without any external API call"*. But:

- it produces a document in the wrong currency,
- carrying a tax number from the wrong jurisdiction,
- with fabricated lines,
- lacking every ZATCA Phase 2 element (`cbc:UUID`, previous-invoice hash, cryptographic stamp,
  certificate) that would make it submittable,
- while the jurisdiction the customer is actually in has **no e-invoicing support at all**.

Either it targets a real Saudi market — in which case currency, VAT number, lines and Phase 2 signing
all need building — or it should be removed before a customer scans that QR and believes it.

---

|---|---|---|
| R2-412 | 🟠 | Rupees are emitted as `SAR` and the company's GSTIN is presented as a Saudi VAT number in the QR a tax authority scans; no Indian e-invoicing exists |
| R2-413 | 🟠 | The UBL carries one fabricated line — `Item`, 10.00 — against a 100,000 total, because `items_json` is empty (R2-401) |

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 39: the client progress report — generated, downloaded and read. Three findings proved on the one document that reaches a customer

Seventh document type, and the most consequential: this is the only artefact SiteFlow produces that
is **sent to the client**. It was generated on the clean-room project, downloaded and its text
extracted.

**Disclosure:** this wrote **one `ClientReport` row and one PDF file** to the clean-room project
`4ab9616c`, the first write to that project in this audit. It is arithmetically inert — a report row
touches no bill, payment, task or stock record — so the project still reproduces **₹6,61,154 /
₹1,18,000** exactly, verified in Batch 2 and unchanged. Cleanup SQL is at the end.

## R2-339 proved live — `Average Completion: 0%`

Filed in Batch 6 from source: nothing in the product ever writes `Task.status = "completed"`, so
`tasks_completion_pct` is structurally zero. The document confirms it — **2 tasks, 0 completed, 0 in
progress, 0%** — and note that `Tasks in Progress` is also 0, so both counters miss. A client reading
this sees a project that has not started.

## R2-343 proved live, and harder than filed — `Total Net Certified Amount: 0.00`

This is the stronger result. The clean-room project holds a **subcontractor bill of ₹5,90,000**
(verified in Batch 2's ground truth). The report tells the client:

```
Total RA Bills Submitted: 0
Total Net Certified Amount: 0.00
```

`generate_report` counts only bills whose `approval_flag.lower() in ("approved","auto_approved")`
(`reports.py:84`). Every bill is created `pending` (`billing.py:626`) and the **only** way to change
that is `PATCH /finance/approve/{id}` — the endpoint R2-342 showed has no rule, no level, no state
check and no recorded actor, and which the console has no path to for subcontractor bills.

So the certified-amount line on the client-facing document is **0.00 on every project, for every
company, unless someone calls an API endpoint directly.** Batch 13 filed this as "depends on a
decorative flag"; it is in fact the difference between reporting ₹5.9 lakh of subcontractor work and
reporting nothing.

---

## FINDING R2-414 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the quality pass rate prints `0%` when no tests exist, asserting failure where there is no data

```
Material Lab Tests Pass Rate: 0% (0 pass / 0 total)
```

`quality_tests_pass_rate = int((pass/total)*100) if total > 0 else 0` (`reports.py:100`) — the
divide-by-zero guard returns **0**, and the template prints it as a percentage. A project that has run
**no** lab tests is reported to the client as having a **0% pass rate**, which reads as *every test
failed*.

The parenthetical `(0 pass / 0 total)` is the only thing distinguishing it from genuine total
failure, and it appears after the headline number. The honest rendering is `n/a` or *"no tests
recorded"*. This is the third defect in this document's four quality/financial metrics, alongside
R2-364 (unassessed tests counted as failures when tests *do* exist) — the guard is wrong in the empty
case and the arithmetic is wrong in the populated one.

---

## What the client report does NOT contain

Recorded because it shapes the fix: the document a client receives carries **no cost or revenue figure
of any kind**. No contract value, no billed-to-date, no spend, no variation total, no retention held.
The clean-room project has ₹6,61,154 of cost and ₹1,18,000 of revenue and the report mentions neither.
Its "FINANCIALS" section contains three subcontractor counters, two of which are structurally zero.

**Scorecard for the only outbound document in the product:**

| Metric | State |
|---|---|
| `Average Completion` | ❌ always 0% — **R2-339, proved** |
| `Total Net Certified Amount` | ❌ always 0.00 — **R2-343, proved** |
| `Material Lab Tests Pass Rate` | ❌ 0% when no tests; counts unassessed as failures when there are — **R2-414, R2-364** |
| `Open / Closed NCRs` | ✅ correct — NCR is the clean status machine |
| Counts of tasks, WOs, indents, POs, inspections | ✅ correct |
| Any financial value | — absent by design |

**Four of the six computed metrics are wrong, and the two that a client would act on — progress and
certified value — are wrong in the same direction: they under-report the project to zero.**

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 40: the last document type — the BOCW cess return, and the full export inventory

Eighth and final document type. `GET /labour/bocw/{project_id}/export` produces the **BOCW return** —
the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess record, a statutory filing under the BOCW
Act. Both live projects return:

```
GET /labour/bocw/a1376092-…/export → 404 {"detail":"No BOCW records found"}
GET /labour/bocw/4ab9616c-…/export → 404 {"detail":"No BOCW records found"}
```

The table is empty, so the export could not be exercised against data — but the writer is short enough
to audit in full, and its input schema is the finding.

---

## FINDING R2-415 — 🟠 HIGH: the BOCW cess return is typed by hand — nothing derives it, nothing validates it, and it is disconnected from the labour records in the same module

`BOCWCreate` (`labour.py:72-81`):

```python
class BOCWCreate(BaseModel):
    company_id: UUID
    project_id: UUID
    contractor_id: Optional[UUID] = None
    contractor_name: str                       # free text, not resolved from contractor_id
    month_year: str                            # "YYYY-MM", no pattern, no range check
    workers_count: int   = Field(0, ge=0)
    wages_paid: float    = Field(0.0, ge=0)
    contribution_amount: float = Field(0.0, ge=0)
    acknowledgement_number: Optional[str] = None
```

Every material figure is caller-supplied and nothing reconciles them:

- **`workers_count` is not derived from anything.** The same module holds `MusterRoll`
  (`workers_present`, `workers_absent`) and `SubcontractorAttendance` (`worker_count`) for the same
  project and month — neither is consulted. R2-333 established the muster roll has no consumer; this
  is the surface that should have been it.
- **`wages_paid` is not derived from payroll.** `PayrollLineItem.net_payable` exists for the period
  and is not read.
- **`contribution_amount` is not computed.** BOCW cess is **1% of the cost of construction**, a
  statutory rate — and nothing multiplies anything. A user can file ₹1 of cess against ₹50,00,000 of
  wages, or ₹50,00,000 of cess against ₹1, and both are accepted (`ge=0` is the only constraint).
- **`contractor_name` is free text beside an optional `contractor_id`** — the label-instead-of-id
  pattern again (R2-314), and the export prints the string, so the return can name a contractor who
  does not exist in the system.
- **`month_year` has no pattern**, unlike `payroll_month`'s `^\d{4}-\d{2}$` (R2-355) — `"last month"`
  is accepted and exported verbatim into a statutory return.

So the BOCW module is a **data-entry form that prints what it was given**, in a product that already
holds the attendance, wage and cost records the return is supposed to be built from. This is the
second statutory register in the same module with the same shape, after the muster roll (R2-333) —
and both sit beside the payroll engine that has the numbers.

**A recorded positive:** the export uses Python's `csv.writer`, which quotes correctly — unlike the
frontend's hand-rolled `"${c.replace(/"/g,'""')}"` (R2-396). Embedded quotes, commas and newlines are
handled properly here.

**But it shares the injection gap:** `csv.writer` does not neutralise formula prefixes either, and
`contractor_name` is unvalidated free text, so **`=HYPERLINK(...)` as a contractor name exports
executable** exactly as R2-407 proved for the DPR export. That makes **three** export paths carrying
the same defect — frontend reports (R2-396), DPR (R2-407) and BOCW — and the fix is one shared helper.

---

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 41: the Finance dashboard shows ₹0 for everything, and the reason is a project gate on a company-level screen

Clicked to `/c/{cid}/d/finance` in the browser. The screen renders:

```
TOTAL INVOICE   ₹0        Unpaid Invoice: ₹0
TOTAL EXPENSE   ₹0        Unpaid Expense: ₹0
COMPANY BALANCE ₹0        In: ₹0 | Out: ₹0
Unbilled Materials: New 0 · Pending Entries: 0
PARTY | DETAILS | AMOUNT (₹) | STATUS
No Data Transaction
```

Every figure is zero and the transaction table says **"No Data Transaction"**. The API disagrees, and
this was verified **from the page's own session**, using the token in its `localStorage`:

```js
await fetch(`${H}/finance/transactions/${company_id}`, {headers:{Authorization:'Bearer '+token}})
→ 200 · total_invoice 236000 · total_expense 815144 · in_total 90000 · transactions: 18
```

Ten further endpoints were called the same way — payment-requests, parties, transactions, zoho status,
hr/employees, accounts, cash-account, pl, and four tally endpoints — **all returned 200**. Nothing the
page needs is failing.

---

## FINDING R2-416 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the company-level Finance dashboard never loads its data, because its effect is gated on a project being selected

`finance/page.tsx:373-377`:

```tsx
  useEffect(() => {
    if (projectId) {
      fetchData();
    }
  }, [projectId, companyId]);
```

`fetchData` is the single function that populates the summary tiles, the transaction list, parties,
payment requests, bank and cash accounts, and the Tally panel. **It only runs when a project is
selected**, and the route it lives on — `/c/{company_id}/d/finance` — is **company-level**: there is
no project in the path (`hasProjectInUrl: false`), and the screen's own headings are
`TOTAL INVOICE`, `TOTAL EXPENSE`, `COMPANY BALANCE`.

So a user who opens Finance from the sidebar, without first entering a project, sees a company
dashboard reporting that the company has **no invoices, no expenses, no balance and no
transactions** — on a company holding ₹2,36,000 of invoices, ₹8,15,144 of expense and 18 recorded
transactions.

`txnSummary` is initialised to zeros at `:255` (`{total_invoice: 0, unpaid_invoice: 0,
total_expense: 0, …}`), so the tiles render those defaults as though they were measured values.
**There is no loading state and no empty-vs-unloaded distinction** — the same class as R2-405's
"No team members found" and R2-394's "No expense transactions recorded yet", now on the company's
primary financial screen.

Note what this means for the audit itself: **every financial defect proved through the API in Batches
2, 22 and 23 is invisible on this screen — not because the UI corrects them, but because the UI shows
nothing at all.** The wrong numbers (R2-326's ₹8,15,144, R2-315's ₹0 bank balance) would appear only
after a project is selected, which changes what a user is looking at without changing the
company-level labels.

**Fix:** call `fetchData()` unconditionally and gate only the two project-scoped calls inside it
(`/finance/pl?project_id=…` at `:298` and `/hr/employees/{projectId}` at `:353`, both already guarded
by their own `if (projectId)`). The effect's gate is the only thing stopping the other eleven calls.

---

## FINDING R2-417 — 🟠 HIGH: `GET /finance/ledger` returns 500, and to the browser it is indistinguishable from being offline

Testing each endpoint from the page's own origin produced one failure among twelve:

```js
try { await fetch(`${H}/finance/ledger?project_id=${p}`, …) }
catch (e) { … }
→ THREW: "Failed to fetch"
```

and by direct request, `GET /apis/v3/finance/ledger?project_id=a1376092-…` → **HTTP 500**.

This is **R2-236 reproduced in the browser, on demand**: an unhandled server error whose response
never passes back through the CORS middleware, so the browser cannot read the status and `fetch`
rejects with `TypeError: Failed to fetch` — the same string it produces when the network is down.
Any caller that wraps its fetches in one `try/catch` (as `fetchData` does, `:294-360`) loses every
subsequent call in the block.

The Finance page's Dashboard sub-tab is not currently a victim of this — the ledger call lives
elsewhere (`:120`) — but the mechanism is live in the product's most-used module, and R2-236's fix
(a catch-all handler returning JSON *through* CORS) is what separates "the server is broken" from
"the user is offline" for every screen.

The ledger 500 itself is a distinct defect from R2-356's P&L 500: it fires with **no open equipment
deployment involved**, on a project whose `/finance/pl` returns 200 in the same second. Its cause is
unidentified — a Render traceback for `/apis/v3/finance/ledger` would name it in one line, and the
founder has supplied those before.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 42: R2-417 is not a new defect — it is R2-236, and its trigger condition is now known

## Correction to Batch 41

Batch 41 filed **R2-417** as *"a distinct 500 in the finance module, cause unidentified"* and asked the
founder for a Render traceback. **No traceback is needed. It is R2-236**, and one more probe found the
condition that fires it.

```js
GET /finance/ledger?project_id=a1376092-…  (messy project)      → THREW "Failed to fetch"  (500)
GET /finance/ledger?project_id=4ab9616c-…  (clean-room project) → 200
```

**The same endpoint, same token, same second — 500 on one project and 200 on the other.** The
difference is payroll: the messy project has payroll runs (its P&L shows `Labour Cost 44,113.84`, and
Batch 28 added two more runs to it); the clean room has none (`Labour Cost 0.0`).

`get_ledger` (`finance.py:223`) joins `PayrollLineItem` for the project and, in its salary branch
(`:334-341`):

```python
        elif entry_type == "salary":
            party_name = "Staff Member"
            if obj.employee_id:
                emp = db.query(StaffEmployee).filter(StaffEmployee.id == obj.employee_id).first()
                if emp and emp.company_user_id:                    # ← line 338
```

`StaffEmployee` has no `company_user_id` (`models.py:1470-1490`). **This is the exact line the Round 5
handoff names as the real cause of R2-236**, and the exact expression `reports.py:649` carries for the
Party Ledger (R2-312).

### What is genuinely new here

R2-236 has been open since Round 4 with one loose end: **why an unhandled `AttributeError` at
`finance.py:338` never reached a Sentry board carrying seventeen other issues.** The answer is now
visible:

- **It only fires on projects that have payroll line items.** A company with no payroll never hits it,
  and this deployment's only payroll-bearing project is the messy test one.
- **The console never calls it in a way that surfaces.** The Finance page's ledger call sits inside a
  `try/catch` (`finance/page.tsx:120`), and the response — being an unhandled 500 that bypasses CORS
  (R2-236's other half) — reaches the browser as `TypeError: Failed to fetch`, which is caught and
  swallowed like an offline blip.

So the finding does not reach Sentry because the *server* records it (it should) and does not reach a
user because the *client* discards it. **Round 5's open item "R2-236's narrow Sentry gap" is closed as
far as reproduction goes: the endpoint, the line, the trigger condition and the swallow path are all
identified.** Whether the exception is *captured and grouped* by Sentry is now the only residue, and
that is a dashboard question rather than a code one.

**R2-417 is therefore withdrawn as a separate finding and folded into R2-236**, with this batch as its
reproduction recipe. The register keeps the number as a cross-reference rather than reusing it.

**Fix #8 in the handoff — the four-site `StaffEmployee.company_user_id` correction — now has a fifth
consumer measured:** `finance.py:338` breaks `/finance/ledger` for any project with payroll, on top of
`finance.py` (R2-236), `reports.py:649` (R2-312), and the two statutory/face sites.

---

The founder's screenshot of `/d/finance` **with a project selected** shows the tiles populated, which
independently confirms three findings and R2-416's mechanism:

```
TOTAL INVOICE    ₹2,36,000     Unpaid Invoice: ₹1,96,000

PARTY                DETAILS                     AMOUNT      STATUS
```

| Tiles populated only with a project selected | **R2-416** | Confirms the gate — the same screen showed all zeros without one |

**Five findings visible in a single screenshot of the product's main financial screen**, four of them
previously proved only through the API.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 43: two tabs of the Finance page disagree with each other, on screen, in the same second

Read from rendered screenshots of `/c/{cid}/d/finance` rather than from the API. Two sub-tabs were
captured seconds apart with a project selected.

**Transaction tab:**
```
TOTAL INVOICE ₹2,36,000   ·   TOTAL EXPENSE ₹8,15,144   ·   COMPANY BALANCE ₹0 (In ₹90,000 | Out ₹0)
PARTY                DETAILS                              AMOUNT       STATUS
Unknown Party        Invoice ZZ-R5-SUB-1  Project: 4ab9616c   ₹5,90,000   UNPAID
upadhyayprateek574   Invoice ZZ-R5-CF-1   Project: 4ab9616c   ₹118        UNPAID
```

**Party tab:**
```
ADVANCE PAID ₹0   ·   TO PAY ₹8,15,144   ·   TO RECEIVE ₹1,96,000   ·   ADVANCE RECEIVED ₹0
PARTY DETAILS              TYPE            BALANCE (₹)     STATUS
upadhyayprateek574 PID-1   —               ₹-3,08,808      TO PAY
ZZ QA Subcon Co            Subcontractor   ₹-7,01,218      TO PAY
ZZ QA NoGST Vendor         Subcontractor   ₹-1,118         TO PAY
```

---

## FINDING R2-418 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the party balances and the TO PAY tile on the same screen differ by ₹1,96,000 — exactly the receivable

Adding the three party balances the screen itself lists:

```
3,08,808 + 7,01,218 + 1,118 = 10,11,144
TO PAY tile                  =  8,15,144
difference                   =  1,96,000   ← exactly the TO RECEIVE tile
```

The per-party balances are **net** figures — each party's payables minus receivables rolled into one
number — while the tiles above them **separate** the two directions. So the same screen presents
₹10,11,144 of party liabilities beside a ₹8,15,144 headline, and the discrepancy is precisely the
₹1,96,000 it displays two inches higher as `TO RECEIVE`.

The two halves come from different sources: the tile row is the finance summary
(`/finance/transactions/{cid}` — the endpoint R2-326 proved is itself ₹12,390 too high), while the
party rows are computed per party by id. **Neither reconciles to the other, and a user reading down
the page has no way to know which number to trust.** A finance lead asked "what do we owe?" can
answer ₹8,15,144 or ₹10,11,144 from one screenshot.

This is the seventh financial surface found to disagree, and the first where **two of the
disagreeing figures are visible simultaneously** rather than on different endpoints.

---

## FINDING R2-419 — 🟠 HIGH: the same page names a party in one tab and calls it "Unknown Party" in the other

The Transaction tab renders the ₹5,90,000 subcontractor bill as **`Unknown Party`**. The Party tab, in
the same module and the same session, lists **`ZZ QA Subcon Co · Subcontractor · ₹-7,01,218`** — and
that balance is arithmetically the same party: `5,90,000 + 1,11,100 + 118 = 7,01,218`, the subcon
bills this audit measured in Batch 2.

**So the name exists, the module has it, and one tab cannot see it.** This is R2-400 (`Party: N/A` on
the invoice PDF) narrowed to its cause: the Transaction row resolves the counterparty through
`CompanyTeam → User` — which only works for platform logins — while the Party tab reads
`LibraryParty`, where the real business names live. The evidence:

- `upadhyayprateek574` — a **User** — renders correctly in *both* tabs.
- `ZZ QA Subcon Co` — a **LibraryParty with no user** — renders in the Party tab only.

The largest single liability on the company (₹5,90,000, 72% of `TO PAY`) is therefore attributed to
`Unknown Party` on the screen a finance lead uses, and to a named subcontractor one tab away.

---

## FINDING R2-420 — 🟡 MEDIUM: balances are shown negative *and* labelled `TO PAY`, and project ids are printed as truncated UUIDs

Two presentation defects visible in the same screenshots.

**(a) Double-encoded direction.** Each row reads `₹-3,08,808` with a `TO PAY` badge. The sign and the
badge both encode the same thing, so the row literally states *"we owe minus ₹3,08,808."* The tiles
above use the opposite convention — `TO PAY ₹8,15,144`, unsigned — so the same quantity is positive in
one place and negative six lines below.

**(b) Raw ids on screen.** Each transaction row prints `Project: 4ab9616c` —
`finance/page.tsx:1204`:

```tsx
{t.project_id ? <span className="text-[10px] text-muted block">Project: {String(t.project_id).slice(0, 8)}</span> : null}
```

The first eight characters of a UUID, shown to a user, where the project's name belongs. Both projects
in this company are distinguishable to the product (`ZZ QA R5 Second Project`, `Zoho Test Project`) and
neither name appears. A user cannot tell which project a transaction belongs to without decoding
hex — and the transaction list is the screen where project attribution matters most, given R2-345
(FIFO settles across projects) and R2-328 (project-less payments vanish).

`upadhyayprateek574` also appears in the Party tab with `TYPE —` (blank) and id `PID-1`: the founder's
own login is a trading party with no party type, carrying a ₹3,08,808 liability. That is the
users-double-as-parties consequence of R2-314, rendered.

---

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 44: the Company Dashboard — a project that exists in no tile, a hardcoded "Connected" badge, and four fabricated projects waiting behind a failed fetch

Screenshot of `/c/{cid}/dashboard`, Operational tab:

```
Tally Agent: ● Connected          [Trigger Sync]

NOT STARTED PROJECTS  0        ONGOING PROJECTS   1
ONHOLD PROJECTS       0        COMPLETED PROJECTS 0

PROJECT HEALTH  ◕ 100% … 2
```

The four status tiles total **1**. The health donut immediately below reports **2**. The company has
two projects.

---

## FINDING R2-421 — 🟠 HIGH: a project whose status is `Planning` is counted in none of the dashboard's four status tiles

Queried from the page's own session:

```js
GET /projects/company/{cid}
→ [{name: "Zoho Test Project",       status: "Planning"},
   {name: "ZZ QA R5 Second Project", status: "Ongoing"}]
```

The tiles recognise **Not Started · Ongoing · Onhold · Completed**. `Planning` matches none of them, so
`Zoho Test Project` — which holds ₹1,41,600 of cost, both duplicate payroll runs and 16 of the 18
finance transactions — **appears in no tile on the company's landing screen.** The project census
silently loses it, while the health chart (which counts every project regardless of status) shows the
true total two inches lower.

This is the `Task.status` pattern of R2-340 repeated on `Project.status`: a free-text status column
(`Project.status`, no enum, no constraint), a fixed vocabulary hardcoded in the consumer, and no
overlap check. It is also the sixth status column found with disagreeing vocabularies, after
`Bill.status`, `AttendanceLog.status`, `Task.status`, `MaterialWastage.status` and
`PurchaseOrder.status`.

**A dashboard whose tiles do not sum to its own chart is the first thing a user sees on login.**

---

## FINDING R2-422 — 🟠 HIGH: the "Tally Agent: Connected" badge is a hardcoded string with a green dot, and no agent is registered

`dashboard/page.tsx:14` and `:525-529`:

```tsx
const [tallySyncStatus, setTallySyncStatus] = useState("Connected");
…
<span className="h-2 w-2 rounded-full bg-success" />
<span>Tally Agent: {tallySyncStatus}</span>
```

`setTallySyncStatus` is **never called** — grep returns the declaration and the render, nothing else.
The badge is the literal `"Connected"` with a permanently green dot.

Verified against the API from the same page:

```js
GET /tally/agents?company_id={cid} → 200 []
```

**Zero registered agents.** The dashboard asserts a live desktop-agent connection that does not exist,
beside a `Trigger Sync` button. A user seeing "Connected" reasonably concludes their accounting sync
is running — while R2-369 (the export never marks anything synced) and R2-410 (no tax ledgers) mean
that even a real agent would produce wrong books.

This is the fabricated-status class the audit has recorded before (R2-068 photo evidence, R2-091/092
fabricated vendors): **a UI element that reports system state it never queries.**

---

## FINDING R2-423 — 🔴 CRITICAL: four fabricated projects with invented clients and personnel are the initial state of the dashboard, and they render whenever the projects fetch fails

`dashboard/page.tsx:188-193` initialises `useState` with real-looking data:

```tsx
const [projects, setProjects] = useState<any[]>([
  {name: "Metro Terminal (Phase 2)",   city: "Mumbai",    customerName: "Prestige Group",  keyPersonnel: "Yash Desai",         progress: 12.5, health: "Healthy"},
  {name: "Bypass Highway Flyover",     city: "Pune",      customerName: "Developers Inc",  keyPersonnel: "Amit Sharma",        progress: 0.0,  health: "Warning"},
  {name: "Alpha Premium Residences",   city: "Delhi",     customerName: "Alpha Group",     keyPersonnel: "Rohan Gupta",        progress: 45.0, health: "Critical"},
  {name: "Prestige Commercial Hub",    city: "Bangalore", customerName: "Acme Corp",       keyPersonnel: "Siddharth Malhotra", progress: 0.0,  health: "Healthy"},
]);
```

Named clients (**Prestige Group**, **Acme Corp**), named individuals, addresses (`Andheri East Metro
Line`, `Sector 62, Dwarka`), progress percentages and health ratings — none of it real.

The projects fetch that would replace it ends in `.catch((err) => console.error("Failed to fetch
projects list", err))` (`:167`). **On any failure the state is never replaced, so the four invented
projects remain rendered** — and R2-236 guarantees such failures arrive as `TypeError: Failed to
fetch`, indistinguishable from being offline, which is exactly the path this `catch` handles.

So the failure mode of the company's landing page is **not** an empty state or an error: it is a
dashboard showing four construction projects the customer does not have, with client names belonging
to real Indian developers, complete with health ratings and progress bars.

Round 4 recorded fake data as scrubbed. It was scrubbed from the *rendered* paths; it survives as the
**initial state**, which is a strictly worse place for it — it needs no code path to be reached, only
a slow network. The same file also carries `fallbackWorkforceEmployees` (`:321`).

**This is the most customer-damaging finding of Round 9**, because it does not misreport the
customer's data — it invents somebody else's.

R2-423 found four invented projects as the dashboard's initial state. Sweeping the console for those
names shows the same fiction reused in three more places, and two of them are **not** fallbacks — they
are the permanent, hardcoded contents of controls the user is meant to operate.

## FINDING R2-424 — 🟠 HIGH: two report screens filter by a hardcoded list of projects that do not exist, so their filters can never match the company's data

`reports/dpr/page.tsx:129-133`:

```tsx
<select value={selectedProject} onChange={…}>
  <option value="All">All Projects</option>
  <option value="Metro Terminal">Metro Terminal (Phase 2)</option>
  <option value="Bypass Highway">Bypass Highway Flyover</option>
  <option value="Alpha Premium">Alpha Premium Residences</option>
</select>
```

`reports/item-wise-sales/page.tsx:75-78` carries the same three, abbreviated
(`Metro Terminal`, `Bypass Flyover`, `Alpha Residences`).

These are **not** initial state awaiting a fetch — they are static `<option>` elements. No request
populates them. So on both screens:

- the project filter lists three projects **the company does not have**, and lists **none** of the two
  it does (`Zoho Test Project`, `ZZ QA R5 Second Project`);
- selecting any of them filters the data to **nothing**, because no row can match a project that does
  not exist. The user sees an empty report and concludes they have no DPRs or no item-wise sales —
  the same misread as R2-394 and R2-405, arrived at by a different route;
- the only usable option is `All`.

The DPR report is also the screen whose export carries R2-407's formula-injection payload, so the two
defects sit on one page: a filter that cannot work above a file that executes attacker input.

## FINDING R2-425 — 🟠 HIGH: the HR "Live Geofence Map" is a static drawing with invented workers and a hardcoded site name

`d/hr/page.tsx:922-928`:

```tsx
<div className="absolute top-5  left-8  w-2 h-2 rounded-full bg-yellow-400" title="Sanjay — outside" />
<div className="absolute top-20 left-28 w-2 h-2 rounded-full bg-green-400"  title="Meera — inside" />

<p className="text-[10px] text-muted mt-1">Radius: 500m  •  Site: Metro Terminal Phase 2, Mumbai</p>
```

Two coloured dots at fixed CSS offsets, labelled with invented worker names — **Sanjay** outside the
fence, **Meera** inside — over a caption claiming the map is *"Live"* and *"PostGIS-powered in

Nothing here reads `AttendanceLog.lat_in/lng_in`, `is_within_geofence` or
`distance_from_site_m` — all of which exist and are populated (`models.py:680-685`). The product

This compounds R2-106 (Round 3: *"GPS verification is a checkbox"*) with a display that actively
asserts the opposite: a supervisor looking at this screen believes they are watching live worker
positions, including one worker flagged as outside the geofence. **The caption's own parenthetical —
"in production" — is a developer's note that the feature is unbuilt, shipped to production.**

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 46: a "Create Demo Request" button that writes a real ₹45,000 payment request, and two modules that fabricate their contents when the API fails

Continuing the sweep begun in Batch 45. Grepping the console for demo/sample/fallback language finds
three more classes, one of which **writes to the production database on click**.

---

## FINDING R2-426 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the Payment Approval screen ships a "+ Create Demo Request" button that creates a genuine ₹45,000 payment request against a real party

`d/payment-approval/page.tsx:136-153`:

```tsx
const res = await fetch(`${apiHost}/apis/v3/finance/payment-requests/${companyId}`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {"Authorization": `Bearer ${accessToken}`, …},
  body: JSON.stringify({
    party_company_user_id: userId,
    amount: 45000.0,
    details: "Steel structures delivery invoice ST-1092",
    due_date: new Date(Date.now() + 7*24*60*60*1000).toISOString(),
  }),
});
if (res.ok) { setToastMessage("Demo payment request created!"); … }
```

and the control, rendered as a primary action on the page (`:186-191`), with the empty state telling
the user to press it (`:250`, *"Click + Create Demo Request"*).

**Nothing about this is a demo.** It calls the same production endpoint as the real feature, with the
caller's own token, against `party_company_user_id: userId` — **the logged-in user as the counterparty**
— and creates a ₹45,000 liability with a fabricated invoice reference (`Steel structures delivery
invoice ST-1092`) and a due date seven days out. The record is indistinguishable from a genuine
request afterwards: it enters `/finance/payment-requests/{cid}`, the Payment Requests tab, the
`payment-request` report, and any approval workflow configured for that feature type.

Three multipliers make this worse than a stray test button:

1. **It is the page's call to action.** The empty state instructs the user to click it, so the first
   thing a new company does on this screen is create a fake ₹45,000 payable.
2. **There is no delete route for payment requests** except `DELETE /finance/payment-requests/{id}`
   — which exists, but nothing on this screen offers it, and the toast implies the record is
   disposable.
3. **`amount: 45000.0` is hardcoded**, so every click adds another ₹45,000. The button is idempotent
   in appearance and cumulative in effect.

This is the same class as R2-423 (fabricated projects) with the crucial difference that R2-423 only
*displays* fiction, while this one **persists it**. It is the only finding in 426 where the product
ships a control whose documented purpose is to write false financial data.

---

## FINDING R2-427 — 🟠 HIGH: Equipment and BOQ silently replace the company's data with invented records when a request fails

`d/equipment/page.tsx:130-136`:

```tsx
} catch (err) {
  console.error("Error loading equipment data, using fallback mock data:", err);
  setError("Using demo data — backend connection unavailable");
  setFleet([
    {id:"EQ-01", name:"JCB Excavator 3DX",   code:"JCB-001", category:"Excavator", ownership_type:"Owned",  status:"Active", hourly_rate:1500},
    {id:"EQ-02", name:"Concrete Mixer 10/7", code:"MIX-002", category:"Mixer",     ownership_type:"Rented", status:"Active", hourly_rate:600},
    …
  ]);
```

`d/budgeting/boq/page.tsx:143`: `setImportMsg("Backend not reachable. — using demo data.")`.

Both modules respond to a failed fetch by **populating themselves with invented equipment and BOQ
rows** — named machines, codes, ownership types and hourly rates that look exactly like real fleet
data. The user is warned by a small `error` string, but the table beneath fills with plausible
records, and R2-357 established that `hourly_rate` drives Plant & Machinery cost — so a user could
read a rate off a fabricated row and enter it as real.

The trigger is not hypothetical. **R2-236 guarantees that any unhandled 500 reaches the browser as
`TypeError: Failed to fetch`**, which lands in exactly this `catch`. The equipment module already has
a proven 500 in its neighbourhood (R2-356, `/finance/pl` with an open deployment), and this session
saw `/finance/ledger` throw the same way.

Better behaviour is one line: leave the list empty and show the error. **Showing invented rows beside
a warning is worse than showing nothing**, because the rows outlive the warning in a screenshot, an
export or a memory.

---

## FINDING R2-428 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the payments CSV template ships sample rows that name fictitious parties and a project that does not exist

`d/finance/page.tsx:2277` builds the downloadable import template:

```
Payment Type,Party Name,Amount,Project Name,Payment Date,Mode of Payment,Category,Payment Request ID,Remark
out,Sample Vendor Pvt Ltd,12500,Sample Project,2026-07-09,Cash,Material,PR-1,June material advance
in,Sample Client Ltd,80000,Sample Project,2026-07-09,Bank,Client,INV-1,July milestone
```

A template with example rows is reasonable practice — but these rows reference `Sample Project`, and
the importer matches parties and projects **by name** (the R2-314 family). A user who fills the file
below the samples and uploads it without deleting them imports **two payments totalling ₹92,500**
against a non-existent project and two non-existent parties.

Whether those rows are skipped or created depends on the importer's name-matching, which this batch
did not exercise. Filed as MEDIUM with the mechanism named rather than tested; the safe fix is a
commented header or a template with headers only.

**`₹0/hr` is displayed as an ordinary rate**, with no warning and no distinction from ₹1,200/hr — and
R2-358(a) established that `if eq and eq.hourly_rate:` treats it as falsy, so that machine is excluded
from Plant & Machinery costing entirely while appearing perfectly normal on this screen. A `Hired`
machine whose rate lives on the hire invoice looks identical to a costed one.

*(Reminder: the two `ZZ R6` probes are this audit's artefacts and are in Batch 11's cleanup SQL.)*

---

## FINDING R2-429 — 🟠 HIGH: the payroll roster lists the same employee twice, and the screen's own default filter hides most of the workforce it pays

`/d/payroll-attendance` → People. **Office Staff** (the default tab) shows **one** row. Switching to
**Site Staff** shows **four**:

```
PARTY                   ASSOCIATED PROJECTS   DESIGNATION     DEPARTMENT   MOBILE        SALARY
ZZ QA Employee One      Zoho Test Project     Site Engineer   Civil        9000000001    ₹23,400.00
ZZ QA Employee One      Zoho Test Project     Site Engineer   Civil        9000000001    ₹23,400.00
ZZ QA Verify Employee   Zoho Test Project     QA              —            —             ₹23,400.00
ZZ QA DOM Employee      Zoho Test Project     —               —            —             ₹23,400.00
```

Two defects, both visible in that block.

**(a) Two rows are byte-identical** — same name, same project, same designation, same department, the
**same mobile number** `9000000001`, same salary. `StaffEmployee` has an `employee_code` column
(`models.py:1474`) and the table does not show it, so **nothing on screen distinguishes them.** This
is the roster view of what Batch 28 measured in the payslip export — three payslips reading
`ZZ QA Employee One` — and Batch 36 filed as R2-409. Here it is on the screen where a payroll manager
decides who gets paid: **two people, or one person duplicated, and the UI cannot say which.**

**(b) The default view hides four of five employees.** The page opens on `Office Staff`, showing one
row. The payroll engine selects on `StaffEmployee.status == "active"` **company-wide with no
office/site distinction** (`hr.py:608-613`), so `POST /hr/payroll/run` pays all five — including the
four this screen only reveals after a second click. A manager reviewing the roster before running
payroll sees 20% of the people they are about to pay.

The `Office Staff` / `Site Staff` split is a frontend filter with no corresponding backend concept:
`StaffEmployee` has `department` and `designation`, and neither is `staff_type`. So the split is
computed client-side from data that does not encode it, which is why one employee lands on one side
and four on the other with no rule a user could predict.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 48: the Attendance tab — the rollup 500s whenever attendance exists, and the screen renders "Absent" for a worker who punched in

Browser: `/d/payroll-attendance` → **Attendance** tab, date `2026-07-27`.

```
● 0 Present    ● 1 Absent    ● 0 Paid Leave    ● 0 Week Off

NAME                    ATTENDANCE STATUS
ZZ QA Employee One      Absent
```

---

## FINDING R2-430 — 🔴 CRITICAL: `GET /hr/attendance/company/{cid}/{date}` returns 500 whenever the day has any attendance rows, and 200 when it has none

Three calls isolate it without guessing:

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `/hr/attendance/company/{cid}/2026-07-27` (rows exist) | **500** |
| `/hr/attendance/company/{cid}/2026-07-01` (no rows) | **200 `[]`** |
| `/hr/attendance/{project_id}/2026-07-27` (same date, same rows) | **200**, returns the row |

So the query, the date parsing and the naive/aware comparison are all **fine** — the project-scoped
endpoint runs the identical date logic against the same rows and succeeds. **The failure is in
per-row handling**, `hr.py:1497-1502`:

```python
    for log, emp_name in results:
        res = CompanyAttendanceResponse.model_validate(log)
        res.employee_name = emp_name
        response.append(res)
```

An empty result set never enters the loop, which is exactly the observed 200/500 split. The precise
cause is a response-model mapping failure (`model_validate` over the ORM row, or the
`response_model=List[CompanyAttendanceResponse]` re-validation of the mutated object) — **narrowed to
these five lines and deliberately not guessed further**; a Render traceback for this path would name
it, as one did for R2-291 and R2-356.

**The endpoint therefore fails for every company that records attendance and works for every company
that does not.** It is the third such data-conditional 500 in the audit, after R2-356 (P&L fails when
a machine is deployed) and R2-236/R2-417 (the ledger fails when a project has payroll) — a pattern
worth naming: **these endpoints are tested on empty data and break on populated data.**

---

## FINDING R2-431 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the same missing data makes the attendance screen say "Absent" and the payroll engine pay a full month

The screen above reports `ZZ QA Employee One` as **Absent**, with counters `0 Present · 1 Absent`.
That employee **has an attendance row for that exact date**, returned by the project endpoint in the
same minute:

```json
{"id":"d3242f75-7529-4313-835f-7cf90cc7325f",
 "employee_id":"0057179f-…","project_id":"a1376092-…",
 "attendance_date":"2026-07-27T06:21:04.963463Z", …}
```

*(This is the stranded open punch from R2-262 — punched in, punch-out 500s, listed in Round 5's
cleanup SQL.)*

So the person **punched in at 06:21**, the record exists, and the console shows **Absent** — because
the company rollup 500s (R2-430) and the UI falls back to marking everyone absent rather than
surfacing the error. That is the fourth instance of the frontend's swallow pattern, and the most
consequential, because it silently inverts the record's meaning.

### The same fact produces three different answers

| Surface | What it says about 2026-07-27 for this employee |
|---|---|
| `AttendanceLog` row | **Punched in at 06:21**, never punched out (R2-262) |
| Payroll → Attendance tab | **Absent** |
| `POST /hr/payroll/run` | **Present for the full month** — the zero-attendance fallback pays `days_in_month` (R2-352, proved at ₹23,400 in Batch 28) |
| `_rep_attendance_salary` report | counts only exact `"Present"`, so this row contributes **nothing** (R2-325) |

**One worker, one day, four surfaces, four different answers** — and the two that matter commercially
disagree in opposite directions: the screen a supervisor checks says the worker was absent, and the
engine that pays them assumes a full month.

This is the sharpest statement available of the thesis this audit has been building since Round 5:
the product's defects are not missing features but **the same fact computed independently in several
places with no reconciliation** — here, without even a shared definition of what "present" means.

---

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 49: R2-430's mechanism closed by the founder's traceback — the field is assigned one line after it is required

The founder supplied the Render log for `/apis/v3/hr/attendance/company/{cid}/2026-07-27` within
minutes of the request. It names the line:

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for CompanyAttendanceResponse
employee_name
  Field required [type=missing, input_value=<app.models.AttendanceLog...bject at 0x7e4376384d70>,
                 input_type=AttendanceLog]
For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.13/v/missing
```

and the surrounding access lines confirm the split Batch 48 measured:

```
GET /apis/v3/hr/attendance/a1376092-…/2026-07-27          200 OK   ← project scope, same rows
GET /apis/v3/hr/attendance/company/d3724ec3-…/2026-07-01  200 OK   ← company scope, no rows
```

## The cause, exactly

`hr.py:1497-1502`:

```python
    for log, emp_name in results:
        res = CompanyAttendanceResponse.model_validate(log)   # ← raises here
        res.employee_name = emp_name                          # ← the field is supplied on the NEXT line
        response.append(res)
```

`CompanyAttendanceResponse` declares `employee_name` as **required**. `model_validate(log)` is handed
an `AttendanceLog` ORM object, which has no such attribute, so Pydantic raises before the assignment
that would have provided it. **The value is available — it is sitting in `emp_name`, selected by the
query one line above — and it is applied one statement too late.**

This is why the endpoint is data-conditional: an empty result set never enters the loop, so a company
with no attendance gets `200 []` and a company with attendance gets a 500. **Batch 48's narrowing was
correct and its restraint was justified** — the finding named the five lines and declined to guess
which; the answer was the ordering, not the mapping.

**Fix, one line:**

```python
res = CompanyAttendanceResponse.model_validate({**log.__dict__, "employee_name": emp_name})
```

or make `employee_name` `Optional[str] = None` on the response model.

## What this adds to the register

**A fourth member of the response-model failure family**, which is now distinct enough to name
alongside the schema/model column mismatches of fix #6:

| Endpoint | Failure | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /face/punch` | `ResponseValidationError` — commits, then fails serialising | R2-307 |
| `POST /statutory/{cid}/auto-populate` | `ValidationError: 3 errors for StatutoryReportResponse … filed_at Field required` | R2-283 |
| `PUT /settings/team/{id}/role` | commits, then 500s on the missing `User.phone` | R2-390 |
| **`GET /hr/attendance/company/{cid}/{date}`** | **`ValidationError: employee_name Field required`** | **R2-430** |

All four are **response-shape defects, not logic defects** — the work succeeds and the reply cannot be
built. Two of them (R2-307, R2-390) commit first, so the caller is told the operation failed when it
did not. **None of these would be caught by a test that asserts on status codes against empty
fixtures**, which is the same gap Batch 48 identified: *tested on empty data, broken on populated
data.*

Recommended alongside fix #6: **a contract test that exercises every `response_model` against one
populated row.** Four CRITICAL/HIGH findings share a root cause that a single such test would have
caught before deploy.

---

| **R2-430** | ✅ **cause confirmed** — `employee_name` is required and assigned one line after `model_validate`; one-line fix recorded |
| Response-model failure family | Now four members — R2-283, R2-307, R2-390, R2-430 |

**Register unchanged at 431.**

Browser: `/d/procurement`, PO and Inventory tabs.

```
PURCHASE ORDERS
PO No.          Vendor    Item Line(s)                        Approval
ZZ-QA-PO-001    Vendor    UltraTech Cement 100 bags @ ₹410    APPROVED
ZZ-R7-PO-1      Vendor    ZZ R7 Steel Rod 100 tonne @ ₹1,000  PENDING
```

```
REAL-TIME WAREHOUSE STOCK BALANCE
Material Item        Unit    Current Stock   Reserved   Reorder   Status
UltraTech Cement     BAGS     84 bags        0 bags     0 bags    HEALTHY
ZZ R7 Steel Rod      TONNE     0 tonne       0 tonne    0 tonne   HEALTHY
ZZ R8 Phantom Sand   CFT     -500 cft        0 cft      0 cft     NEGATIVE STOCK CONTEXT
```

---

## FINDING R2-432 — 🔴 CRITICAL: goods can be received against a purchase order that has never been approved

`ZZ-R7-PO-1` displays `Approval: PENDING`. That is the purchase order Batch 23 used to prove R2-348 —
it received **10,000 tonne** against a 100-tonne line, its status is `received`, and its approval flag
has never left `pending`.

`create_grn` (`procurement.py:600-607`) checks that the PO exists and that its company and project
match the request. **It does not read `po.approval_flag`.** So the sequence is:

1. raise a PO — `approval_flag = "pending"` (`procurement.py:444`),
2. receive goods against it — accepted, no approval consulted,
3. inventory increments, `po.status` becomes `received`,
4. the PO still shows **PENDING** on this screen.

**A purchase order that no one authorised has been fully received**, and the screen displays both
facts side by side without reconciling them.

This is the third and most serious instance of a pattern the audit has now measured end to end —
**approval gates nothing in procure-to-pay**:

| Stage | Approval exists? | Does it gate the next step? |
|---|---|---|
| Indent → PO | `POST /indents/{id}/approve` | ❌ **R2-372** — no `indent_id` on the PO; one approval can be ordered repeatedly |
| PO → GRN | `approval_flag`, `pending_approval`, an `ApprovalRule` engine | ❌ **R2-432** — receipt never checks it |
| Bill → Payment | `PATCH /finance/approve/{id}` | ❌ **R2-346** — FIFO settles unapproved bills |

Every stage has an approval mechanism; **no stage's approval is a precondition for the next.** The
multi-level approval engine (R2-119: 15 categories offered, 2 wired) sits above a chain in which
approval is advisory at every link.

---

## FINDING R2-433 — 🟠 HIGH: the vendor column on every purchase order reads the literal string "Vendor"

Both POs show `Vendor` in the Vendor column — not a name, not a blank, the word itself. `ZZ-QA-PO-001`
was created by a previous audit round with a real vendor party, and `PurchaseOrder.vendor_id` is a
nullable FK to `company_team` (`models.py:419`).

This is the **fourth screen** on which the counterparty cannot be named, each failing differently:

| Surface | Renders | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Invoice PDF | `Party: N/A` | R2-400 |
| Finance → Transaction | `Unknown Party` | R2-419 |
| Finance → Party tab | ✅ the real name, from `LibraryParty` | — |
| **Procurement → PO** | **`Vendor`** | **R2-433** |
| Tally XML | ✅ the real name | R2-410 (recorded positive) |

Two surfaces resolve it correctly and three do not, in three different ways. The vendor's identity is
in the database — `/finance/parties/{cid}` lists `ZZ QA NoGST Vendor`, `ZZ QA Subcon Co` — and each
screen re-implements the lookup with a different fallback string. **R2-314's label-versus-id defect,
compounded by every consumer inventing its own placeholder.**

The practical effect on this screen is worse than cosmetic: a purchase-order list where every row says
`Vendor` cannot be used to answer *"which supplier is this order with?"* — the primary question a PO
list exists to answer.

---

## Confirmed on screen

**R2-380 / R2-297 — negative stock is rendered as a status, not an error.** `ZZ R8 Phantom Sand` shows
`-500 cft` with the badge **`NEGATIVE STOCK CONTEXT`**. The DPR that created it (Batch 27) consumed
material that never existed, with `negative_stock_lock` **enabled**, and the product's response is a
label acknowledging the state rather than preventing it. The badge text also appears truncated
(`… CONTEXT`), suggesting a longer string the column cannot fit.

**R2-387 confirmed** — `ZZ R7 Steel Rod` reads `0 tonne` because Batch 23 had to neutralise 10,000
phantom tonnes by recording a **consumption that never happened**; there is still no adjustment
operation, and the stock ledger now carries that false consumption permanently.

*(Both `ZZ R7 Steel Rod` and `ZZ R8 Phantom Sand` are this audit's artefacts and are covered by the
cleanup SQL in Batches 23 and 27.)*

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 51: the Quality register — every inspection is signed by a fictional inspector, and R2-362's four failures are invisible at every level

Browser: `/d/quality`. The screen renders the inspection Batch 26 created:

```
TOTAL INSPECTIONS 1    ALL PASS 1    PARTIAL 0    FAIL 0

INSPECTION REGISTER          1 inspection shown
INSPECTED BY: [All Inspectors | Meera Nair]      STATUS: [All | pending | pass | partial | fail]

Zone              Checklist                  Date         Inspected By   Pass / Fail   Status
ZZ R8 probe zone  ZZ R8 Structural Checklist 2026-07-27   Meera Nair     ✓ 1 / ✕ 0     pass
```

---

## FINDING R2-434 — 🔴 CRITICAL: every inspection is attributed to a hardcoded fictional inspector, and the filter offers her as the only choice

`d/quality/page.tsx:222-232` maps each inspection from the API:

```tsx
return {
  id: insp.id, checklistId: insp.checklist_id,
  zone: insp.zone || "General Site",
  checklist: foundCl ? foundCl.title : "IS 456 Concrete Pre-Pour",
  date: …, status: insp.status,
  passCount: insp.pass_count, failCount: insp.fail_count, naCount: insp.na_count,
  inspector: "Meera Nair"                       // ← :231, hardcoded for every row
};
```

**`inspector` is a literal.** It is not read from `SiteInspection.inspected_by`, which exists
(`models.py:827`, `# user_id ref`) and which this audit left `NULL` when creating the inspection —
yet the register names a person. The same literal appears in the project-scoped copy of the screen
(`p/[project_id]/quality/page.tsx:229`).

Three consequences, in order of seriousness:

1. **A quality record carries a false signature.** An inspection register is the document that says
   *who checked this work*. Every row in this product names **Meera Nair** — a person who does not
   exist in the company, invented in the same fabricated data set as the HR geofence map's
   `"Meera — inside"` (R2-425).
2. **The `INSPECTED BY` filter lists her as the only inspector**, so the control that exists to
   answer *"show me everything Ramesh inspected"* can only ever return everything or nothing.
3. **`checklist` falls back to `"IS 456 Concrete Pre-Pour"`** when the checklist is not found — an
   invented reference to a real Indian standard, on a record about structural concrete.

This is the fabricated-data family (R2-423 → R2-428) landing on a **compliance record** rather than a
dashboard tile. Nine sites became ten; this one is the first where the fiction is attached to an
individual's professional accountability.

---

## R2-362 confirmed on screen — and the failures are invisible at three levels

Batch 26 proved that submitting one passing item after `1 Pass / 4 Fail` flips the inspection to
`pass`. The register now shows what a user sees afterwards:

| Level | Shows | Truth |
|---|---|---|
| Summary tiles | `ALL PASS 1 · PARTIAL 0 · FAIL 0` | four `Fail` rows exist |
| Row counter | `✓ 1 / ✕ 0` | 1 pass, 4 fail recorded |
| Row status | `pass` | the inspection failed four checks |

**Nothing on this screen can reveal the four failures**, and R2-391 established that no endpoint
returns the per-item responses at all — so the contradiction is unreachable from the product
entirely. The `FAIL` tile reading `0` is the strongest form of the defect: a quality dashboard
asserting that nothing has failed, on a company whose only inspection failed four of six checks.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 52: drawing pins cannot be saved at all — the console sends the string `"current-user"` into a UUID field

Sweeping the console for other hardcoded person attributions after R2-434 found two more sites. One
of them does not merely mislabel the author — it makes the write impossible.

---

## FINDING R2-435 — 🔴 CRITICAL: every drawing pin created from the console is rejected with 422, and the failure is caught and hidden behind a local-only pin

`d/drawings/page.tsx:213-228`:

```tsx
const res = await fetch(`…/drawings/revisions/${revisionId}/pins`, {
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify({
    x_coordinate: tempXY.x,
    y_coordinate: tempXY.y,
    comment: newPinComment,
    created_by: "current-user",          // ← :221, a literal string
  }),
});
if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Failed to save pin");
…
} catch (err) {
  console.error("Pin save error, using local only:", err);   // ← :228
```

`DrawingPin.created_by` is a foreign key to `company_team.id` (`models.py:392`) and
`PinCreateRequest.created_by` is `Optional[UUID]` (`drawings.py:79`). The literal `"current-user"` is
not a UUID. **Verified against the live API:**

```
POST /drawings/revisions/{id}/pins  {"x_coordinate":10,"y_coordinate":20,
                                     "comment":"…","created_by":"current-user"}
→ 422 {"detail":[{"type":"uuid_parsing","loc":["body","created_by"],
                  "msg":"Input should be a valid UUID, invalid character: found `u` at 2",
                  "input":"current-user"}]}
```

Body validation runs before the route's own lookups, so **this fails for every revision, every
drawing, every company** — the request never reaches the handler.

### Why nobody has reported it

The `catch` logs `"Pin save error, using local only:"` and keeps the pin in React state
(`pinData.id` is simply never replaced with a server id). **So the user places a pin on the drawing,
types a comment, sees it appear exactly where they put it — and it exists only in their browser tab.**
It survives until the page reloads, then it is gone. No error is shown.

This is the audit's fifth instance of the frontend swallowing a backend failure (after R2-394,
R2-405, R2-427, R2-431), and the only one where the swallow **fabricates a successful outcome in the
UI**: the others render an empty state, this one renders the thing the user just created.

Drawing pins are how a site engineer marks a defect or a query on a drawing for someone else to
answer. **None of those marks has ever been saved.** The `drawing_pins` table's only rows are the
ones this audit created directly through the API in Round 5 (R2-277's `Numeric(6,2)` overflow probes).

**Fix is one line** — send the authenticated user's `company_team.id`, or omit the field entirely
since it is `Optional`. Note the endpoint would then still accept a *caller-supplied* actor
(R2-367's family), so the correct fix derives it server-side from `current_user`.

---

## FINDING R2-436 — 🟡 MEDIUM: MOM records are created with an empty `created_by`

`d/mom/page.tsx:70` and `:128`, and the project-scoped copy (`p/[project_id]/mom/page.tsx:66`, `:124`),
initialise and reset the create form with:

```tsx
created_by: "",
```

An empty string is sent as the author of a **Minutes of Meeting** record — the document that records
who said what and who agreed to what. Unlike the pin case this does not fail validation (the field is
a nullable string on the model), so the record is created with no author and no error.

Fourteenth site of the caller-supplied-actor pattern (fix #8), and the second where the client sends
a **placeholder rather than an identity** — `"current-user"` in one screen, `""` in another, in a
product where `current_user` is available on every request.

---

| # | Severity | One line |
|---|---|---|
| R2-435 | 🔴 | The console posts `created_by: "current-user"` into a UUID field, so **every** pin save returns 422 and the catch shows the pin locally as though it saved |
| R2-436 | 🟡 | MOM records are created with `created_by: ""` — no author on the record of who agreed to what |

**The actor-identity pattern now has fourteen sites and three distinct failure modes:** the caller
supplies someone else's id (R2-367, R2-241), the caller supplies a placeholder that is discarded
(R2-436), and the caller supplies a placeholder that **breaks the write** (R2-435). Fix #8 —
"derive every actor field from the authenticated user" — closes all three, and R2-435 makes it
urgent rather than hygienic.

| `Contacted` | — |
| `Qualified` | — |
| `Site Visit` | — |
| `Proposal Sent` | `Proposal Stage` ✗ |
| `Negotiation` | — |
| `Won` | `Converted` ✗ |
| — | `Follow-Up`, `Irrelevant Lead`, `Lost`, `New Lead`, `No Response` |

**The intersection is empty.** Not one of the seven statuses a user can actually select appears in any
of the funnel's four filter arrays. `Proposal Stage` and `Proposal Sent` differ by a word;
`Converted` and `Won` are the same concept under different names.

So the Lead Status Funnel — a report the product ships, with a five-stage diagram, conversion
percentages and a **WIN RATE** headline — is **arithmetically incapable of showing anything but
`100% at stage 1` and `0%` everywhere below**, for every company, forever, regardless of how much
work they win. A sales manager who converts every lead sees `WIN RATE 0%`.

This upgrades R2-393 from "fragile against custom vocabularies" to "**broken against the product's own
defaults**", and it is the clearest example yet of the audit's central pattern: two parts of one
product computing the same concept with vocabularies nobody reconciled. It also explains why
`lead-status-funnel` was left unimplemented on the backend (R2-075) — the frontend's client-side
version could never have worked either.

---

## FINDING R2-438 — 🟠 HIGH: invalid contact data renders as valid contact data, decorated by the UI

Row 2 displays:

- **`+91 not-a-phone`** — the string `not-a-phone` stored in `phone_no`, and the screen **prefixes the
  country code**, presenting nonsense in the format of a dialable Indian number;
- **`not-an-email`** in the Email column, rendered like any address;
- **`Expected Closure: 01 Jan 2020`** — a closure date six and a half years in the past, accepted and
  displayed without comment.

R2-273 filed phone and email as free text on the backend. What the screen adds is that **the UI
actively formats the invalid values**, so a user scanning the list cannot distinguish a real contact
from a broken one — and the CRM list is exactly where someone picks a number to call.

`priority` also renders as **`Medium`** on row 1 and **`medium`** on row 2 — the same value in two
cases, sorted and filtered as different strings (R2-359's unvalidated `priority`), visible side by
side.

A past `expected_closure` has no validation anywhere: nothing rejects it on write and nothing flags it
on read, so a pipeline report weighted by closure date would treat this lead as six years overdue or
silently drop it depending on the query.

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 54: the Party Library — two parties share an ID, two have none, and the ID generator is a row count

Browser: `/d/library` → Party Library.

```
PARTY ID   PARTY NAME             PARTY TYPE       TAX NO.            CREATOR NAME
PID-1      upadhyayprateek574     -                27AAPFU0939F1ZV    -
PID-2      ZZ QA Client Ltd       CLIENT           -                  -
PID-2      ZZ QA Client Probe     CLIENT           -                  -
PID-4      ZZ QA Timing Test      CLIENT           -                  -
PID-5      ZZ QA WithProject      CLIENT           -                  -
  -        ZZ QA Subcon Co        SUBCONTRACTOR    -                  -
  -        ZZ QA NoGST Vendor     SUBCONTRACTOR    -                  -
```

`PID-2` twice. `PID-3` absent. Two parties with no ID at all.

---

## FINDING R2-439 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the party ID is generated from a row count, so it repeats after any deletion and is not unique in the database

`library.py:139-142`:

```python
    if not payload.party_id_custom:
        count = db.query(models.LibraryParty).filter(models.LibraryParty.company_id == payload.company_id).count()
        payload.party_id_custom = f"PID-{count + 1}"
```

The identifier is **`COUNT(*) + 1`**. Delete any party and the next insert reuses the number of the
one that was deleted — which is exactly the sequence the live data shows: a party was created as
`PID-3`, deleted, and the next creation recomputed `count + 1` and landed on `PID-2`… or `PID-2` was
created twice around a deletion. Either way the ledger now holds **two distinct parties presenting
the same ID**, and one number is missing entirely.

`party_id_custom` is `String(100), nullable=True` with **no unique constraint**
(`models.py:1883`), so nothing at any level prevents it. This is the eighth document-number-style
identifier without a DB constraint (R2-386's seven, plus this one) — and the only one whose generator
**guarantees** collisions rather than merely permitting them.

**Why it matters beyond tidiness:** `PID-n` is the human-readable key a construction company uses on
purchase orders, cheques and correspondence to refer to a vendor. Two parties sharing `PID-2` means
any reconciliation keyed on it — a bank statement narration, a manual ledger, an accountant's
spreadsheet — merges two counterparties. It is R2-314's label-versus-id defect **created by the
product itself**: the company did not choose a bad key, the product minted a colliding one.

The correct generator is `MAX(suffix) + 1` scoped to the company, or a per-company sequence, plus a
`UniqueConstraint(company_id, party_id_custom)`.

---

## FINDING R2-440 — 🟠 HIGH: the two subcontractors — including the ₹5,90,000 counterparty — have no party ID at all

`ZZ QA Subcon Co` and `ZZ QA NoGST Vendor` both show `-` in the PARTY ID column. These are not
incidental records: `ZZ QA Subcon Co` is the counterparty on the **₹5,90,000** subcontractor bill —
72% of the company's `TO PAY` — and the party the Finance Transaction tab renders as
`Unknown Party` (R2-419).

The generator only runs `if not payload.party_id_custom`, so a caller that sends an **empty string**
gets an empty string stored (`""` is falsy in Python, so the branch *should* fire — meaning these rows
were created by a path that supplied a non-empty value that later became blank, or by a direct write
that bypassed this endpoint entirely). Whichever it was, the product's own screens show two parties
with no identifier and no warning, alongside five that have one.

So the same counterparty is, across four surfaces: `ZZ QA Subcon Co` (Party Library, no ID),
`Unknown Party` (Finance → Transaction, R2-419), `Vendor` (Procurement → PO, R2-433) and `Party: N/A`
(invoice PDF, R2-400). **Four screens, four different renderings, one vendor owed ₹5.9 lakh.**

## FINDING R2-441 — 🟠 HIGH: every project reports 0% progress on the list screen, including one with recorded execution

completed}` — while the only status the product ever writes is `in_progress`, which is not a key in
that dict. `.get(t.status, 0.0)` returns `0.0`, so **`earned` is zero for every task that is under
way**, and the project rolls up to 0%.

The consequence on this screen is broader than the client PDF's (R2-339): this is the list a manager
opens to see how their portfolio is doing, and **it reports every project at 0% regardless of work
done** — while the same row displays ₹6,61,154 of spend against it. A project cannot be 0% complete
and ₹6.6 lakh spent, and the screen states both.

here either.

## FINDING R2-442 — 🟠 HIGH: a stored `javascript:` URL is still live in production and now renders on a screen with a Delete action but no way to see or clear the URL

`url: "javascript:alert(1)"` is R2-278's payload, filed in Round 5 with cleanup SQL that has not been
run. Two things this batch adds:

1. **The screen does not show the URL at all.** The row renders `ZZ R5 Todo` with no link column, so a
   user cannot see that the item carries a URL, cannot inspect it, and cannot clear it — only
   `Delete` the whole to-do. A field that accepts any scheme (R2-257's family) and is invisible in the
   UI is the worst combination: unreviewable and unremovable in place.
2. **Whether it executes depends on a renderer this audit has not found.** No `<a href>` appears in
   the To-Do list markup. If any future view, export or notification renders `todo.url` as a link,
   this row becomes a live XSS on whoever clicks it. **The stored payload outlives every screen that
   might be added later** — which is precisely why input validation, not render-time escaping, is the
   correct fix.

The correct fix is an allow-list of `http`/`https` at the schema (`todos.py`), matching what R2-366
needs for `file_url` and R2-257 for the other URL fields. **Three URL columns, one validator.**

The same record carries **`repeat_type: "daily"`**. Per R2-383 the product has **no scheduler of any
