# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 58: two screens — R2-310's fetch loop measured in the browser, and MOM's status vocabulary

## R2-310 proved live — 44 requests in 18 seconds, and the page never renders

Browser: `/d/delete-logs`. The screen renders its filters and then:

```
Date | Entity Type | Summary | Party | Deleted By | Action
Loading...
```

**It stays there.** Two page-text reads seconds apart returned the identical `Loading...`. Meanwhile,
measured from the page's own Performance API:

```js
performance.getEntriesByType('resource').filter(r => r.name.includes('/apis/v3/'))
→ 49 API calls in an 18-second window
   • /apis/v3/{company_id}              44 ×
   • auth/me, auth/my-companies, settings/company, planning/projects   1 × each
```

**44 identical requests to the delete-logs endpoint in 18 seconds — about 2.4 per second — on an idle
tab that has finished loading and is displaying nothing.** The loop is unbounded: it continues for as
long as the page is open.

This is **R2-310 confirmed from the client side**. Round 5 derived it from source
(`delete-logs/page.tsx:43` — an object literal in component scope → `useCallback` dep → `useEffect`
dep → `setLoading(true)` → re-render → refetch) and estimated ~16 req/s; the measured rate on this
machine and connection is lower but the mechanism and the unboundedness are exactly as filed. The
permanent `Loading...` is the same defect seen from the other side: `setLoading(true)` fires on every
iteration, so the table can never render.

**Fix #1 remains one `useMemo`.** What this measurement adds is the user-visible half — the module
is not merely expensive, it **does not work**: nobody has ever seen the delete-log table on this
deployment.

### Correction made before filing

I drafted this finding claiming each looped request was a **500** that consumed a pooled connection,
tying it to R2-291. **That was wrong and the check caught it:**

```
GET /apis/v3/d3724ec3-…            → 200
GET /apis/v3/d3724ec3-…?limit=100  → 200
```

`GET /apis/v3/{company_id}` **is** the delete-logs route, and it succeeds when the path segment is a
valid UUID. R2-291's 500 occurs only when the segment is *not* a UUID (`/apis/v3/projects`,
`/apis/v3/todos`). The two findings share a router and are otherwise independent: the loop fires 200s,
the wildcard fires 500s.

The pool-exhaustion link (R2-308) survives regardless — **44 successful requests still take 44
connections from a pool of 10 + 20 overflow**, which is precisely how `/auth/me` times out.
*Eighth correction of this audit, and the fourth caught by testing an assumption rather than
reasoning about it.*

---

## FINDING R2-446 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the MOM register's status filter cannot select the status its own records carry

Browser: `/d/mom`.

```
STATUS filter:  All Statuses · Open · Closed · Action Pending

Attendee(s)   Project                   Type          Status   Notes         Action
ZZ A, ZZ B    ZZ QA R5 Second Project   Site Review   Draft    ZZ R5 probe   Edit Delete
```

The one record in the register has status **`Draft`**, and `Draft` is **not one of the four filter
options**. Selecting any status therefore hides it; only `All Statuses` shows it.

`mom/page.tsx:70` initialises the create form with `status: "Open"`, so the product writes `Open` by
default — yet this record carries `Draft`, meaning some path (an earlier audit round's API call, or a
different form) wrote a value the filter does not know. `Mom.status` has no enum on the model and no
pattern on the schema.

**Eighth status column with a writer/reader vocabulary mismatch**, after `Bill`, `AttendanceLog`,
`Task`, `MaterialWastage`, `PurchaseOrder`, `Project` and `CRMLead`. The shape is identical every
time: a free-text column, a hardcoded consumer list, no overlap check, and a filter that silently
excludes real records.

Also on that screen: **`created_by` is not displayed at all** — consistent with R2-436, which found
the create form sends `created_by: ""`. The register of *who agreed to what* shows attendees and

# 🔎 ROUND 9 — BATCH 59: Team Schedule never loads — the company task rollup 500s, and the screen shows "0 tasks" while it waits forever

Browser: `/d/team-action`.

```
Team Schedule — Company-wide task rollup across all projects and party-linked time logs.
[Schedule Gantt | Timesheet]  [Day|Week|Month|Year]  All assignees ▾  All statuses ▾  All projects ▾
Unassigned | Assigned        0 tasks
Loading schedule…
```

Measured from the same session:

```
GET /planning/tasks/company/{cid}          → 500 Internal Server Error
GET /team-schedule/timesheets?company_id=… → 200
```

---

## FINDING R2-447 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the company-wide task rollup returns 500, so Team Schedule renders "0 tasks" and "Loading schedule…" permanently

`/planning/tasks/company/{cid}` is the only source of tasks for this screen, and it fails. The
sibling timesheet endpoint succeeds, so the page is not misconfigured or unauthenticated — one
endpoint is broken and the module built on it is unusable.

Both projects have tasks: the client report PDF (Batch 39) counted `Total Tasks in WBS: 2` on the
clean room alone, and the projects list shows a WBS for each. **The screen reports `0 tasks`.**

Two failures compound, and both are patterns this audit has already named:

1. **The 500 itself** joins the data-conditional family — R2-356 (P&L fails when a machine is
   deployed), R2-236/R2-417 (ledger fails when a project has payroll), R2-430 (attendance rollup
   fails when the day has rows). Each works on empty data and breaks on populated data; this one is
   the fifth. Given `CompanyAttendanceResponse` (R2-430) and `StatutoryReportResponse` (R2-283), a
   response-model mismatch on the company-scoped task schema is the leading candidate — **stated as a
   hypothesis, not a finding**, exactly as Batch 48 did before the founder's traceback settled it.
2. **The screen renders two contradictory states at once** — `0 tasks` (a completed count) and
   `Loading schedule…` (an in-flight state) — because the counter reads an initialised empty array
   while the loader waits on a promise that rejected. Sixth instance of the frontend swallow, and the
   only one that displays *both* a false result and a false progress indicator simultaneously.

The Gantt, the assignee filter, the status filter and the Day/Week/Month/Year controls are all
rendered and all operate on an empty set. **The status filter offers `Not Started · Ongoing ·
Completed`** — a fourth vocabulary for `Task.status`, alongside the four already catalogued in
R2-339/R2-340 (`analytics` accepts `{completed, done, closed, finished}`; the client PDF matches
exact `"completed"`; `projects.py` keys on `{not_started, start, ongoing, completed}`; the product
writes `in_progress`). **`in_progress` — the only value the product ever writes — appears in none of
the four.**

**Founder: a Render traceback for `/apis/v3/planning/tasks/company/{company_id}` names this one**, as
the last one did for R2-430 in a single line.

   the project row's To Do count vs the header tile (R2-455 note), and more.

# 🔎 ROUND 10 — BATCH 1: the project dashboard recognises three of the five invoice types the product writes, and prints two different expense totals in one frame

**Round 10 opens the `/p/[project_id]/*` module set — 34 screens, none of them opened before this
round.** Browser: `/c/d3724ec3-…/p/a1376092-…/dashboard` (Zoho Test Project, the messy room).

Session note: the Round 9 browser session was gone, so the founder logged in fresh. The account
landed on a new empty company `1fa705a4-…` "ZZ R8 Throwaway" (0 projects). `localStorage.company_id`
was repointed to `d3724ec3-…`; the same user is a member of both, so this is legitimate access, not a
tenant break — `verify_company_access` (`auth.py:199`) was re-read and it does check
`CompanyTeam(company_id, user_id)` correctly. **Tenant isolation on the company-scoped path
parameter: checked, sound, not a finding.**

## What the screen shows — one frame, transcribed

```
Zoho Test Project — PROGRESS 0%   CASH IN ₹1,18,000.00   CASH OUT ₹1,41,600.00   NET MARGIN ₹-23,600.00

FINANCIAL VIEW
ESTIMATED BUDGET      ₹0.00           across 0 cost codes
TOTAL BOQ VALUE       ₹0.00           Estimated Margin: ₹0.00
TOTAL SALES INVOICE   ₹1,18,000.00    — of BOQ value
TOTAL EXPENSE (TILL DATE)  ₹1,35,700.00   — of Budget used
WORK DONE VALUE       ₹0.00           — of BOQ value
NET CASH POSITION     ₹-17,700.00     Project Balance + Receivables − Payables
```

**Two expense figures — ₹1,41,600 and ₹1,35,700 — and two net figures — ₹-23,600 and ₹-17,700 — are
on the screen at the same time, six lines apart.**

## The ledger, fetched from the page origin

`GET /billing/bills?project_id=a1376092-…` → 7 bills:

| `invoice_type` | subtotal | gst | `total_payable` | `paid_amount` | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| purchase | 10,000 | 1,800 | 11,800 | 0 | Unpaid |
| **sale** | 1,00,000 | 18,000 | **1,18,000** | **40,000** | Partially Paid |
| **expense** | 5,000 | 900 | **5,900** | 0 | Unpaid |
| **payment_in** | 10,000 | 1,800 | **11,800** | 0 | Unpaid |
| purchase | 1,000 | 0 | 1,000 | 0 | Unpaid |
| subcon | 1,00,000 | 18,000 | 1,11,100 | 0 | Unpaid |
| purchase | 10,000 | 1,800 | 11,800 | 0 | Unpaid |

Sums: `purchase` 24,600 · `subcon` 1,11,100 · `expense` 5,900 · `payment_in` 11,800 · `sale` 1,18,000.

- **1,41,600** (the `CASH OUT` tile, server-side `Project.cash_out`) = 24,600 + 1,11,100 + **5,900**.
- **1,35,700** (the `TOTAL EXPENSE` tile, computed in the browser) = 24,600 + 1,11,100. **The
  ₹5,900 bill is missing.**

---

## FINDING R2-448 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the project dashboard's financial view drops the `expense` and `payment_in` invoice types entirely, so a ₹5,900 expense and an ₹11,800 payment-in appear in no tile, and the screen prints two contradictory expense totals

`dashboard/page.tsx:237-256` filters the ledger into exactly three buckets and nothing else:

```ts
const sale     = bills.filter((b) => b.invoice_type === "sale");
const purchase = bills.filter((b) => b.invoice_type === "purchase");
const subcon   = bills.filter((b) => b.invoice_type === "subcon");
…
const expense  = purchase.concat(subcon).reduce((s, b) => s + (b.total_payable || 0), 0);
const cashIn   = sale.reduce((s, b) => s + (b.paid_amount || 0), 0);
const cashOut  = purchase.concat(subcon).reduce((s, b) => s + (b.paid_amount || 0), 0);
const receivables = sale.filter(b => b.status !== "Cancelled").reduce((s,b)=>s+((b.total_payable||0)-(b.paid_amount||0)),0);
const payables    = purchase.concat(subcon).filter(b => b.status !== "Cancelled").reduce(…);
const netCash  = (cashIn - cashOut) + receivables - payables;
```

`expense` and `payment_in` match no branch. They are not misclassified — they are **discarded**. Every
figure below the header on this screen is computed from 5 of the 7 bills.

**This is the third mutually incompatible reading of the same two types in the same product:**

| Surface | `expense` bill | `payment_in` bill |
|---|---|---|
| `Project.cash_out` (server, projects.py) | counted as spend | not counted |
| Company Finance dashboard | counted as spend | **counted as spend** — that is R2-326, the ₹12,390 overstatement |
| **Project dashboard (this finding)** | **ignored** | **ignored** |

So an operator who records an expense bill sees it in the company total, sees it in `CASH OUT`, and
does **not** see it in `TOTAL EXPENSE` on the project it belongs to. A payment received against a
`payment_in` bill is visible only in the one place it is wrong (R2-326).

**Why this is CRITICAL and not a rounding nit:**

1. **`NET CASH POSITION` is the tile the earlier rounds recorded as the one sound number on this
   screen** (Batch 3: "That card is sound; only CASH IN / CASH OUT are wrong"). It is no longer sound
   — `-17,700` = 40,000 balance + 78,000 receivables − 1,35,700 payables, and the payables base is
   the truncated one. With the ₹5,900 included it is `-23,600`. The audit's own designated
   trustworthy figure on this screen is off by the size of whatever `expense` bills the project
   carries.
2. **The contradiction is inside one frame.** No API test can catch it: both endpoints answer 200 and
   both are individually defensible. Only the rendered screen shows ₹1,41,600 and ₹1,35,700 together.
3. **It scales with usage.** `expense` is the type the product offers for site overheads, and it is
   the type most likely to dominate on a running project. On this seeded project it hides 4% of
   spend; on a project run on petty-cash expense bills it hides most of it.

**Fix:** this is fix-list item 7 — one shared `invoice_type` → cost-head map — reaching the client for
the first time. Two correct server-side reference implementations already exist
(`/analytics/company/{cid}/financial`, `/projects/company/{cid}`). The client must consume a
classification, not re-derive one with a three-value whitelist. **A hardcoded whitelist of literal
`invoice_type` strings in a component is the defect; there are now four independent copies of that
mistake in the codebase.**

## FINDING R2-449 — 🟠 HIGH: a BOQ line item can only be created by uploading an Excel file, and once created it can never be edited or deleted through the product

The entire router surface for BOQ items (`backend/app/routers/budgeting.py`):

```
GET   /budgeting/boq                       ← read
POST  /budgeting/boq/import                ← multipart Excel, the ONLY writer
POST  /budgeting/allocation
GET   /budgeting/boq-documents
POST  /budgeting/boq-documents
PATCH /budgeting/boq-documents/{doc_id}
GET   /budgeting/boq-documents/{doc_id}/pdf
GET   /budgeting/boq-documents/{doc_id}/revisions
POST  /budgeting/boq-documents/{doc_id}/revisions
GET   /budgeting/boq-revisions
```

**There is no `POST /boq`, no `PATCH /boq/{id}`, no `DELETE /boq/{id}`, and no delete for a BOQ
document either.** The empty state is honest about it: *"import an Excel with item_name, unit, qty,
rate."* That is not a hint, it is the only path.

Consequences that follow directly, none of them recoverable in-product:

1. **A single wrong rate on one line means re-importing.** Import only ever `db.add()`s
   (`budgeting.py:184-199`) — it never replaces or dedupes against the document's existing rows. So the
   corrective import **doubles the BOQ** instead of fixing it, and with no delete endpoint there is no
   way back. The BOQ value feeds `TOTAL BOQ VALUE`, `Estimated Margin`, `WORK DONE VALUE` and the
   billing `% of BOQ` on the dashboard audited in Batch 1.
2. **No contractor can build a BOQ inside the product**, which is the module's stated purpose. A BOQ
   is the document a construction business negotiates line by line.
3. **The `Milestone Done / Milestone Total` fields are free-typed integers**, both in the create modal
   and as two inline `<input type=number>` boxes on the row. `PHYSICAL PROGRESS 0.0%` is therefore a
   self-declared number, not derived from the milestone rows or from any measured work — and it is one
   of the two inputs to `WORK DONE VALUE` on the project dashboard
   (`workDone = Σ boq_value × physical_progress/100`).

---

## FINDING R2-450 — 🟠 HIGH: the importer silently discards rows and reports only the rows it kept, so a partial import is indistinguishable from a complete one

`budgeting.py:151-168`:

```python
item_name = row[name_col]
if not item_name:
    continue                     # blank line — dropped, not counted
…
try:
    quantity = float(qty_val) if qty_val is not None else 0.0
    …
except ValueError:
    continue                     # non-numeric qty or rate — dropped, not counted
```

The response is `{"success": true, "imported_count": N, "total_estimated_cost": X}`. **There is no
skipped count, no row numbers, no warnings list.** A 400-line BOQ whose quantity column contains
`"2 nos"`, `"LS"`, `"as per drawing"` or a merged-cell blank — all ordinary in a real Indian BOQ —
imports as 300 rows and reports success. The user's only clue is a total they have no reason to
distrust, on a screen that has never shown them the file's true row count.

Compounding: `except ValueError` does not catch `TypeError`, which is what `float()` raises on a
`datetime` or `None`-typed cell object — those rows abort the whole import into the 500 of R2-453
instead of being skipped.

---

## FINDING R2-451 — 🟠 HIGH: an item's amount is `qty × (rate + supply_rate + installation_rate)`, so a sheet carrying both a composite rate and its split double-counts the whole line

`budgeting.py:181`:

```python
amount = quantity * (rate + supply_rate + installation_rate)
```

The parser deliberately accepts all three columns (`rate`/`unit_rate`, `supply_rate`,
`installation_rate`/`install_rate`, `budgeting.py:127-131`) and the required-columns check passes if
**either** `rate` **or** `supply_rate` is present — proof that both layouts are expected in the wild.

In Indian BOQ practice a supply-and-fix item is quoted either as one composite rate **or** as a
supply rate plus an installation rate, and templates routinely carry a `Rate` column holding the
composite **alongside** the split. This code adds all three. A ₹1,000 item quoted as
`rate 1000 / supply 600 / install 400` is stored at **₹2,000 per unit — exactly double**.

There is no validation, no warning, and — per R2-449 — no way to correct the resulting line. The
inflated figure then propagates to `TOTAL BOQ VALUE`, `Estimated Margin` and every `% of BOQ value`
ratio on the project dashboard.

---

## FINDING R2-452 — 🟡 MEDIUM: imported quantities are silently rounded, to whole numbers for `Nos`, bags and bricks

`budgeting.py:172-180`:

```python
float_limit = 2
if unit.lower() in ("kg", "ton", "t", "steel"):   float_limit = 3
elif unit.lower() in ("no", "nos", "brick", "bag", "bags"): float_limit = 0
quantity = round(quantity, float_limit)
```

The quantity the user typed is not the quantity stored. `2.5 Nos` becomes `2` (Python's round-half-to-
even), `0.5 bags` becomes `0` — and a zero-quantity line is a zero-amount line that still occupies a
row in a BOQ the user cannot edit. `unit` is also silently defaulted to `"Nos"` when the cell is blank
(`:170`), which can move a `cum` line into the whole-number bucket.

Rounding a *quantity* is not a display concern — it changes the contracted scope of work. If a
rounding base is wanted it belongs on presentation, or it belongs in a validation error the user can
answer.

---

## FINDING R2-453 — 🟠 HIGH: every user-fixable import error is returned as a 500 with a raw library message, because the handler's outer `except Exception` also swallows its own `HTTPException`s

`budgeting.py:206-208`:

```python
    except Exception as e:
        db.rollback()
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=f"Import failed: {str(e)}")
```

Both deliberate 400s — `"Excel file is empty"` (`:114`) and `"Invalid headers. Excel must contain:
Description/Item Name, Qty, Unit, and Rate (or Supply Rate)."` (`:136`) — are raised **inside** that
`try`. `HTTPException` is an `Exception`, so both are caught and re-raised as **500 `Import failed:
400: Invalid headers…`**. The one message in this module that tells the user exactly how to fix their
file is delivered as a server fault.

**Proved live** — a 19-byte blob posted with the filename `probe.xlsx`:

```
POST /apis/v3/budgeting/boq/import   (multipart: project_id, boq_document_id, file=probe.xlsx)
→ 500  {"detail":"Import failed: File is not a zip file"}          (3.8 s)
```

"File is not a zip file" is openpyxl's internal message for *you uploaded something that is not an
Excel file* — a pure user error, surfaced as a 500 carrying library internals.

**Correction to a standing claim, for the record:** this 500 *did* come back through CORS readably —
`fetch` resolved and the JSON body was legible from the page. R2-236's pattern ("every 500 reaches
the browser as `Failed to fetch`") is therefore **not universal**; it holds for the unhandled-exception
path, not for a 500 raised explicitly inside a route. Worth checking before attributing any future
`Failed to fetch` to R2-236.

---

## FINDING R2-454 — 🟠 HIGH: every document-download control in the console is a plain link carrying no Authorization header, and every one of those endpoints requires one — so the downloads have never worked

The BOQ document's `Download PDF` is an `<a>` (`boq/page.tsx:433-440`):

```tsx
<a href={getApi(`/budgeting/boq-documents/${d.id}/pdf`)} target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">
  Download PDF
</a>
```

`getApi` (`lib/siteflow.ts:3`) returns a bare URL — `${host}/apis/v3${path}` — with no token, no query
parameter and no cookie involvement. The token lives in `localStorage`, which a browser navigation
cannot attach. The sibling helper `authHeaders()` sits in the same file, ten lines below, and is used
by every `fetch` on the same page.

Measured from the page, with credentials omitted, exactly as a link navigation would arrive:

| Control | Endpoint | Unauthenticated result |
|---|---|---|
| BOQ · `Download PDF` | `GET /budgeting/boq-documents/{id}/pdf` | **401** `Could not validate credentials` |
| Billing · invoice PDF (`billing/page.tsx:669`) | `GET /billing/bills/{id}/pdf` | **401** |
| Procurement · PO PDF (`procurement/page.tsx:737`) | `GET /procurement/pos/{id}/pdf` | **401** |
| Reports · download (`d/reports/page.tsx:226`) | `GET /reports/{id}/download` | **401** |
| Labour · BOCW export (`d/labour/page.tsx:116`, `window.open`) | `GET /labour/bocw/{pid}/export` | **401** |

**Five modules, one defect.** The user clicks Download PDF and gets a blank tab or a raw JSON error
body — never a document. The console offers no other route to these files.

This also revises how Round 9's document audit should be read: **all eight document types were
verified by fetching them with the bearer token from `javascript_tool`, which is not how the product
delivers them.** The documents render correctly; the buttons that are supposed to hand them to a user
do not work. That gap was invisible to every method used before this batch.

**Fix:** these must go through `fetch(..., { headers: authHeaders() })` → `blob()` →
`URL.createObjectURL` → programmatic anchor, or the endpoints must accept a short-lived signed
download token. The former is a one-helper change and matches the code already in these files.

## Recorded, not filed

- `PINNED PROJECTS` rendered only `Zoho Test Project` on first paint of this screen and both projects
  a moment later — a render-order artefact, not a data fault.
- The `.xlsx`/`.xlsm` extension check (`:106`) runs before the `try`, so a wrong extension is the one
  input error that does return a clean 400.
- The probe uploaded nothing that persisted (`db.rollback()` on the 500 path) — **no cleanup needed
  for this batch.**

Browser: clicked **Planning** in the project sidebar from `/p/a1376092-…/`.

**The tab does not go to a project route.** It lands on `/c/undefined/d/planning/gantt` — the
company-level Gantt, with the literal string `undefined` where the company id belongs.

## FINDING R2-457 — 🟠 HIGH: the project Planning tab navigates to `/c/undefined/…`, and three company-scoped requests fail with `undefined` as the id

Requests fired on arrival, read from `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')` and re-run by hand:

```
GET /settings/company/undefined        → 422  {"type":"uuid_parsing","loc":["path","company_id"],
                                               "msg":"Input should be a valid UUID…","input":"undefined"}
GET /auth/resolve-company/undefined    → 404  {"detail":"Company not found"}
GET /planning/projects?company_id=undefined → 422  uuid_parsing on the query parameter
```

User-visible consequences on the rendered screen:

- the header reads **`Workspace`** instead of `AK Construction`;
- the sidebar's `PINNED PROJECTS` sits on **`Loading projects...` permanently**;
- the project `<select>` at the top of the page has exactly one option whose **label is the string
  `Loading projects...`** and whose value is the correct project UUID — a control that can never be
  used to switch projects, showing a loading message as a project name;
- company settings never load, so every currency/decimal preference on this screen falls back to
  defaults rather than the company's own.

The task data itself still renders, because the task queries key off `project_id`, which survives.
That is why the screen looks like it works.

---

## FINDING R2-455 — 🔴 CRITICAL: every task comment and every progress entry is written under a hardcoded fictional identity, "Vikram Joshi (Site Engineer)", and the server stores whatever name and user id the client sends

`d/planning/gantt/page.tsx:416-434`:

```ts
const body = {
  user_id: "e0000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000100", // simulated logged-in user ID
  user_name: "Vikram Joshi (Site Engineer)",
  message_text: newCommentText || (customVoiceUrl ? "Voice note logged" : `Logged progress takeoff: ${evaluatedQty}`),
  progress_qty_added: evaluatedQty,
  voice_note_url: customVoiceUrl || null
};
await fetch(`${getApiHost()}/apis/v3/planning/tasks/${selectedTask.id}/comments`, { method: "POST", … });
```

and the server takes it at face value (`planning.py:722-730`):

```python
comment = TaskComment(
    task_id=task_id,
    user_id=payload.user_id,          # ← client-supplied
    user_name=payload.user_name,      # ← client-supplied
    …
)
```

`current_user` is resolved on this route — it is used for the membership check and the
`planning:edit` permission — and then **not used for the field that records who wrote the message.**

Two distinct defects in one payload:

1. **Fabricated attribution, shipping.** "Vikram Joshi (Site Engineer)" is a person who does not
   exist in any company. Every entry in the "TASK ACTIVITY CHAT FEED" — the module the UI calls the
   *real-time collaboration feed* — is signed by them, in every company, for every customer. This is
   the same class as R2-434 (`inspector: "Meera Nair"`), which was fixed in commit `34d44b9`; the
   grep that verified that fix covered `Meera Nair`, `Sanjay`, `Siddharth Malhotra`, `Acme Corp` and
   the four project names. **`Vikram Joshi` was not on the list and is still in the tree.** The
   fabricated-actor sweep is not complete.
2. **The identity is forgeable.** Because the server writes `payload.user_name` and `payload.user_id`
   verbatim, any authenticated member can post to a task feed under any name and any user id —
   including a real colleague's — with a hand-made request. The comment then displays that name
   beside the message with no indication it was supplied by the poster. This is not an
   authentication or RBAC gap (both closed): the caller is authenticated and permitted to comment.
   It is that the *actor field on the record* is taken from the request body. This is fix-list item
   9 — "derive every actor field from `current_user`" — and it now has a sixteenth site, the one
   where the field is also displayed back to other users as the author.

## FINDING R2-456 — 🔴 CRITICAL: "PROGRESS ENTRY & MEASUREMENT BOOK" does not record progress — the button labelled `Log Progress` posts a comment, and the measured quantity never reaches `Task.progress`

The drawer (opened by clicking a task card — this works) contains:

```
SUBTASK CHECKLIST                    [+ Todo]
PROGRESS ENTRY & MEASUREMENT BOOK    ☐ Use Takeoff (N x L x W x H)
  [Enter qty or formula (e.g. 2+3+6)…]   [Log Progress]
TASK ACTIVITY CHAT FEED              [Audio Memo]
```

`Log Progress`'s `onClick` is `handleSaveComment()` (`gantt/page.tsx:943`) — the same handler as the
chat feed's Send. It posts to `/planning/tasks/{id}/comments` with `progress_qty_added`, and the
server (`planning.py:733-737`) does exactly one thing with that quantity:

```python
if payload.progress_qty_added is not None and payload.progress_qty_added > 0:
    if task.status == "not_started":
        task.status = "in_progress"
```

**`Task.progress` is never touched.** The only writer of `Task.progress` in the whole backend is
`planning.py:501`, reached by `PATCH /planning/tasks/{task_id}` — a call the Gantt page never makes
(its single `PATCH` is the todo toggle, `:388`).

So the measurement book is a write-only log:

- the takeoff calculator (N × L × W × H) computes a quantity, and the formula box evaluates
  expressions like `2+3+6` with a hand-written shunting-yard parser (`:67-95`) — genuinely working
  arithmetic;
- the result is stored on a comment row as `progress_qty_added` and rendered nowhere;
- the task's percentage, the Baseline tab's `75% done`, the critical-path calculation, the project
  dashboard's `WORK DONE VALUE` and every `% of BOQ` ratio are all unaffected by it.

A site engineer who books 40 cum of concrete against a task sees a chat line reading *"Logged progress
takeoff: 40"* and a schedule that has not moved. **The one screen in the product that collects
measured site quantities discards them into a message feed.**

The disconnect is two-sided: the project-level Task screen *can* set progress
(`p/[project_id]/task/page.tsx:115` PATCHes `{progress}` from a slider), so the product has two
progress mechanisms that share no data — a typed percentage that counts, and a measured quantity that
does not.

## FINDING R2-458 — 🟠 HIGH: the 14-Day Lookahead excludes overdue open work, so a critical task 23 days late at 75% complete appears in no forward schedule

Tab `14-Day Lookahead` renders:

```
14-Day Lookahead Schedule — Rolling 2-week plan derived from real scheduled tasks
Next 14 days
No tasks scheduled in the next 14 days.
```

The project's only task, read from `/planning/tasks?project_id=…`:

```json
{"name":"ZZ QA Task - Foundation","start_date":"2026-07-01","end_date":"2026-07-06",
 "status":"not_started","progress":75.0,"is_critical":true,"duration_days":5}
```

Today is 2026-07-29. The task is **23 days past its end date, 75% complete, and on the critical
path.** `planning.py:290-299` windows purely on dates:

```python
window_start = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
window_end   = window_start + timedelta(days=days)
… .filter(Task.start_date <= window_end).filter(Task.end_date >= window_start)
```

There is no `status != "completed"` clause. A task drops out of the lookahead when its planned end
date passes, **whether or not the work is finished** — which is the exact opposite of what a
lookahead is for. The one class of work a two-week look-ahead exists to surface is work that has
slipped, and this one hides it.

The same row also carries `status: "not_started"` alongside `progress: 75.0` — a contradiction the
API returns and no screen flags.

---

## FINDING R2-459 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a task card shows neither progress, status, end date nor overdue state, so a 75%-complete critical task 23 days late is visually identical to a fresh one

`WBS EXECUTION NODES` renders per task (`gantt/page.tsx:807-828`) only: name, a priority chip, start
date and duration.

```
ZZ QA Task - Foundation   MEDIUM
Start: 7/1/2026 · Duration: 5 Days                                    →
```

`progress`, `status`, `end_date` and `is_critical` are all present in the fetched object and all
dropped. The `Baseline` tab does show `CRITICAL … 75% done`, so the data reaches the client — it is
the primary list, the one the page tells you to work from, that omits it. The drawer is no better:
`PROGRESS ENTRY` offers an input with **no display of the current value**, so progress is entered
blind.

## FINDING R2-460 — 🟡 MEDIUM: schedule dates render in US month-first order in a rupee/IST product, so 1 July displays as `7/1/2026`

`gantt/page.tsx:823` uses `new Date(task.start_date).toLocaleDateString()` with no locale, which
follows the *browser's* locale — `en-US` on a default install — and prints `7/1/2026` for
2026-07-01. The date input directly above it, on the same screen, is rendered by the browser as
`dd-mm-yyyy`.

For an Indian construction product this is not cosmetic: `7/1/2026` reads as 7 January to the
intended user, and the same screen teaches both orders. Every other date on the page inherits the
same call.

---

## FINDING R2-461 — 🟡 MEDIUM: `end_date = start_date + duration_days` makes every task span one day too many

`planning.py:449` (create), `:510` (update) and `:222` (predecessor propagation) all compute:

```python
end_date = request.start_date + timedelta(days=request.duration_days)
```

A 5-day task starting 1 July ends **6 July** — six calendar days occupied. Inclusive-day duration is
the construction convention (a 5-day activity starting Monday finishes Friday), and it is what the
form asks for: `Duration (Days)`. The off-by-one is applied consistently, so it also inflates every
finish-to-start propagation down the chain and every critical-path length by one day per task.

# 🔎 ROUND 10 — BATCH 4: twenty-one project tabs throw away both ids on the way in, and the Blueprints module has no file upload anywhere in it

Batch 3 found the project **Planning** tab landing on `/c/undefined/d/planning/gantt`. This batch
establishes the scope of that, then drives the drawings module it also affects.

## The scope: 21 of 34 project-module routes are broken redirect stubs

Every `/p/[project_id]/*` directory was inventoried. Twenty-two are four-line redirect stubs; twenty-one
of them read `params` synchronously:

```tsx
// p/[project_id]/drawings/page.tsx — the entire file
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";

export default function LegacyRedirect({ params }: { params: { company_id: string; project_id: string } }) {
  redirect(`/c/${params.company_id}/d/drawings`);
}
```

In Next.js 15 `params` is a **Promise**, so `params.company_id` is `undefined` and the template
interpolates the literal string. **One sibling does it correctly** —
`p/[project_id]/budgeting/page.tsx` awaits the params before reading them — which is both the proof
of the cause and the one-line fix, twenty-one times.

| Broken (21) | Correct (1) |
|---|---|
| billing · budget · chat · crm · custom-fields · depreciation · dpr · drawings · face-recognition · finance · hr · labour · planning · procurement · production · reports · safety · statutory · three-way · towers · wastage | budgeting |

---

## FINDING R2-464 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the drawings module contains no file input at all, and `Upload New Revision` attaches the *first existing revision's* file to the new one

`d/drawings/page.tsx` has **zero occurrences of `type="file"`, `FormData` or any upload call.** The
button labelled `↑ Upload New Revision` opens a form that collects a version code and a comment, and
publishes this (`:247-270`):

```ts
const newRev: Revision = {
  id: `rev-${Date.now()}`,
  version: newRevCode.toUpperCase(),
  fileUrl: activeDrawing?.revisions[0]?.fileUrl ?? "",   // ← the OLD file
  status: "current",
  uploadedBy: "Current User",
  …
};
await fetch(`${apiHost}/apis/v3/drawings/${activeDrawingId}/revisions`, {
  method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ version_code: …, file_url: newRev.fileUrl, comments: … }),
});
```

So issuing revision R2 of a drawing **publishes the R0 drawing file under the R2 label**, and marks it
`status: "current"`. On a drawing whose first revision has no file, every subsequent revision carries
`file_url: ""`.

For a construction drawing register this is the worst possible failure: the module's entire purpose
is that the revision label and the sheet in front of the site engineer agree. Here the label always
advances and the sheet never changes. A superseded sheet is issued for construction under a current
revision code, with a `Locked` badge and an approval workflow around it — every signal the product
gives says "this is the latest drawing".

There is also no way to get a real drawing into the system in the first place: `POST /drawings` and
`POST /drawings/{id}/revisions` both take `file_url: str` as a plain string (`drawings.py:35,62,66`),
and no screen ever produces one. Both `file_url` values in the seeded data are strings a probe typed
by hand.

---

## FINDING R2-465 — 🟠 HIGH: a failed revision publish is caught, logged, and then rendered as a successful revision anyway

`d/drawings/page.tsx:271-280`:

```ts
} catch (err) {
  console.error("Revision publish error, using local only:", err);
}
setDrawings(prev => …);   // ← runs regardless: the revision is added to the UI
```

The comment states the intent outright — *"using local only"*. The user sees the new revision in the
history list, marked `current`, with its version code and date, when the server rejected or never
received it. Reloading loses it silently.

This is R2-435's twin (the drawing pin rendered from a catch block after a 422), in the same module,
on the more consequential write. **Seventh instance of the frontend swallow**, and the second one
where the swallow specifically fabricates a *successful write*.

---

## FINDING R2-466 — 🟠 HIGH: `file_url` is an unvalidated arbitrary URL and the viewer loads it as `<img src>`, so opening a drawing makes every viewer's browser call an attacker-chosen host — proved live

The seeded revisions on the clean room hold, from the API:

```json
{"version_code":"V1","file_url":"https://evil.example.com/zz.pdf","approval_status":"pending"}
{"version_code":"R0","file_url":"javascript:alert(1)","approval_status":"rejected"}
```

The viewer renders the active revision's URL directly (`page.tsx:398-399`):

```tsx
{activeRev?.fileUrl && (
  <img key={activeRev.id} src={activeRev.fileUrl} alt={activeDrawing.name} … />
```

Measured on the rendered page:

```js
[...document.querySelectorAll('img')].map(i => i.src)
  → ["https://evil.example.com/zz.pdf"]
performance.getEntriesByType('resource').filter(e => e.name.includes('evil.example')).length
  → 1        // the request was made
```

**The browser did contact `evil.example.com`.** The deployed CSP is otherwise tight —
`default-src 'self'`, `object-src 'none'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`, a pinned `connect-src` — but
`img-src` is `'self' data: blob: https:`, which permits **any** https origin. So the one directive
that matters here is the one left open.

Impact, without any script executing: every user who opens that drawing leaks their IP, user-agent and
a referrer to a third party of the uploader's choosing, on a page behind authentication, repeatedly.
The `javascript:` URL is inert in an `<img>`, but it is stored, and it will not be inert the first
time someone renders `file_url` in an `<a href>` or a "open in new tab" control — which is the natural
next feature for this screen.

**Fix:** validate `file_url` server-side against an allowlist of the product's own storage origins, at
`POST /drawings` and `POST /drawings/{id}/revisions`. Reject non-`https` schemes outright.

### ⚠️ Live cleanup outstanding — a second stored `javascript:` payload

```sql
-- drawing revision 839a3703-e2af-447a-8e1b-996e4d7b9578 holds file_url = 'https://evil.example.com/zz.pdf'
DELETE FROM drawing_revisions WHERE id IN ('2f4d7d80-64f2-40b9-beb5-a5a955d22d7d',
                                           '839a3703-e2af-447a-8e1b-996e4d7b9578');
DELETE FROM drawings WHERE id = 'c13be875-9985-4eb3-90f7-7a95129a11fd';
```

to-do that stood from Round 5 until it was deleted last session. **This one is currently causing an

# 🔎 ROUND 10 — BATCH 5: Chat cannot work for anyone — the membership check tests a column against a value its own foreign key forbids

Browser: `/c/d3724ec3-…/d/chat`, project switched to the clean room. One group exists —
`ZZ R5 Chat 2 · Site · 0 Members` — left by a Round 5 probe. Opening it renders an empty message pane
and a composer. Typing a message and pressing **Send** does nothing at all: no message, no error, no
toast.

Everything below was then established by driving the API from the page.

---

## FINDING R2-468 — 🔴 CRITICAL: no chat group can ever be readable, because `verify_group_membership` compares `chat_group_members.user_id` to `users.id` while the column is a foreign key to `company_team.id`

`chat.py:14-21`:

```python
def verify_group_membership(db, current_user, group_id):
    membership = db.query(ChatGroupMember).filter(
        ChatGroupMember.group_id == group_id,
        ChatGroupMember.user_id == current_user.id,      # ← a users.id
    ).first()
    if not membership:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Not a member of this chat group")
```

`models.py:1659`:

```python
class ChatGroupMember(Base):
    user_id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), ForeignKey("company_team.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), nullable=False)
```

**The predicate is unsatisfiable.** A row that satisfies the foreign key holds a `company_team.id`,
which can never equal a `users.id`; a value that would satisfy the check violates the foreign key and
cannot be inserted. There is no state of the database in which any user passes this gate.

`verify_group_membership` guards **every** meaningful route in the module — `GET /chat/messages/{gid}`,
`POST /chat/messages`, `GET /chat/groups/{gid}/members`, `POST /chat/groups/{gid}/members`,
`DELETE`/role changes. So chat is not "broken for this account": **it is inoperable for every user of
every company, and always has been.**

Measured, as the owner of the company, on a group created seconds earlier by the same account:

```
GET /chat/messages/{gid}          → 403 {"detail":"Not a member of this chat group"}
GET /chat/groups/{gid}/members    → 403 {"detail":"Not a member of this chat group"}
```

This is the sixth instance of the `users.id` vs `company_team.id` confusion catalogued by this audit
(`StaffEmployee.company_user_id` ×2, `ChatGroup.created_by`, `ChatGroupMember.user_id`,
`ChatMessage.user_id`, and R2-435's `"current-user"` string). **It is now the single most productive
root cause in the register.** Fix-list item 6 should be restated as: *one helper,
`company_team_id_for(current_user, company_id)`, used at every site that writes or compares a
`company_team` foreign key.*

The same file already contains the correct implementation, with a comment explaining exactly why
(`chat.py:146-153`, `send_message`):

```python
# The server owns the sender identity, not the client payload. user_id links to company_team.id.
ct = db.query(CompanyTeam).filter(
    CompanyTeam.company_id == group.company_id,
    CompanyTeam.user_id == current_user.id
).first()
if ct is not None:
    msg.user_id = ct.id
```

That resolution exists in one function and in none of the other five.

---

## FINDING R2-469 — 🔴 CRITICAL: creating a chat group from the console always returns a CORS-less 500, because the client sends `users.id` into `ChatGroup.created_by`, a foreign key to `company_team.id`

`d/chat/page.tsx:151-163` reads the id out of `localStorage` and posts it:

```ts
const currentLoggedUserId = localStorage.getItem("user_id") || "e0000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000";
… body: JSON.stringify({ company_id, project_id, name, group_type, created_by: currentLoggedUserId })
```

`chat.py:112-122` inserts it straight into the FK column and then into `ChatGroupMember.user_id`:

```python
group = ChatGroup(**payload.model_dump())      # created_by → FK company_team.id
…
if payload.created_by:
    member = ChatGroupMember(group_id=group.id, user_id=payload.created_by, role="admin")
```

**Proved by differential probe** — the identical request, once with the field and once without:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| `POST /chat/groups` **with** `created_by: "7f6c0bcf-…"` (the value the console sends) | **`TypeError: Failed to fetch`** — a 500 with no CORS header, i.e. R2-236's pattern |
| `POST /chat/groups` with `created_by` **omitted** | **201**, `member_count: 0` |

So the button in the UI can never succeed. The observed behaviour matches exactly: the Create Group
modal stays open, no group appears, and nothing is reported — `handleCreateGroupSubmit` has no
non-`res.ok` branch.

Note the second-order effect: the *only* code path that would ever insert a `ChatGroupMember` row is
the `if payload.created_by:` block, and that block is only reached by the request that 500s. **The
membership table is therefore permanently empty**, which is why every group in the product displays
`0 Members`.

---

## FINDING R2-470 — 🔴 CRITICAL: a group with no members can never gain one — the add-member route is itself gated on being a member

```
POST /chat/groups/{gid}/members   {group_id, user_id, role:"admin"}   → 403 "Not a member of this chat group"
```

`chat.py:222-231` calls `verify_group_membership` before inserting. Combined with R2-468 and R2-469
this closes the loop completely:

- creating a group with the creator recorded → **500**;
- creating a group without one → **succeeds with zero members**;
- adding the first member to that group → **403, because you are not a member**;
- reading it → **403**.

There is no bootstrap. Even if R2-468's predicate were satisfiable, a group could never acquire its
first member through the API. **Three independent defects each sufficient to make the module
unusable.**

---

## FINDING R2-471 — 🟠 HIGH: the group list is not membership-filtered, so the sidebar advertises conversations that every route behind it refuses

`GET /chat/groups/{project_id}` (`chat.py:125-135`) filters on `project_id` and `is_archived` only —
no membership clause — and it is the one chat route **not** guarded by `verify_group_membership`.

The result is the worst possible pairing: the sidebar lists the group, the header renders its name and
`0 Members`, the composer is enabled, and the message pane says *"No messages yet — This is the
beginning of the chat group."* while the fetch behind it returned **403**. A permission failure is
rendered as an empty conversation.

Eighth instance of the frontend swallow, and the second where a 403 specifically is displayed as
emptiness. `handleSendMessage` (`page.tsx:233`) is `if (res.ok) { … }` with no `else` — the send that
the server refused leaves no trace on screen.

---

## FINDING R2-472 — 🟡 MEDIUM: message attachments are a free-text "Image URL" field, comma-split into `<img>` tags — the same unvalidated-URL surface as R2-466

The composer's second input is `Image URL (optional)`. `page.tsx:226`:

```ts
image_urls: imageUrl ? imageUrl.split(",").map(s => s.trim()).filter(Boolean) : [],
```

and the renderer (`:494-497`) maps each straight into `<img src={url}>`. As with drawings, there is no
file upload anywhere in the module, no scheme check and no origin allowlist, and the deployed CSP's
`img-src 'self' data: blob: https:` permits any https host. One helper — validate on write, allowlist
on render — closes this and R2-466 together.

---

## ⚠️ Cleanup created by this batch

The differential probe required creating one group. It holds no messages and no members.

```sql
DELETE FROM chat_groups WHERE id = '81970dc8-7274-45dc-bc08-17d094bc13c8';  -- "ZZ R10 Chat Probe"
-- and, still outstanding from Round 5:
DELETE FROM chat_groups WHERE id = 'dca82067-05f1-47bc-9c79-059f4fe23889';  -- "ZZ R5 Chat 2"
```

There is **no DELETE or archive endpoint for a chat group**, so these cannot be removed through the
product — worth noting as a finding-adjacent gap: `is_archived` exists on the model and no route sets
it.

## FINDING R2-473 — 🔴 CRITICAL: "Today's Attendance" opens on a hardcoded date literal, so today's punches are never displayed — and four more screens ship the same fiction

`p/[project_id]/attendance/page.tsx:144` and `d/attendance/page.tsx:148`, identical:

```ts
const [date, setDate] = useState("2026-06-30");
```

Measured on the live screen, today being **2026-07-29**:

```
GET /apis/v3/hr/attendance/a1376092-…/2026-06-30   → 200  []
```

The tab is labelled `Today's Attendance`, the table is labelled `● Real-time Logs`, and the empty
state reads *"No attendance logs logged yet for today."* All three are false: the screen is showing
**30 June 2026**, twenty-nine days earlier, and it will keep showing that date for every user until
they notice the picker and change it.

A punch recorded through the API seconds earlier (see R2-474) was returned as `201` and did **not**
appear after a full page reload — because the screen never asks for today.

A grep for the pattern finds **five hardcoded date literals across four files**:

| File | Literal | What it controls |
|---|---|---|
| `p/[project_id]/attendance/page.tsx:144` | `"2026-06-30"` | the project attendance log date |
| `d/attendance/page.tsx:148` | `"2026-06-30"` | the company attendance log date |
| `d/hr/page.tsx:234` | `"2026-06-26"` | the HR module's selected attendance date |
| `d/hr/page.tsx:235` | `"2026-06"` | **the payroll month the HR screen defaults to** |
| `d/todo/page.tsx:55` | `"2026-12-05"` | a to-do end date |

This is the same class as the fabricated projects and `inspector: "Meera Nair"` closed in `34d44b9` —
a developer's convenience value shipped as initial state — but expressed as dates, which the
fabrication sweep's grep (`Sample|Demo|mock|fallback` + names) could not have found. **The sweep needs
a second pass for hardcoded dates and ids**, and `payrollMonth = "2026-06"` is the most dangerous of
the five: a payroll screen that silently defaults to a fixed past month.

---

## FINDING R2-474 — 🔴 CRITICAL: "GPS Verified" is a checkbox the user ticks, not a measurement — a punch submitted from London coordinates was accepted as verified and Present

The punch form's control is labelled **`Simulate GPS lock (On-Site)`** and is `checked` by default
(`attendance/page.tsx:290`, `:651-657`):

```ts
const [isGpsSimulatedVerified, setIsGpsSimulatedVerified] = useState<boolean>(true);
…
location_verified: isGpsSimulatedVerified,
notes: `Punch recorded at shift multiplier ${multiplier}. Location verified: ${isGpsSimulatedVerified}`
```

and the log table renders **that** field, not the server's computed one (`:712`):

```tsx
{log.location_verified ? ( … ✓ GPS Verified … ) : ( … )}
```

**Proved live.** A punch posted for `ZZ QA Employee One` with the coordinates of central London
(51.5074, −0.1278) against an Indian construction project:

```
POST /apis/v3/hr/attendance/punch  → 201
{
  "lat_in": 51.5074, "lng_in": -0.1278,
  "distance_from_site_m": null,
  "is_within_geofence": true,
  "status": "Present",
  "location_verified": true
}
```

Accepted, marked **Present**, marked **within geofence**, marked **verified** — from 7,000 km away.

The two fields are not the same thing and the UI shows the wrong one:

| Field | Where it comes from | Trustworthy? | Shown? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `is_within_geofence` | server, `haversine_distance_m(...) <= radius` (`hr.py:280-286`) | **yes, when the site has coordinates** | **no** |
| `location_verified` | **the client checkbox**, passed through untouched (`hr.py:314`) | no | **yes, as "GPS Verified"** |

So the column a payroll clerk reads to decide whether a day's wage is legitimate is the one the
person clocking in controls. The product's own marketing line on this screen is *"GPS Punch-in · Face
Recognition"*, and the header badge says `Geofence: Active`.

**Fix:** delete `location_verified` from the punch payload entirely and render `is_within_geofence`
in the "GPS Verified" column. The honest value already exists and is already computed correctly.

---

## FINDING R2-475 — 🟠 HIGH: a project with no site coordinates passes every geofence check, and the log prints `0m (Inside)` for a distance that was never measured

`hr.py:281-287`:

```python
if site_lat is not None:
    distance_m = round(haversine_distance_m(payload.lat, payload.lng, site_lat, site_lng), 2)
    within_geofence = distance_m <= radius
else:
    # No site coords configured → allow punch without GPS enforcement
    within_geofence = True
```

`GET /planning/projects/a1376092-…` returns `"location": null` with
`"attendance_radius_meters": 500` — a radius configured around a point that does not exist. Every
punch on this project is therefore unconditionally inside the fence, which is how the London punch
above passed.

The client then compounds it (`attendance/page.tsx:720`):

```tsx
<td>{log.distance_from_site_m ? `${log.distance_from_site_m}m` : "0m (Inside)"}</td>
```

`distance_from_site_m` is `null` — *not measured*. The screen prints **`0m (Inside)`**, asserting the
worker was standing on the site marker. A missing measurement is rendered as a perfect one. Same
falsifying-fallback shape as R2-467's `Auto-synced` and R2-471's "No messages yet", now on a field
that determines whether a wage is payable.

The header badge `Geofence: Active` is displayed unconditionally, with no reference to whether the
project has coordinates at all.

## FINDING R2-476 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the subcontractor crew drawer is pre-loaded with fifteen invented workers, and submitting posts them as real attendance without checking a single response

`attendance/page.tsx:295-299`, in **both** the project and company copies:

```ts
const [subconRows, setSubconRows] = useState<any[]>([
  { role: "Mason",      count: 5, shift: 1.0, ot: 0, allowance: 250, deduction: 0, notes: "" },
  { role: "Helper",     count: 8, shift: 1.0, ot: 0, allowance: 100, deduction: 0, notes: "" },
  { role: "Supervisor", count: 2, shift: 1.0, ot: 0, allowance: 300, deduction: 0, notes: "" },
]);
```

and `submitSubconAttendance` (`:482-510`) posts every row with `count > 0` straight to
`POST /subcon/attendance`:

```ts
for (const row of subconRows) {
  if (row.count <= 0) continue;
  await fetch(`${getApiHost()}/apis/v3/subcon/attendance`, { method: "POST", … });
}
alert(`Subcontractor crew attendance saved for ${selectedSubcon.name}!`);
```

Opening the drawer for a subcontractor and pressing save — with no data entered — books **15 workers
(5 masons, 8 helpers, 2 supervisors) with ₹250/₹100/₹300 allowances** against that subcontractor, for
today, as a measured site record. Subcontractor attendance is the basis of an RA bill.

This is the *fourth* category of the fabricated-data family — after initial state, static markup and
catch-block fallbacks — and the only one where the fabricated values are **written to the database by
a normal user action**. It is the same shape as `+ Create Demo Request` writing a real ₹45,000
payment request (R2-426, fixed), and it survived that sweep because the values are numbers and role
names, not the strings the grep looked for.

Two further defects in the same eleven lines:

- **No response is ever inspected.** `await fetch(...)` with no `res.ok` check, inside a loop. Any or
  all of the posts can fail.
- **The success alert is unconditional.** `alert("Subcontractor crew attendance saved for …!")` fires
  outside any check; only a thrown network error reaches the `catch`. Ninth instance of the frontend
  swallow, and the second that announces a success that may not have happened.

---

## Recorded, not filed

- `attendance_date` and `punch_in` are stamped with `datetime.utcnow()` (`hr.py:303-305`). The probe
  punch, made at **10:32 IST**, was stored as `2026-07-29T05:02:17Z`. For any punch between 00:00 and
  05:30 IST the stored *date* is the previous day, which shifts the day into the wrong attendance
  bucket and the wrong payroll month at a month boundary. This is fix-list item 3 (`datetime.utcnow()`
  ban, already seven findings); recorded here as its attendance-specific consequence rather than a new
  number.
- The employee `<select>` renders `ZZ QA Employee One (Site Engineer)` twice — once as the placeholder
  and once as an option — so the list appears to contain a duplicate worker.
- `SELECTED DATE:` renders with an empty value beside the label while `date` holds `"2026-06-30"`.
- The punch handler *does* have a real error branch (`:461-463`,
  `setSyncMessage("Punch rejected: …")`) — worth recording as correct, and as the counter-example
  proving the swallows elsewhere are not a house style.

# 🔎 ROUND 10 — BATCH 7: Settings — a back-dating control that covers three write paths out of fifteen, six toggles wired to nothing, an approval engine that was never built, and engineering notes shipped as customer copy

Browser: `/c/d3724ec3-…/settings`. Ten sub-tabs: **Company · Roles & Access · Team · Payroll ·
Holiday & Weekoff · Workflow Controls · Document & Fields · Multi Level Approval · Integrations ·
Subscription.** Company, Roles & Access and Team were driven in earlier rounds; this batch opens the
remaining seven.

---

## FINDING R2-477 — 🔴 CRITICAL: "Restrict creating entries older than N days" is enforced on three write paths and silently ignored by every other dated write — proved on one company, one setting, in one minute

`Workflow Controls → Entry Controls` offers *"Restrict creating entries older than (N) days —
Block creating entries dated more than N days in the past."*

The control was enabled through the API exactly as the screen would (`PUT /settings/company/{cid}`,
`restrict_entry_creation_enabled: true, restrict_entry_creation_days: 1` → **200**), then two
back-dated writes were attempted against the same company, both dated 2026-01-15 (195 days old):

| Write | Endpoint | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Daily Progress Report | `POST /dpr` | **400** — `"Entry Controls: cannot create an entry dated more than 1 day(s) in the past (this entry is 195 day(s) old)."` |
| **Subcontractor labour attendance** | `POST /subcon/attendance` | **201 — created**, `attendance_date: "2026-01-15T00:00:00Z"` |

The setting was restored to `false / 0` immediately afterwards (verified `200`, `[false, 0]`).

The enforcement helper exists and works. It is simply called in almost nowhere —
`enforce_entry_creation_window` has **three** call sites in the entire backend:

```
billing.py:587    enforce_entry_creation_window(db, req.company_id, req.invoice_date)
dpr.py:68         enforce_entry_creation_window(db, project.company_id, req.dpr_date)
planning.py:445   enforce_entry_creation_window(db, project.company_id, request.start_date)
```

and its editing counterpart has exactly **one** (`planning.py:518`).

Everything else that accepts a client-supplied date is unguarded — subcontractor labour attendance,
material consumption and wastage, quality inspections, MOM, transactions, payment entries, equipment
logs, leave applications, GRNs. **Subcontractor labour attendance is the worst possible omission**:
it is the primary input to a subcontractor's RA bill, it accepts an arbitrary `attendance_date` from
the client, and back-dating labour claims is the specific fraud this control exists to stop.

The failure is worse than "not implemented", because the setting *appears* to work: an administrator
who enables it, tests it on a DPR, and sees the block will reasonably conclude the company is
protected.

**Fix:** the helper is already written and already correct. Call it from every route that accepts a
date field — a mechanical sweep of `POST`/`PUT` bodies containing `*_date`.

## FINDING R2-481 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the Holiday Calendar and Weekly Off configuration feed nothing — payroll divides by a client-supplied `days_in_month` that defaults to 26

`Holiday & Weekoff` holds a real holiday (`ZZ QA Holiday · 15/8/2026`) and a seven-day toggle strip on

  ```python
  …
  ```

calendar changes nothing downstream.

The holiday date also renders as `15/8/2026` — day-first — on a screen in the same console where the
scheduler renders `7/1/2026` month-first (R2-460). Both formats ship.

# 🔎 ROUND 10 — BATCH 8: the calculators, formula by formula — two mix grades that contradict the app's own stated ratio, a brick geometry mismatch that doubles the mortar, and a currency selector that changes nothing

Browser: `/c/{cid}/d/reports/calculators`. Eleven calculators in one screen —
**Col Steel · 1-Way Slab · 2-Way Slab · Concrete Vol · RMC Mixer · Bricks · Plaster · Paint · Tile ·
Waterproofing · House Cost**. Header claim: *"IS 456 & CPWD standard quantity takeoff engine"*.

Each was checked against the ratios, factors and rules **the screen itself prints in its own
"Engineering & Takeoff Reference Notes"**, so every finding below is an internal contradiction, not an
external opinion about which code to follow.

---

## FINDING R2-482 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the M5 and M7.5 cement factors do not follow the mix ratios and the 1.54 dry factor the same screen declares — M7.5 over-orders cement by 17%

`calculators/page.tsx:243-250`:

```ts
const mixLib: Record<string, [number, number, number]> = {   // [cement bags/m³, sand m³, agg m³]
  M5:   [3.2,  0.48, 0.96],
  M7_5: [4.0,  0.47, 0.94],
  M10:  [4.4,  0.46, 0.92],
  M15:  [6.3,  0.44, 0.88],
  M20:  [8.2,  0.42, 0.84],
  M25:  [11.1, 0.38, 0.76],
};
```

The screen states the ratio for each grade in its own dropdown and states the dry factor in its own
result panel — `DRY MIX MATERIALS (1.54 FACTOR)`. From those two published values,
cement bags per m³ = `(1.54 / Σparts) × 1440 / 50`:

| Grade | Ratio (the app's own label) | Σ | Cement bags/m³ implied | Shipped | Error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M5 | 1:5:10 | 16 | **2.77** | 3.2 | **+15.4%** |
| M7.5 | 1:4:8 | 13 | **3.41** | 4.0 | **+17.2%** |
| M10 | 1:3:6 | 10 | 4.43 | 4.4 | −0.8% ✓ |
| M15 | 1:2:4 | 7 | 6.34 | 6.3 | −0.6% ✓ |
| M20 | 1:1.5:3 | 5.5 | 8.06 | 8.2 | +1.7% ✓ |
| M25 | 1:1:2 | 4 | 11.09 | 11.1 | +0.1% ✓ |

**Every sand and aggregate factor in the table is internally consistent** — `1.54 × parts / Σ` to two
decimals for all six grades, M5 and M7.5 included. Only the two cement figures are outliers, which
rules out a different-but-defensible convention: the same table computes the other two columns the
orthodox way.

**Proved on screen.** Concrete Vol → M7.5, slab 2.25 m³, wastage 5%:

```
WET CONCRETE VOLUME  2.250 m³
DRY MIX MATERIALS (1.54 FACTOR)
  10  CEMENT BAGS      1.11  SAND (M³)      2.22  AGGREGATE (M³)
```

Sand `2.25 × 0.47 × 1.05 = 1.110` ✓ and aggregate `2.25 × 0.94 × 1.05 = 2.221` ✓ both follow 1.54.
Cement should be `2.25 × (1.54/13) × 28.8 × 1.05 = 8.06 bags → 9 rounded up`. **The screen says 10.**

M5 and M7.5 are the PCC grades — blinding, levelling course, mass concrete — the ones poured in the
largest volumes on a site. A 17% cement over-order on a 200 m³ PCC raft is roughly 120 extra bags.

---

## FINDING R2-483 — 🟠 HIGH: the brick calculator's default state pairs modular bricks with a wall-thickness list calibrated to traditional bricks, and the mortar it reports is 2.1× the real figure

The wall thickness control offers exactly two options and derives the leaf count from them
(`page.tsx:1213-1223`):

```tsx
<option value={115}>4.5 inch (Half Brick - Single Leaf)</option>
<option value={230}>9 inch (Full Brick - Double Leaf)</option>
…
setBrickLeaves(Number(e.target.value) > 115 ? 2 : 1);
```

115 and 230 mm are the **traditional** brick dimensions (110 + 10 joint, 2×110 + 10). The brick size
selector defaults to **modular, 190 × 90 × 90** (`:115`), for which the corresponding wall thicknesses
are 100 and 190 mm. The two controls are never reconciled, and mortar is computed as the *residual*:

```ts
const wallVol   = wallArea * (brickThickness / 1000.0);
const mortarVol = Math.max(0, wallVol - netBricksNoWaste * actualVol);
```

so every millimetre of the mismatch is booked as mortar.

**Measured on the default screen** — 5 m × 3 m wall, 230 mm, modular, 10 mm joint, 1:6:

```
BRICKS REQUIRED   1,650 nos      DRY MORTAR MATERIAL SPLIT   6.2 CEMENT BAGS   1.30 SAND (M³)
```

| | Shipped (230 mm) | Correct for modular double leaf (190 mm) |
|---|---|---|
| Wall volume | 15 × 0.23 = 3.450 m³ | 15 × 0.19 = 2.850 m³ |
| Brick volume (1,500 net) | 2.309 m³ | 2.309 m³ |
| Mortar | **1.142 m³ (33% of wall)** | 0.542 m³ (19%) |
| Cement | **6.2 bags** | **2.97 bags** |

**2.1× the cement, in the calculator's out-of-the-box state**, with nothing on screen to indicate the
two selections are incompatible. The reference note *"Mortar volume constitutes ~30% of total brick
wall volume"* rationalises the wrong number rather than flagging it — 30% is the rule of thumb for
**traditional** brickwork, and it is being quoted under a modular default.

**Fix:** derive the thickness options from the selected brick preset (modular → 100/190, traditional →
115/230), or validate `thickness ≈ leaves × brickWidth + joints` and refuse the combination.

---

## FINDING R2-484 — 🟠 HIGH: the stirrup cutting length adds 14d while the screen's own note describes a method that yields 6d–8d

Reference note, rendered under the Col Steel result:

> *"Stirrups cutting lengths account for 2 hooks of 10D and bend deductions: 90° = 2d, 135° = 3d."*

Implementation (`page.tsx:180`):

```ts
const colStirrupLen = (2 * ((sizeA - 80) + (sizeB - 80)) + 14 * stirrupDia) / 1000;
```

The documented method gives `2 × 10d − (bend deductions)`. A rectangular stirrup has four 90° corners
and two 135° hooks, so the deduction is `4 × 2d + 2 × 3d = 14d` → **6d**; counting three corners it is
`3 × 2d + 2 × 3d = 12d` → **8d**. The code adds **14d**, which is `20d − 6d` — the two 135° hooks
deducted and **every 90° bend deduction omitted**, precisely the term the note promises to include.

Per stirrup the overstatement is 6d–8d: 48–64 mm at 8 mm dia. On the default column the screen reports
`19 stirrups (End zone 5×2 + Mid span 9)` and `9.70 kg` of ties — the error is ~5% of stirrup steel, on
every column, always in the same direction.

Two further notes on the same calculator, recorded rather than filed:

- The `(sizeA − 80)` term hardcodes 40 mm clear cover on each face. That is the IS 456 nominal cover
  for a column, so it is right here — but there is **no cover input**, so the same helper cannot be
  reused for a beam (25 mm) or slab (20 mm) without being wrong.
- `colLo = max(colHeight/6, max(sizeA, sizeB), 450)` is **exactly IS 13920's confinement length** and
  is implemented correctly. Recorded as correct.
- `midCount = floor((h − 2·lo)/spacing) − 1` subtracts one bar where the standard count adds one;
  it under-counts mid-span ties by about two.

---

## FINDING R2-485 — 🟠 HIGH: the House Cost estimator silently adds a 120-foot compound wall and a 10% contingency the user never entered, and its Currency Mode selector changes nothing

Only four inputs are rendered — `Built-Up Area (sqft)`, `Floors Count`, `Construction Grade`,
`Currency Mode`. The formula uses seven state values. The three with no control are fixed at their
initial values for every user, forever (`page.tsx:154-160`):

```ts
const [houseCompoundWall, setHouseCompoundWall] = useState(120);  // ft   — no input rendered
const [houseContingency,  setHouseContingency]  = useState(10);   // %    — no input rendered
const [houseCity,         setHouseCity]         = useState("default"); // — no input rendered
```

**Measured** — 1,500 sqft, G floor, Standard:

```
ESTIMATED BUDGET  ₹3,731,640     Includes 10% contingency buffer (₹339,240)
```

`1500 × 2200 = 3,300,000` **+ `120 ft × (2200 × 0.35) = ₹92,400` of compound wall** → `× 1.10` =
₹3,731,640. **₹92,400 of fence nobody asked for is inside every estimate**, and the only hint is a
reference note reading *"Compound wall base rate is budgeted at 35% of building base rate"* — which
does not say that 120 feet of it are assumed.

That 35% figure is also dimensionally incoherent: it multiplies a **₹/sqft** building rate by a
**running-foot** length.

**The Currency Mode selector is inert — proved.** Setting it to `UAE (AED)`:

```
Currency Mode = AED   →   ESTIMATED BUDGET  ₹3,731,640      (unchanged, still rupees)
```

because `effCurrency = cityData.cur || houseCurrency` (`:358`) and `cityData` is always the `default`
entry, whose `cur` is `"INR"` — a truthy value, so the user's choice is never reached.

Behind that same unreachable branch sits a complete ten-city rate table (Mumbai ×1.25, Delhi ×1.20,
Bengaluru ×1.18, Pune ×1.15, Hyderabad ×1.10, Jaipur ×0.95, Lucknow ×0.90, Dubai, Riyadh) that **no
control exposes** — dead code carrying two latent errors for whenever a city picker is added:
**Riyadh is priced in `USD`** (Saudi Arabia uses SAR), and the floor multiplier compounds upward
(`1 + 0.12 × f`, so upper floors cost *more* per sqft, which is the opposite of the usual
foundation-amortisation effect).

Finally, the five split percentages (40/25/15/12/8) are applied to the total **after** contingency, so
the ₹339,240 buffer is silently distributed across Structure, Finishing, MEP, Interior and Consultants
rather than shown as its own line.

---

## FINDING R2-486 — 🟡 MEDIUM: the Paint calculator's quality dropdown advertises a coverage it does not use, and its Interior/Exterior selector is never read

```
Paint Context:      [Interior Walls] [Exterior Walls]
Paint Type/Quality: Economy Emulsion (120 sqft/L) | Premium (140) | Luxury (155) | Texture (80)
```

`page.tsx:307-312`:

```ts
const coverageMap = { economy: 115.0, premium: 140.0, luxury: 155.0, texture: 80.0 };
const coverage = coverageMap[paintQuality] || 135.0;
```

- **Economy is labelled 120 sqft/L and computed at 115** — a 4% discrepancy between what the user is
  told and what is used. The other three agree.
- `paintMode` (`:131`) is declared, bound to the Interior/Exterior control, and **never read by any
  formula**. Exterior work differs in coverage, primer and coats; the selector does nothing.
- The `|| 135.0` fallback is a fifth coverage value that matches none of the four options and is
  unreachable.

## ✅ RECORDED AS CORRECT — most of the takeoff engine is sound

Stated as firmly as the failures:

| Check | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Steel unit weight `D²/162` | correct, all three steel calculators |
| Column lap length `50d` | standard site practice, consistent |
| IS 13920 confinement zone `max(h/6, max(a,b), 450)` | **correct** |
| M10 / M15 / M20 / M25 cement, and **all six** sand and aggregate factors | correct against 1.54 |
| Staircase volume `steps × width × [(R×T/2) + waist×√(R²+T²)]` | correct, and the note states it |
| Brick face area `(len+joint) × (height+joint)` | correct |
| Mortar as `wallVol − brickVol`, dry factor 1.33 | correct method |
| Plaster: `area × thickness × 1.33`, cement `dry × ratio × 1440/50` | correct |
| Tile: grout converted `mm/25.4` and added before division | correct, and the note states it |
| Paint door 21 sqft / window 12 sqft deductions | correct, units consistent (all inputs in ft) |
| RMC truck count `ceil(totalVol / mixerSize)` | correct |
| Waterproofing `area/coverage × coats × (1+waste)` | correct |

**The arithmetic is largely right.** What fails is at the seams — a lookup table that two of its six
rows do not obey, two controls whose geometries disagree, and three inputs that exist in the formula
but not on the screen.

## ⚠️ CORRECTION TO METHOD — `Failed to fetch` does **not** imply a 500

Trap 4 / R2-236 has been used throughout this audit to read `TypeError: Failed to fetch` as "a 500
that lost its CORS headers". A control probe run this batch shows the inference is unsound:

```
GET /apis/v3/nonexistent-path-probe        → TypeError: Failed to fetch
```

An **unmatched route — an ordinary 404 — produces the identical symptom**, because the CORS headers
are attached inside the routed application and a route miss never reaches it. So `Failed to fetch`
means *"the browser could not read the response"*, which covers at least: a 500 raised outside a
route, a 404 on a path that does not exist, and a cross-origin redirect the browser will not follow.

Consequences, applied honestly:

- Three endpoints probed at the start of this batch — `/files?project_id=…`, `/mom?project_id=…`,
  `/materials/wastage` — returned `Failed to fetch` and were **wrong paths**. The real ones
  (`/files/files`, `/mom/{company_id}`) return **200**. Had the old inference been applied, this batch
  would have filed three fictitious 500s.
- Batch 4's claim that `/planning/tasks/company/{cid}` is a CORS-less 500 **is still correct** — but
  because the founder's log shows `"GET /apis/v3/planning/tasks/company/d3724ec3-… HTTP/1.1" 500
  Internal Server Error`, not because of the symptom.
- **Batch 2's contrast holds and is now better stated:** a 500 raised *inside* a route
  (`raise HTTPException(500)`) returns readable JSON through CORS; an unhandled exception, and a route
  miss, do not.

**Rule going forward: never attribute a status code to `Failed to fetch` without a server log.**
This is the tenth correction the audit has made to itself, and the fifth found by testing rather than
reasoning.

## FINDING R2-487 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the project's Party register is empty and reports ₹0 payable, on a project carrying ₹1,35,700 of unpaid bills — raising a bill against a party never links that party to the project

Browser: `/p/a1376092-…/party`.

```
ADVANCE PAID  ₹0.00      TO PAY  ₹0.00
Party Details | Type | Balance | Status | Action
No parties linked to this project.
```

Fetched from the page in the same frame:

```
GET /projects/a1376092-…/parties           → 200  []
GET /projects/a1376092-…/parties/balances  → 200  {"advance_paid": 0.0, "to_pay": 0.0}
GET /library/parties/d3724ec3-…            → 200  [ … 4 real parties incl. ZZ QA Client Ltd … ]
GET /billing/bills?project_id=a1376092-…   → 200  7 bills, ₹1,35,700 unpaid to purchase + subcon parties
```

The bills carry `party_company_user_id` — including the ₹1,11,100 subcontractor bill to
`ZZ QA Subcon Co` audited in Batch 1. The parties exist. The bills exist. The link table does not.

`_party_settlement` (`projects.py:26-60`) is written correctly — it bridges a library party to
`CompanyTeam.library_party_id`, rolls opening advance/payable together with live bill activity, and
returns Advance Paid / To Pay. **It is iterated over the project's linked parties, and nothing in the
billing flow ever creates that link**, so the loop runs zero times and the correct helper returns
zero.

Why this is CRITICAL rather than an empty-state cosmetic:

1. **It is the screen a site accountant opens to answer "who do we owe on this project".** It answers
   ₹0.00, with a definite-sounding sentence — *"No parties linked to this project."* — and no
   indication that ₹1.36 lakh of unpaid bills exist one tab away.
2. **The two tiles are not blank, they are zero.** Same shape as R2-416 and R2-405: an uninitialised
   value rendered as a measured one.
3. It is the project-level mirror of **R2-418** (company party balances disagreeing with the TO PAY
   tile). Round 9 filed the disagreement; this is the cause on the project side — the linkage the
   whole party-ledger feature depends on is never written.
4. `+ Add Party` exists on this screen, so the link *can* be made manually. Every payable is therefore
   invisible until somebody remembers to also register the party against the project — a step no
   billing flow prompts for and nothing warns about.

## FINDING R2-488 — 🟠 HIGH: the Material screen adds bags, tonnes and cft together and prints the sum as a headline stock figure

Browser: `/p/a1376092-…/material`.

```
Material Stock — Current Stock = Received − Consumed
Materials 3      Received 10,100      Consumed 10,516      Over-consumed 1

#  MATERIAL             UNIT    RECEIVED  CONSUMED  CURRENT STOCK
1  UltraTech Cement     bags       100        16         84
2  ZZ R7 Steel Rod      tonne   10,000    10,000          0
3  ZZ R8 Phantom Sand   cft          0       500      -500 OVER
```

`Received 10,100` = 100 **bags** + 10,000 **tonnes** + 0 **cft**. `Consumed 10,516` = 16 bags +
10,000 tonnes + 500 cft. The per-row arithmetic is correct and the `Over-consumed 1` counter is
correct; the two headline totals are dimensionally meaningless.

The product knows the units — they are a column on the same table, and `unit` is a required field on
`MaterialConsumptionSchema`. The totals ignore them.

This matters beyond tidiness: those two tiles are the first numbers on the module, they move when
anything is received or issued, and they will read as "we have taken in 10,100 units of material" to
anyone who does not stop to add the column by hand. The honest options are a per-unit breakdown, a
count of distinct materials, or no total at all.

*(Recorded, not filed: `Current Stock -500 OVER` for Phantom Sand is the negative-stock case working
as configured — `negative_stock_lock` is `false` on this company, and `procurement.py:821` honours it.
The badge is honest.)*

## FINDING R2-490 — 🔴 CRITICAL: `TOTAL OUT ₹0.00` is printed immediately above a table of ₹1,41,600 of outflows, and the four tiles use three different bases — none of them money actually moved

`transaction/page.tsx:181-207`:

```ts
for (const b of bills) {
  const amt = Number(b.total_payable) || 0;
  const sub = Number(b.subtotal) || 0;
  if (REVENUE_TYPES.includes(t))        sales   += sub;      // pre-GST
  else if (EXPENSE_TYPES.includes(t))   expense += sub;      // pre-GST
  else if (SETTLEMENT_TYPES.includes(t)) {
    if (t === "payment_in" || t === "i_received") totalIn  += amt;   // post-GST
    else if (t === "payment_out" || t === "i_paid") totalOut += amt; // post-GST
  }
}
return { totalIn, totalOut, sales, expense, balance: totalIn - totalOut, margin: sales - expense };
```

Reconciled against the ledger beneath it:

| Tile | Shown | What it actually counts | What the table shows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TOTAL IN` | ₹11,800 | **only** `payment_in`/`i_received`, at `total_payable` | +₹1,29,800 of inflow rows |
| `TOTAL OUT` | **₹0.00** | **only** `payment_out`/`i_paid` — and this project has none | **−₹1,41,600 of outflow rows** |
| `PROJECT BALANCE (IN − OUT)` | ₹11,800 | inherits both | — |
| `MARGIN (SALES − EXPENSE)` | −₹26,000 | `subtotal` sums: 1,00,000 − 1,26,000 | pre-GST, a different basis from the tiles above |

**Three separate defects in four tiles:**

1. **`TOTAL OUT ₹0.00` sits four lines above five outflow rows totalling ₹1,41,600**, each rendered in
   red with a minus sign. This is the starkest same-frame contradiction the audit has recorded — the
   refuting evidence is not on another screen or another tab, it is in the table the tile heads.
2. **Two tax bases on one card row.** `TOTAL IN`/`TOTAL OUT` are post-GST `total_payable`; `MARGIN` is
   pre-GST `subtotal`. A user comparing ₹11,800 with −₹26,000 is comparing different quantities.
3. **`paid_amount` appears in none of them.** ₹40,000 has actually been received against
   `ZZ-QA-AUDIT-001` (`status: Partially Paid`, visible on the same row). The only card labelled with
   real cash — `PROJECT BALANCE` — does not contain it.

This project now has **four mutually inconsistent financial summaries across three screens**, all
computed in the browser from the same seven bills:

| Screen | Spend figure | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Project dashboard `CASH OUT` | ₹1,41,600 | server `Project.cash_out`, all expense types, post-GST |
| Project dashboard `TOTAL EXPENSE` | ₹1,35,700 | client, `purchase`+`subcon` only, post-GST (R2-448) |
| **Project transaction `TOTAL OUT`** | **₹0** | client, settlement types only, post-GST |
| **Project transaction `MARGIN` expense leg** | **₹1,26,000** | client, revenue/expense types, **pre-GST** |

The correct fix is the same one as R2-448 — a single shared classification of `invoice_type` into
cost heads, plus one decision about whether a screen reports accrual or cash, applied consistently.
The `SETTLEMENT_TYPES` split is defensible in itself; labelling its result `TOTAL OUT` on a screen
whose table shows every outflow is not.
