# 🔎 ROUND 10 — BATCH 36: concurrency tested, the whole report layer re-measured, and a real improvement recorded

The last untested condition (**concurrency**) plus a full re-measurement of the report layer that
Round 5 recorded as broken.

---

## Concurrency — tested, and the result is narrower than expected

**First attempt:** four concurrent `POST /billing/bills` with an identical `invoice_number`. All four
were still in flight when the shell timed out at 120 s, and **zero rows landed**. Inconclusive — the
free-tier instance does not serve four concurrent writes inside two minutes. Recorded rather than
inferred.

**Second attempt**, a lighter endpoint — three concurrent `POST /library/cost-codes` with an identical
`code`:

```
req1 HTTP 200   req2 HTTP 200   req3 HTTP 200
ZZR10RACE rows now present: 3
  04c17b26-…   3afd03f8-…   1cd3eac7-…
```

Three identical codes created. **But reading the handler shows this is not a race** —
`create_library_cost_code` (`library.py:263-278`) performs **no duplicate check of any kind**; it
constructs the row and commits. Three concurrent requests produce three rows for the same reason one
sequential request would produce a second: nothing looks.

**So the honest result is: concurrency is not what breaks here, uniqueness is.** R2-386's specific
claim — that six *check-then-insert* endpoints would race — remains **untested**, because the endpoint
that would demonstrate it (bills) could not be driven concurrently within the timeout. That is a gap,
not a finding, and it is recorded as such.

*(The three probe rows were deleted through the product — `DELETE /library/cost-codes/{id}` ×3, all
200.)*

---

## FINDING R2-559 — 🟠 HIGH: the entire schema carries 13 unique constraints, and not one of them is on a document number

Counted across `models.py`:

```
unique=True columns: 13
  reports.slug · users.mobile · users.email · equipment.code · bi_api_keys.auth_key
  payroll_profiles.employee_id
  + 6 company_id columns on one-row-per-company settings tables
UniqueConstraint(...) declarations: 0
```

So the only business identifier the database protects is **equipment code**. Every document number the
product issues — `invoice_number`, `po_number`, `grn_number`, `ncr_number`, `wo_number`,
`reference_number`, cost-code `code` — is unconstrained.

This is R2-386 with a measured denominator, and Batch 36's probe shows the practical consequence at
its simplest: **three cost codes with the same code, created in one second, through the product.** The
live data already carries the same pattern from earlier rounds — two NCRs numbered `ZZ-R8-NCR-DUP`,
three three-way matches on one PO/GRN pair.

The gradient across the codebase is worth naming, because it shows the intent existed and was applied
unevenly:

| Level of protection | Where |
|---|---|
| DB unique constraint | `equipment.code` only |
| Application check-then-insert (racy, but present) | six endpoints, per R2-386 |
| **Advisory endpoint the client may call** | `/procurement/duplicate-po-check` — and it is case-sensitive and untrimmed (R2-535) |
| **Nothing at all** | `library/cost-codes`, `quality/ncr`, and the rest |

**Fix:** `UniqueConstraint("company_id", "<number>")` per document table — company-scoped, so two
tenants may legitimately use the same number. That single change also removes the race in R2-386's six
endpoints, because the database becomes the arbiter instead of the pre-check.

## FINDING R2-560 — 🟠 HIGH: the two party reports return `rows: []` behind a bare `except Exception: return []`, on a company with six parties and ₹2.71 lakh of bills against them

All 21 report slugs were driven live against AK Construction. **16 return data.** Five return zero
rows, and two of those five should not:

| Report | Rows | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `party-ledger` | **0** | ✗ the company has 4 library parties, 2 subcontractors, 7 bills |
| `all-party-balances` | **0** | ✗ same |
| `payment-request` | 0 | ✓ genuinely empty (`/finance/payment-requests` → `[]`) |
| `bank-statement` | 0 | ✓ genuinely empty (`/finance/accounts` → `[]`) |
| `item-wise-sales` | 0 | ✓ sources CRM quotation items, of which there are none |

`reports.py:688-711`:

```python
def _rep_party_ledger(db, cid, pid):
    try:
        rows, _ = _build_party_ledger(db, cid, pid)
        return rows
    except Exception:
        return []

def _rep_all_party_balances(db, cid, pid):
    try:
        _, party_final = _build_party_ledger(db, cid, pid)
        …
    except Exception:
        return []
```

Both call the same helper and both swallow every exception into an empty list. So a zero-row party
ledger on a company that demonstrably has parties and bills is **indistinguishable from a company with
no activity** — and per R2-491/R2-499 the party-name resolution that helper depends on is exactly the
join that fails elsewhere in the product.

This is the R2-312/R2-324 swallow, now isolated: it is no longer hiding a systemic failure, it is
hiding **precisely the two reports that do not work.**

## 🥇 FIX LIST — final, ordered by damage

1. **Delete the offline-sync button** (R2-515). `flushQueue` has no `fetch`; it wipes the queue and
   prints *"Synced N queued punches successfully"*. Proved live: server rows 1 → 1, two punches
   destroyed. The only finding that destroys data a user already entered. Rebuilding it needs R2-516
   first — the queued record has no `employee_id`, no `project_id`, and a display-string time.
2. **`--forwarded-allow-ips` on uvicorn** (R2-511). One flag. Today six unauthenticated requests
   exhaust the 5/minute login limit for **every customer**, because every rate limit keys on Render's
   proxy IP — proved from three rotating `10.30.x.x` client addresses for one browser in the founder's
   access log.
3. **A `company_team_id_for()` helper** (root cause 1, six sites). Makes chat work at all
   (R2-468/469/470) and fixes R2-491/R2-499. `chat.py:146-153` already holds the correct resolution
   and uses it exactly once.
4. **One shared `invoice_type` → cost-head map**. One project currently ships **five** different spend
   figures. Two correct server-side reference implementations already exist.
5. **Project delete safety** (R2-557). 51 cascades, no impact count, no undo, an audit line naming
   nobody. Add a preflight count and soft-delete.
6. **`await params` in 21 redirect stubs** (R2-462). `budgeting/page.tsx` is the working template.
7. **The 13 missing `require_permission` calls** (R2-541), starting with
   `POST /settings/company-file/{cid}` — it governs the **signature and stamp printed on tax
   invoices**, resolves no `current_user`, and writes no audit record.
8. **`useMemo` the `authHeaders` object** (`delete-logs/page.tsx:43`, R2-310) — still 44 requests/18 s.
9. **Ban `datetime.utcnow()`** — seven findings plus R2-473's attendance-date consequence.
10. **The eleven missing/mismatched columns** — R2-540 (`Timesheet.company_id`) is a guaranteed 500.
11. **Validation sweep** — `Field(ge=, le=)` on the 42 unbounded numerics, `max_length` on the 448
    unbounded strings (widths already declared in `models.py`), `UniqueConstraint(company_id, number)`
    per document table, and a resolve-and-404 helper for foreign keys.
12. **Delete the swallow handlers** — twelve instances, including an audit trail (R2-513), a 403
    rendered as "No messages yet" (R2-471), and the two party reports (R2-560).

## 🧠 THE SIX ROOT CAUSES

1. **`users.id` vs `company_team.id`** — 6 sites.
2. **No shared `invoice_type` map** — 5 spend figures for one project, all shipped.
3. **Actor fields taken from the client** — 20 sites, including all 30 `log_deletion` calls omitting
   `deleted_by`, so **no deletion in the product records who performed it** (R2-536; proved 9/9 null).
4. **Company-level rollups that 500** — five, each with a working project-level sibling. One contract
   test per `response_model` against a populated row catches all five.
5. **Captured data, absent engine** — six modules: measurement book, depreciation, BOCW/muster roll,
   approval chains, statutory returns, fuel logs.
6. **The database is the validation layer.** Where the app validates, a precise **422**; where it does
   not, the database refuses and the user gets a **500**. That one sentence explains R2-547, R2-551,
   R2-552, R2-555 and R2-556 — and why so much of this audit has been spent telling real faults from
   user error: *the product returns the same status code for both.*

---

## ⚠️ CORRECTIONS THIS ROUND MADE TO ITSELF

1. **`Failed to fetch` does NOT imply a 500.** An unmatched route (404) produces the identical
   symptom — proved with `/apis/v3/nonexistent-path-probe`. Never attribute a status code without a
   server log.
2. **R2-236 is not universal** — a 500 raised *inside* a route returns readable JSON through CORS.
3. **R2-356 is not fixed** — `/finance/pl` returns 200 only because every equipment deployment now
   carries an `end_date`. The trigger is absent, not repaired.
4. **Coverage was claimed twice and wrong twice.** "Backend complete / calculators 100%" was disproved
   by counting (Batch 19); the batch footers written *after* that correction were themselves asserted
   and had to be retracted (Batch 26). Every coverage figure now carries its command.
5. **A mail-hang hypothesis was formed and disproved** before filing — the 90 s timeout was Render's
   cold start; the warm request returns in 1.95 s.
6. **A leave-balance name-collision hypothesis was disproved by testing** before filing — the code
   keys on `employee_id` when present. The real defect (R2-527) is narrower and different.

## Batch 1 — HR timesheets (cluster: HR, 9 sites)

Probes created and removed: one timesheet header + four entries, `DELETE /hr/timesheets/{id}` → 204,
read-back shows 0 residual `ZZ R11` rows. No cleanup SQL needed for this batch.

### FINDING R2-561 — 🟠 HIGH: a timesheet entry carries three independent representations of the same time and the server cross-validates none of them; `duration` is taken from the client verbatim

`POST /apis/v3/hr/timesheets/{ts_id}/entries` accepts `hours`, `start_time`/`end_time`, and
`duration` as three separate fields. `hours` is the only one validated (`Field(..., gt=0, le=24)`,
`hr.py:153`). The other two are free.

`hr.py:399-401`:

```python
if entry_data.get("start_time") and entry_data.get("end_time") and not entry_data.get("duration"):
    delta = entry_data["end_time"] - entry_data["start_time"]
    entry_data["duration"] = int(delta.total_seconds() / 60)
```

The guard is `not entry_data.get("duration")` — so when the client supplies `duration`, the server
does not compute it and does not check it. `duration` is declared client-writable at `hr.py:157`.

Proved live:

```
POST /hr/timesheets/{ts}/entries
  {"hours":1,"start_time":"2026-08-05T09:00:00Z","end_time":"2026-08-05T10:00:00Z","duration":99999}
→ 201 {"duration":99999,"start_time":"...09:00:00+00:00","end_time":"...10:00:00+00:00"}
```

One row now says the work took 1 hour, that it ran 09:00–10:00, and that it lasted 99,999 minutes
(1,666 hours). The timesheet grid renders the third: `hr/page.tsx:1012-1015` formats `log.duration`
as `1666 Hr 39 Min` next to a start and end time one hour apart.

**Why it matters:** `hours` drives `total_hours` and payroll; `duration` is what the operator reads
on screen. They can disagree without limit, and the disagreement is client-controlled. This is root
cause 3 (values taken from the client) applied to a quantity rather than an actor.

**Fix:** drop `duration` from `TimesheetEntryCreate` and always derive it; reject `end_time <=
start_time`; reject `abs(duration/60 - hours) > tolerance`.

### FINDING R2-562 — 🟠 HIGH: `end_time` before `start_time` is accepted and stored as a negative duration, which the console prints as "-8 Hr 0 Min"

Same endpoint, no ordering check. Proved live:

```
{"hours":8,"start_time":"2026-08-05T17:00:00Z","end_time":"2026-08-05T09:00:00Z"} → 201
GET /hr/timesheets/project/{project_id} → "duration":-480
```

`-480` is persisted and returned by the endpoint the timesheets tab reads. `hr/page.tsx:1012-1015`
computes `Math.floor(-480/60)` = `-8` and `-480 % 60` = `-0`, so the row reads **"-8 Hr 0 Min"**.
Note `if (log.duration)` also means a genuine zero-minute entry falls through to `"—"`.

`total_hours` still incremented by the full 8, because it sums `hours`, not `duration` — so the
header total and the visible line disagree in sign.

**Fix:** validate ordering at the schema level.

### FINDING R2-563 — 🟡 MEDIUM: an entry's `entry_date` is not constrained to its own timesheet's week

The header is explicitly week-scoped (`week_start`, `week_end`, `models.py:702-703`) and the console
computes Monday–Sunday before posting (`hr/page.tsx:490-491`). The entry endpoint ignores it.

Proved live against a header spanning `2026-08-03` → `2026-08-09`:

```
{"entry_date":"1899-01-01T00:00:00Z","hours":8,...} → 201, and total_hours became 8.0
```

An entry dated **1 January 1899** sits inside an August 2026 weekly timesheet and counts toward its
total. Weekly reporting that groups by header will attribute it to that week; anything grouping by
`entry_date` will not. Same class as the unbounded-numeric family, on a date.

**Fix:** reject `entry_date` outside `[week_start, week_end]`.

### FINDING R2-564 — 🟠 HIGH: when the timesheet header fails, the console silently discards the hours the user typed and shows neither an error nor a success

`hr/page.tsx:496-533`. The Save handler POSTs the header, then posts the entry:

```ts
let tsId = "";
if (tsHeaderRes.ok) { tsId = (await tsHeaderRes.json()).id; }
else { tsId = "d0000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001"; }   // "Fallback default"
const res = await fetch(`.../hr/timesheets/${tsId}/entries`, { method: "POST", ... });
if (res.ok) { setShowNewTimesheetDrawer(false); fetchTimesheetLogs(); }
```

Three defects in eight lines:

1. **The fallback id is dead.** `d0000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001` is a hardcoded literal that
   does not exist in this database — proved live: `POST /hr/timesheets/d0000000-…-000000000001/entries`
   → **404 `{"detail":"Timesheet not found"}`**. It is not a fallback, it is a guaranteed failure. In
   any deployment where that id *does* resolve, the outcome is worse: the hours are written into an
   unrelated employee's timesheet.
2. **`if (res.ok)` has no `else`.** On failure nothing happens — the drawer stays open, no error is
   set, no toast. The user's hours are gone with no message. The outer `catch` only
   `console.error`s.
3. **The header failure is a 500, not a 4xx.** Proved live: posting a header with an unresolvable
   `employee_id` returns **500 "Internal Server Error"**, not a 422 — the FK is enforced only by the
   database. Root cause 6 exactly.

**Reachability:** the normal path selects an employee from `/hr/employees/{projectId}`, so the FK
usually resolves. It fails whenever the employee was removed from the project between page load and
save, or the row is stale — and the failure mode is silent loss, not an error.

This is the R2-515 shape — a write that fails while the UI says nothing — but discarding rather than
destroying, so HIGH rather than CRITICAL.

**Fix:** delete the fallback branch, `return` on `!tsHeaderRes.ok`, and add an `else` that surfaces
the error.

### Batch 1 tally — R2-561 … R2-564 (4 findings: 3 🟠 HIGH, 1 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Also tested, and NOT filed:**

- `hours` **is** properly bounded — `-40` → 422 `"Input should be greater than 0"`, `9999` → 422
  `"Input should be less than or equal to 24"`. One of the few bounded numerics in the product.
- `ts.status not in ("draft","rejected")` correctly blocks entries on submitted timesheets
  (`hr.py:395`).
- **A `total_hours` double-count hypothesis was formed and disproved before filing.** `hr.py:406-410`
  `db.add()`s the entry before summing existing entries and then adds `payload.hours` again, which
  reads as a double count under autoflush. The live numbers refute it: successive 8-hour entries
  produced `total_hours` 8.0 then 16.0, not 16.0 then 32.0. The pending entry is not flushed into
  that query. **Correct as written.**
- **R2-540 re-verified still live:** `GET /hr/timesheets/company/{cid}` → **500**. Unfixed.

## Batch 2 — planning / Gantt (cluster: gantt, 7 sites)

### FINDING R2-565 — 🔴 CRITICAL: adding a task dependency permanently breaks the planning module for that project, and no route exists to undo it

**The single highest-impact finding of Round 11.** Dependencies are the reason a Gantt chart exists;
using the feature destroys the screen it lives on.

**Proved live, from a clean state, in one sequence** (project `a1376092` "Zoho Test Project"):

```
GET /apis/v3/planning/tasks?project_id=a1376092…      → 200   (two tasks, no links)
POST /apis/v3/planning/tasks/{T1b}/predecessors
     {"predecessor_id":"{T1}"}                        → 201 {"success":true,
                                                              "message":"Predecessor dependency added successfully"}
GET /apis/v3/planning/tasks?project_id=a1376092…      → 500
POST /apis/v3/planning/tasks {…same shape that just worked…} → 500
```

`ZZ QA R5 Second Project` (`4ab9616c`) was **already in this state before this session touched it** —
that is how the defect was found: an identical task-create payload succeeded in one project and 500'd
in the other. The difference between the two projects was the presence of a predecessor link.

**Cause — `planning.py:146`:**

```python
value = min(latest_finish(s) - dur_by_id.get(s, 1) for s in sc)
```

`latest_finish(s)` returns a **datetime** — it bottoms out at `project_end`, itself a datetime
(`planning.py:131`, `max(end_by_id.values())`). `dur_by_id[s]` is a **float number of days**
(`planning.py:130`, `.total_seconds() / 86400.0`). `datetime - float` raises `TypeError`.

The line is guarded by `sc = succ.get(tid)` being non-empty (`:142-145`), and `succ` is built only
from rows in `task_predecessors` (`:133-136`). **With zero dependency links the branch is
unreachable and everything works. With one link it is reached on every call.**

`compute_critical_task_ids` is called from `annotate_critical` (`:171`), which runs in both the task
**list** endpoint and the task **create** endpoint (`:469`) — so one link takes out reading and
writing together.

**Why it is unrecoverable through the product:**

```bash
grep -nE '@router\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)\(".*predecessor' backend/app/routers/planning.py
# => 534:@router.post("/tasks/{task_id}/predecessors")     ← the only one
grep -nE '@router\.delete' backend/app/routers/planning.py
# => 415:/milestones/{id}   675:/tasks/todos/{todo_id}     ← no task delete, no predecessor delete
```

`DELETE /planning/tasks/{id}` → **405**. `DELETE` on the predecessor → **405**. The Gantt page has no
remove-link control (`grep -i 'predecessor.*(delete|remove)'` on `gantt/page.tsx` → no match). A user
who clicks "Add Predecessor" once has no path back, and neither did this audit — restoring the probe
project required SQL.

**Aggravating: the create endpoint commits before it crashes.** `planning.py:466-471` runs
`db.add()` → `db.commit()` → `db.refresh()` → **then** `annotate_critical`. Once a project is in this
state, `POST /planning/tasks` **writes the row and then returns 500**, so the client is told the
creation failed while the task exists. Retrying multiplies it.

**Fix (one line):** subtract a `timedelta`, not a float —
`latest_finish(s) - timedelta(days=dur_by_id.get(s, 1))`. Then move `annotate_critical` above
`db.commit()` or wrap it, so a derived-field failure cannot report a completed write as an error.
Then add `DELETE /tasks/{task_id}/predecessors/{predecessor_id}` and a control for it, so the
feature is reversible.

**Status: CLOSED — traceback observed in the founder's Render live tail, verbatim:**

```
File "/app/app/routers/planning.py", line 171, in annotate_critical
    critical = compute_critical_task_ids(proj_tasks, db)
File "/app/app/routers/planning.py", line 157, in compute_critical_task_ids
    slack = (latest_finish(t.id) - end_by_id[t.id]).total_seconds() / 86400.0
File "/app/app/routers/planning.py", line 146, in latest_finish
    value = min(latest_finish(s) - dur_by_id.get(s, 1) for s in sc)
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'datetime.datetime' and 'float'
```

The exception type, the line and the operand types match the prediction made from source exactly.
The call chain in the log also confirms the entry point is `annotate_critical` (`:171`), which is the
shared helper behind both the list and the create endpoint — so one link disabling both reads and
writes is confirmed by the server, not only inferred.

**Restoration verified:** after the cleanup SQL, `GET /planning/tasks?project_id=a1376092…` → **200**,
0 residual `ZZ R11` rows. `4ab9616c` remains **500** — pre-existing, not caused by this audit, and it
stays broken until its own predecessor rows are cleared or R2-565 is fixed.

### FINDING R2-566 — 🟡 MEDIUM: `POST /planning/tasks` silently discards the client's `status`

The Gantt create form sends `status: "pending"` (`gantt/page.tsx:322`). `create_task`
(`planning.py:451-464`) never reads `request.status`; the row is created with the model default and
the response comes back `"status":"not_started"`. Proved live — sent `"pending"`, stored
`"not_started"`. Harmless today because the form only ever sends one value, but it is a field the
client believes it controls and does not.

### Batch 2 tally — R2-565 … R2-566 (2 findings: 1 🔴 CRITICAL, 1 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Also tested, and NOT filed — the dependency guards that DO work:**

- **Self-predecessor rejected:** `{"predecessor_id": <same task>}` → **400 "A task cannot be its own
  predecessor"**.
- `check_circular_dependency` (`planning.py:177-195`) is a correct DFS over the transitive
  predecessor set.
- Both were verified before R2-565 was framed, so the CRITICAL is specifically *not* "loop detection
  is broken" — the validation is fine; the critical-path computation behind it is not.

```sql
-- ZZ QA R5 Second Project (4ab9616c) is in the SAME broken state and was NOT caused by this audit.
```

## Batch 3 — scripted: irreversibility across the whole API

R2-565's second limb — *a record you can create but no route can remove* — is a schema-level
question, so it was scripted rather than sampled.

```bash
# pair every @router.post path against @router.delete paths in the same router
python - <<'PY'   # (full script in session; normalises {param} -> *)
PY
# => 111 of 144 POST-able paths have no DELETE in the same router
```

111/144 overstates it: calculators, auth actions, `/approve`, `/reject` and the backfills are not
meant to be deletable. Filtering to **endpoints that create a persistent business record** gives the
finding below.

### FINDING R2-567 — 🔴 CRITICAL: no financial, procurement, quality or safety document can be deleted, voided, cancelled or reversed — four entire routers contain zero delete routes and the API has no void mechanism at all

```bash
grep -nE '@router\.delete' app/routers/{billing,procurement,quality,safety}.py
# => no output. Zero delete routes across all four files.

grep -rnE '@router\.(post|put|patch|delete)\([\x27"][^\x27"]*(void|cancel|reverse|revoke)' app/routers/*.py
# => no output. No void/cancel/reverse route exists anywhere in the product.
```

The affected document types, all created through the console and all permanent once created:

| Router | Documents with no delete and no void |
|---|---|
| `billing.py` | bills, **credit notes**, **debit notes**, work orders, subcontractors |
| `procurement.py` | purchase orders, GRNs, indents, transactions |
| `quality.py` | NCRs, inspections, checklists, material tests |
| `safety.py` | incidents, PPE checks, toolbox talks |
| also | production batches/recipes, BOCW + muster roll, chat messages, equipment fuel/maintenance/deploy |

Confirmed live for each: `DELETE …/{well-formed-uuid}` returns 404 or 405 in every case.

**On 404 vs 405 — a correction to the obvious reading.** The split is not meaningful. FastAPI returns
**405** when the path matches a registered route under another method and **404** when no route
matches that path at all. `billing.py` has `/bills/{id}/zatca` and `/bills/{id}/pdf` but no bare
`/bills/{id}`, so the bare path 404s; `quality.py` has other methods on `/ncr/{id}`, so it 405s.
**Both mean the same thing: there is no DELETE.** The grep above, not the status code, is the
authority here — recorded because the status code invites exactly the wrong inference. Same family
as Trap 16.

**Why this is CRITICAL rather than correct-by-design.** Immutability of a posted financial document
is normal accounting practice — *when a reversal mechanism exists*. Here neither exists. The product
has no delete, no void, no cancel, no credit-note-against-a-bill workflow reachable as a correction.
Combined with two findings already in this register:

- **no uniqueness constraint on any document number** (Round 10: 13 unique constraints in the schema,
  zero on a document number), so a duplicate bill number can be created; and
- **correcting a bill is provably broken** (Round 5),

the full sequence is: a user can post a wrong bill, cannot correct it, cannot void it, cannot delete
it, and can then post a second bill carrying the same number. For statutory documents — credit and
debit notes are GST instruments — that is a compliance problem, not only a usability one.

**Fix:** a `status`/`is_void` column plus a void route per document type, restricted by permission and
writing a `log_deletion` record with a real actor (see root cause 3 — all 30 existing `log_deletion`
calls omit `deleted_by`).

### Batch 3 tally — R2-567 (1 finding: 1 🔴 CRITICAL)

**Also checked, and NOT filed:** the two apparent void-ish routes are false positives —
`crm.py:451 POST /lead-statuses/{company_id}` creates a lookup value, and
`wastage.py:69 PATCH /{wastage_id}/status` is the only document-status transition in the product and
is scoped to wastage alone.

**Method note for the next session:** no financial documents were created to prove this. Creating a
bill to test whether a bill can be deleted would have left an undeletable bill in the founder's data —
which is the finding. Route-level evidence was used instead.

## Batch 4 — equipment (cluster: equipment, 8 sites)

### FINDING R2-568 — 🔴 CRITICAL: one physical machine can be deployed to unlimited projects at the same time, and every concurrent deployment bills the project separately

`POST /apis/v3/equipment/{equipment_id}/deploy` performs no availability check. Proved live with
`ZZ R5 Excavator` (`f4eac72e`, `hourly_rate` 1200):

```
POST /equipment/f4eac72e…/deploy {"project_id":"a1376092…"}  → 201   (Zoho Test Project)
POST /equipment/f4eac72e…/deploy {"project_id":"4ab9616c…"}  → 201   (ZZ QA R5 Second Project)
POST /equipment/f4eac72e…/deploy {"project_id":"a1376092…"}  → 201   (same project again)
```

Three open deployments (`end_date: null`) of one excavator, across two projects, all accepted. The
row's own `status` field flips to `"deployed"` after the first — so the product **records** that the
machine is unavailable and then never consults it. There is no overlap check on dates either.

**The cost consequence is not cosmetic.** `finance.py:411-419` computes plant cost by iterating
deployments and multiplying elapsed time by `hourly_rate`:

```python
for dep in deployments:
    ...
    end = dep.end_date if dep.end_date else datetime.utcnow()
    hours = (end - dep.start_date).total_seconds() / 3600.0
    dep_cost += max(0.0, hours * rate)
```

Nothing deduplicates by equipment. Two open deployments of the same machine on one project charge it
**twice**, three charge it three times, at ₹1,200/hour each. A machine double-booked across two
projects is charged in full to both — the same rupee of plant cost appears in two projects' P&L.

**Also note the accrual model:** elapsed **wall-clock** time, 24 hours a day, including nights,
weekends and holidays, for as long as the deployment stays open. A machine deployed once and never
returned accrues ₹28,800/day forever. That is a separate modelling problem from the duplication and
should be decided deliberately, not by omission.

**Fix:** reject a deploy when an open deployment exists for that equipment (or when date ranges
overlap); consult the `status` the product already maintains.

### FINDING R2-569 — 🔴 CRITICAL: R2-356 re-proved live — `/finance/pl` 500s whenever any equipment deployment is open, and the mechanism is now isolated

Round 10 recorded R2-356 as "not fixed — `/finance/pl` returns 200 only because every deployment now
carries an `end_date`. The trigger is absent, not repaired." **This session restored the trigger and
the endpoint failed, then removed it and the endpoint recovered:**

```
(3 open deployments created)   GET /apis/v3/finance/pl?project_id=a1376092…  → 500
(all 3 returned via PATCH /equipment/deployments/{id}/return → 200)
(0 open deployments)           GET /apis/v3/finance/pl?project_id=a1376092…  → 200
```

Two states, two outcomes, one variable. R2-356 is **confirmed live and still unfixed**, and its
severity is higher than "a report is broken": the project P&L is unavailable for exactly as long as
any machine is on site, which is the normal operating condition of a construction project.

**Mechanism** — `finance.py:417`, `end = dep.end_date if dep.end_date else datetime.utcnow()`.
`datetime.utcnow()` returns a **naive** datetime; `dep.start_date` is `DateTime(timezone=True)` and
comes back **aware**. Subtracting them raises
`TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. With `end_date` populated both
operands are aware and the arithmetic succeeds — which is precisely why populating every `end_date`
masked it.

This is the eighth finding attributable to `datetime.utcnow()` and moves that item up the fix list:
it is a one-word change (`datetime.now(timezone.utc)`) that restores the P&L.

**Note on route shape:** the endpoint is `GET /finance/pl?project_id=…` (query parameter,
`finance.py:371`). `/finance/pl/{project_id}` returns **404**, not 500 — a path shape that does not
exist. Recorded because the two are easy to confuse and 404-vs-500 has already misled this audit
twice (Trap 16).

### FINDING R2-570 — 🟠 HIGH: fuel logs accept a backwards odometer, a date 73 years in the future, and fuel for a machine that was never deployed to the project being charged

`POST /apis/v3/equipment/{equipment_id}/fuel` validates only that `liters > 0` and
`cost_per_liter >= 0` (`equipment.py:64-70`). Everything relational and temporal is unchecked. All
four proved live, all `201`:

| Probe | Sent | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Odometer forward | `odometer_hours: 9000` | 201 |
| **Odometer backwards** | `odometer_hours: 5` immediately after 9000 | **201** — no monotonicity check |
| **Date in 2099** | `logged_date: "2099-12-31"` | **201** |
| **Machine not deployed there** | fuel for `ZZ QA Excavator` charged to a project it has no deployment on | **201** |

The last is the significant one. `finance.py:422-424` sums **all** `FuelLog` rows by `project_id`
with no join to a deployment, so fuel for a machine that was never on that site lands directly in
that project's Plant & Machinery actual. Combined with R2-568, plant cost has two independent ways to
be attributed to the wrong project.

A backwards odometer also silently breaks any consumption-per-hour calculation built on these rows,
and the 2099 date will sit in every date-bounded fuel report forever.

**Fix:** require the equipment to have a deployment covering `logged_date` on that project; bound
`logged_date`; validate `odometer_hours` against the previous log for that machine.

### Batch 4 tally — R2-568 … R2-570 (3 findings: 2 🔴 CRITICAL, 1 🟠 HIGH)

**Also tested, and NOT filed:**

- `liters` and `cost_per_liter` **are** bounded (`gt=0`, `ge=0`) and `odometer_hours` has `ge=0` —
  the numeric guards are present; it is the relational and temporal ones that are absent.
- `PATCH /equipment/deployments/{id}/return` works, sets `end_date`, and correctly returns the
  equipment `status` to `available`. Deployments are reversible; **fuel logs are not** (no DELETE
  route — see R2-567).

### ⚠️ CLEANUP SQL — Batch 4 (required; no DELETE route exists for fuel logs)

Four probe fuel logs totalling **₹23,501** are now charged to Zoho Test Project's Plant & Machinery
actual and cannot be removed through the product. This is R2-567 encountered directly:

```sql
DELETE FROM equipment_fuel_logs WHERE remarks LIKE 'ZZ R11 fuel%';
```

Deployments needed no SQL — all three were returned via the API and `/finance/pl` verified back to 200.

## Batch 5 — procurement (cluster: procurement, 5 sites)

**Headline negative result: procurement is the best-validated module found in this audit.** Every
tenancy and relational probe was correctly refused. The findings below are the gaps that remain
around a core that is otherwise sound — which makes the first one more surprising, not less.

### FINDING R2-571 — 🔴 CRITICAL: goods can be received against a purchase order that was never approved, which silently bypasses the entire PO approval chain

`create_grn` (`procurement.py:583`) checks permission, company/project ownership, GRN-number
uniqueness, PO existence, and that each `po_item_id` belongs to the supplied PO. **It never checks the
PO's `status` or `approval_flag`.**

Proved live end to end:

```
POST /procurement/pos  {"po_number":"ZZ-R11-PO-DRAFT", items:[100 kg steel @ ₹60]}
  → 201  status "draft",  approval_flag "pending",  total ₹7,080     (never approved)

POST /procurement/grns {"po_id": <that PO>, items:[{received_qty: 100}]}
  → 201  GRN-0004                                                    (goods received)

GET  /procurement/pos → ZZ-R11-PO-DRAFT | status "received" | approval_flag "pending" | ₹7,080
```

₹7,080 of steel booked as received against an order nobody ever authorised. The PO moved
`draft → received` while `approval_flag` stayed `pending` — the two fields now contradict each other,
and the approval flag is the one the approval UI reads.

**Why this is the significant one.** The approval chain is the product's only spend control before
money is committed. `approve_po` is properly guarded — this session verified that a PO cannot be
approved twice, cannot be rejected once approved, and cannot be approved after rejection (all
`400 "Purchase order is already fully approved"`). All of that is bypassed by not calling it. The
control is enforced on the door and the wall next to it is open.

**Consequences beyond the bypass:**

- The PO is now `status: "received"`, so `approve_po`/`reject_po` can never run on it. It is
  permanently stuck as an unapproved-but-received order, and per R2-567 it cannot be deleted or
  voided either.
- It feeds the three-way match, which already takes its verdict from the client (Round 10) — so an
  unapproved order can reach a matched, payable state.
- `ApprovalRule`/`approvals_required` machinery (`procurement.py:429-445`) is bypassed wholesale, not
  degraded. This is root cause 5 — captured data, absent engine — but here the engine exists and is
  simply not consulted.

**Fix:** reject a GRN whose PO is not in an approved/sent state, and reconcile `status` with
`approval_flag` so the two cannot disagree.

### FINDING R2-572 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a purchase order with no line items is accepted, creating a ₹0 order

```
POST /procurement/pos {"po_number":"ZZ-R11-PO-EMPTY", "items": []}
  → 201  status "draft", gross 0.0, tax 0.0, total 0.0, items []
```

`items: List[POCreateItemSchema]` has no `min_length` (`procurement.py:66`). The loop at `:417`
iterates nothing, so every total computes to zero and `find_matching_rule` is called with
`total_amount = 0.0` — meaning a zero-value PO also **matches no approval rule** and needs no
sign-off. An order for nothing, approvable by nobody, sitting in the PO register.

**Fix:** `Field(..., min_length=1)`.

### FINDING R2-573 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a GRN can be dated 73 years in the future

```
POST /procurement/grns {"received_date":"2099-12-31T00:00:00Z", ...} → 201  GRN-0003
```

Same unbounded-date class as R2-570 (fuel) and R2-563 (timesheet entries). `received_date` is a bare
`datetime` (`procurement.py:109`). A goods receipt dated 2099 sits in every date-bounded stock,
ageing and three-way-match report from now on, and receipt dates are what inventory valuation cuts on.

### Batch 5 tally — R2-571 … R2-573 (3 findings: 1 🔴 CRITICAL, 2 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Also tested, and NOT filed — everything procurement gets right.** Recorded because it is the
strongest set of guards found anywhere in this product, and a future round should not re-probe it:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| PO for another company (`company_id` is client-supplied) | refused — `get_company_membership` + `verify_project_in_company` + `require_permission` (`procurement.py:402-404`) |
| **Duplicate `po_number`** | **400 "PO number already exists for this company"** |
| Duplicate `grn_number` | 400 |
| GRN whose `project_id` ≠ the PO's project | **403 "Purchase Order does not belong to the supplied company/project"** |
| GRN whose `po_item_id` belongs to a different PO | **400 "PO Item … does not belong to PO …"** |
| Approve an already-approved PO | 400 |
| Reject an approved PO / approve after reject | 400 |

**Correction to a Round 10 figure.** The register records *"13 unique constraints in the schema, 0 on
any document number"*. That is true at the **database** level and remains a race window, but it
understates the product: `po_number` and `grn_number` **are** enforced unique per company in
application code (`procurement.py:406-411`). The correct statement is *no document number is
protected by a database constraint*, not *no document number is checked*.

evidence and is now permanently stuck in `received`/`pending`.

```sql

  SELECT id FROM goods_receipt_notes WHERE po_id IN (
    SELECT id FROM purchase_orders WHERE po_number LIKE 'ZZ-R11-%'));

  SELECT id FROM purchase_orders WHERE po_number LIKE 'ZZ-R11-%');
```

## Batch 6 — quality (cluster: quality, 10 sites across `d/quality` and `p/{id}/quality`)

### FINDING R2-574 — 🟠 HIGH: a Critical NCR can be closed straight from `open`, skipping the review step entirely — the guard exists on one transition and is missing on the next

The NCR lifecycle is `open → under_review → closed`. `ncr_under_review` enforces its precondition
(`quality.py:343`, `if ncr.status != "open"` → 400). `close_ncr` checks only that the NCR is not
*already* closed (`quality.py:365`):

```python
if ncr.status == "closed":
    raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="NCR is already closed")
ncr.status = "closed"
```

Nothing requires `under_review`. Proved live on a **Critical**-severity NCR, four seconds after
raising it:

```
POST  /quality/ncr {"ncr_number":"ZZ-R11-NCR-1","severity":"Critical"}  → 201  status "open"
PATCH /quality/ncr/{id}/close {"resolution_notes":"…"}                  → 200  status "closed"
PATCH /quality/ncr/{id}/review                                          → 400  (too late)
```

A non-conformance on a construction site — the record that says something was built wrong — can be
raised and closed without anyone reviewing it, and once closed the review transition is unreachable.
`resolution_notes` is required by the schema, so the closure looks fully documented.

**This is the same shape as R2-571** (goods received against an unapproved PO): a state machine whose
individual transitions are guarded, with one path that skips the gate. Two independent modules, same
defect class — worth treating as a pattern rather than two bugs. **Recommend auditing every remaining
`status` transition in the product for the same omission.**

**Fix:** require `ncr.status == "under_review"` in `close_ncr`, or make the allowed transitions
explicit in one table rather than as per-endpoint conditionals.

### FINDING R2-575 — 🟠 HIGH: a material test logged without acceptance limits is reported to the user as **Failed**

`log_material_test` computes a verdict only when bounds are supplied (`quality.py:387-395`); with
neither `min_acceptable` nor `max_acceptable`, `is_pass` stays `None`. Both fields are optional
(`quality.py:153-154`). Proved live:

```
POST /quality/material-tests {"test_type":"ZZ R11 NoBounds","result_value":5}
  → 201  "is_pass": null
```

The console has no third state. `d/quality/page.tsx:775` and `:806-813`:

```tsx
{ label: "Failed", val: labTests.filter(t => !t.pass).length, … }
<span className={t.pass ? "text-green-400" : "text-red-400"}>
```

`!null` is `true`, so **an unevaluated test is counted as Failed, printed in red, and drags down the
"Pass Rate" tile** on the same screen. A cube test that nobody assigned limits to is indistinguishable
from concrete that failed. The failure direction is at least the safe one — nothing unevaluated is
reported as a pass — but the quality record and the pass-rate metric are both wrong, and on a
construction project a false failed-concrete record has its own cost.

**Also unvalidated: the acceptance band itself.** `min_acceptable: 40` with `max_acceptable: 20` is
accepted (201). `mn <= val <= mx` can then never be true, so **every test against an inverted band
fails regardless of the reading** — a transposed pair of numbers silently condemns every subsequent
sample. And `result_value: -999` MPa is accepted; there is no plausibility bound on a physical
measurement.

**Fix:** reject `min_acceptable > max_acceptable`; render `is_pass === null` as a distinct
"Not evaluated" state and exclude it from both tallies; require at least one bound, or bound
`result_value`.

### FINDING R2-576 — 🟡 MEDIUM: `ncr_number` is not unique — duplicates are accepted

```
POST /quality/ncr {"ncr_number":"ZZ-R11-NCR-1", …}  → 201
POST /quality/ncr {"ncr_number":"ZZ-R11-NCR-1", …}  → 201   (same number, same project)
```

Two NCRs now share an identifier in the same project. `create_ncr` has no equivalent of the
`po_number`/`grn_number` check that procurement performs.

**This sharpens the register's uniqueness picture into a three-way split**, which matters for the fix:

| Document | Uniqueness |
|---|---|
| `po_number`, `grn_number` | **enforced in application code**, per company (racy, but present) |
| `ncr_number` | **not enforced anywhere** |
| every document number | **no database constraint** — so even the enforced ones race |

The Round 10 statement *"0 unique constraints on any document number"* is correct about the database
and should not be read as "nothing is checked" — procurement checks, quality does not.

### Batch 6 tally — R2-574 … R2-576 (3 findings: 2 🟠 HIGH, 1 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Also observed:**

- `severity` **is** properly constrained — `Field("Major", pattern="^(Minor|Major|Critical)$")`
  (`quality.py:123`). Enum validation remains the product's strongest validation class, consistent
  with Round 10's profile.
- `test_date: "2099-12-31"` accepted — the **fourth** unbounded-date instance this round after
  R2-563 (timesheet entry), R2-570 (fuel log) and R2-573 (GRN). Not filed separately; recorded here
  so the fix is scoped as one sweep across every bare `datetime` field in a write schema rather than
  four point fixes.
- `close_ncr` sets `closed_at = datetime.utcnow()` (`quality.py:369`) — another naive-`utcnow` site,
  same family as R2-569.

```sql

DELETE FROM material_test_results WHERE test_type LIKE 'ZZ R11%';
```

## Batch 7 — chat (cluster: chat, 5 sites)

Round 10 recorded chat as inoperable via R2-468/469/470 — `ChatGroupMember.user_id` holds a
`company_team.id` while `verify_group_membership` compares it to `users.id`, an unsatisfiable
predicate. That is confirmed still live (`chat.py:14-21`) and is **not** re-filed. What follows is a
**second, independent** reason chat cannot work, which survives the fix for the first.

### FINDING R2-577 — 🔴 CRITICAL: chat groups are unusable by construction — creating a group enrols nobody, and every route that could add the first member requires already being a member

Four routes, one closed loop. `chat.py`:

| Route | Guard | Line |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /chat/groups` | creates the group, **adds no members** | `111` |
| `POST /chat/groups/{id}/members` | `verify_group_membership(...)` | `230` |
| `POST /chat/messages` | `verify_group_membership(...)` | `144` |
| `GET /chat/groups/{id}/members` | `verify_group_membership(...)` | `201` |

`create_group` never inserts a `ChatGroupMember` row for its creator, and **the only route that adds
members demands membership as its precondition**. A new group therefore has zero members forever:
there is no API path that produces the first one.

Proved live as the company **Owner**, `permissions: {"all": true}`:

```
POST /chat/groups {"name":"ZZ R11 Chat Probe"}   → 201  member_count: 0,  created_by: null
POST /chat/messages {"group_id": <that group>}   → 403  "Not a member of this chat group"
POST /chat/groups/{id}/members {me, "admin"}     → 403  "Not a member of this chat group"
GET  /chat/groups/{id}/members                   → 403  "Not a member of this chat group"
```

The pre-existing group `a0beb919` ("ZZ QA Audit Chat B", `member_count: 0`) behaves identically — its
member list cannot even be *read*.

**Why this is separate from R2-468 and matters for fix ordering.** R2-468 is an identity-type
mismatch: fix `verify_group_membership` to resolve `company_team.id` and existing memberships start
matching. **That fix alone does not make chat work**, because no group has any members to match
against and none can be added. Both must be fixed together:

1. `create_group` must insert its creator as an `admin` member, and
2. `add_member` needs a bootstrap exception — a company admin, or the group creator, may add the
   first member without being one.

Bootstrapping any existing group today requires a direct `INSERT` into `chat_group_members`.

**Also observed on the same routes:**

- `created_by` comes back **null** on a freshly created group even though `ChatGroupCreate` exposes
  it (`chat.py:29`) — the server never stamps it. **No chat group records who created it.** Root
  cause 3.
- `remove_member` wraps its audit call in `try: … except Exception: pass` (`chat.py:255-259`) — a
  swallow handler on an audit trail, the R2-513 class — and its `log_deletion` omits `deleted_by`,
  consistent with all 30 sites in root cause 3.

### FINDING R2-578 — 🟡 MEDIUM (latent): `send_message` stamps the real sender only conditionally — the client-supplied `user_id` survives when the sender has no `company_team` row

`send_message` is written correctly and says so (`chat.py:145-153`):

```python
ct = db.query(CompanyTeam).filter(
    CompanyTeam.company_id == group.company_id,
    CompanyTeam.user_id == current_user.id
).first()
if ct is not None:
    msg.user_id = ct.id
msg.user_name = current_user.name
```

But `msg` was built as `ChatMessage(**payload.model_dump())` at `:144`, and `ChatMessageCreate`
exposes `user_id` to the client (`chat.py:49`). **When `ct is None` the overwrite is skipped and the
client's `user_id` persists** — authorship attributable to any id the sender chooses. `user_name` is
always stamped, so the displayed name stays honest while the stored foreign key does not; `GET
/chat/messages` resolves the display name through `ChatMessage.user_id` (`chat.py:170-172`), so the
forged id decides which name is shown once the join succeeds.

**Filed as MEDIUM and latent, not HIGH,** because R2-577 makes it currently unreachable — no one can
post at all. **It becomes live the moment chat is fixed**, and a user who is a company member without
a `company_team` row is exactly the case R2-468's root cause creates. Recorded here so the chat fix
does not ship this.

**Fix:** drop `user_id` and `user_name` from `ChatMessageCreate`; stamp unconditionally and 403 when
`ct is None`.

### Batch 7 tally — R2-577 … R2-578 (2 findings: 1 🔴 CRITICAL, 1 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Also noted:** `add_member` correctly rejects a `group_id` in the body that disagrees with the path
(`400 "Group ID mismatch"`, `chat.py:224`).

```sql

```

## Batch 8 — projects (cluster: projects, 6 sites)

Projects is one of the few modules with a full CRUD surface, so this batch round-tripped cleanly: a
probe project was created, mutated, read back and **deleted through the API** (`200`, 0 residual).
No cleanup SQL.

### FINDING R2-579 — 🟠 HIGH: the attendance geofence radius accepts negative and absurd values, and a radius of `0` is silently turned into 500 metres

`attendance_radius_meters` is a bare `int` in both create and update (`projects.py:182`,
`projects.py:206`) with no bounds. Every value below was accepted and stored verbatim (`200`):

| Sent | Stored | Effect at `hr.py:285`, `within_geofence = distance_m <= radius` |
|---|---|---|
| `-50`, `-1` | `-50`, `-1` | `distance_m` is a haversine distance, always `>= 0`, so the comparison is **never true** — every punch at that project is permanently labelled off-site |
| `999999999` | `999999999` | ~1,000,000 km — roughly 25× the Earth's circumference. **Every punch on the planet is inside the geofence** |
| `0` | `0` | **silently becomes 500** — see below |

**The `0` case is the subtle one.** `hr.py:279` reads:

```python
radius = project.attendance_radius_meters or 500
```

`0 or 500` evaluates to `500`. An administrator who sets the radius to zero — the natural way to
express "require an exact match" or "I am configuring this now, lock it down" — silently gets a
**500-metre** geofence instead. The stored value and the enforced value disagree, and the console
shows the stored one.

**Severity note.** This does not by itself let anyone punch from anywhere, because the geofence is
already advisory: `hr.py:311-312` only sets `is_within_geofence` and
`status = "Present" if within_geofence else "Present (Off-Site)"`. Both count as present, which is
R2-474 and is **not** re-filed here. The finding is that the one field an administrator can tune to
make that label meaningful is itself unvalidated in both directions — and the direction that reads as
"tighter" (`0`) is the one that silently loosens to 500 m.

**Fix:** `Field(ge=1, le=10000)`, and replace `or 500` with an explicit `is None` check so a
configured `0` is honoured or rejected rather than reinterpreted.

### FINDING R2-580 — 🟠 HIGH: project `status` is a free-text string — any value is accepted and stored

```
PUT /projects/{id} {"status":"ZZ R11 not-a-real-status"}  → 200
                    "status":"ZZ R11 not-a-real-status"
```

`ProjectUpdate.status` is `Optional[str]` with no pattern (`projects.py:191`), unlike `NCRCreate.severity`
which is correctly constrained. Project status drives dashboard grouping, project filters and several
report cut-offs; a value outside the expected set does not error anywhere — it silently drops the
project out of every status-filtered view while still counting in totals. This is the
string-validation gap (Round 10: 448/458 unbounded) landing on a field that is functionally an enum.

**Fix:** `Field(pattern=…)` over the real status set, the same treatment `severity` already gets.

### FINDING R2-581 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a project can be created with a negative contract value and an end date before its start date; an oversized value 500s instead of validating

All accepted in a single create (`200`):

```json
{"project_value": -5000000, "planned_start_date": "2026-12-31", "planned_end_date": "2020-01-01",
 "attendance_radius_meters": -50}
```

- **`project_value: -5000000`** — a contract worth minus fifty lakh. `project_value: float = 0.0`
  (`projects.py:176`), no `ge=`. It feeds budget-vs-actual and every margin calculation.
- **End date six years before the start date** — no ordering check on
  `planned_start_date`/`planned_end_date`. Any duration derived from these is negative, the same
  class as R2-562's negative timesheet duration.
- **`project_value: 1e20` → 500 Internal Server Error**, not a 422. The database's `Numeric`
  precision refuses it and the app has no bound of its own — **root cause 6 again**, and the third
  instance recorded this round after R2-564's timesheet header and the task-create FK.

**Fix:** `Field(ge=0)` with a sane upper bound, and an ordering validator on the date pair.

### Batch 8 tally — R2-579 … R2-581 (2 🟠 HIGH, 1 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Also verified:** `DELETE /projects/{id}` → `200` and the project disappears from the company list.
The 51-table cascade behind it is R2-557 and is unchanged; this batch deliberately did not re-probe it.

## Batch 9 — party + BOQ (clusters: party 4 sites, boq 4 sites)

### FINDING R2-582 — 🟠 HIGH: attempting to deactivate a project party silently **activates** it — every unrecognised status is coerced to `Active`

`set_project_party_status` (`projects.py:496`) takes an **untyped `dict`** — no Pydantic schema at all —
and resolves the status like this (`projects.py:510-513`):

```python
status = (payload.get("status") or "Active")
if status not in ("Active", "Inactive"):
    status = "Active"
```

Anything that is not exactly `"Inactive"` becomes `"Active"`. Proved live, all `200`:

| Sent | Stored |
|---|---|
| `"Inactive"` | `Inactive` ✅ |
| `"inactive"` | **`Active`** |
| `"INACTIVE"` | **`Active`** |
| `"Disabled"` | **`Active`** |
| omitted entirely | **`Active`** |

**The failure mode of a deactivation attempt is activation**, returned as a `200` success with no
warning. A casing slip, a client sending a different vocabulary, or a missing field all re-enable a
party that someone intended to switch off — and project parties gate who can be selected for payments
and bills. The safe coercion for an unrecognised value is to reject it, or at minimum to fall back to
the *restrictive* state, never the permissive one.

Because the endpoint is an untyped `dict`, FastAPI performs no validation and generates no schema for
it, so this is invisible in `openapi.json` too.

**Fix:** a real Pydantic model with `Field(pattern="^(Active|Inactive)$")`, returning 422 on anything else.

### FINDING R2-583 — 🟠 HIGH: setting an opening balance on a party already linked to the project is silently discarded and reported as success

`add_project_party` (`projects.py:466-487`) looks up an existing link and **only builds the row when
none exists** (`if not existing:`). When the link is already there, every field in the payload is
ignored and the pre-existing row is returned with `200`. Proved live:

```
POST /projects/{p}/parties {"party_id":X,"opening_balance_direction":"will_pay",   "amount":250000}
  → 200  balance -250000.0, to_pay 250000.0                                  (created)

POST /projects/{p}/parties {"party_id":X,"opening_balance_direction":"will_receive","amount":900000}
  → 200  balance -250000.0, to_pay 250000.0        ← the ₹9,00,000 is gone, and the direction too

POST /projects/{p}/parties {"party_id":X,"opening_balance_direction":"will_pay",   "amount":-500000}
  → 200  balance -250000.0                          ← negative amount also silently ignored
```

The response is a `200` carrying the *old* balance, so a client that displays the response shows the
correct-looking number while the user's new figure was never stored. There is no "already linked"
error and no update path — `PUT /{project_id}/parties/{party_id}` only sets `status` (see R2-582), so
**an opening balance entered wrongly the first time cannot be corrected through the product at all.**

Same family as R2-564 (hours silently discarded) and R2-515: a write that does nothing and says it
worked — except here the discarded value is a money figure on a party ledger.

**Fix:** update the existing link, or return 409; either way stop returning 200 for a no-op.

### FINDING R2-584 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a BOQ document accepts more completed milestones than it has

```
POST /budgeting/boq-documents {"title":"ZZ R11 BOQ","milestone_done":9999,"milestone_total":1}
  → 201  milestone_done 9999, milestone_total 1
```

Both fields carry `ge=0` (`budgeting.py:254-255`) but there is no cross-field check, so a document can
report 9,999 of 1 milestones complete. Any progress percentage derived from the pair is 999,900%.
Same cross-field-validation gap as R2-575's inverted acceptance band and R2-581's inverted date pair —
**three instances this round of paired fields validated individually and never against each other.**

### Batch 9 tally — R2-582 … R2-584 (2 🟠 HIGH, 1 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Also tested, and NOT filed:**

- **BOQ revisions get the actor right.** `revised_by_user_id` came back as the real caller
  (`7f6c0bcf…`) with `revised_by_name` resolved server-side — a correct implementation of the identity
  handling that root cause 3 says is wrong in 20 other places. **Worth using as the reference pattern
  when fixing those.**
- `revised_amount` is properly bounded — `-1000000` → **422 "Input should be greater than 0"**.
- `party_type` is pattern-constrained on `PartyCreate` (`library.py:24`) — enums continue to be the
  product's strongest validation class.
- Attaching a `party_id` that does not exist → **500**, not 422 (the FK is enforced only by the
  database). Not filed separately: it is the **fourth** instance of root cause 6 recorded this round,
  after R2-564, the task-create FK and R2-581's `1e20`. The pattern, not the instance, is the finding.
- `DELETE /projects/{id}/parties/{party_id}` resolves **no `current_user` and calls no
  `require_permission`** (`projects.py:530-531`), unlike the POST and PUT on the same resource which
  both require `projects:edit`. Recorded as a new instance of **R2-541**'s missing-permission family
  rather than a new finding, per the standing instruction not to re-audit RBAC.

## Batch 10 — transaction + team-action (clusters: transaction 4 sites, team-action 4 sites)

No cleanup SQL. Team-schedule timesheets were removed through the API; the credit-note probe was
refused by the database, so nothing was written.

### FINDING R2-585 — 🟠 HIGH: the product contains two timesheet engines that return **opposite** answers for the same start/end times — one wraps past midnight, the other stores a negative duration

Identical input, two endpoints, both `201`:

| Endpoint | `start 17:00 → end 09:00` | Stored |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /hr/timesheets/{id}/entries` | `hr.py:399-401`, plain subtraction | **`duration: -480`** (minus 8 hours) |
| `POST /team-schedule/timesheets` | `team_schedule.py:76-82` | **`duration_minutes: 960`** (plus 16 hours) |

`team_schedule._compute_duration` handles the negative case deliberately:

```python
seconds = (end - start).total_seconds()
if seconds < 0:
    seconds += 24 * 3600  # wrap-around past midnight
```

`hr.py` has no such branch — that is R2-562. **Both screens are labelled "timesheet" in the console.**
The same shift entered on one screen is minus eight hours and on the other is plus sixteen; a 24-hour
spread on a payroll-adjacent number, decided by which tab the user happened to open.

**Neither behaviour is safe on its own.** The HR side records an impossible negative. The
team-schedule side is worse in a quieter way: a typed-in transposition (`17:00`–`09:00` when the user
meant `09:00`–`17:00`) is **silently converted into a legitimate-looking 16-hour overnight shift**
rather than rejected. There is no flag distinguishing "this was a real night shift" from "this was a
typo the server repaired", so the record cannot be audited after the fact.

**Fix:** one shared duration helper. Require an explicit overnight flag (or an end date) rather than
inferring intent from the sign, and reject the ambiguous case in both places.

### FINDING R2-586 — 🟡 MEDIUM: a team-schedule timesheet stores any `file_url` the client sends, including an arbitrary external host

```
POST /team-schedule/timesheets {"file_url":"https://evil.example.com/zz.pdf","file_name":"x.pdf"}
  → 201, stored verbatim
```

`file_url` is an unvalidated `Optional[str]` (`team_schedule.py:30`) — no scheme allow-list, no
restriction to the product's own storage. This is the **R2-466 class on a new surface**: that finding
(a drawing revision holding `https://evil.example.com/zz.pdf`, fetched on every view) has been
outstanding since Round 5, and the same gap exists here. Whether it becomes an active beacon depends
on how the attachment is rendered, which was not exercised.

**Fix:** validate `file_url` against the storage origin at the schema level, in both places and
anywhere else a client-supplied URL is persisted.

### FINDING R2-587 — 🟡 MEDIUM (latent, no live defect): the field name `party_company_user_id` means two different things across five models

```
Bill.party_company_user_id            -> FK company_team.id
DebitNote.party_company_user_id       -> FK company_team.id
CreditNote.party_company_user_id      -> FK company_team.id
Payment.party_company_user_id         -> FK company_team.id
PaymentRequest.party_company_user_id  -> FK users.id          ← the odd one
```

The console mirrors the split correctly on a single screen —
`transaction/page.tsx:530` and `:544` send `member.company_team_id` for debit and credit notes, while
`:553` sends `member.user_id` for the payment request, three adjacent branches of one `if/else`.

**Every resolution site was checked and every one matches its own model.** `_txn_party_name`
(`finance.py:914-921`) resolves via `CompanyTeam` and is used only for `Bill` and `Payment`;
`_pr_response` (`finance.py:1047`) resolves `PaymentRequest` via `User.id`. **There is no live bug
here** — filed as a latent hazard only, because this is root cause 1's exact shape (`users.id` vs
`company_team.id`) sitting behind an identical field name, and root cause 1 has already produced six
real defects elsewhere. The next generic join over this column will be wrong for exactly one of the
five models.

**Fix:** rename `PaymentRequest.party_company_user_id` to `party_user_id`, or migrate it to
`company_team.id` for consistency with the other four.

### Batch 10 tally — R2-585 … R2-587 (1 🟠 HIGH, 2 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Hypothesis formed and DISPROVED before filing** — recorded because it was nearly filed as CRITICAL:

> *"`finance.py:267` resolves `party_company_user_id` through `CompanyTeam.id` while
> `PaymentRequest.party_company_user_id` is an FK to `users.id`, so payment-request party names must
> resolve to nothing."*

Wrong. The block at `finance.py:260-275` handles `Payment`, not `PaymentRequest`, and
`Payment.party_company_user_id` **is** an FK to `company_team.id`. Reading the model list before the
call sites would have prevented the hypothesis. What survives is R2-587's naming hazard, which is a
much weaker claim. **This is the third time this round that a plausible CRITICAL dissolved on
verification** — the standing lesson holds: identify the *model* a resolution site operates on before
asserting a mismatch.

**Also tested, and NOT filed:**

- `POST /team-schedule/timesheets` with a `project_id` belonging to another company →
  **403 "Project does not belong to this company"**. Tenancy correct.
- Credit note with a nonexistent `bill_id` and a nonexistent party → **500**, the transaction rolled
  back and nothing was written. Fifth instance of root cause 6; both `bill_id` and
  `party_company_user_id` are FK-protected at the database level and by nothing above it.
- `CreditNoteCreateRequest.total_amount` / `DebitNoteCreateRequest.total_amount` carry `ge=0` but
  **no upper bound and no check against the referenced bill** (`billing.py:149,177`) — a credit note
  may exceed the invoice it credits. Not proved live: doing so would have written an undeletable
  financial document (R2-567). **Flagged for a session that can accept that residue.**

## Batch 11 — payroll-attendance + quality/HR render verification (BROWSER)

**Method change, and the reason for it.** Batches 1–10 drove the API with `curl`. That tests what the
server accepts; it does **not** test what the console does with the response. Round 9's lesson was
that the browser finds a class of defect nothing else can, and this batch proves it again: the
CRITICAL below is invisible from the API — every endpoint involved works perfectly.

Two findings already filed from source reading were also **confirmed on screen** for the first time,
per [[feedback_visual_verification_required]].

### FINDING R2-588 — 🔴 CRITICAL: the Weekly Timesheet Approvals table is never populated, so no timesheet can ever be submitted or approved through the console

Observed first as an empty table with headers rendered under "WEEKLY TIMESHEET APPROVALS" while
timesheets demonstrably existed. Traced in `d/hr/page.tsx`:

```ts
const [timesheets, setTimesheets] = useState<Timesheet[]>([]);   // :181  — initialised empty
…
{timesheets.map(ts => (                                          // :955  — the approvals table
    … {ts.status === "draft"     && <button onClick={() => handleTimesheetAction(ts.id,"submit")}>}
      {ts.status === "submitted" && <button onClick={() => handleTimesheetAction(ts.id,"approve")}>}
```

**`setTimesheets` is called in exactly two places — `:455` and `:459` — both inside
`handleTimesheetAction`, as an optimistic post-click update.** No fetch ever populates the array.
`fetchTimesheetLogs` (`:209-217`) loads `timesheetLogs`, a different state used by the separate
"Daily Activity" table below it.

Consequences, all following from one missing fetch:

- `timesheets.map` iterates `[]` forever — the approvals table is **permanently empty**.
- The **Submit** and **Approve** buttons exist only inside those rows, so they can never render.
  **The entire weekly timesheet approval workflow is unreachable from the console.**
- The optimistic updater at `:455`/`:459` maps over an empty array, so even the click path is inert.
- Every timesheet therefore stays `draft` forever. This retro-explains a Batch 1 observation: entries
  could always be added because `hr.py:395` only blocks non-`draft` timesheets, and **nothing can ever
  leave `draft`.**

The backend is not at fault — `POST /hr/timesheets` works, the status guard works, and
`handleTimesheetAction` calls real endpoints. The approval feature is complete on the server and
unreachable in the UI.

**Why no API probe could find this.** Every request the screen makes returns 200 with correct data.
The defect is a state variable that is read but never written. It is only visible by looking at the
rendered page and asking why a table with rows of data behind it is empty.

**Fix:** fetch the timesheet headers into `timesheets` on the same effect that loads `timesheetLogs`.

> ⚠️ **CORRECTION (Round 11 wave-0 review):** an earlier version of this line claimed "the project
> endpoint already exists and returns them". **It does not.** Both `GET /hr/timesheets/project/{id}`
> and `GET /hr/timesheets/company/{id}` return `List[TimesheetEntryResponse]` (entries, not headers),
> and the company variant 500s on the missing `Timesheet.company_id` (R2-540). A **new**
> `GET /hr/timesheets/project/{project_id}/headers` endpoint is required. Treat every "Fix:" note in
> this register as a hypothesis to verify against live code, not a specification.

### FINDING R2-589 — 🟠 HIGH: a lab test with no acceptance limits is displayed with a **fabricated** "0–100" range and simultaneously marked FAIL — the row contradicts itself

This is R2-575 seen on screen, and the render is worse than the API suggested.
`d/quality/page.tsx:278-279`:

```ts
min: t.min_acceptable || 0,
max: t.max_acceptable || 100,
```

When a test has no bounds the console **invents** `0` and `100` and prints them as a real acceptance
range (`:810`, `{t.min}–{t.max} {t.unit}`). Combined with `!t.pass` treating `is_pass: null` as
failure, the rendered row for a probe logged with **no limits at all** reads:

| TEST TYPE | RESULT | RANGE | STATUS |
|---|---|---|---|
| ZZ R11 VISUAL NoBounds | **32 MPa** (red) | **0–100 MPa** | **● FAIL** |

**32 is inside 0–100.** The screen states an acceptance range, a result within it, and a verdict of
FAIL, all on one line. An engineer reading it cannot reconcile the three, and the range shown was
never entered by anyone. Screen tiles read **TOTAL 4 · PASSED 0 · FAILED 4 · PASS RATE 0%**.

`|| 0` / `|| 100` is also the same falsy-coercion footgun as `radius … or 500` in R2-579 — a
legitimate `max_acceptable: 0` would render as `100`. **Third instance of `||`/`or` defaulting
silently overriding a real value this round.**

**Fix:** render "Not evaluated" and a blank range when bounds are absent; never substitute display
values for missing data.

**Confirmed on screen (previously filed from source only):**

- **R2-562** — the HR timesheet row renders `-8 Hr 0 Min` in DURATION, **directly beside `8h` in
  HOURS**, with START `10:30 PM` and END `02:30 PM`. R2-561 and R2-562 are visible together on one

- **R2-575** — inverted and absent acceptance bands render as shown above; a pre-existing row from an

## Batch 12 — library + a scripted render-layer sweep over ALL 52 write-bearing screens

**Why scripted rather than screen-by-screen.** Batches 1-10 drove the API only. Rather than re-open
ten screens by eye, the three render-layer defect classes found in Batch 11 were turned into
detectors and run over **all 98 console `.tsx` files at once** — which covers the API-only batches
retrospectively and measures the residue instead of sampling it.

### FINDING R2-590 — 🟠 HIGH: **91 of 189 write controls (48%) fail silently** — `if (res.ok)` with no `else` and no error surfacing anywhere in the handler

```bash
# for each mutating call site, look 40 lines ahead for `if (res.ok)` with no `} else`,
# and additionally require that no setError / toast / alert / throw appears in that window
cd frontend/src/app/c && python <detector>     # full script in session transcript
# => 99 hits on the if/else test alone
# => 91 of those ALSO surface no error by any mechanism   <-- the defensible number
```

**Validation:** a random sample of 6 was pulled and 3 read in full — `d/quality/page.tsx:432`
(inspection responses), `d/equipment/page.tsx:254` (fuel log), `p/{id}/boq/page.tsx:176` (create
client party). **All 3 were true positives**: `if (res.ok) { …close drawer, reload… }` with no `else`,
and a `catch` that only `console.error`s.

The user-visible behaviour is identical in all 91 cases: the server refuses the write, **the drawer
stays open, no message appears, and the typed data is silently discarded.** R2-564 (timesheet hours)
and R2-583 (party opening balance) are two instances that were found individually; this is the
population they belong to.

**This is the measured answer to Round 4's standing question.** Round 4 asked "does the button do
anything" (100%) and "does it check the response" (100%). The unmeasured third question was whether
the check *does anything when it fails*. It does not, in **48%** of cases.

Severity is HIGH rather than CRITICAL because no data already saved is destroyed — but combined with
root cause 6 (the database, not the app, rejects bad input, returning 500), the common path is: user
types a legitimate-looking value the app never validated → database refuses → 500 → **the console says
nothing at all.**

**Fix:** one shared `submit()` helper with a mandatory error branch. This is a single refactor that
closes 91 sites.

### FINDING R2-591 — 🟠 HIGH: library Party IDs are generated from a row **count**, so they duplicate after any deletion — two parties in this company share `PID-2`

`library.py:139-142`:

```python
if not payload.party_id_custom:
    count = db.query(models.LibraryParty).filter(models.LibraryParty.company_id == …).count()
    payload.party_id_custom = f"PID-{count + 1}"
```

A **count is not a sequence.** Delete any party and the next one created reuses an identifier that is
already in use. There is no unique constraint on `party_id_custom` to catch it, and the expression is
also racy — two concurrent creates read the same count.

**Observed on screen first** (the PARTY ID column showed `PID-1, PID-2, PID-2, PID-4, PID-5, -`), then
confirmed in the data via `GET /library/parties/{cid}`:

```
'PID-1' | upadhyayprateek574        'PID-4' | ZZ QA Timing Test
'PID-2' | ZZ QA Client Ltd          'PID-5' | ZZ QA WithProject
'PID-2' | ZZ QA Client Probe   <--  None    | ZZ QA Subcon Co
                                    None    | ZZ QA NoGST Vendor
DUPLICATES: {'PID-2': 2}   —  PID-3 missing, 2 parties have no ID at all
```

**These rows predate this session** — the collision is pre-existing, not audit-induced. `PID-3` is
gone (deleted), its number was reissued as a duplicate rather than retired, and two parties carry no
identifier and render as `-`.

`party_id_custom` is the user-facing key in the Party Library — the string someone quotes to identify
a vendor. Two vendors answering to `PID-2` is ambiguous for any human process built on it, and for any
lookup keyed on that string.

**Fix:** a real per-company sequence (or `max(suffix)+1`), plus
`UniqueConstraint(company_id, party_id_custom)` — the same treatment recommended for document numbers
in R2-576.

### FINDING R2-592 — 🟡 MEDIUM: nine display fields substitute invented values for missing data, including the geofence radius on two screens

```bash
grep -rE '\w+:\s*\w+\.\w+\s*\|\|\s*[0-9]+' src/app/c   # => 9
```

| File | Expression | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `d/quality`, `p/{id}/quality` | `min: t.min_acceptable \|\| 0` / `max: … \|\| 100` | **R2-589** — fabricated "0-100" range shown beside a FAIL verdict, on **both** quality screens |
| `projects/page.tsx`, `dashboard/page.tsx` | `attendance_radius_meters: … \|\| 500` | the console **mirrors the server's `or 500`** (R2-579) — a stored `0` displays as `500`, so the UI corroborates the wrong value rather than exposing the disagreement |
| `d/hr` | `hoursWorked: att.hours_worked \|\| 0`, `overtime: … \|\| 0` | benign for display, but erases the distinction between "zero hours" and "no record" |
| `dashboard` | `progress: dbProj.progress \|\| 0` | same |

The `attendance_radius_meters` pair is the notable one: **a client-side default that happens to match
a server-side default hides the bug instead of revealing it.** An administrator who sets `0` sees
`500` on screen and is enforced at `500` — fully self-consistent, and wrong.

### Batch 12 tally — R2-590 … R2-592 (2 🟠 HIGH, 1 🟡 MEDIUM)

**Negative result, measured — R2-588 is unique, not systemic:**

```bash
# state arrays rendered via .map() but never populated by anything except an optimistic prev=> update
# scanned 98 .tsx files (os.walk, NOT glob — glob treats "[company_id]" as a character class)
# => 1 hit: d/hr/page.tsx `timesheets`  (= R2-588)
```

Only one screen in the console has a permanently-empty rendered collection. **The other 51
write-bearing screens do populate what they render**, so no further hidden-workflow findings of the
R2-588 class remain. This closes that question rather than leaving it as projected residue.

**Method note for the next session:** `glob.glob('**/*.tsx')` silently returns **zero** results under
`app/c` because `[company_id]` is parsed as a character class. The first run of this detector reported
"0 suspect state arrays" and was wrong. Use `os.walk`. Any earlier round that globbed these paths
should be re-checked.

# ⛔ ROUND 11 — DUPLICATE RETRACTION

**Seven of this round's thirty-two findings duplicate findings already in this register.** They were
filed without grepping the prior register first. The numbers are **retained as withdrawn** so that
the register keeps its no-gaps property and so nothing already cited shifts.

**Cause of the failure.** Batches 1 and 2 were dedup-checked (`Vikram Joshi`, `tsId`,
`00000000-…`, which correctly caught R2-455 and the finance party dropdown before filing). From
Batch 4 onward the check was dropped and never resumed. It was only restored at Batch 13, which found
all seven at once. **Dedup is not a batch-1 activity; it is a per-finding precondition.**

| Withdrawn | Duplicates | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **R2-571** | **R2-432** | **Full duplicate.** Goods received against an unapproved PO; same cause (`create_grn` never reads `approval_flag`), same severity. R2-432 additionally places it in the measured three-stage table (indent→PO→GRN→payment) showing approval gates nothing anywhere. |
| **R2-575** | **R2-364** | **Duplicate on the core claim** — a test with no bounds counted as a failure. R2-364 proves it in the *client report* pass rate; the console-screen render is genuinely new and survives separately as **R2-589**. The inverted-band observation (`min 40 > max 20`) is new but too thin to stand alone; folded into R2-589. |
| **R2-579** | **R2-552** | **Full duplicate**, including the subtle part — R2-552 already states *"`attendance_radius_meters: 0` is falsy, so a deliberate zero-metre radius silently becomes 500 m."* Only the `999999999` upper-bound probe was new, which does not warrant a finding. |
| **R2-581** | **R2-552** | **Full duplicate.** Same three probes (negative `project_value`, end date before start, negative radius) in a single create. R2-552 used `-999`, this round used `-50`. |
| **R2-585** | **R2-258** | **Duplicate on the defect.** R2-258 already covers `_compute_duration`'s unguarded midnight wrap turning a transposition into a 23-hour shift. The *cross-engine comparison* — HR yields `-480` where team-schedule yields `+960` for identical input — is a new framing of two already-filed defects (R2-258 + R2-562), not a new defect. Worth keeping as a note on R2-258. |
| **R2-586** | **R2-257** | **Full duplicate, and R2-257 is stronger** — it proves a `javascript:` URL in a timesheet `file_url` rendered as a clickable link (stored XSS). This round only re-observed an external `https://` host. |
| **R2-591** | **R2-098** | **Full duplicate, on identical data.** R2-098 records the same table: `PID-2` twice, `PID-3` never issued, one blank, same root cause (`count + 1`), and already links it to R2-054 (`request_no = f"PR-{count+1}"`). This round added nothing. |

**Round 11 corrected total: 25 findings — R2-561 … R2-592 less the seven above.**
**6 🔴 CRITICAL · 13 🟠 HIGH · 6 🟡 MEDIUM.**

The CRITICAL count drops from 7 to 6 (R2-571 withdrawn). **R2-565, R2-567, R2-577 and R2-588 are the
surviving CRITICALs**, all four dedup-verified against the prior register.

## What the duplicates say about the product (worth more than the retraction)

Five of the seven were re-found **independently, by a different method, months apart** — R2-098 and
R2-552 came from browser sessions, this round re-derived them from the API and source. That is
evidence about the codebase, not just about the audit:

- **Nothing has been fixed.** Every duplicate reproduced live today, unchanged. R2-098's `PID-2`
  collision is the *same two party rows*.
- **The defects are re-findable from any direction**, which means they are structural rather than
  incidental — a fix list, not a bug list.

## Dedup procedure for the next session — run BEFORE filing each finding

```bash
CUT=$(grep -n "^# ROUND 11" docs/AUDIT_ROUND2_FINDINGS.md | head -1 | cut -d: -f1)
head -n $((CUT-1)) docs/AUDIT_ROUND2_FINDINGS.md > /tmp/prior.md   # exclude your own round
grep -inE "<the mechanism, not the symptom>" /tmp/prior.md | grep -iE "FINDING R2-"
```

Grep the **mechanism** (`annotate_critical`, `count + 1`, `_compute_duration`, `approval_flag`), not
the symptom ("duplicate id", "wrong duration") — symptoms are worded differently every round, code
identifiers are not.

```bash
# every settings/finance/custom_fields write endpoint, normalised, grepped against the prior register
for r in settings finance custom_fields; do

    rx=$(echo "$path" | sed 's/{[^}]*}/[^\/ ]*/g')
    grep -qE -- "$rx" /tmp/prior.md || echo "UNCOVERED $r $verb $path"
  done
```
